This game had potential for success, but in the end (and more importantly, the beginning and middle) failed to deliver on multiple fronts.
In this episode of Watch_dogs, you are a token black character. Lovable, easy going, and so smart, you set out to hack the world and free everyone from big brother. Big brother, known as Blume or ctOS, conducts malicious acts on the innocent american people, turning them into a big paycheck. Profiling and record keeping is exploited at the most egregious of levels, allowing Blume to not only assess your abilty to commit crime, but to assess your spending habits, internet habits, and other various habits you have to turn you into a big paycheck.
But don't worry! The prodigal script kiddies are here with their suave lingo and giant words you don't understand to save the day. The game opens up with you already playing to your racial sterotypes and immediatly breaking and entering. Don't worry - You think you're robin hood so you get a free pass to commit any crimes you as you see fit, no matter the severity. In this case, It's murdering security gaurds who are just doing their job, and then deleting your criminal record (which is extensive) and profile from Blume's database.
After the first mission, which was apparently a test for a elitest group of hackers called "dedsec", you are invited to their basement hideout where you'll meet the ragtag group of misfits, most annoying of which is Wrench who wears some digital mask and a pointy leather jacket. He is the "Heroic Comedic Sociopath" in this group, providing you with some humor and comedy to relieve a serious situation. It's hard to be immersed in Dedsec's goals with this one around. The only other character of importance is Sitara, who is pretty cool but comes off a little too strong as the "Cool Big Sis" and the "Cultured Badass".
After that, the world is opened to you to encounter one meme and trope after another, continung down a very predictable and rather uninteresting storyline. It failed to keep my attention at multiple times, and after a while just felt like a chore to play the game.
Watch_dogs 1 was about fighting crime and avenging your neice. Watch_dogs 2 is about being a silly young prankster who steals everything from everyone else while complaining about the same thing. Which sounds more interesting to you?

Punch Club is a surprisingly interesting and different twist on a multitude of genres, and leaves both very good and very mixed results.
I really wish that Steam Reviews had a “Neutral” option. Because while I really do like this game in a lot of aspects, I found it hard to enjoy it in many others.
Punch Club is a really difficult game to discuss about, because what it does is so different. That’s what I like about it, however.
Let’s start off with what’s great. The game’s aesthetic and visuals are really well-done. They’re ripe with detail, and full of color. That’s really all I can say on it.
The game’s concept is also really cool. Basically, take one of those epic training montages and make it an entire game, and you get this. Punch Club doesn’t shy away from its inspirations and ideas, and goes full throttle on it. And this leads to a unique game that’s immensely fun to play in short bursts.
But the short bursts is where the game’s main issue lies. I can’t bring myself to play the game for more than maybe 10 minutes, and really couldn’t bring myself to play through the game. That was, until I later got the iOS version of the game, and I was able to enjoy it much more.
You see, despite its intentions with features such as Twitch integration, Punch Club really feels like a game built for mobile. There’s no microtransactions (Which is superb!), but the game, from it’s UI, to its very design, was most likely built from the ground up.
I can vouch for the fact that it’s a mobile game because the game’s mechanics are designed to have a lot of stopping points; the game has a calendar/time system where you need to create and follow a strong schedule to keep your character up to shape while he’s able to afford food and advance on his quest. How you manage this schedule will arguably affect the chance you have of winning the game’s battles.
And it doesn’t help that the UI seems to be entirely built for mobile as well. It’s unacceptable that on PC, I have to constantly click on a ton of buttons to get actions working. From what I’m aware of, the game has no keybind shortcuts, so you have to leave so much of your actions to moving your cursor around and clicking buttons.
While managing your schedule and building your character is really, really fun (in small bursts), the combat sort of leaves you to the fate of a number roll to determine your victory. It emphasizes training because you want your character to be stronger so he has a higher chance of getting that lucky win roll, but I feel like without that much input (other than deciding his moves during battle), battles slowly change from really tense fights, to really boring and long matches. The game’s fights will really put a lot of people off, since you really have no direct control over winning the battles.
That said, while I have a lot of gripes with the game, I don’t think the entire design of the game is bad. For something that could had been just a simulator, they did a outstanding job creating a story that weaves with the game mechanics, and they definitely put a lot of thought in the game’s mechanics and the connection they share.
The game provides a huge payoff to those who can get through it, and that’s what I like about it. Versus (the literal bane of my existence) Knights of Pen and Paper, the game understands how much work the player has to put into getting a solid character going, and rewards the player with satisfying victories and tons of paths down the game’s narrative.
Unfortunately, I didn’t find the game to click for me. What kept me going was the meaty mechanics, which outweighed the repetition that brought me down on the game. I think that if you really like the idea of a game that incentivizes tons of planning and rewards the player for said planning, then you’re going to absolutely love this game.
So, do I recommend Punch Club? It’s hard to say, because while I don’t think this is the game for me, I can still totally recommend it to others. I like it because of how interesting the game’s mechanics are, and how it encourages the player to think and plan out their actions to ultimately create the number #1 boxing king. But if it doesn't look like your thing, then it won't be.

Solid addition to the franchise and some cool new additions, but some glaring problems as well. The story and characters is top notch as usual, with some food for thought and philosophical musing. It has some interesting commentary on North America as it is today as well. The combat has some new combos and enemies to try out, muskets being an interesting addition that is handled well. The funnest addition is probably the naval combat, great fun and very atmospheric, can't wait to play 4. The wilderness parkour is incredibly intuitive and natural, it's fantastic how seamlessly and fluidly you travel through the trees, with subtle directional hints that are still easy on the eye. However that's the only real appeal of the frontier, for the space you have to travel to, there is very little to do apart from hunting, which gets dull pretty fast. This is the games primary problem, there is insufficent interesting mid and end game content outside of the story, it is far too grindy and unoriginal. I did not look forward to completing missions in the same way as previous titles and I didn't feel the same incentives from the rewards. Hopefully something to be rectified in AC IV.*Some Spoilers* As with all games the ending is very important, yet for all the build-up and hype that I'd generated for it over all the previous games, waiting to find out finally what actually happens, the word to best describe my reaction was honestly just 'meh'. It had the hint of a rushed finish to it, not that it was bad necessarily, just that it didn't live up to the expectations I had of it. Whether that's simply because I had my sights too high for the series story finale is up to the judgement of anyone else who plays it of course.

Remeber ROAD RASH? Rejoice fellow 16 bit and uppers! ROAD RASH is back, and slightly better than ever!
In this updated version of the classic illegal motorcycle racing game, you get to play a more RPG style character, (through multiple playthoughs) with upgradable skills that follow you through multiple deaths... and there will be deaths... Even for a veteran rasher from genesis to ps1 this game is HARD!
I had to play almost a full day (according to steam timer) to upgrade absolutely everything in the skills page at game over, although it was worth it. Now my guy actually catches up to first, second, and third placers off the get go. Starting off in this game is INFURIATING. I broke 2 keyboards and a mouse trying to beat level 3. I had to lower the mouse sensitivity to .1 as to avoid overlooking left or right while I'm turning. Which is a main issue, but now I can only shoot about a half block behind my target. Then I discovered the xbox360 controller works for this game! Now I am a fricken PRO!  Ripping across the side road on nitrous, C4ing as I pass, hitting every ramp jumping over cars, etc! Shooting is still hard, tho I might boost the up and down axis to get a little more aim maneuvering.
Besides the jumpy keyboard controls, the game is pretty solid, the store purchases make losing almost every race tolerable, and I loved that you can stack damage upgrades you buy at the store, making your current playthough character a one hit killer! (store upgrades do not carry over after game over) The upgrade for an extra life DOES NOT WORK. A waste of 2.2k$ I don't know if its buggy right now (early access game) or that I died and it didn't register because I bought other store upgrades after it and it lost track? The store prices are ridiculous. Even with the skillpoints for better store deals, a hot dog is 750$ when you race for 1,000$? math needs to make sense here.
DEVs need to get on patching the glitchyness of the game. So many times I have been dragged by random taxis I tried to bounce off the sides of (ala classic road rash) and end up catching a hitbox corner to be dragged allllll the way into last place. (Even have a snapshot of me being dragged on my profile page on steam) Every golden gate style bridge in the game has a center curb at the beginning of afforementioned bridge that causes either a small ramping jump, or total collison. NOT SURE WHY? Oh and the random collison with nothing every once in a while, either skimming too close to a cliffside wall, or barely passing a random turning sign that just stops you cold dead. The signs should just breakaway as per this game's predecessor, it would help the fun factor of this game. Also cut out the bullstuff crash as you fall off a bridge melodramatic camera work. It wastes precious racetime, and pisses me off. The rooftop levels are nototrious for 25 second falling camera angle (staring at the side of a building you didnt gap )proceeded by losing the race entirely. And forget takedown missions on rooftops, you can hardly get a shot in before they either kill themselves not jumping a gap, or you waste your entire killtime falling, dealing with the camerawork, or jump boosting riiiight over their heads just to have to slow down and maybe clip one of the other players, but still slow down just enough to not make the next roof jump. And whats with the grappling hook? I have not successfully saved myself from a fall with that nor have I ever hooked anything thats worth even using the damn thing for. The mechanics to that weapon need tweaking to say the least.
The AI of the cars and semi trucks are godawful, they really intend to destroy your race times by flipping cars onto your bike and just all out ram the poop outta you. TOO HARD. Even the random cars change lanes right into you, or a disabled car smashed to death and stalled will just come to life as you pass it, T-boning you into losing the race. Oh gotta LOVE the random van in traffic that can't make the steep hill and starts rolling backwards into your bike as your neck and neck with a [sigma] rider...BAM! SUCH FUN. (all sarchasm)
I loved the use of guns, C4, stickybombs, and grenade launchers make takedown missions ultra fun... better than GTA fun! There needs to be an autoaim option, because shooting is really frustrating, half the time you overlook and shoot above or below the target, only to hit oncoming traffic! A difficulty option would be grand.
The graphics vary obviously from system to system, so don't expect to have jacksepticeye quality framerates/crystal clarity if you got a 2.5 gig processor running one GPU. I have a 3.5 gig one GPU and still have blurry road ahead of me and skippy framerates. I haven't tried any steam machines, or supercomputers so all I have is my experience. Regardless, I do recommend this game to anyone who loves racing games, and F.ing S. Up.

To be honest, I didn't expect a Star Wars game to be this short.
But I've played shorter, and as my father always told me, "It's never about the length. It's how well you do with what you've got."
That did't save Star Wars Starfighter, though.
I'm supposing Starfighter is a spiritual successor to the beloved Rogue Squadron (a game I only casually played as a child), since a lot of the mechanics in the game seem similar. Flying ships, and performing various tasks for your side during a certain period of time in the Star Wars film cannon.
I was honestly a little excited to play this. I always say it and Jedi Starfighter at GameStop when I was littler, and always thought that if I had enough money, I'd totally buy it. But when the time came, I ended up spending it on Star Wars Bounty Hunter.
A wise decision, in hindsight.
In Starfighter, you play through the critically appraised and widely beloved... Phantom Menace... See, this game was made two years after Episode I. The designers must've thought that the hatred for this film would wear off, and people would want to play through their "favorite" moments in this "excellent" movie.
Well, enough with beating around the bush. In Starfighter, you play through 14 missions across the whole Naboo-Blockade crisis, between three characters and play in their three separate ships. And the story linking the battles is incredibly dull. Nothing of any emotional weight happens. It's merely a vehicle for you to shoot mercenaries and pirates from one venue to the next.
And for a game about Starfighting, the levels you play in are so... vapid. There's only one decent mission- the canyon mission- which has you progress through very tight canyons to new valleys in order to shoot down more enemies. And it got reused. No changes. Just more enemies, and a night filter. The rest of the levels are you piddling about, waiting for whatever next objective awaits you with little else going on. And it wouldn't be anywhere near as bad, if the flying weren't so damn clunky.
To be fair, I did get used to it. But why the hell did the developers think that players wanted the default set to first person? In a flying and shooting game? I had no idea what key triggered the change to third person until 3/4 through, and that was entirely by accident (it's ~, by the way), and when you DO play third person, it's a hell of a lot easier to control. And it's close to fun when you're zooming through the sky- or space- and nailing whatever shots you can through enemy fighters.
And then you see another god-awful cutscene, and forget why you enjoyed this game. Seriously, the pre-rendered cutscenes look BAD. Like Just Cause 1 bad. Like it would have been better if they used the in-game graphics, bad. And the voice acting all around ranges from mediocre at best, to flat out ridiculously horrible at worst. Especially Rhys. His voice actor is trying so hard to emote with his voice, and it's so obvious I cringe everytime he speaks.
While there are tons of things in Starfighter that I abominate... there are those few things I did enjoy while playing. Again, few things. But I feel like everything kind of averages out in the end, to a nice even 5/10. Unless you're an absolute die-hard Star Wars fan that wants to play every game in the Star Wars library, give this one a pass.

Star Wars Starfighter is a broken mess. When you boot up the game, the iconic Lucasarts logo flashes rapidly, and this trend carries on through all the cinematics including the title crawl. Unfortunately, those were the only 2 cinematics I was able to see. Why? The game won't stop spinning. From the second you boot up the game's first mission, the screen spins around wildly, rendering the game unplayable.

Star Wars: Starfighter doesn’t hold up well, and is plagued by bad controls. The story is promising at first, but goes by too fast to leave any impact. You get to play as three different pilots who each hate the Trade Federation and decide to help Naboo. The pilots are cool, but, despite their enjoyable banter, and meaningful backstories, the game does not take enough time to develop their relationship, and makes their friendship seem unearned.
In 2001 the game must have been impressive, and even now you can see how good it must have looked. This is especially evident in the final mission which has you take down the droid control ship. Unfortunately, that same mission is immensely frustrating because its exiting first part is completely nullified by its second part, where an almost unbeatable boss (who remains invincible until the final stage) gets to pound you repeatedly with high damage missiles, which are hard to dodge. It leaves a very sour taste over what is otherwise a (nowadays) flawed but enjoyable game.
Finally, a strange omission for a Starfighter game is a radar, which means you often don’t know where the enemies are, or can’t find the objects to defend. There’s a limited amount of replayability and some bonus missions, though whether it’s worth going through some frustrating levels again to unlock them is something I’ll leave to you.
It’s a short and disappointing ride, and makes you long for the Rogue Squadron games.

Worms has been around for years and still has new releases, yet this game remains on top.  There are two primary gameplay modes: Campaign and Deathmatch.
The campaign is comprised of different levels that teach you the gameplay mechanics and give you different goals to reach with a given set of weapons.  It starts out explaining how aiming, power, and wind effect different weapon such as grenades and the bazooka.  You quickly learn how different weapons react to different environments.  The game then puts you in situations where you have to get from point A to point B while only using specific utilities.  There are many levels that will only be completed through trial and error--and that is one of the best parts of the game--it doesn't hold your hand.  You learn how everything works through experimentation.  You learn for example, that a girder can be used for protection as well as to traverse the maps.
Death Match is a simple 1 on 1 where each player takes turns controlling an individual worm trying to eliminate the other team.  It starts out simple, giving you the obvious advantage in team size and poor ai aiming, while slowing ramping up the difficulty with each match.  By the end, you have a smaller team size and the ai has impeccable aim.  The last match will likely take many tries.  But, when you do win, you will feel like you truly earned it.
All Worms games follow the same mold, but what makes this one truly stand out is the customization.  You choose the name of every worm on your team as well as their gravestone and voice from a huge list of options.  When you want to face off with a friend or the ai, the game gives an astounding amount of options that are sadly lacking from more recent titles.  You can choose which weapons and utilities you want available (there is a lot to choose from!), how much ammo they have, when they can be used, etc.  You can choose how often health/weapons/utilities drop.  You have control over worm life and sudden death options.  You can essentially change anything you would possibly want.  Don't like the random stages the game gives you?  You can create your own stages as well!
One of the things that makes Worms Armageddon so great is that you can play multiplayer locally as well as online.  Sure, you can see all of your opponent's crate pickups during local play, but nothing beats being able to see their face when you land that amazing grenade toss to win the game.
Although newer titles may look nicer in the graphics department, this game still reigns supreme in terms of content and customizability.  This game was amazing in 1999, and it still holds up today in 2015.

Reviews of old games: are they worth the time to read or write? Most likely not. And a lot of what there is out there is dripping with obvious nostalgia factored in, to the point where it is hard to take anything written as credible (because fan boys are stupid). But this game stands to this day as an example of a game so well designed, it will continue to be playable and should be played until there is a game of this type capable of replacing it (still waiting).
While I would have preferred that Worms World Party as available (as it's basically Armageddon with a few extras), this is a rare game indeed. At least for me. Many games that I've poured so much time into I've felt as if I've thrown away my life. So many games have also made me feel like I wish I didn't purchase them (like the majority of my steam library). This game is a rarity because I've enjoyed pretty much every moment of it. For the past 15 years of playing it. Hundreds of hours in Armageddon (not including playtime on steam), double that with World Party. Regrets? Maybe not having enough people to play with in offline multiplayer.
While an humongous understatement: This game is excellent.
For one, it can run on anything now. The graphics are still excellent, crisp, adorable, and the animations are great... but who cares about such superficial♥♥♥♥♥♥
Gameplay is where this game becomes a timeless classic, as it is more or less a game of chess with so much complexity.  It feels like a turn based fighting game, as you need to take out the enemies, while holding favorable ground, and requires a lot of forethought. So many factors have effects on the outcomes of your actions.
Many weapons that have different effects, many of which make craters and are (sometimes) accompanied by a blast radius, and depending on how close you hit an opponent, and the incline of terrain they're on, and if there is any overhang or terrain features for them to bounce off, of if there are barrels and mines, the wind, the momentum of their inevitable flights and the possibility of sending one worm into another for a tackle, etc etc long run-on sentence.
There is so much to learn, so much to experiment with: I think this game should be available to all school computer labs for little kids just to give them all a good lesson in physics (as well as coming up with creative problem solving).
This game is really deep though, and it can actually be very daunting for someone who hasn't put the time to learn all the many facets of this game. Like learning the best digging techniques, how to be mindful of having the proper coverage at the end of your move to mitigate a too severe reprisal, efficient movement and how the terrain can be either helpful or detrimental (I hate you GRASS), how to take advantage of the pleasantly wonky ninja-rope physics, and more.
There is a lot you can do with this game, like playing multiplayer (offline is always best, enjoyment is dependent on the number of friends and their willingness to play this game) or deathmatch with the A.I. (at elite level the game becomes a puzzle that changes with every play), or all the fun training modes and missions.
A final note: this game is the definintion of replayable.  Randomized maps and with time and practice pulling off perfectly placed shots, this game can lead to awesome and hilarious experiences.
I’m going back to putting more time into this gem.  And you should be playing this as well.

Anyway, good memories here, but no nostalgia goggles are worn.

First and foremost an extremely fun game to play.  It brings aspects of GTA and assassins creed together with some fun “hacking.”  You don’t do any actual code writing or anything you just hack the appropriate pieces together until you beat the mission.  At times the game was very difficult.  The bullets hurt you and bad so if you go into a gun fight you better use cover and choke points.  Many missions were so hard to try and sneak around it was easier to just find a choke point and kill anything that came after you.  The nice thing about each mission is that there is more than one way to get through it.  You can go sneaky and not kill anyone.  You can kill everyone.  You can hack from behind and they never see you.  It was a lot of fun playing this game.  It never felt boring.  All the way through the different main missions you felt yourself getting more powerful and the enemy getting more powerful in different ways.  The “Heavy” AI can soak up a whole round of bullets so if you plan to go in gung ho, you better have the best weapons…even with the best weapons the AI still soak up bullets.  Your technique will adjust per mission and the puzzles were lots of fun.  Graphics were great.  Lots of things to do.  I did maybe half the side quests and got about 30 hours in.  But those 30 hours were a lot of fun.  The message the game sends is also very fitting for the US’ current state of affairs.
The drawbacks? Driving is easy and more of an arcade feel.  Cars didn’t take the damage I thought they would take.  You can run down a heavy lightpost with a motorcycle and not see any damage.  You can rear-end a car and not much damage.  Not a huge deal but just weird.  I loved the game.  Very fun.  Not sure I will play it again but I got it on sale and had a fun time so it was definitely money well spent.  Also watch out for a specific mission with satellites.  If you do the mission in the wrong order you will run into a bug that will basically stop the mission from progressing.  I went through that mission too many times till I turned to the internet for the appropriate order.
Pros: the multiplayer aspect of the game was great fun.  Occasionally another actual person will come to steal your data.  You have to find them and eliminate them before they steal it all.  If gives some points if you win.  You can also try and steal other peoples data (the tables turn) and if you get away you get a good amount of points or followers.  You can do many missions with other people and the game matches you up with another person. The multiplayer is a lot of fun.  I played with a few fun people and we conquered missions.  It would have been nice to have some chat feature because in the missions you play with others, when there is no communication, it is hard to plan how things will go down.  For instance, another player and I decided to play a few hard missions together.  After a little I realized how the other person worked.  He distracted all the guards and what not while I went in and hacked a computer or rescued a person.  Some chat ability would be nice.
Tons of fun.  Never felt boring.  Graphics were awesome.

Watch_Dogs 2 is, you guessed it, the sequel to the successful, if a bit polarizing, Ubisoft game. It retains its open world and general mechanics while having a new protagonist and city to explore, San Francisco and the Bay Area more specifically. Its plot is rather independent from its predecessor, so Watch_Dogs 2 can be played without worries even by those who didn't play the first game.
PROS
+The world map is large, detailed and frankly a pleasure to explore. It's full of personality, a decently faithful and iconic representation of the San Francisco Bay Area, and hides tons and tons of collectibles to give your exploration more incentive.
+The drone mechanics are quite cool and make for interesting approach options to most missions, without either of them being excessively overpowered in what it does.
+Hacking options are much more extensive in this game, and while not being nearly close to the potential of such a good (and currently still wasted) idea they're satisfying to use.
+While non-violence is hardly a convenient path (what with the stunned enemies getting up on their own after a quite short amount of time), it is an option in a game with LOTS of guns, while nobody will judge you for going medieval and wrecking everything if that's what you want. Gameplay and story segregation? Yes. Less tedious than the reputation system, that forced you to be boring as hell if you wanted to be considered "good"? Hell yes.
+While the PC port has highs and lows depending on the sheer randomness of your configuration (it runs horribly on mine, for example, for unexplained reasons), it is mostly a decent conversion with lots of options and a good, albeit not stunning, graphical fidelity. Facial expressions are very realistic inside cutscenes though (while during gameplay everyone has the good old plain-face of genericness). The texture pack sure helps making this game look good, while it requires an ungodly amount of memory.
+The challenge this game will give you in some missions is surprisingly above average. Enemies are not excessively terrible at spotting you or whatever sign of your tinkering, though they have some easily exploitable behavior, and their massive damage and sharpshooter accuracy in a firefight makes them a serious threat in a frontal assault, with the game subtly encouraging a stealthier approach that makes a better use of what your hacking and drones can do, while at the same time giving you a pile of high powered guns to make some noise if you want to. Shame you can only carry around two guns at once though.
+While i never felt like "WOAH!" while playing this game, Watch_Dogs 2 is a fun, entertaining experience with good longevity (i took 45 hours to finish the game with some co-op, all the sidequests completed and a good amount of exploring) and the game is really above average in constantly giving you new stuff to do inside missions, along with the usual "infiltrate in X however you want" that is where most of the third person shooting action happens. It's a solid game, while not being perfect.
+The music selection from the radios, while not the largest and the most varied, is pretty solid. Same goes for the original score, which doesn't disappoint.
*I can't say anything about the voice talents of this game since i couldn't switch languages after installing it in my native tongue, which is italian. For whoever's interested: the italian dub is mostly excellent.
CONS
-Shooting and driving are REALLY so-so. The vehicles' handling is not terribly inaccurate, but it's heavily on the arcade side and feels too rough sometimes, leading to police chases not being exactly the funniest thing ever. Same goes for shooting, which can feel sluggish and isn't very funny, especially since your enemies hit EXTREMELY hard and force you to fight in a chickeny way.
-While expanded, hacking is still a gimmicky gameplay element that only exists to be this or the way the plot advances. The things you can do are pretty awesome, but still seem very disconnected from the actual hacking, that only happens offscreen or in cutscene and requires no interaction other than the occasional button tap (or, at its extreme, staying around a specific area for some time). Hollywood hacking at its finest.
-The plot and characterization leaves something to be desired. While your protagonist and (particularly) his friends aren't horribly bland or clichéd, they're still really one-dimensional and don't go through a lot of character development. You become instant bros with everyone since the moment you meet them, and there's hardly any conflict going on from there onwards. As for the actual plot, it's a rather by-the-book "f*ck the system" crusade with the obvious corrupt corporate executives being the villains of the situation. Oh, and did I mention the absolutely intolerable leader of your hacking competitors, the Prime Eight group? Yeah, she's really terrible.
-Extra activities still feel really limited compared to other, extremely obvious open world games. You can drive people around for cash and occasionally some interesting chatter, take selfies all over SF, collect the usual bazillion collectibles (which for once are at least something useful to your skill progression), race some bikes/boats/e-karts and that's about it, without counting the online. It also feels like you could spend your money in more ways than just clothes, weapons and cars, albeit the variety there is good enough.
-I feel like this game tries way too hard to be far from the brooding atmosphere of its predecessor. I welcome the fact that the city is way more colored, the game doesn't take itself too seriously and the characters are chipper and funnier to listen to, but at the same time i can't help but think they were REALLY heavy handed with the modern hipster-geeky-cool aura, that sometimes feels simply exaggerated or out of place. It's not terrible, but can you really get caught up by the plot if there's this much levity in the atmosphere?
In conclusion, if you liked Watch_Dogs you may find this sequel a bit too much on the lighter and softer side, but you will appreciate the better gameplay, the puzzles, the exploration and the better online. This is not a bad open world game even for those who never touched the previous one, since its plot is pretty much autonomous (excluding some recurring characters that work perfectly even if you never saw them before), but it's not exactly a majestic game. It's decent to good, and it's worth its money if bought at a reasonable price. Unless you're absolutely crazy for the genre though, i wouldn't buy it at its full price.

Assassin's Creed III is an action-adventure stealth game with open world environment from Ubisoft and also the next instalment of the Assassin's Creed series. Assassin's Creed III is a sequel to the previous game Assassin's Creed: Revelations.
Desmond has regained his conscious and is now back in action. Desmond, Rebecca, Shaun and now his father, have traveled to the Grand Temple of "Those Who Came Before", an ancient race of powerful beings who created humankind before a global calamity thousands of years before the events of the game made them almost extinct and ravaged the Earth. There, Desmond needs to uncover how to open the secrets in the temple, but on his arrival, Desmond then falls into a fugue state, to which Desmond is returned to the Animus and bleeds back to Haytham Kenway.
Assassin's Creed III has many major overhaul on the gameplay, some might think this good, some will not. The setting now takes place in the 18th century, in the North American continent, on the city of Boston, New York and the frontiers of America. This mean, we can expect less building to be climbed but instead replaced with tree running and jumping, somehow like Tarzan. This style of gameplay can offer a new way to play Assassin's Creed. The game also feature many mini games and animal hunting, a new way to earn some money in the game. The combat system are also improved here, some may find this easier or harder but it makes the combat feels more epic. Stealth have been completely overhauled with new features, such as double-counters, multiple takedowns, and chain kills. New heavy weapons type also present, the musket rifle, you can use it in melee combat with its attached bayonets or just fire it. And when the enemies are about to fire at you with rifle or pistol, you can use a human shield to protect yourself. The best part of the new gameplay is naval combat. It's so epic. You command your own ship and crew, and engage in many naval battles including the battle that involves the American and British navy. Assassins recruit are different in this game, its harder for you to recruit Assassins as the only way to do that is doing liberation missions. There are still many feature of the game that yet you can try.
Graphics then. I must say, the game has far better graphics, textures, effects and better animation which make movement feels so smooth. The effects are also incredible. Assassin's Creed III does has better and improved graphics. The downside is the blinding white loading screen. Seriously they can use blue or maybe grey but white? It burns your eye when the game is loading a map, level or save games. Some minor graphics glitch also still present in the game. Despite that, the game runs optimized for me.
Multiplayer has also been expanded in this sequel. New gamemodes where you have to work together to assassinate a target has been added. But Ubisoft seems to have decided to add a microtransactions in the multiplayer. That can be good or bad. But seriously the game is expensive already.
Overall, Assassin's Creed III has better gameplay and graphics, the naval combat are the most epic part of the game. But the story isn't that interesting. Maybe because the main characters, Ratonhnhaké:ton or by his family name, Connor Kenway is just boring. Compared to Ezio and Altaïr, Connor is just plain I think. Other than that, this game is good.
Rating 7/10

*I've done my best to avoid any spoilers in this review*
Assassin Creed III's depiction of Revolutionary America is a joy to behold. It's too bad that it gets dragged down by technical flaws and uninteresting characters.

I can't comment on the stability of the console version of this game, but the PC version certainly has issues. The game crashed and had to be restarted numerous times throughout my time with it. At the beginning the crashes were very frequent until I went online and found something that helped, but didn't completely resolve the problem. Here it is:
Beyond the crashes, I got stuck between a rock and a tree once and glitched through the roof of a horse drawn carriage and was unable to escape the inside of it. Some movements within the game were overly sticky in terms of climbing on objects when I didn't want to, or jittering on the top of a fence when I'm clearly directing it to jump down. While it controls very similarly to past games, this is a small step backward for the series.

A hallmark of the Assassin's Creed series is its ability to recreate a historical time and place that feels alive and packed with places to explore. By and large, AC3 succeeds in that category. This is the most graphically impressive game in the series so far. There were numerous moments where I had to just stop and take in the scenery, particularly in the game's Frontier region. At no point did I regret the change in setting from the vast cityscapes of the previous games in the series to this new rural wilderness.

In fact, it was the cities of AC3 that held some disappointment. Perhaps this could be blamed on the setting. For instance, the historical architecture of 1700s America just can't hold up next to Jerusalem or Venice. Not only that but the people of the time were less colorful. Frontiers men and women ARE interesting, but compared to Italian Carnevale attendees? Despite those limitations I do think Ubisoft could have done a better job. There just wasn't enough variety throughout the cities to keep things interesting. Gone are the Mercenary, Romanies, and Thieves Guild buildings and their members roaming the streets. Gone are the purchasable shops and landmarks. I'm not saying either of those were particularly compelling gameplay wise but they weren't replaced by anything in AC3 and I think that resulted in a lack of depth and connection with AC3's New York and Boston.

Perhaps my biggest disappointment was with the characters. Connor has a neat backstory being half British and half Native American. But as a character he's relatively flat, poorly voiced and comes off as childish at times (you play as a young Connor at one point but I'm referring to the adult here). The character I enjoyed the most is the one you play as in the opening few chapters of the game, Haytham. He has a charisma somewhat reminiscent of Ezio but is still unique as a character in the AC series. Unfortunately even his depiction is flawed over the course of the game. I found it baffling and unnecessary the way Haytham and his companions' personalities and overall demeanors were changed quite dramatically as you switched from playing as Haytham to Connor. I understand that Ubisoft was likely trying to highlight how differently each character sees the world, but what they did was too heavy handed and ultimately dehumanized a significant portion of the cast of characters.

Lorne Balfe did an admirable job with the soundtrack and I'm glad it was included in the deluxe version of the game. However, he's no Jesper Kyd (who composed for all the previous games). I admit I'm biased in that Kyd is one of my favorite composers while I'm not familiar with Balfe outside of his collaboration with Kyd on the AC: Revelations OST.

The 3 King Washington DLCs were a pleasant surprise to me. In them you gain animal spirit powers that can drastically change how you play the game. I had a lot of fun putting them to use. I won't be surprised if I find myself wishing I had the Eagle power available to me in future AC titles. The revisionist history that makes up the story is a fun reimagining of events. I was also satisfied with how they went about tying it in with the main story.

I love the Assassin's Creed series and I really enjoyed this game. But it's hard deny that in a lot of ways the series took a step backwards with this iteration.

Before I get into specifics about the game I want to highlight something very important about it, something that in contemporary games is often so drowned in an abyss of complexity and glamour that we forget to even reflect on it: Road Redemption is FUN.  Every single time, without fail, laugh-out-loud duck-and-flinch old school video game FUN.  I spend most of my game time in that aforementioned abyss, straining my intellect and grasping for immersion. Road Redemption has taken its place in my apothecary as a balm, a revitalizer for my spirit, after such sessions.
This game flashed by on my front page for weeks before I really looked into it; I didn't look too closely because I figured it was some sort of glorified street-moto Trials clone.  What opened my eyes to it was a search by tag "Permadeath."  I'm a big fan of permadeath mechanics in general so I became ravenously curious and dove into a game forum spiral,
Turns out, at its core, Road Redemption is a fiercely indie, happily absurd, fresh, new, and ridiculously satisfying roguelite.  Let me clarify by discussing the major gameplay elements.
The loose premise is that you are a gang biker trekking across USA, west coast to east coast, for some reason that somehow involves a boss level at the end.  RR does not for a moment pretend to have a rich and nuanced plot.  The trek is divided into more than a dozen stages that take between five or ten minutes each to complete. Gameplay is traditional 3rd-person motorcycle race style with the control schemes to match (this will show my age, but it reminds me fondly of playing Road Rage in the arcade back in the day).
So how is it roguelite?
First off, each playthrough is entirely procedurally generated- the road maps, terrain, and absurdity variables (sometimes you'll get a level with "hallucinogenic chemical zones" that are filled with bright colors and cars falling out of the sky, other times the whole course is made of skyscraper rooftops, etc, etc); the enemies, their names, attributes, and gang affiliations; the weapon and item drops; and the game type for the level (for example, one level may involve getting the police to really notice you, another will be about smashing a rival gang, another will be a simple race).
Second, Road Redemption uses the modern meta roguelite paradigm that more or less rules the genre at the moment.  You permadie again and again and again but you can earn xp during your playthrough that can then be spent on permanent meta-perks like more health per level or higher base melee damage.  It's more challenging than some of the examples out there, because if you don't earn enough xp to buy a perk, all that xp dissappears.  Nonetheless, bit by bit, I find myself (sometimes) stringing together more and more levels before the inevitable fatality (other times, I just die- but man is it a fun ride).
RR shows great economy of design. It's indie in the beautiful way only our age allows and it does not strut like it's AAA. There is no chaff, no filler. It doesn't pretend to be something great or profound. In fact, if anything, it is proudly and defiantly banal.  And therein lies the magic, that special something that makes a game fun with no pressure and no strings. Just FUN.
And in our lives of overwork, overextension, and exhaustion= I have to say I really appreciate that.

Management game with RPG elements in theme of boxing a la "Rocky".
Gameplay comes down to managing your time and statistics, balancing between training, fightning to the top and earning money to progress. It's pretty straightforward, but it's simple mechanics are really fun. Fights are limited to selecting abilities best suited to fight and watch our protagonist on a ring. Additionally there's a CU (content update) deployed lately which adds 3 hours additional game time.
Punch Club has really nice pixelart style and 8 bit soundtrack, which makes it feel really comfy and not forced like many indie games today does. Story is a major drawback - it's utter gibberish and♥♥♥♥♥♥with poorly written dialogues, especially of your character. It would be better if he would be mute completely through the whole game. Also a lot of easter eggs to older martial artists or fightning games, but not that much to obscure original elements of this title.
It may get a bit repetetive when you find your own tempo of doing things. Personally I find it fitting this theme, like real sportsman you must train everyday according to your daily routine to get better. Also big thing for me was that, even losing a fight awards you some skill points, which makes you slowly better - every fight makes you learn new things.
TL;DR If you like management games with a bit of RPG elements, don't care about story and you're here just to progress to be better and better - this is good purchase for you.

Okay, I have to be honest. Watch_Dogs 2 IS a good game. There are a few flaws however, but let's get into the Pros first. Well, first things first, I love Marcus Holloway better than Aiden Peirce. Why? Well, Aiden kind of rubbed off as sort of a creep or just someone who was always out to get revenge. Marcus on the other hand, has more personality and even expresses more of himself throughout the story than Aiden. The second thing I liked, was the gameplay. It does feel simular from the first game and I did expect that but towards the end of the game, it did start to feel TOO simular but I will get to that when I start talking about the cons. I like the added features; the drones and the style of hacking, even the hackable cars interested me. I find this game to have a thantastic story, it did feel short however I barely did side missions and I did do tons of them in one day so it makes sense.
Okay, now on to the cons. First things first, is the FPS and Optimization. As much as Watch Dogs is a good game, it does have alot of optimization issues. Like for example, I am running a GTX 950, and the auto detect settings force me to play at Low. When most titles (even high graphical and recent releases), allow me to play at full settings. I do acknowledge that my GPU isn't the best, but it's not the worst either. Another issue with optimization is all the spikes of freezing I get. The fortunate side of this, is Ubisoft can fix this problem so it will not damage my rating that much. Another thing as stated in the Pros, is the fact that the game felt too simular to the first towards the end. I'm not going to exactly say why for spoiler reasons but all I can say, it just does a little.
My final answer, as you probably know from my (Thumbs Up) is yes, I do recommend this game if you are into heavy puzzle/stealth games. I hope Ubisoft continues to create great games. I give this game a 8.9/10

I think this is how Arkham Knight ran at launch. First boot, I almost think it's crashed, but finally the menu decides to show up for work. Dress code must be pretty lax here, as the UI looks like a placeholder. Probably is the case, as the Keybindings button is blanked and unusable. The background environments take me back to PS2 days, but it's Fastest graphics quality. Alright, no big deal, let's do this.
Campaign supports 4 players locally, neat. I'll come to wonder how, eventually. 5 bikes, 2 of which look about the same in stats and looks. Shovel Knight character looks cool, let's go. OH GOD. Loading screen visuals make me think this is a mod, and the mission starts with no notice. No countdown to go, not even a quick overview of the controls and mechanics. Maybe it's supposed to be old-school, and you're supposed to read the manual? It's easy enough to play I guess, but WOW that framerate is schizophrenic. 1280x720 resolution, Fastest Quality, and a computer above Recommended specs, and I'm lucky to break 50 frames per second. Controls are a mess when frames are dropping and flying between 20 and 40 fps, and packed races can bring it to a halt. Trying to quit to play something else, it tops it all off with a crash to desktop, losing any XP progression I had. I gave it some extra time later, to see if things were a fluke. No changes, other than no other crashes. Maybe I came in after a bad patch, but it sounds like I'm not alone with issues on the forums.
Aside from optimization and bugs, I'm really not impressed with the gameplay. Maybe there is more depth to the combat I haven't found, but I did alright just by attacking, moving aside so I never needed to deflect. Missions get pretty repetitive, along with the lifeless desert roads. The progression system is mostly stats, and nothing interesting, just a way to make the game harder until you grind more. I really haven't enjoyed the game to justify the $8 USD I spent on the sale, and I would be very disappointed at full price. Honestly, I don't think the game is ready to launch this year, unless the developers really go into overdrive before the end of the year. It has good potential, but the performance issues really held me back. Maybe it's just a small unlucky group having issues, but I really would've appreciated a demo to see how good/bad it ran for me.
I jumped on the sale, expecting the game would easily be worth under $10 USD. Unfortunately I was mistaken. I should've looked at playtimes of more reviews, I think 16 hours is the most I've seen, and most people stop in a few hours. It's not nearly ready for launch, and the performance issues may mean you won't be able to enjoy the game properly. Check out videos to see if there is enough content for you to enjoy, and be careful. I've learned to treat Early Access games as effectively finalized, as you never know when progress will stop. *I've done my best to avoid any spoilers in this review*
Assassin Creed III's depiction of Revolutionary America is a joy to behold. It's too bad that it gets dragged down by technical flaws and uninteresting characters.

I can't comment on the stability of the console version of this game, but the PC version certainly has issues. The game crashed and had to be restarted numerous times throughout my time with it. At the beginning the crashes were very frequent until I went online and found something that helped, but didn't completely resolve the problem. Here it is:
Beyond the crashes, I got stuck between a rock and a tree once and glitched through the roof of a horse drawn carriage and was unable to escape the inside of it. Some movements within the game were overly sticky in terms of climbing on objects when I didn't want to, or jittering on the top of a fence when I'm clearly directing it to jump down. While it controls very similarly to past games, this is a small step backward for the series.

A hallmark of the Assassin's Creed series is its ability to recreate a historical time and place that feels alive and packed with places to explore. By and large, AC3 succeeds in that category. This is the most graphically impressive game in the series so far. There were numerous moments where I had to just stop and take in the scenery, particularly in the game's Frontier region. At no point did I regret the change in setting from the vast cityscapes of the previous games in the series to this new rural wilderness.

In fact, it was the cities of AC3 that held some disappointment. Perhaps this could be blamed on the setting. For instance, the historical architecture of 1700s America just can't hold up next to Jerusalem or Venice. Not only that but the people of the time were less colorful. Frontiers men and women ARE interesting, but compared to Italian Carnevale attendees? Despite those limitations I do think Ubisoft could have done a better job. There just wasn't enough variety throughout the cities to keep things interesting. Gone are the Mercenary, Romanies, and Thieves Guild buildings and their members roaming the streets. Gone are the purchasable shops and landmarks. I'm not saying either of those were particularly compelling gameplay wise but they weren't replaced by anything in AC3 and I think that resulted in a lack of depth and connection with AC3's New York and Boston.

Perhaps my biggest disappointment was with the characters. Connor has a neat backstory being half British and half Native American. But as a character he's relatively flat, poorly voiced and comes off as childish at times (you play as a young Connor at one point but I'm referring to the adult here). The character I enjoyed the most is the one you play as in the opening few chapters of the game, Haytham. He has a charisma somewhat reminiscent of Ezio but is still unique as a character in the AC series. Unfortunately even his depiction is flawed over the course of the game. I found it baffling and unnecessary the way Haytham and his companions' personalities and overall demeanors were changed quite dramatically as you switched from playing as Haytham to Connor. I understand that Ubisoft was likely trying to highlight how differently each character sees the world, but what they did was too heavy handed and ultimately dehumanized a significant portion of the cast of characters.

Lorne Balfe did an admirable job with the soundtrack and I'm glad it was included in the deluxe version of the game. However, he's no Jesper Kyd (who composed for all the previous games). I admit I'm biased in that Kyd is one of my favorite composers while I'm not familiar with Balfe outside of his collaboration with Kyd on the AC: Revelations OST.

The 3 King Washington DLCs were a pleasant surprise to me. In them you gain animal spirit powers that can drastically change how you play the game. I had a lot of fun putting them to use. I won't be surprised if I find myself wishing I had the Eagle power available to me in future AC titles. The revisionist history that makes up the story is a fun reimagining of events. I was also satisfied with how they went about tying it in with the main story.

I love the Assassin's Creed series and I really enjoyed this game. But it's hard deny that in a lot of ways the series took a step backwards with this iteration.

TL;DR first, in depth review after the TL;DR.
Watch_Dogs 2 is a fantastic example of how great something can become when developers listen to the fans.
In the first Watch_Dogs, we played as
Aiden Pearce, a generic angry white dude with an even more generic backstory who goes through a kind of generic if not wacky series of events to "avenge" the death of his niece, Lena Pearce. While this game was overall a pretty neat concept for a new IP from Ubisoft, complete with fun gameplay and cool mechanics, the game's story and lack of personality from the main character made it a mediocre release at best. The fans of the game complained on subreddits, Ubisoft forums, anywhere they could go. "Aiden is too bland!" "The tone doesn't fit the gameplay!" "The story is generic and predictable!" And thus, Ubisoft created Watch_Dogs 2.
In Watch_Dogs 2, you play as Marcus Holloway, a man who came to DedSec after being accused of a crime he didn't commit. As cliché as his backstory is, he is actually a pretty cool character, along with the rest of the DedSec crew you'll work with in this game. Each character in the story has a unique personality and a very unique way of solving problems. Playing as Marcus, a happy-go-lucky type with an eagerness to shed light on the shady dealings of ctOS 2.0, I found myself unable to actually use lethal force in any missions, because I believe that Marcus doesn't seem like a murdering type. Wrench is the only character in the DedSec crew that I could see being a killer, with his fantastically cute mask, and fabulous (if not a little insane) way of thinking. Sitara is the artist and voice of the team, graced with the ability to use art, marketing, and speech to rally public support for DedSec. Her talents make her a valuble asset to the group, and her personality helps her make sure we do the right things for the right reasons.
Josh, the typical antisocial dreamer of any misfit team, sounds generic at first glance, but his personality goes a little deeper than being antisocial. He's a dreamer, and excellent at coming up with solutions that aren't really obivous at all, using his odd creations (which usually seem like they shouldn't work) to get out of bad situations. Due to his skillset, he's more valuble behind a screen than out in battle. Horatio is.. uh, a little bare when it comes to unique abilities, but he is (along with the rest of the team) loveable. T-Bone/Raymond Kenny is one of the characters from the first Watch_Dogs. His personality was established in the first game as someone who thinks outside the box, and has a personal beef with Blume. Ray was directly involved with the creation of ctOS, and, after being fired, tried to use it to send a message to Blume by causing a massive blackout, which accidentally killed 11 people. His vendetta against Blume is continued flawlessly in Watch_Dogs 2 when he teams up with DedSec to take out the corrupt corporation. Characters are 10/10.
The main story is, well, take down Blume. The real story is the side missions and other main missions that you go through on your way to Blume, exposing smaller corporations and making your way up to Blume by gaining enough support and followers who allow you to use the processing power of their devices to perform bigger and bigger hacks. There's a few spoilerific plot twists along the way which actually surprised me, which is neat in its own way. Overall I would say the game's story/stories are fantastic and worth checking out.
The combat of Watch_Dogs 2 is fantastically smooth and well thought out, the new UI is way sleeker and less gloomy than the UI of the first Watch_Dogs, and the improved toolset gives you many unique ways to complete your objectives. You can go full stealth, guns blazing, a mixture of both, or you can not even enter the area, using your drone to complete objectives so you won't risk getting spotted and shot up. The game rewards you for every playstyle, which is a great thing for an open world game like this. In the almost completely seamless multiplayer which is included while you're playing singleplayer, you can hack other players or be hacked, turning the game into hide and seek. Finding the hacker or completing the hack without getting spotted feels really intense and rewarding. Bounty hunter mode occurs when a player is at a level 5 wanted level during a police chase. If you achieve this level, other players will join your session and attempt to kill you, it becomes kill or be killed while you try to escape from both the other players and the police. Bounty hunter mode is intense and fast paced, making chases exhilarating. Finally, in co-op mode, you and a co-op partner (or up to three other players come June) can complete little missions together in any playstle you wish. While you complete small missions and free roam through the entire map with your friends, hacking invasions and bounty hunting can still occour, so don't think playing in co-op makes you immune. It's not really more than that, though, which makes me wish for a co-op story in the next game, or maybe in future content for this game. Overall, I would say the gameplay and multiplayer is a very great experience.

This game is a breath of fresh air in a world of graphically impressive overhyped nonsense.
Not only does it  prove that a pixel-graphics game can still be fun these days, but also manages to become a great title and (i hope) the beginning of great series of games in their own right.
If you watched movies like Rocky, Enter the Dragon, Blood Sport, Mortal Kombat, Batman (originals - not Dark Knight remakes, you silly child), if you read TMNT comics, seen Biker Mice cartoon and loved them all - you will certainly love and enjoy every moment, dialogue and appearance in this little game. Ammount of classic "hollywood-movie" cliches and easter eggs relating to all sorts of old blockbusters is through the roof.
The game itself is pretty much like old "Tamagotchi" games (for those of us old enough to remember what that bloody thing is), only you are not raising cute puppy or little purrry kitten. Instead you raise one bad*** tough b*****d with a hunger for a good scrap and a score to settle. But the concept is just the same - feed him, train him, take him for a walk, make sure he has some rest now and then and watch him kick some heads in. Awww - so cute!
In a number of other reviews I've read (negative ones), people claim this game being to grindy, difficult and frustraiting. You can safely ignore these whimp-written, casual gamer whinings. Those guys who wrote them, have no idea what the grindy game really is. Let them play games like "Sunless Sea" for a week and watch them beating themselves to death with a keyboard *evil laughter*. Now THAT is a f****g grindy game (although it's still great). As for the "Punch Club" - I am barely 7 hours into it. Already beaten it once and about to start over with a different character build. Seven hours to beat the game (and have some great laughs in the process) is not too grindy now is it? So please ignore those who say it is - they just suck and don't even have courage to admit to it.
To sum it all up, let's do the standard pros and cons list, as it is the custom of all steam-reviewers. So it was once said, so it was written in our holy blackish-blue app and so shall it be done. Ahem... let's get on with it.
Pros:
* Easter Eggs - there is one or another waiting for you on every step you make throughout this game. Literally. The references to comics, cartoons and movies are too numerous to list. Enter the Dragon, Mortal Combat, Street Fighter, TMNT, Batman, Rocky, Kickboxer, Terminator, Snatch, Double Impact, Blood Sport, Big Trouble in Little China, Biker Mice from Mars and so on - it's all there.
* Humour - the dialogues can be entertaining, funny, random or downright ridiculous - anything but boring.
* Russians - no proper hollywood action movie can be without them, can it? Being Russian-born myself I just had to appreciate every Russian stereotype being squeezed into one little room you encounter in the game. Vodka, AK, bear, sputnik, balalaika, ushanka and tons of snow. I can just see some guys from Europe and US reading this and rushing off to google to find out what the f**k is "balalaika".
* Huge possibilities to vary your character build and tactics during the combat.
* Little bit of a grind - in my view it is a good thing, delivered in right proportion. You have to train your fighter - right? Also you have to feed, go to work, hang out with your friends and solve other people's s**t, which they were capable of getting into, but aren't capable to solve it them f****g selves. Typical. Such is life... I guess. Massively adds to realism for adults and introduces kids to what life will be, once they leave school or college. Thumbs up for that.
CONS:
* The only one I can think of - not enough of a good thing. I want more quests, more perks, more adventure, more fights, more encounters. More of everything! But that's just me being greedy.
So that is it - short and sweet. I hope my review helps to set some minds in place to go an buy this game. You won't regret it :)

An exhilarating game of tactics where the maps are ever-changing entities and the operator choices can help deal with the opposition if picked appropriately but in the end a skillful shooter can overcome seemingly stacked odds.
Release version players will tell you this title was a mess that seemed destined to fail but after months of patching, from balance changes to bug fixing to optimization, the game is currently at a sweet spot where work is still required but the experience has been drastically improved; all of this gives confidence that the developer will keep supporting the game.
The business model may not be ideal, with cosmetic-only loot boxes and new operators requiring in-game or real-money based currency to unlock all on top of an initial purchase, but the game offers several options to quickly unlock base operators that can hold their ground against the newer ones.
There's much to learn for a new player: guns, operator gadgets, maps, attacker/defender asymmetric tactics and camera/drone management. However the game greatly rewards persistence, and after several hours of dying and being outplayed getting a kill, using a gadget to help you push forward or simply being able to use smart callouts to help your team secure a win feel just as great as they did the first time.

This game is mostly about traffic. It has the usual house/commerce/industry zoning and building city infrastructure, but traffic is where it shines. And it's where it collapses. Building efficient roads and optimizing based on what all the little vehicles driving around is really the one thing that sets this game apart from other city games. At first, it'll be fun. Once your city gets large enough, though, the games problems really start to become breaking.
Yes, big cities have traffic. This game is hardly a big city game. Even with a dumpy 20k to 40k population, you can have traffic backed up to the entry highway 24/7 blocking all your delivery trucks, garbage trucks, cemetary cars, etc., that in the real world, don't operate during rush hour for obvious reasons. This would still almost be ok, if they weren't so abysmally bad at optimizing routes. You can have buildings burn down right next to a firestation, because, for some reason, the game decides to only dispatch trucks from another station half your city away.
These delays will ruin your game. In the real world, if a delivery takes 2 hours, it takes 2 hours. In this game, if it takes too long, that's a couple weeks of production lost, possibly power blackouts if it's a fuel delivery, and sometimes the trucks just disappear.
The death rate in this game is unreal. With 100k population, I lose 500 people per week. That means the entire population of my city dies every 4 years. With over 10 times the number of crematoriums supposedly needed to deal with the death rate, dead bodies still manage to pile up like crazy, as well, thanks to the vehicles not seeming to be able to figure out anything that resembles an optimum route. This game should be called Ghost Cities with the number of dead and abandoned buildings that keep piling up.
And then comes the non-intuitive traffic lanes. Give your cars 3 lanes, you expect them to use 3 lanes. Instead, they use 1. And then they all wait behind the vehicles at an offramp instead of just going around in the other 2 completely empty lanes.
This game isn't exactly slow in the sense that it hitches, but rather, in that the game speed itself slows down. Once you have a relatively large complicated city, expect your fast forward to be more like slow motion. At least it'll still run smoothly, though.
If this game were called Towns instead of Cities, I might be able to overlook how poorly it scales. But it's not, and the game scales poorly.

After 15 hours in game:

Other than that my main issue with this game so far is that while it is a large open world that seems to have taken heavy inspiration from The Witcher 3, it is still very linear when it comes to the story. What made The Witcher 3 so great were the many decisions the player had to make. Those decisions would have a real effect on the story. In AC: Origins, there aren't any decisions to make. Dialogue options are not present at all. I can see Ubisoft not wanting to allow player choice in main quests for lore purposes but they could have at least given fake decisions in the main quests and real impactful ones in the side quests. In 3 hours I have gotten hooked into the world of Assassin's Creed once more. The free roaming, at first, was something I was not entirely sold on as well as the RPG elements they added to the game. I thought it would subtract from the overall of what makes Assassin's Creed games have 'that' feel but I was wrong. The combat is smooth, the characters are incredibly well voiced, the world it self is masterfully built, and the crafting/loot system isn't burdensome or too overly complicated.
Performance wise it took some fine tuning to get where I'd like it to be since I play in 21:9. At first I was incredibly turned off at the performance when I remembered that I had recently updated my GTX 1080 driver with a clean install and that my settings reset. After fixing that I am stable and steady at a constant 60fps on a mix of high to medium settings.
If you are like me and clean installed your game driver update for your video card go into Nvidia settings and make sure to change back to prefer maximum performance under power settings, and whatever else you may like to change. This will help some of the performance issues.

Functionaly PC port, works nicely with my Xbox360 controller plugged in. Keyboard keys are rebindable. No graphic options, but they're not really needed, considering the artstyle and the low system requirements. It's an old game anyways.
Now as for the game itself...
This was the first game and it is very obvious. Revolutionary at its time with a new and simple combat system, never before seen cell-shading technology. Everybody watching the anime was hyped to play the game, but today? There's so many tedious little flaws in this game. Like how it forces you to do boring sidequests to be able to do main quests. All the pointless platforming in the hub city, collecting garbage on the map and my personal favorite: unlocking doors by placing boxes on pressure pads, which take FOREVER to carry from 1 point to the other. ...It's a timefiller drag, no question about it.
It is very much flawed and I expected as much, it being the first game. But the real reason I'm giving this the red thumb is because you might as well just buy Naruto Shippuden UNS 3, which has all of the old, most memorable fights from previous games on the timeline and play them that way, with a more fleshed out combat system, without the stupid race gamemodes.
Really, you don't miss out on anything if you skip this. UNS 3 has beatufiul 10+ min cutscenes to tell the story in great detail, completely true to the source material. This game has 1 or 2 cutscenes for each storyarc. You're just jumping from 1 fight/race to the next from the menu. It's a very... disconnected experience. It's similar to how it's done in UNS4, but even worse and more dry. Don't expect to see a lot of awesome QTE battles (yes, those can actually be awesome, and UNS3 proved this) here either. There's about 3 of those in the entire game.
I bought it becuase I'm a fan. If you're interested in the roots of the UNS franchise like I was (having only played 3rd and 4th game), or looking to buy the complete bundle of Naruto games just so you have the complete set, sure, go ahead. Satisfy your curiousity. If you just want one Naruto game that you can play with friends or something, I recommend either the 3rd or the 4th. I have yet to play the 2nd, but the 3rd is certainly the best so far - one of the best games ever, in fact.
This is an old game, things will be different than games today. If you don't like it then refund it. Quit complaining saying that it's forcing you to do things and you have no control over anything.

All right so this is my review of Naruto:Ultimate Ninja Storm.I decided to write a review because i see a lot of Mixed ones.Which i think is false because the game is definetly a good game with flaws.

Music/Sound Design:The voice acting is OK but i reccomend the original voices because well thats the original.Sometimes the lip syncing is off a little,The Music is really good sounding and has no problem.Again a solid 10/10

I REALLY wanted to like this game, since it has a pretty unique visual style in a sea of 16-bit monstrosities and it appeals to  two interests of mine -- stats and punching things.
And then everything goes downhill from there.
The game is very short, and while there are a few different paths to reach the end, the ending is so abrupt it'll give you whiplash and it reeks of being nothing but unfinished. I also made the mistake of assuming this would have been a completed game, so the new content that came out for it was pretty much unplayable because you lose the ability to access it at the halfway point of the main story.
As for the game mechanics: the daily stat decay is so extreme you have to formulate a very strict training routine and ABSOLUTELY NOT DIVERT from it in order to keep your stats from going through the floor while making very minimal gains. While progressing through the game, you can minimize the reduction of your main stat, but all three are very important. That said, a look at the forums for this game seem to show that the developer is currently in a state of chasing their own tail trying to balance it out, and it's really a mess to behold. I did a little research and it looks like the stat decay works the way it does because if stats get too high, it's fully possible to have a character that's completely  unplayable due to the way stamina/energy is spent during attacks.
In the end, I guess I'm really just disappointed. After pretty much boycotting indie titles for a long time on Steam, I got my hand bit again and I'll remember to be more mindful in the future when choosing games to buy.

The 80s tribute pixel art game by a small russian team, which previously specialized on browser builders, and this is also a resourse managment strategy pretty seamlessly combined with choose your own adventure storyline of an aspiring brawler's career. Train your hero - build stats, collect perks & special moves through series of decisions day to day to achieve an effective profile. From the food he consumes, to the means of getting money for a new training device, friendship with useful people in town and so on - everything will change the overall experience. The game's full of grotesque humor and still rather hard emotionally, for you'll come across different random situations aimed to exhaust your nerves both during the battles & in the civic life.
The fighting process is fully automatic, just like in 'Football Manager' series where you have control only over the general setup before the round, then you just find yourself yelling at the screen: 'C'mon, you can do it! Look, he's loosing energy fast! You'll get your chance, just hold on there! Don't you dare to fall, you hear me?!' - like a real coach by the ring, unable to even pause the action. The greatest thing about it - the techniques choice is very strategic & you really can counter and get your chance to win even against most dreadful of enemies of different fighting skills. To my mind this is an almost perfectly balanced masterpiece and a must-play for any manager nerd who ever wondered about what for do those bulky guys gather in the local gym every night? ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)
------------------
Дань уважения 80ым в игре с точечной графикой от маленькой русской команды, до того подвизавшейся на браузерных строительных симуляторах, и здесь также стратегия с управлением ресурсами, которую умело совместили с гибким интерактивным сюжетом о карьере начинающего борцухи. Тренируйте своего героя - качайте параметры, собирайте особенные черты и спецприемы, принимая повседневные решения, выстраивая эффективный профиль. Начиная с продуктов питания, до способов заработка на новый тренажер, дружбы с полезными людьми в городе - все будет оказывать влияние на игровой опыт. Игра полна гротескного юмора, и в то же время эмоционально тяжела, так как вы будете попадать во множество случайных ситуаций, нацеленных пощекотать вам нервы как в боевой практике, так и в гражданской жизни.
Процесс сражения полностью автоматический, точно как в серии "Управляющий ногамяча", где контролируешь лишь подготовительную фазу перед раундом, затем обнаруживашь себя вопящим в монитор: "Давай, ты сможешь! Смотри, как быстро он расходует энергию! Жди своего шанса, только держись! Не смей падать, ты слышишь меня?!" - как настоящий тренер у ринга, наспособный даже прерывать происходящее. Самое прекрасное то, что выбор приемов весьма стратегичен, и есть возможность противопоставить что-то и добиться шанса на победу даже во встрече с наиболее пугающими врагами разных бойцовых школ. На мой взгляд, это почти идеально сбалансированный шедевр, который обязателен к ознакомлению каждому заучке-управленцу, недоумевюшему по поводу того, с какой целью все эти здоровые ребята собираются темными вечерами в местной качалке?
