Ah, here we are again with another adventure into Scott Cawthon's world of Five Nights At Freddy's, how swell!
Having the opportunity to have played every game prior up to this point has been a ride
of mostly good and fresh experiences of gaming, with a few disappointing moments and
bumps on the road. However, that doesn't necessarily have to be a bad thing considering
how frequently these games have been pushed out for the public mass while simultaneously
trying to keep itself entertaining by introducing new mechanics, animatronics, environments
without tinkering too much with the original concept and idea for the game.
That being said, though, I still stand by the fact that while FNAF 2 & 3 both amped up the
difficulty of the game while going in-depth with its cryptic background story, after a while,
especially in the third, I was hoping for something to completely throw me off, something
vastly different that would further add to the surprise factor the first two installments had,
but the third's attempts at this quickly fell flat in my opinion. I was actually really sceptical
about where the franchise would go from here, but alas, all my worries was for naught.
Honestly, after having played this game for a while, I can honestly say that the 4th installment
makes up for all the minor flaws I saw in its two older siblings (not counting the 1st game, seeing
as it's the first of its kind as far as i'm aware) and overall created a new fun experience in Freddy
Fazbear's universe.
The game opens up with one of its atari-like mini-games together with our favorite buddies Freddy,
Chica, Bonnie and Foxy, with Golden Freddy talking to you and following you with each step you take.
And from there we're placed in a familiar position, static in place in the middle of a room,
using a flashlight, doors and whatever else a youngin has got in his arsenal. Eh, to be fair
you're not quite as "static" as in previous games, you actually move around.
Yes, unlike the previous installments, this one allows you to click your way
around your room, so by gosh, you've got to be quick about checking every
hallway, the closet infront of you and the seemingly "cute" and seldom harmful looking
Freddy Fazbear plush ever so neatly placed in the center of your bed, otherwise
you're in for quite a surprise. Oh, they also implemented some other cool ideas
and little games for you to do in between certain nights, so.. have fun with "Plushtrap"
Not only has the gameplay evolved in a very smart way while maintaining
its roots, the game relies A LOT MORE heavily on the atmosphere. Sorry, kids,
turning your volume down won't keep you alive this time. The game forces you
to crank up the volume in order to tell when an animatronic is getting close.
The game is kind enough to tell you to listen for certain sounds such as breathing,
and then making you hold the door closed to stop whatever it is out there from
getting in. It's REALLY cool and while i'm usually not one to be easily budged
by a horror game, this one had me on my toes during certain stressful situations it
put me in.
There's not much to say in terms of the sound department, it stays consistent
and that's good 'cause I don't think it needed much change anyway. Great ambience
and eerie noises all around to keep you busy, what else is there to say really?
Well, i'm glad that the somewhat annoying screech from the first two games have been
replaced with a much more aggressive, mechanical buzz / scream. Just makes more
sense, really, eh?
After having completed most of the nights, bonus nights and whatnot, you unlock
a bunch of neat things other than bragging rights. Thus, increasing the replay value
and overall playability to give you a ' completionist goal' I suppose if you want more than just
a "story" and challenging experience. I won't say what the bonuses and unlocks are, not sure
if that would count as a spoiler for anyone that wants to see for themselves, but it'd be so un-cool.
You're welcome.
So would I recommend this game? Yes, I would actually. For anyone that likes the FNAF franchise,
and even the people that got turned off by it after the first game, they should most definitely
give this one a try. It stays with the traditional FNAF concept but spicing it up in interesting
ways. It's like being invited over to your friend's place and he's cooking up spaghetti.
You know how YOUR spaghetti tastes, but his is just.. mm. Delicious. How did he cook it?
What little extra did he put in to make the taste interesting again? *wink* That's exactly what
FNAF 4 did for me.
Happy Gaming!

Hello, after Simcity finished its course I decided to to purchase Cities: Skylines. This game is everything that the city builder should have. A large map size, nice interface, disasters, day and night cycle, and much more! The games graphics are very nice, but you do need a decent computer to run it on medium settings. In the beginning stages of your town you will be fine with FPS, but as you get more citizens your FPS will decrease slightly. The AI in the game is well scripted and put together, citizens not being dumb a living a complete life cycle. Sometimes your city will slow down in population growth due to citizens dieing of old age or other scenarios. Crime in your city is not much at all, and I wish there was more crime, and I wish that there were more penalties to the crime system, fire system and health system. Money in the beginning is difficult, but then you will gradualy increase and money is never a problem (only if you constantly place down very expensive structures when your taxpayers cannot support it). I also wish that the income you receive is lowered. The game other than that is great, and the different zoning options really is cool, especially the "Office" zones. I think this game is good for its $30 price tag compared to Simcitys $60 price tag. I think you should get it if you are very interested in city builders, or if you are a new person looking to jump into this genre. 8/10 for me!

Watch Dogs 2 is probably Ubisoft's best open world single player game yet. I had not liked the first one because the protagonist and his story were simply not interesting. I'm also one of those people who is getting tired of open world maps full of icons for bland and repetitive activities that Ubisoft is known for (among others).
The Watch Dogs 2 characters, story and gameplay are the complete oposite of the first one. The characters have interesting personalities and they have fun and realistic interactions. They don't feel like video game characters, they feel like actors in a movie with a good script.
The map is still full of icons, but this time almost every activity is fun. For example, you can go around town to collect skill point to spend in a skill tree, but they are hidden in hard to reach places like roof tops and the like, so getting to them is an environmental puzzle. You get to use a drone and a remote control car to solve these puzzles, and they can be used to hack and collect items too.

I have never cursed at a game as much as I have at this one, but it's also the most fun I've had with a game in quite some time. At times it's frustratingly difficult, but that just makes the times you make it through all the more special. I would name myself a jaded gamer, I struggle to find as much joy with games these days. However this little gem of a game has come along and helped me rediscover a bit of gaming joy.
There's a definite feeling of speed, and both the combat and dodging of obstacles can give that on-edge feeling where your breath stops for just a moment as you wait those milliseconds to see if you edged it.
There's rightly a lot of comparisons to Road Rash, but this game stands out on its own merit. It has a whackyness that surpasses the prior game, and the feeling of progression is different as well, at least in this early access edition. Road rash felt more gradual, whereas this game throws you right into things. Said progression is a bit strange in Road Redemption, but it has its own charm if you have the patience.
The game still needs work, there are some strange occurances and the odd crash, but the patches have been coming thick and fast and I am confident it will only get better. It is already an extremely enjoyable game and I highly recommend it.

I don't have a ton of time in it so far, but what I've played of Road Redemption have been fun. It is very much the spiritual successor to Road Rash, which I greatly enjoyed on my PS1. Besides the basic combat, which this title mimics well as far as my memory serves, it also layers a progression system. You can purchase perks with the money you've won but they vanish after you die. You also earn experience, which can be used to upgrade other facets of your character than remain even through death. This adds almost an RPG/roguelike experience to the game.
I only have a few quibbles. The rooftop levels are the least enjoyable for me. They seemed neat at first, but it's very easy to miss the same jump over and over again or become stuck on parts of the roof geometry. Still, it's nice to have something besides the same basic roads to race over repeatedly. I also have some periodic issues with getting knocked off my bike for no apparent reason.
Minor issues aside, Road Redemption is an excellent way to get your Road Rash fix. I look forward to future updates to refine the polish on this already fun game.

For some reason this game is very addictive to me.  It's satisfying to build up a fighter and evolve techniques to win.  I've always been a re-roller in every game I've ever played in order to try different playstyles, unfortunately not all playstyles seem to work in this game with a balance issue where Agility is the key to victory and if you build a character with that in mind you can develop really strong.
Time management is the real pain in this game, the timer that moves from day to day seems to move too fast for the amount of either money earned or recovery gained from sleep.  It's almost impossible to eat/sleep/work/workout in a single day because BOOM, it's the next day.  One of the annoying little ticks I hope they fix is, when the day rolls over from one to the next it stops you in the middle of what you started, just started lifting weights 5 minutes ago, well you'll have to click to acknowledge the change from one day to the next, then click to initiate the thing you were doing before the day change or, and sometimes this is more efficent move on to something else.
In spite of the balance issues I'm still having fun with it.  Also, quick tip, don't buy workout equipment for your home, for some reason the "fun" level doesn't seem to go up as high as it does when you just go to the gym and workout there. Dunno if that's a glitch or a mechanic of the game to get you to go out and burn time going from point A to B or what, but it makes little sense to have a "fun" rating on a piece of workout equipment if when you use it at home your "fun" level doesn't rise accordingly while using it.
As long as the devs remain engaged in this and impliment a few tweeks this game has a lot of potential.  But like any other game, it's not for everyone it's a niche game to be sure.
EDIT: Now that I've spent more time in the game the grindfest of it becomes really apparent and there are aspects to it which make it very difficult to advance from the amature side of things to the pro.  But once you break into the pros the game becomes much much easier, but still grindy, never sleep, always workout, make enough money to support yourself and build up your skills. Lots of energy drinks, lots of protein bars in the gym, I prefer to use the public gym because I can step out the door once a day to do the sparring and get some free skill points.  Lather rinse repeat, lather rinse repeat.... It's grindy, but not in the worst way possible. There are little things you learn early on which make the grind less grindy, but that's the fun in the game, figuring it out.
Still recommend, and for 10 bucks you get a lot of gameplay from it. I'm running it again because there were achievements I haven't unlocked and storyline I cut myself off from by choosing one path over another, or even not meeting my "girlfriend" to help me work out. Gonna see how that works out.

============================================================
SINGLEPLAYER REVIEW
============================================================
During my first hour playing this game, I couldn't help but compare it to its predecessor in every aspect. Up until now, I'm still not sure which one I like more, but I do know that after I decided to give this game a chance and play through the campaign missions I found myself addicted.
While its predecessor was all about Aiden "The Vigilante" Pearce, a protagonist seeking revenge as well as justice. The story really had me there and Aiden was doubtlessly a character I related to.
However, here comes Marcus, a brilliant hacker who joins DedSec and seems to be in it for the same reasons as the rest of the group - but you don't know what personal reasons motivate him (at least at the point where I am right now in the campaign).
Some missions
All I said so far was rather neutral or even slightly negative, but I cannot stress out how interesting the game gets. I get a good laugh from the cutscenes; there's a lot of humor all over this game.
And even though I can't relate with the protagonist, I found myself attached to the DedSec group as a whole, as if I'm actually feeling what they're feeling when they're going through their ups and downs as a group.
Watch Dogs 2 may not be as fun as Watch Dogs, but it definitely does bring its own unique attributes that make this game a fun experience.
============================================================
MULTIPLAYER REVIEW
============================================================
1. HACKING INVASION
When I first tried the hacking invasion back in Watch Dogs, I fell in love with the concept. Entering another player's world, stalking them while they remain completely unaware, starting the hack when the opportunity's in hand -- it's fun and even addictive. Whether you choose to blend in with NPCs or hide in cover, you'll definitely enjoy messing with another player's world.
However, in Watch Dogs 2, the drones make it quite easy for seekers to find the intruder. They fly up and profile pretty much everything. If you hide on a rooftop you'll be spotted easily.
That's not even the worst part, though. When you're connected with a player that's far away from you on the map, you'll be positioned about 100 meters away from them. If they were running your way, they'll realize you're an actual player and profile you right away, before you had the chance to do anything.
Moreover, you'll so often be connected to a player and then see the victim leave the session almost right away. Assuming they went peer-to-peer with the connections (if they did that with For Honor why won't they do that here?), then it's probably players you have bad connectivity with. Other reasons could be intended, such as when players start a mission or fast-travel somewhere. In other words, any player that's not just free-roaming or idle is not likely to appear as a target for you.
I entered the game of more than a hundred players through hacking invasion, but no one has ever entered mine for some reason. I suppose it might be because I'm usually doing missions or fast traveling towards them, but it's sad that I've yet to be victimized in this game.
2. BOUNTY HUNT
Straight up awesome. While it's likely that a match would not be found for you for this type of multiplayer - if you do get lucky, you'll find yourself joining the police in pursuit of a fellow player. If you or the police kill them, you win and the session is over. However, if you're killed by the rival player you may choose to respawn and keep on trying.
To say the truth, I most enjoyed this feature as a victim. I picked myself some trouble with the police and soon found myself escaping 3 rival players at the same time. Killing them brings great satisfaction, but you'll have to make a run for it if you want to actually win. The difference between a pursuit with the police and a pursuit with players, is that you don't get those easy "press F to wreck the cruiser" opportunities. If you want to use environmental hacking to give your pursuers a hard time, you'll actually have to look back and activate hacks or otherwise set proximity triggers.
3. CO-OP
Only joined one co-op session, where the other guy did the objective and I was simply following him, trying to understand how to use VoIP and communicate with no luck.

Assassin's Creed III allows gamers to experience Connor Kenway and his father Haytham Kenway (possibly the most awesome character in the series so far) in the New World. It's refreshing to see the Assassin's Creed series properly progress past Assassin's Creed II and its two rather similar sequels. The graphics are beautiful and the environments are very detailed. There are also a host of new mechanics such as different fighting mechanics, hiding in undergrowth, climbing trees, and hunting. In a bizarre twist of fate, Connor also gets hold of a sailing ship, which opens a whole new realm of naval combat.
AC III continues to have the 'fun factor' of the Assassin's Creed games - free-running around in different environments is inherently an absolute gas. Unfortunately, the storyline is forgettable and a big deal is made out of hunting, which is much less fun than it sounds. The naval combat is fun and ambitious, but many other new features, such as the Assassins' abilities, are much less interesting than they seem on face value.
AC III closes the atrocious 'solar flare' overall storyline and progresses the story of Desmond Miles. I suggest you play AC III once and appreciate it for what it is - a quantum leap forwards from the AC II series, not an increment - then move straight onto AC IV: Black Flag, which is much better in every single way.

Love the AC games, but this is the lowest contribution thus far.  It's not that it's Boston, and the American frontier - I love that it's come to the New World, and Connor, though he's a bit too solemn and colorless for me, is not the worst hero I've played.  But what does it for me are the glitches and mechanical errors, and the problems in pacing.  The menus are obviously developed for the XBox, and are only half-heartedly converted to the PC (mouse + keyboard) (which is how I prefer to play these games).  Sometimes WASD, sometimes scroll wheel, sometimes arrows, click with mouse, confirm with enter, you're moving all over the keyboard just to exit the game, reload a checkpoint, or sell something.  Weapon select and assassin send menus are bad.  Since these weren't issues in previous games, why are they now?  The mechanical glitches are bad: horses get stuck, etc.  The pacing is also bad: it puts you into a mission, just to walk for about two minutes.  Why? Either walk further, or focus on the important bits.
The ship sailing dynamic is good. Boston is nice, though the assassin/templar contest for territory seems less American than European (would a quebecois butcher really swear allegiance to me?).  I think it needed another two months of playtesting on the PC.

I love the whole series, but this one has me wrapped around its little finger. It's so different from the others. I find it scarier and less predictable. There is also less room for error.
The previous 3 games were based largely on visual cues, with audio added to enhance things. This game is based on audio cues, with visuals enhancing the fright.
No cameras, no phone calls, no sitting still. It still has the claustrophobia and paranoia of the previous games, since you still stay in one room waiting for the break of day while trying not to die, but the overall feel of it makes my heart race and stomach drop out like it never has before in this series.
The story is extremely compelling, in the parts I have seen so far (I've survived only the first two nights as I'm writing this).
Also Plushtrap is adorable and my love for his (its? their? I mean, it is a plush toy) inclusion is deeper than the dread I feel every time I play a short burst of this game. (I can only play in short bursts because of the adrenaline making me run off to do something else. Thanks fight-or-flight mechanism!)
Random note: there is a grandfather clock in the left-hand hallway. Part of me imagines that it is alluding to the music box from FNaF 2, which played the chorus to "My Grandfather's Clock." But that's just a theory.
Overall my rating is 10/10, would boop Freddy's nose again before being mercilessly jumpscared by an animatronic.

An otherwise enhanced gameplay experience for a CoD game, tarnished by the horrible story
utterly disappoints as the last game of the series.
As always my experience reflects
the singleplayer aspect of the game.
Call of Duty®: Black Ops III is the final (for now) installment Treyarch have developed for their critically acclaimed series of Call of Duty games and boy they saved the worst for last.
But first lets talk about some of the better qualities of Black Ops 3 and what do you know, gameplay has actually a few new additions which make for much more interesting playthroughs. The Player, a cybernetic enhanced soldier, not only just uses weapons to take down the enemy but also has access to several augmentations and powers. You have access to 3 cyber core trees: Control, Chaos and Martial.
All 3 cores include 7 different powers (plus their upgraded versions). These powers range from summoning a swarm of nanomachines to overwhelm the enemy, a cloak device, smokescreen, faster movement and reload for the player, a sonic attack and many more. You can unlock these powers by using fabrication kits which you acquire when you level up in the game. Leveling up is done by completing several accolades, most of them unique to each of the 11 missions of the game. Accolades such as completing the mission without dying once, getting a high score and finding all collectibles are shared for all missions.
Getting those fabrication kits also allows you to unlock weapons, wildcards and extra bonuses, such as walking on walls, a single use auto-revive, extra attachments to your weapons and a few others. Weapon attachments include various scopes, grips for increased accuracy and other various stat modifiers for increased range/accuracy/damage.
I loved the ability to modify and prepare for each mission accordingly since you get a short briefing with what you should expect in terms of combat, be it short or medium or long range engagements.
Graphically the game looks pretty good for 2015 and dare I say, despite some bad textures here and there, even up for 2017 standards. The models and animations are good, weapons look modern without being ridiculous and the environments which you fight are for the most part decently looking although the level design itself leaves a lot to be desired.
Performance wise the game played out really well however I will mention a couple of weird hitches every now and then between loading of different chapters but nothing that impacts gameplay or any crashes.
So where's does Call of Duty®: Black Ops III fail? For me Call of Duty is all about a nice decent story and fun gameplay. That's my 'fun' formula and when either part fails hard, then the whole game collapses. I should have seen Treyarch slipping badly from the 2nd Black Ops game which had a very weaker, albeit well presented, story.
I'm gonna try and keep it as spoiler free as I can.
The story is as nonsensical as they come, completely wasting all the potential they had with an otherwise strong first couple of missions, in a setting where characters, plot points and revelations are shoehorned in the game with absolute zero explanation and the end result is a mishmash of very bad common sci-fi tropes. The surprise 'twist' ending of the game had me in complete apathy as the credits started to roll.
The characters, with very few exceptions, are never explored in a good way and instead serve as cheap padding for an already tiring and convoluted story which begs for some kind of sanity.
Not to mention the disconnection with any of the previous work of Treyarch which reaches its peak with a single voiced reference to Raul Menendez from Black Ops 2 during one of the missions... and that's about it.
What mostly annoyed me though was the frequent appearance of bullet spongy mini-bosses, in the form of giant mechs, which
a lot of playtime in order to bring down. To put this in perspective, there are mobile armories and ammo crates placed when you're expected to fight these mini-bosses, just in case you DONT run out of ammo and get stuck fighting the boss. This cheap mechanic screams of a horrible gameplay design and is a poor indicator of the artificial difficulty the game is trying to impose on the player. Some previous CoD games might have been guilty of the same sin but those moments sparingly appeared. However in Black Ops 3 they are
frequent to the point of almost being in a every single mission. I hated those fights because they would bring the fluid gameplay of wall running and using the cyber powers to take down the enemy to a standstill; all to keep shooting bullets at the underbelly armor of a mech so it can open, you can fire a rocket and then repeat the same thing 4 more times so you could finally proceed to the next section of the game.
Sound design is alright for the most part but the soundtrack is forgettable and doesn't even come to close to being as good as the ones featured in the previous games. There's not much in terms of music and sound layering and it just plays out as generic futuristic FPS soundtrack.
Treyarch made one step forward and 2 steps backwards with Blacks Ops 3. The engaging gameplay, which features robotic and human enemies, with several powers to unlock and use, perks and weapon customization is all squandered on a horrible story which unravels from an intriguing mystery to a non-sensical and tiring plotline which bored me to tears. I can't believe I'm saying this but I prefer the story of Ghosts to this. Which is a sad statement in itself... Fact of the matter is, Black Ops 3 story was probably the

So I had a review in here and it wasn't a very good one. This time I'll flesh it out a bit more.
First of all, this game is NOT a spiritual successor to Road Rash. The internet is calling it that and I'm sorry but it absolutely is not.
Road Redemption lacks any and all of the original charm that was Road Rash.
Road Rash sucked you in by giving you the choice of the gang you affiliated with, giving the characters quirky and memorable personas that were funny and interesting.
It was also clear that you were just a gang member, racing against rival gangs for money and respect.
It had a licensed sound track that was bad to the bone! The music from the road rash games shaped my musical taste today. You wont find that here.
The story in Road Redemption is such an after thought to the actual game that I feel sorry for it. The aliens and robots riding futuristic motorcycles against you makes zero sense...
Story aside, the gameplay is just....odd.
Motorcycles have the wrong sounds associated with them, cruisers sound like sports bikes and vice-versa.
The playable characters are different not only by skin but also by stats, meaning you will pick a favorite based on what it gets you in game not just by whether you think they're cool or not. (Which is why you picked a character in Road Rash)
The game will leave you wondering, why can't I have a bike like that? Why do all these random dudes get a cool cafe racer and I have the option of a 675 Ducati, a Sportster and a CBR.
When you turn, the front wheel of the bike turns like 45 degrees and the bike barely leans over.
When you're turning the bike is constantly leaving a skid mark.
There's jump jet sections and a grappling hook.
The environments are mainly bland roads surrounded by mountains that are copy pasted.
The combat is nice at times, but a lot of the time just seems too zany. Combat in Road Rash seemed slightly believable, with a short crow bar in your leather jacket for example.
In this you're just riding down the highway at 250+ with a long sword across your handlebars.
The roguelike gameplay is sucky in my opinion. Works for some games but here I just find it annoying.
I've tried really hard to enjoy this game as its the most recent Motorcycle Combat game that someone has given a red hot crack but I just can't advise anyone to get into it.
TL:DR
Ridiculous gameplay that makes zero sense.
Physics and Audio is odd and often doesn't match the game.
Unity Engine so the graphics are trash on the highest settings.
You'll want to mute the in-game music and run spotify with the original road rash OST.
Combat is odd. Animations interrupt each other weird.
Non-Memorable story with non-memorable characters.
Guns and explosives.... Why?
Game is still in Early Access and devs are already talking about a sequel... Alarm bells anyone?
To the devs, be more than happy to discuss these things further if you would like :)

============================================================
SINGLEPLAYER REVIEW
============================================================
During my first hour playing this game, I couldn't help but compare it to its predecessor in every aspect. Up until now, I'm still not sure which one I like more, but I do know that after I decided to give this game a chance and play through the campaign missions I found myself addicted.
While its predecessor was all about Aiden "The Vigilante" Pearce, a protagonist seeking revenge as well as justice. The story really had me there and Aiden was doubtlessly a character I related to.
However, here comes Marcus, a brilliant hacker who joins DedSec and seems to be in it for the same reasons as the rest of the group - but you don't know what personal reasons motivate him (at least at the point where I am right now in the campaign).
Some missions
All I said so far was rather neutral or even slightly negative, but I cannot stress out how interesting the game gets. I get a good laugh from the cutscenes; there's a lot of humor all over this game.
And even though I can't relate with the protagonist, I found myself attached to the DedSec group as a whole, as if I'm actually feeling what they're feeling when they're going through their ups and downs as a group.
Watch Dogs 2 may not be as fun as Watch Dogs, but it definitely does bring its own unique attributes that make this game a fun experience.
============================================================
MULTIPLAYER REVIEW
============================================================
1. HACKING INVASION
When I first tried the hacking invasion back in Watch Dogs, I fell in love with the concept. Entering another player's world, stalking them while they remain completely unaware, starting the hack when the opportunity's in hand -- it's fun and even addictive. Whether you choose to blend in with NPCs or hide in cover, you'll definitely enjoy messing with another player's world.
However, in Watch Dogs 2, the drones make it quite easy for seekers to find the intruder. They fly up and profile pretty much everything. If you hide on a rooftop you'll be spotted easily.
That's not even the worst part, though. When you're connected with a player that's far away from you on the map, you'll be positioned about 100 meters away from them. If they were running your way, they'll realize you're an actual player and profile you right away, before you had the chance to do anything.
Moreover, you'll so often be connected to a player and then see the victim leave the session almost right away. Assuming they went peer-to-peer with the connections (if they did that with For Honor why won't they do that here?), then it's probably players you have bad connectivity with. Other reasons could be intended, such as when players start a mission or fast-travel somewhere. In other words, any player that's not just free-roaming or idle is not likely to appear as a target for you.
I entered the game of more than a hundred players through hacking invasion, but no one has ever entered mine for some reason. I suppose it might be because I'm usually doing missions or fast traveling towards them, but it's sad that I've yet to be victimized in this game.
2. BOUNTY HUNT
Straight up awesome. While it's likely that a match would not be found for you for this type of multiplayer - if you do get lucky, you'll find yourself joining the police in pursuit of a fellow player. If you or the police kill them, you win and the session is over. However, if you're killed by the rival player you may choose to respawn and keep on trying.
To say the truth, I most enjoyed this feature as a victim. I picked myself some trouble with the police and soon found myself escaping 3 rival players at the same time. Killing them brings great satisfaction, but you'll have to make a run for it if you want to actually win. The difference between a pursuit with the police and a pursuit with players, is that you don't get those easy "press F to wreck the cruiser" opportunities. If you want to use environmental hacking to give your pursuers a hard time, you'll actually have to look back and activate hacks or otherwise set proximity triggers.
3. CO-OP
Only joined one co-op session, where the other guy did the objective and I was simply following him, trying to understand how to use VoIP and communicate with no luck.

-Set Shadows to Very High or High.
-Turn OFF these options: "Headlight Shadows", "ScreenSpace Reflections" and "San Francisco Fog" (huge FPS improvement)

The previous 3 games were based largely on visual cues, with audio added to enhance things. This game is based on audio cues, with visuals enhancing the fright.
No cameras, no phone calls, no sitting still. It still has the claustrophobia and paranoia of the previous games, since you still stay in one room waiting for the break of day while trying not to die, but the overall feel of it makes my heart race and stomach drop out like it never has before in this series.
The story is extremely compelling, in the parts I have seen so far (I've survived only the first two nights as I'm writing this).
Also Plushtrap is adorable and my love for his (its? their? I mean, it is a plush toy) inclusion is deeper than the dread I feel every time I play a short burst of this game. Bland, repetitive and frustrating to play.  Constantly pulls the rug out from under the player in a bad way (particularly at the end of the very long prologue), and has a terrible ending to a story we've all been forced to sit through as we tried to get through the Ezio goodness in the previous 3 games.  The new world setting means the game lacks the impressive scope of the buildings in 1, 2, Brotherhood and Revelations, and the open world frontier sections just feel empty and not at all fun to play through.  The side-activities have lost all charm or interest, I didn't care about trading lumber for barrels or getting salt shipped over to Boston and ended up ignoring almost all of them/forgetting they were there.
Most frustrating of all is the feeling that all the emotional or story beats the game is trying to hit don't feel earned - Desmond's relationship with his father; Connor's so-called anguish over HIS father; Achilles' conflicts with Connor don't feel genuine; and the homestead lacks the family/community feel they seemed to be going for.
A massive letdown after the Ezio trilogy and not at all a game I'd recommend.  Read up on what happened and skip to Black Flag, or just wait for the new French Revolution game.

Assassin's Creed 3 is the final installment in the series of Assassin's Creed games featuring Desmond, an unambitious man turned hero of the Assassin order. From a story standpoint, Assassin's Creed 3, honestly, didn't live up to the title. It almost felt like the writers were running out of ideas, and really fell short in this 'big finale'. Now, from a gameplay standpoint, AC3 is, well alright. The mechanics are easy to master, and, with only a combination of pressing 'e' and clicking the mouse buttons, become quickly repetitive. I found myself growing bored of the gameplay halfway through the story, and found myself taking several breaks in between sessions. Now, don't get me wrong, though I've been harsh on this game so far, that doesn't make it bad. The game is solid enough. For the hardcore Assassin's Creed fans like myslef, AC3 didn't deliver, but for the casual gamer, it's a great game, and definitely worth the $20 price tag. All in all, I would rate Assassin's Creed 3 a 7/10.

Assassin's Creed III is a monument to everything you SHOULDN'T do in a video game, especially the third entry in a high-profile series. It's so foolishly ambitious that it trips over ever flaw it could possibly have, not stumbling, but falling down a flight of game-breaking glitches, buggy mechanics, shoehorned features, and the smallest focus on actual assassinations in the entire series.
I do have to give it credit though, the story they went for was a good idea. Setting up Haytham as the main character only to bait and switch him is clever. The issue was making an interesting character out of Conor, which they downright failed to do. Conor never seems to change gears throughout the entireity of the story, helped by mediocre voicework.
4 times I had to restart the game due to glitches, either being unable to complete a mission or due to the world disappearing around me. Not to mention crashes I encountered.
In all honesty, just skip this game and go straight to 4. If you're really interested in the story, it's available by Wikipedia or in cutscene form on Youtube. The game itself is not worth the time of day. I gave up on the game after I realized I was still going through what was essentially tutorials 8 hours into the game.

Before I begin, I would like to note that I've played this game for a while outside of steam, having one maxed out priest, and several midrange characters.
Visuals: Excellent
This game is beautiful both in raw graphical output and in a more general aesthetic sense. The world is entertaining to explore and adore; Character and enemy models are are clear, attack and action animations are well done and add to the experience, the the overal visual design scheme is appropriate for the for each area, with only a few dungeons being somewhat bland.  While the female character designs are certainly over-sexualized, TERA attempts to do so in a *slightly* more balanced way by including some sexualized male armor sets: if you like your games sexy, this game has it in spades for what it's worth.
Pacing: Good
The rate at which you aquire loot and levels keeps things entertaining for most of the game; only a couple of times did I find my progress sluggish enough to evoke frumpiness. As with any MMO there is a grind to worry about (especially once you get to max level, you'll be running certain dungeons a sickening number of times for loot or enchanting fodder). You start fast, grow fast, and rarely NEED to grind until the endgame opens up.
Sound: Good
The music is well done, but I found myself eventually turning it off, as it's not entertaining enough to want to listen to on it's own merit; rather, it's more atmospheric. The combat and action sounds are appropriate and are timed properly, making combat aurally viseral enough.   Voice acting is . . . fine.
Mechanics: Great
This score would be lower but this is the first MMO in which I was actally entertained by the combat. Battle is freeform and fast, especially in the PVP department, where clutch timing can be vital. Skill cooldown and hitboxes are mostly appropriate for PVE and PVP. Crafting is tedious, resource heavy, and not immediately rewarding leaving most players to wait until endgame to begin crafting, where resources and harvest points are more available. Enchanting is useful, but unimpressive and higher levels of enchanting can leave you pulling out your hair and spending most of your stockpile of gold. Missions are uninteresting, mostly consisting of "go to X and kill Y"  or "go to X and collect/harvest Y*  The loot boxes make me cry . . .
Balance: Good
Most skills and classes are balanced for their function and are regularly adjusted for fine tuning in updates, with flaws and imbalances existing mainly in the content itself. The game is combat focused, and as such the support classes (Priest and Mystic) have difficulty earning rewards compared to other more damaging or defensive classes. This is most obvious during BAM events, where you may as well switch to a combat alt.

Community: *shrugs*
I'm not sure what to say here. In general the people are good natured, but it's the internet afterall, and freemium MMO's have no monetary barrier/filter to keep the dregs of the MMO culture from freely entering the world and running amok until banned. Their is a strong erotic subculture that one should be wary of, unless that's your kind of thing. Otherwise, I would say the community is largly youth based, with a decent sized pool of older MMO players as well.  Conversation seems to gravitate towards anime culture or School/College stuff, which isn't my cup of tea, but if you are of the age or just a big fan of anime, you'll not want for conversational partners.
Overall, a pretty great MMO. I had a great time leveling my first character to max, not so great a time dungeon grinding and enchanting endgame. Leveling a second character was less fun, but still fast, especially if you join a guild with helpful member.  Give it a shot if you have the room (38 friggan gigs!), you'll likely find yourself pleasantly supprised.

An otherwise enhanced gameplay experience for a CoD game, tarnished by the horrible story
utterly disappoints as the last game of the series.
As always my experience reflects
the singleplayer aspect of the game.
Call of Duty®: Black Ops III is the final (for now) installment Treyarch have developed for their critically acclaimed series of Call of Duty games and boy they saved the worst for last.
But first lets talk about some of the better qualities of Black Ops 3 and what do you know, gameplay has actually a few new additions which make for much more interesting playthroughs. The Player, a cybernetic enhanced soldier, not only just uses weapons to take down the enemy but also has access to several augmentations and powers. You have access to 3 cyber core trees: Control, Chaos and Martial.
All 3 cores include 7 different powers (plus their upgraded versions). These powers range from summoning a swarm of nanomachines to overwhelm the enemy, a cloak device, smokescreen, faster movement and reload for the player, a sonic attack and many more. You can unlock these powers by using fabrication kits which you acquire when you level up in the game. Leveling up is done by completing several accolades, most of them unique to each of the 11 missions of the game. Accolades such as completing the mission without dying once, getting a high score and finding all collectibles are shared for all missions.
Getting those fabrication kits also allows you to unlock weapons, wildcards and extra bonuses, such as walking on walls, a single use auto-revive, extra attachments to your weapons and a few others. Weapon attachments include various scopes, grips for increased accuracy and other various stat modifiers for increased range/accuracy/damage.
I loved the ability to modify and prepare for each mission accordingly since you get a short briefing with what you should expect in terms of combat, be it short or medium or long range engagements.
Graphically the game looks pretty good for 2015 and dare I say, despite some bad textures here and there, even up for 2017 standards. The models and animations are good, weapons look modern without being ridiculous and the environments which you fight are for the most part decently looking although the level design itself leaves a lot to be desired.
Performance wise the game played out really well however I will mention a couple of weird hitches every now and then between loading of different chapters but nothing that impacts gameplay or any crashes.
So where's does Call of Duty®: Black Ops III fail? For me Call of Duty is all about a nice decent story and fun gameplay. That's my 'fun' formula and when either part fails hard, then the whole game collapses. I should have seen Treyarch slipping badly from the 2nd Black Ops game which had a very weaker, albeit well presented, story.
I'm gonna try and keep it as spoiler free as I can.
The story is as nonsensical as they come, completely wasting all the potential they had with an otherwise strong first couple of missions, in a setting where characters, plot points and revelations are shoehorned in the game with absolute zero explanation and the end result is a mishmash of very bad common sci-fi tropes. The surprise 'twist' ending of the game had me in complete apathy as the credits started to roll.
The characters, with very few exceptions, are never explored in a good way and instead serve as cheap padding for an already tiring and convoluted story which begs for some kind of sanity.
Not to mention the disconnection with any of the previous work of Treyarch which reaches its peak with a single voiced reference to Raul Menendez from Black Ops 2 during one of the missions... and that's about it.
What mostly annoyed me though was the frequent appearance of bullet spongy mini-bosses, in the form of giant mechs, which
a lot of playtime in order to bring down. To put this in perspective, there are mobile armories and ammo crates placed when you're expected to fight these mini-bosses, just in case you DONT run out of ammo and get stuck fighting the boss. This cheap mechanic screams of a horrible gameplay design and is a poor indicator of the artificial difficulty the game is trying to impose on the player. Some previous CoD games might have been guilty of the same sin but those moments sparingly appeared. However in Black Ops 3 they are
frequent to the point of almost being in a every single mission. I hated those fights because they would bring the fluid gameplay of wall running and using the cyber powers to take down the enemy to a standstill; all to keep shooting bullets at the underbelly armor of a mech so it can open, you can fire a rocket and then repeat the same thing 4 more times so you could finally proceed to the next section of the game.
Sound design is alright for the most part but the soundtrack is forgettable and doesn't even come to close to being as good as the ones featured in the previous games. There's not much in terms of music and sound layering and it just plays out as generic futuristic FPS soundtrack.
Treyarch made one step forward and 2 steps backwards with Blacks Ops 3. The engaging gameplay, which features robotic and human enemies, with several powers to unlock and use, perks and weapon customization is all squandered on a horrible story which unravels from an intriguing mystery to a non-sensical and tiring plotline which bored me to tears. I can't believe I'm saying this but I prefer the story of Ghosts to this. Which is a sad statement in itself... Fact of the matter is, Black Ops 3 story was probably the
I've ever had the misfortune to experience in a Call of Duty game. For fans of singleplayer FPS games who actually care about storylines and not just mindless (but fun) gameplay, unless you read spoilers and you're OK with what to expect, I'd recommend staying the far away from Black Ops 3 and instead play the first or the second game of the series. As for the future of Black Ops series, maybe I think it's time to take a break for now and come back stronger in the future.

Game doesn't work for me, I reviewed it based on my experience, and with that, I wouldn't recommend it.
The review system is not "This game is good, this game is bad" system. It's "would you tell a friend about this game, and that they should play it"? Based on my experiences, no, they should not.
Even bad games, such as Bad Rats get good reviews, because it's a meme game, and people would recommend it to friends, so they can laugh about the bad game together.

Am I biased? Yes.
Do I like FNAF? No.
Is the series being milked? Yes.
Do I see FNAF's fans as sheep, that will praise the games to high heavens? Yes.

The combat is fairly easy, press X to stab redcoats, but the music is good, which really adds to the setting. It works well as historical tourism. Also, the side missions are pretty essential if you want a full experience, as there is a major spoiler at the end of one of them.
Though worth noting is the protagonist, Connor, has less personality than a potato.

Played this game after hearing a crap ton of recommendations for it and went in expecting a unique experience, boy was I wrong. From the first moments it started dawning on me what overhyped garbage this game really is. The opening is long and drawn out and the dialogue gives off the impression it was written by an 8 year old, the jokes are immature and dumb, the banter between characters is cringy and written with the vocabulary you'd find in Dora The Explorer. The overall feel of the characters is cliche and I cannot believe anyone that has ever played another game can find these characters deep, interesting or endearing.
After the long and needlessly wordy tutorial I was finally ready for my first mission, and what a thrill that was. I was tasked with rescuing 2 kids I know or care nothing about from some silly tower whose purpose, existence or importance is never explained. Boy am I on the edge of my seat now. What a boring way to open up a game, I cared nothing about the consequences of any of these character's actions, thanks in part to how bad the dialogue and presentation of the story is. The second mission wasn't any better, go to some farm and kill the "monster" terrorizing it. Is this an MMORPG? Because the tasks you have to fulfill sure feel like it.
On to the combat. The combat takes place on a grid based battlefield reminiscent of SRPGs but it doesn't have the depth of an SRPG. The existence of this grid is highly questionable as it feels shoddy, the characters can't move manualy and attack on the same turn, you waste turns just moving around to reach faraway enemies which makes the battles needlessly slow. They could have gone with a generic JRPG combat system but instead this "hybrid" combines the worst of both worlds. Silly random encounters in JRPGs that are not fast paced and quick are a chore and get old very quickly. It doesn't feel like the grid adds any sort of strategic depth to the combat.
The slow paced nature of the combat system could maybe be excused if the enemies themselves were at least a tad bit interesting but the enemy design is atrocious. Every single enemy I have seen has looked stupid and not threatening. A squirrel with wings? Seriously? Who would want to fight "monsters" that look like that. I felt bad killing enemies that look as helpless as the lot I faced, they all look like they belong in an injured animal shelter.
And the monsters are not the only thing in this game that looks bad. The entire presentation is uninspired and bland. The game world is barren, the maps between cities are basically corridors with the occasional chest thrown at the side of the road. Truly genius level design. Thanks to this, and the aformentioned combat system, there is 0 incentive to explore the game world. The technical proficiency in which the game was made is also lacking, the game has little aesthetic merit as everything except the menus looks cheap. Textures, models, animations are all medicore.
The only redeeming quality this game has is the music, which was actually quite fun and varied. Other than that, nothing in this game is well done and can even remotely compete with the better games of its genre. I was promised this game excels in "world building" but this just a flat out lie perpetuated by several communities online that operate like an echo chamber. Yeah, all the NPCs have dialogue, but since this dialogue is written so poorly it just feels like a waste of your time. The world, characters and missions were so uninspired that I couldn't find anything that would give me incentive to keep playing this.
Nothing in the game sets it apart in a good way, nothing stood out as exceptional, if I didn't know any better I would have thought this was made with the newest version of RPG Maker. One of the most generic and unimpressive jrpgs I have played in a while and I guess it's no wonder it's totally ignored and forgotten outside of a few niche communities. Skip this game, there is no merit to be had here.
It's boring and archaic. It looks utterly barren, the combat is dull, the dialogue is childish, and it suffers from every JRPG trope imaginable.

MMORPGs are dead. World of Warcraft has considered it necessary to make all of their things, including membership, buyable via in game money which is great for a game that was supposed to be free-to-play from the beginning, but shows how desperate people of this genre are to keep their games alive.
Tera, however, shouldn't even be considered an MMORPG. Sure, its a MMO. Sure, its an RPG. But one thing seperates it from all the other games: it's not dying. It's alive and well and may even be considered the resurrection of the genre that once dominated the PC gaming world.
It's so incredibly smooth, and it offers such versatile gameplay with many races (all with unique features) and many classes that can stack another set of unique features, making for tens of possibilities in playstyle (which doesn't sound like much, but try to consider how many unique combinations you can get from most other MMORPGs).
Character customization is more detailed than a lot of other videogames, allowing you to be personal with the character YOU created.
Sure, it's a little grindy at times. Certain missions (a considerable amount, actually. Especially early.) require you to collect a specific item from a specific type of enemy. Sure, it's really heavy on the requirements. You may have to play on a lower graphics setting. But those are the only two major drawbacks to this game.
Tera is a game with much more pros than cons. Guild creation and management is easy, you can have many characters per server (and there are a few servers, allowing you to amass up 50+ characters if you're really into the game). Combat is flawlessly smooth, with no chunkiness to discourage gameplay.
When the developers created this game, they must have known it would be the game of the genre. This is the new World of Warcraft, but the cost for maintaining a membership isnt $15 a month, or even in game currency. No, the membership is completel free, which is astounding considering how many people would pay for this game.

There is no actual fighting in this fighting game, you just choose what skills you want your character to use during a fight and then sit there and stare as he exchanges blows with the oponent. The rest of the game focuses on having to slave at a boring job to get money for food, you basically just watch a bar go up and get money when it's at the top. Other then that you also have to work out to get your fighters stats up, this is as simple as choosing what training implement to use for different stats and then watch as he repeatedly goes trough the same animation untill he doesn't want to do that specific training anymore and you have to click on another implement.
This is one of those weird games that takes things away from you the further you get into it. After a while you won't have to worry about working or shopping for food as it is provided for you. You also get a home gym so you won't have to leave the house for training. So it basically boils down to watching your fighter work out 95% of the time and then having a fight once in a blue moon. Aparently pro fighters don't fight as often as the rookie ones.
There is also sub plots like a love interest. But it all basically boils down to click something and watch. Click girlfriend, click chat, watch him stand there akwardly flexing his muscles while he talks and gets his relationship up.
The games artstyle is retro and looks good for a retro game. However there is very little originality in the sense of humor or area design. It's all just one screen for each area and every last area is filled to the brim with pop-culture references and memes, no actual creativity or originality went into constructing the characters or the world.
All in all, I'd say don't buy it, don't play it, unless you enjoy sitting motionless watching boring sprite animations for hours on end untill you have enough stats to beat the next fighter.

The gameplay actually has some good mechanics to it that make you feel in control of what is going on, which allows you to get better instead of get lucky. The idea of losing your items and cash when dying, but not your unlocked skills is really interesting.
Now, as an early access game, here are some bugs/issues that I think the devs should glance at:
-The graphics leave something to be desired though, such as unity's new soft shadows and maybe even actual PBR.
-You can grapple a dead biker's unmanned bike. I discovered this because my push to talk button on teamspeak is the same as the grapple button.
-You can easily exploit the "place me on track" button as it only removes your health and doesnt make you wait for the 5 seconds that crashing normally would. I think this button should emulate you crashing your bike instead.
-General optimization issues, I get the same framerate on lowest graphics that I do on highest.
-When starting the game with the music turned all the way down, some strange piano song plays and then suddenly cuts out.
-Additionally, when starting the game it gets stuck on a light blue screen (similar to the color you see on the background of the unity logo), maybe this could be changed to show a loading image instead?
-When switching out weapons at the beginning of the mission, it would be useful to see the durability of my current weapons.
-Having a borderless windowed mode would be neat
-The road is too visually flat, you can tell by the specularity from the sun
-I think that there should be a bit of a minimap, similar to what you already get when racing, on all modes so you can tell whether you should back up or keep going if your goal is to kill cops/bikers.
-When I saw the word "procedural", I imagined endless races that would randomly change, which I didn't get. Not too bad, but an endurance mode would be interesting with impromptu races and objectives.
-Additionally with the procedural stuff, I feel theres not enough variation with each "biome". Maybe add more buildings? Some decals on the road?
Either way, it's a great game, has some real solid gameplay to it, and worth the buy if you like fast paced racing games.

I keep telling myself I won't invest in any more Early Access titles, yet here I am. I remember trading my SNES for my friend's Genesis a lot of weekends in Jr. High, and the Road Rash series was one of the biggest reasons. This game takes the timeless concept of armed crazies on motorcycles racing on public roads for fame and fortune to another level.
Probably the biggest upgrade, online multiplayer, isn't implemented yet, but what is here now is already as fun as the original games. What's already been added to the original schematic is local multiplayer, rooftop levels, "hallucinatory" levels with cars falling from the sky and crashing into each other at every turn, awesome avatars with flaming jack-o-lantern heads, and a permanent experience based upgrade path on top of the cash upgrades that dissapear after each game ends.  I definitely don't regret this purchase.

MMORPGs are dead. World of Warcraft has considered it necessary to make all of their things, including membership, buyable via in game money which is great for a game that was supposed to be free-to-play from the beginning, but shows how desperate people of this genre are to keep their games alive.
Tera, however, shouldn't even be considered an MMORPG. Sure, its a MMO. Sure, its an RPG. But one thing seperates it from all the other games: it's not dying. It's alive and well and may even be considered the resurrection of the genre that once dominated the PC gaming world.
It's so incredibly smooth, and it offers such versatile gameplay with many races (all with unique features) and many classes that can stack another set of unique features, making for tens of possibilities in playstyle (which doesn't sound like much, but try to consider how many unique combinations you can get from most other MMORPGs).
Character customization is more detailed than a lot of other videogames, allowing you to be personal with the character YOU created.
Sure, it's a little grindy at times. Certain missions (a considerable amount, actually. Especially early.) require you to collect a specific item from a specific type of enemy. Sure, it's really heavy on the requirements. You may have to play on a lower graphics setting. But those are the only two major drawbacks to this game.
Tera is a game with much more pros than cons. Guild creation and management is easy, you can have many characters per server (and there are a few servers, allowing you to amass up 50+ characters if you're really into the game). Combat is flawlessly smooth, with no chunkiness to discourage gameplay.
When the developers created this game, they must have known it would be the game of the genre. This is the new World of Warcraft, but the cost for maintaining a membership isnt $15 a month, or even in game currency. No, the membership is completel free, which is astounding considering how many people would pay for this game.

I have to say, I really loved TERA. My friends got into WoW and Runescape whenever those came out, but i never really got into MMOs until TERA, and it felt great finally getting pulled into one. So I guess I'll jump right into it. NOT P2W at ALL.
The game is primarily focused on combat which is fantastic. There are several different classes you can choose from obviously which include healers, ranged dps, melee dps, and tanks. The controls are tight/responsive and really feel like they have a lot of weight behind them (makes for really satisfying gameplay with hard-hitting abilities). I played a slayer (melee dps) until I maxed out my gear and I loved it through and through. Combos get old after a while but that's just because I was playing the same dungeons.
It didn't get boring for me really until I hit the endgame wall. One of the reasons I stopped playing this was because my guild couldn't run higher level dungeons (because of gear and skill). And that is a reoccurring problem with this game. To run higher level dungeons you need significant experience with that specific dungeon or a huge guild to carry you because nobody is going to take an undergeared/underexperienced randy to take on a few-hour dungeon just to wipe. There are wipe-mechanics in pretty much all of the end-game dungeons and if you don't read up before hand you're screwed unless someone else says something/you ask.
I did PvE 99% of the time so I can't say much about PvP but I did play Corsair's Stronghold (CS) a lot. CS is basically just an attack/defend gamemode for anyone level 30-65 (max) where everyone gets normalized gear. I have to say it was a lot of fun on both sides. I would do PvP just for CS if I had the motivation to gear up for it, because the prizes (both daily and rare) are substantial. It was great because it actually required teamwork (for your 20 person team) and it was really satisfying breaking through each of the checkpoints on the map, or successfully defending against waves of attackers. There are several other modes for PvP (single/team/special) which I don't have experience with but are definitely worth looking into.
The crafting/market is really a strong point in this game for me. I mastered etching (creates temporary/permenant buffs for gear) and I have to say that was really exciting crafting those higher-tier etches and selling them on the market for a ton because of the rare chance of crafting them. You can get rewards from PvP (chests) and from other daily events which you can make some serious money off of if you save up. Oh important point I guess. You don't really get any cash until level 50 or so, and nothing you pick up before 65 is worth anything besides crafting materials. But you can sell those crafting materials if you don't plan on using them later (can be worth a lot) and buy your endgame gear later or save the mats and make your stuff after a LOT of grinding. Some mats are REALLY hard to come by (looking at you titan's ember :() and only drop from rare world bosses (drop a lot) or occasionally from high level dungeons (very few drop). The rarity of these is annoying at times but makes the crafting all the more satisfying when it works. It's satisfying because you not only can make the target item but you can crit on it and get an upgraded version of it or get more of the item, which is very cool when it happens.
AVATAR WEAPONS are game-breaking. I have to say it. Avatar weapons are made to help you level up, and they do that all too well. Literally ever other weapon you get before 65 is useless in comparison because you crit so often on avatar weapons. It takes away from the rest of the early parts of the game by reducing your choices. I say just take them out of the game and increase the variation between the weapons that are available during that time.
What else.. guilds are really easy to come by and if you put up a message in global chat saying you want in to one, somebody is bound to invite you. And there are guilds for every aspect of the game.
Oh yeah and of course the other reason I stopped playing was because I maxed out my gear. TERA's endgame is sweet, don't get me wrong, but it's primarily (at least for PvE) focused on gear progression. Once I finished that, I really had no motivation to continue. But again, you still have options. You can continue to master the REAL endgame dungeons (which are a serious challenge and require spot-on teamwork), or do PvP and get ranked. Or you can always just start over, which is what a lot of people do.
Overall amazing game, definitely recommended.
Edit: I used... to love it for the combat, but I've come back a couple times a year expecting something to change because it got boring and I uninstall literally within a minute of starting up the game. Sex-locked classes, terrible optomization, and now an even worse team behind it. What reason is there to play?

Fez is a brilliant platformer. This game's play with 2D projection is one-of-a-kind. A must play.
The projection mechanic is mind-bending at first, but soon you'll find yourself thinking differently about movement. Surfaces that look far away from one perspective are just a step away in another. Long stretches of wall can be flattened to nothing. You'll find yourself spinning the world just to save a few seconds of vine climbing. It's trippy.
The pixel art is minimalist and detailed. The game breaks retro tradition by incorporating some subtle lighting and dazzling shader effects. The music is catchy and nostalgic. The perspective puzzles are great, too. There's even an alien language to decipher. I recommend googling the code rather than scouring for the game's Rosetta Stone, but the choice is yours!
Remember: To climb down ledges, press down and jump.

"Meh" game.
The reason I've been playing it for about 9 hours was that I wanted to know if the story could save the insane grind you'll encounter after about 2 hours or so. Probably I didn't go down the story route the devs have intended (I went full "I wanna be the very best, like no one ever wa...", eh, you get the deal), but what I encountered was pretty much a punch in the face: this route ends with probably one of the worst "what exactly was that?"-endings in video game history, so kudos I guess.
To give you a better idea: you remember those old NES games that seemingly were just produced for the sole purpose of punishing you, yet still were so good that you wanted to push through them? Those, that ended up with a simple "Congratulations! You saved the world!"-text screen and returned to the main menu?
Well, Punch Club is one of those, only in "very mediocre"-mode after hour 2. It's the very definition of a game that could have been much better - the qualities shine through - but leaves the bitter taste of a sudden creativity block dev wise after a certain point.
It's funny, it has awesome pixel art and the music is catchy, but it lacks substance - a lack of substance the promise of an interesting story tries to make up for without ever delivering. I'm not mad that I paid 10€ for it, since this product clearly had a lot of love poured into it (which I absolutely admire), but as a game, I cannot recommend it.

I once considered myself a Five Nights at Freddy's fan, but I'm not so sure anymore. This final installment managed to drop below my most paranoidly low expectations.
The atmosphere is not eerie for long, once you fully explore the very limited features of the bedroom, significantly simpler than the offices of the prior three games.  The "challenge" of the core element of this game is built on inaudible, indistinguishable audio cues.  Turning up the sound to hear any hint of these cues also amplifies the jumpscares to be needlessly, ear-splittingly loud.  It is infuriating, to say the least.  At least in the first three installments, making one mistake and having to restart a night usually felt more like player error than completely vague, punishing game design.
From a graphical standpoint, the animations and character models are solid.  The scenery, not so much; it's all poorly textured, unnaturally shaded, flat-looking rooms with no personality.  These visuals are noticeably lazy compared to what the creator has demonstrated with earlier games in the franchise.
The story, setting, and general identity of this game seems completely misguided after the previous three.  All of the elements that made the others so memorable and noteworthy seem to have been tossed out the window in favor of a cliché, unimaginative attempt at an explanation to tie up all the loose ends of the series--which, in an unsatisfying and largely meaningless way, undermines the sense of mystery which has pervaded the whole series up to this point.  This ending feels like an afterthought in an attempt to appease fans and burn bridges for any more sequels.  Given how unnecessary this sequel was, however, I would not be surprised if there were still more to come.
In short, this game is an unpolished, poorly-conceived, hackneyed mess, and the conclusion is a gigantic letdown to this year-long story.

Are you a fan of JRPGs from the SNES and Playstation eras? Looking for an epic story to sink your teeth into? Well then Trails in the Sky is the game for you!
The Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky is a game in the vein of JRPGs of yore and is the first chapter in a long and epic saga, so if you're in the mood for a massive and detailed story then the Trails series has you covered! That being said you can simply play this game and it's follow-up, Trails in the Sky: SC (Second Chapter), as both games constitute two parts of one story that can be enjoyed on its own.
At first glance both the story and characters appear rather generic. Add to that some very slow pacing at the beginning and you might just think that this game doesn't deserve all the praise it gets. However, what appears to be a bland world populated by unoriginal characters soon becomes the exact opposite. The game's world is rich and full of detail, and the characters are much more than just their archetypes. The plot may take a bit to get going for some players, but the likeable characters and excellent script make the experience very worthwile!
The gameplay is very much like your typical JRPG. You visit towns and cities, speak with NPCs, explore dangerous locations and battle against a variety of foes. The story is rather linear but in each town you have the opportunity to undertake an assortment of optional quests which net you money as well as rare items and equipment. Towns and cities feature a large number of NPCs, each with their own names and personalities, and every time you advance the plot you'll find that they have new dialogue, their individual story arcs advancing little by little.
The combat is turn-based and takes place in a grid. Positioning is important (especially in boss fights) and you'll find yourself trying to land "Arts" (spells) and "Crafts" (skills) on the right spot of the grid so as to damage several enemies at once. The battle animations are quite slow however, so you might feel the need to use the very useful Turbo Mode during battles. Overall the battle system is quite tactical and rewards proper use of strategy. If I had to compare it to anything else I'd say it's a mixture of
and
.
The game isn't terribly impressive when it comes to graphics. It was originally released in 2004 for the PC but you wouldn't really know it seeing as it appears quite dated even for that time. That being said I found the graphics to be quite charming, the juxtaposition of pre-rendered sprites on 3D backgrounds reminding me a lot of PS1-era JRPGs. The artwork can appear to be rather bland but the variety of expressive character portraits really sell the dialogue.
The music in this game is quite pleasing to the ear. Falcom games have a reputation of having great music and whilst I think that this game doesn't have as many great tracks as later games in the series do, it still deserves said reputation. I particularly enjoy the main battle theme ("Sophisticated Fight") and most of the town themes. As for sound effects, they're nothing to write home about but they're not bad either. All in all they're quite serviceable.
I should probably mention that I played the game in Hard difficulty. I chose said difficulty due to past experiences playing JRPGs which I found to be way too easy. Hard difficulty in this game is quite balanced, forcing you to consider your actions during battles, but the beginning of the game can also be quite tough on this difficulty. It's a great difficulty setting to choose if you wish for the game to challenge you and besides a few battles it's never unfair or punishing, nor does it really force you to grind much. There's also the option to active the retry offset, and option that makes each subsequent retry of a battle easier, something which I admit I did have to use in the final battle.
So to summarize (as this review went way longer than I expected) if you're looking for an epic and fun JRPG with great characters and worldbuilding then Trails in the Sky is the game for you! Just know that once your done with this game you'll probably want to immediately jump into its direct sequel, and then the third game, and so on!

The best educational games are the ones that don't feel educational. In Assassin's Creed III you can fight the American War for Independence the sneaky way, meeting real historical leaders, discovering landmarks, and participating in significant events along the way. Every one of these you discover will earn you a humorous and informative entry in the game's encyclopedia, presumably written by one of the main characters. You can also read Ben Franklin's wise and witty proverbs in the various issues of Poor Richard's Almanac, if you're fast enough to catch the pages. For those of us who grew up in the 90's with Carmen Sandiego and the Clue Finders, the Assassin's Creed franchise definitely fills a void. Unlike most modern games, these are guaranteed to yield a return on invested time. Play slowly.

Previously without having played Assassins Creed 3 I was being negative and quite biased when speaking of Assassins Creed series. It all changed upon meeting Connor, the main protagonist, of this entry. Now, I am absolutely positive that this is one of the best action games I have played in years. There are a few misfires that could jeopordize some aspects of the game, yet the good things undermine the significance of the not so good things.
The good thing is the relative freedom that's been given to the player in how he or she interacts with world. Not only you can explore vast cities of Boston and New York you have a whole wilderness in between them to explore. You can harvest, craft and even build your own village. And lets not forget about the sea battles, that are the absolute best of the game.
The story is also satisfying as is it's main subject - Connor. I am not a big fan of the animus thing as I would enjoy the game more if it was a Connor only game, but, hell, all stories need a plot machine.
Now onto the not so good. Let's start with saying that some aspects of the game feel quite dated. The auto run is not good as Connor in times could get stuck in numerous cluster scattered around as well as jump onto the wall you never intended to jump. That's annoying and I've been yelling at my computer at times in desperation.
Overall, the game is fantastic, I do not regret neither the money nor the time spent on it.
