“By God,” you might say if you attended elementary school in the United States in the ‘80s or ‘90s, “
sure was an exciting, unforgiving adventure across a harsh wilderness, surely it must hold up today!” This opinion is shared mostly amongst audiences who have: a) not played it since the ‘80s or ‘90s, or b) the type of grown adults that had trouble getting into all these newfangled concepts of game design such as “gameplay” and “menus”. It’s old, in short.
can get away with being designed like an old game because it came out 38 years ago, and is old.
, on the other hand, first reared its head in 2010 as a Flash-based browser game, making marginal changes when it popped up for iOS in 2012 and Steam in 2013, eventually seeing a PlayStation release in 2015. All of these editions (or ‘strains’, if you were to talk about the game like an infectious disease) are too new to use the
excuse, so each of them needs to have something that makes them better than a bootlegged version of the original that some high school kid retextured in the late ‘90s as part of a game design course.
The only part of
that demonstrates any of the advancements in game development and just ♥♥♥♥ing technology is the addition of mouse control in menus. Whoa there, champ, don’t overdo it! This does, however, segue into the highlight of
- clicking the ‘exit game’ button. It’s not that the game is truly, unashamedly awful. It’s got some charm, and it’s nice to walk around during the shooting and scavenging sections, but developer ‘The Men Who Wear Many Hats’ (♥♥♥♥ing hell) just doesn’t have the basic understanding of the difference between ‘retro’ and ‘retro-styled’.
is retro-styled.
is retro-styled.
is retro-styled. The difference between any of these games and
, is that of gameplay.
Regardless of whether or not you’re going for an old-timey vibe, you need to meet the basic standards of what makes a game at least ‘good enough’.
doesn’t meet these standards. It’s the game equivalent of one joke that was going to be developed into a real game with more mechanics, a story, anything to add depth other than some mildly different flavour texts. Whoever conceived
had a great idea, and was maybe on the right track to make a genuinely enjoyable little game, it’s just a shame he had to pass the project onto his younger cousin as part of the recovery process for his attention deficit disorder.

I once considered myself a Five Nights at Freddy's fan, but I'm not so sure anymore. This final installment managed to drop below my most paranoidly low expectations.
The atmosphere is not eerie for long, once you fully explore the very limited features of the bedroom, significantly simpler than the offices of the prior three games.  The "challenge" of the core element of this game is built on inaudible, indistinguishable audio cues.  Turning up the sound to hear any hint of these cues also amplifies the jumpscares to be needlessly, ear-splittingly loud.  It is infuriating, to say the least.  At least in the first three installments, making one mistake and having to restart a night usually felt more like player error than completely vague, punishing game design.
From a graphical standpoint, the animations and character models are solid.  The scenery, not so much; it's all poorly textured, unnaturally shaded, flat-looking rooms with no personality.  These visuals are noticeably lazy compared to what the creator has demonstrated with earlier games in the franchise.
The story, setting, and general identity of this game seems completely misguided after the previous three.  All of the elements that made the others so memorable and noteworthy seem to have been tossed out the window in favor of a cliché, unimaginative attempt at an explanation to tie up all the loose ends of the series--which, in an unsatisfying and largely meaningless way, undermines the sense of mystery which has pervaded the whole series up to this point.  This ending feels like an afterthought in an attempt to appease fans and burn bridges for any more sequels.  Given how unnecessary this sequel was, however, I would not be surprised if there were still more to come.
In short, this game is an unpolished, poorly-conceived, hackneyed mess, and the conclusion is a gigantic letdown to this year-long story.

In most cases, making a game that's all about exposition is probably a bad idea. Trails in the Sky was most definitely not a bad idea.
You play as Estelle, who is working to become a bracer along with her adopted brother Joshua. They meet a handful of helpful compelling characters (one of whom has seriously unparalleled flirt game) throughout their journey and offer assistance of their own to people around Liberl Kingdom. Somehow, between the crossdressing, saving children from burning buildings, and being sarcastically told off by treasure chests, this game manages to establish a massive world entrenched with real, political issues, yet still only offers a glimpse of what's really going on behind the scenes. And trust me when I say you'll be damn invested in finding out what happens after this game even more so than what happens during it.
This game's soundtrack is amazing. The title track truly captures the essence of the game and the adventure Estelle and Joshua go on. The battle theme, which I think is one of the most important tracks since you're constantly fighting, is catchy while still bringing tension to the battle. And Whereabouts of the Stars...don't get me started on this song. The way in which they weave this song into the storyline is phenomenal, and you'll find yourself filled with emotion every time you hear it. Honestly, this OST is just outstanding.
As the game was released in 2004, the graphics are nothing special, but I thought they cleaned up this version nicely. The evironments look nice and the picture is sharp even on very high quality screens.
The gameplay has similar controls to every other RPG, but the battle system is quite unique. Though it takes some getting used it, it ends up being quite fun. You'll learn to strategize during battles instead of simply spamming attacks. On the downside, once you really figure out how to use crafts, you can basically do just that which takes the strategy out of the big fights.
All of these things together make for a wonderful gaming experience. The localization team did a great job with all the dialogue and you'll want to examine every nook and cranny of this game to find all the hilarious easter eggs hidden throughout. My first playthrough took about 70 hours including all sidequests, so I guarantee Trails is a good investment. Unless you hate having to read lots of dialogue or dislike JRPGs, this is a game that is certainly worth your time. Just make sure you're ready to buy the sequel once you're done this one.

Really good game, satisfied the itch I had for a turn based JRPG on the PC. Not quite in the same league (IMO) as the pre Enix Final Fantasy games, but still quite great. I would describe it as "Rich in content with a lot of depth to the game mechanics, but also family friendly and can be enjoyed by people of virtually any age".
I mean.. I've played this game on other platforms for a billion hours so don't take my game time to mean anything, or something.

Trails in the Sky came to me in a time when I was very disillusioned with games. It had been a long time since I had played a game that impressed me in... even the slightest, most games seeming dull or uninspired. I felt pretty bad about games as a whole, and then I found this absolutely spectacular game. It dazzled me. It confused me. It frustrated me.
I was completely blown away.
A story with an unassuming beginning, blossoming out into tons and tons of individual story lines, all touching upon the world around it and enriching the experience as a whole. The main plot has secrets being revealed left right and center, up until the end, and once you've reached the end, playing through the game again makes you appreciate the writing doubly so, as you now understand certain aspects of the history better.
Lovable characters, each one with unique abilities and proficiencies in combat and charming characteristics in dialogue, mixing together, butting heads, recognizing each other's flaws, and becoming better for it all. They use what is, at times, pretty cheesy dialogue to win me over, but it's good cheese. The kind of cheese that allows for genuine emotion to come through in writing.
A soundtrack made to impress. There's areas where one particular song plays, for instance at a lakeside hotel in the second city, that whenever I hear it I can't help but close my eyes and get swept away in a calmed state, letting everything else melt away. And other times, pumping battle music that rocks so hard I'm ready for battle.
The magic system was really confusing when I first played, and it still is, in this one especially, because like, each gem you put onto a character has different numbers of smaller gems and certain combinations of the smaller gems unlock different spells and none of this is really explained very well. I put two earth gems on the main character and didn't understand where these better earth spells were coming from. Another character is locked into using water gems in a number of their slots, and with water being the healing element, it was very strange to me that they seemed to have ridiculously good healing, sometimes better healing than even necessary, making it frustrating when this very good healer had to leave my party.
This game made me so genuinely happy that
I had spent my time getting to know it. There's no way this one should be passed up by anyone.

I feel like FEZ was a bit overated due to the feeling of nostalgia that the game invoked during its release period (something that many indie games were taking advantage of during that period) however the game is still pretty decent and does a good job of merging the old with the new.
The perspective shifting mechanics are very interesting and pretty well pulled off especially since that is what the game relies mostly on. You use this mechanic to solve puzzle and during platform segments, outside of this the game tends to stick to the basics of platforming games.
Visually the game is very good looking with good use of colors, also uses a simplistic and creative art style that merges well with the game's atmosphere and gameplay. The music didn't really stick to me nor stand out but as with the visuals it merges pretty well with the game's environment.
When it comes to the game's story I think it could of been delivered a bit better and I feel like it tries a bit too hard at being symbolic.
Overall the game is a pretty fun title that any retro and indie fan should have in their library.

This game is horribly optimized and can't even play splitscreen on lowest settings and 480p on my GTX670 MX laptop. On my GTX 970 PC the game still runs astonishingly poorly. The local multiplayer is the main reason I got this game and its simply unplayable in its current state.

Second Edit: This game does not present itself well. The first hour is not very good. The starting areas are ugly and you start out with mostly combat, hardly racing at all. After an hour or so the environments get prettier and you can actually do some 'racing'.
It's not exactly Road Rash either (I've got the Genesis version right here, and still play it), and the Kickstarter backers assuring you of that (and voting this down) are full of crap.  There's not enough racing for that, too much combat.
Good stuff: The soundtrack is great. The combat is meaty and it's quite satisfying to take someone out. I do like the weapons (C4, boom!). The mission structure is interesting - it's basically a roguelike where you gain money from stage to stage and buy upgrades, but lose that all when you die. But then you can use your earned XP on permanent upgrades.  It gets prettier and less 100% combat after an hour or two.
Biggest issues left: As noted, the first hour is crap and this needs a much better out of box experience. The physics are wonky as hell, pure 90s, which is fine for Road Rash, but then they pair it with a rooftop level that sticks bamboo slivers under the fingers of the wonky physics.
Also, the steering is still far too tuned for combat. You can't go off the road unless you're not paying attention, which makes the driving bit kind of boring.
BUT The devs seem to have fixed the worst thing, which was a 180 degree camera rotation if you used the fast turn.  I'd switch from No to Neutral if Steam would let me. And I haven't asked for a refund yet.

Five Nights at Freddy's 4 is a fun, spooky and exhillarating game.
You play as a child who has to survive from getting attack by various animatronic monsters for five nights. You must do this for about 5 to 10 minutes (you can skip 2 in-game hours by completing a short minigame before each night).
There are 3 main things you must do to survive: One is to go up to each door and listen for breathing, if you hear breathing you must hold the door shut for a few seconds, if you don't hear breathing you must flash your torch. The second action is to go up to the cupboard and flash you torch in it to see if Foxy is inside, if he is you must hold the cupboard shut, which will make him cower back. The other thing you must do is to look behind you to ward off any Freddles (small Freddys), they should jump off the bed by a flash of your torch. If you don't keep an eye on the Freddles though, Freddy will arrive. If you fail to do one of these action correctly you will get jumpscared!
The jumpscares in this game are way better than any in the previous titles (FNAF, FNAF2 & FNAF3), as now they are fully 3D and in your face, sometimes the animatronic will pick you up, making it 10x more scary.
I recommend this game to anyone interested into jumpscares, spooky atmospheres, the FNAF franchise, and people that just want to have some fun.

I’ve known about Punch Club for a while now, in fact I was one of the first to be able to make a video of it. I loved the idea from the first moment I heard about it, an 80’s/90’s influenced management sim about fighting. It sounded like Streets of Rage crossed with the Sims, to me this seemed like an amazing combination. But in reality I could sum this game up in one simple sentence “Failed to deliver on all the promise it held!” and that would be accurate.
It would be unfair to say I hate the game, there really is a lot here to like. The visuals are gorgeous and really capture that retro feel, the characters look like who they so often parody and that’s not easy when you choose this 16bit style. The locations are colorful and interesting, again with a huge amount of homages to the films from the 80’s and 90’s.
The story while hugely cheesy is exactly right, it takes all the best bits of Rocky, The Godfather and many other familiar greats. Whether it be facing off against teenage mutant ninja crocodiles or finding yourself in trouble in little china it’s all here, everything you’d expect and probably lots you’ve forgotten if you were a child of the 80’s.
This sounds amazing, what could be so bad? That’s probably what you’re asking yourself and it’s something I’ve been asking too, a game with great music, plot and concept could be bad? The answer of course is yes and it really all comes down to execution, you see the game is a huge grind and I don’t mean that figuratively. No, I mean you’ll spend all your time in the gym just to keep your stats up let alone improving them. There’s so much to see in the game but chances are you won’t as one unexpected trip can really put your progress back. If you want to master the game it’s really as simple as train, eat, work and fight, there really is little else if you wish to succeed.
But it’s a management sim I hear you cry, that’s how they work and you would of course be right. But this game promised so much more, it could have spanned genres and made something amazing. Instead you have very little connection to the main character, not even being able to control them in fights and this is a travesty. A game that’s basis is really about unlocking fighting moves and skills, that gives you zero control of those moves but instead throws them in at random with you left to watch. A frustrating affair and a huge error by the developers if you ask me.
That of course sum’s the game up, it really wouldn’t have taken a lot to make this a great game. Just make training more effective with less degeneration over time and give the player some control in fights, even if it was just a rock, paper, scissors affair it would have been something. But instead I’ve been left a little deflated at the whole experience, it’s not a terrible game but it’s not a great one. Maybe not even a good one, but passable and nothing more. It’s a shame as there are some great moments here and interesting plot lines, but it’s hard to enjoy as your always planning that next trip to the gym!

Ah, Trails In The Sky. The JRPG that set me the new standards and boasted my expectations of a JRPG game. The games title may sound generic but if there's one thing that Trails In The Sky taught me it's this: "Never judge a book by it's cover or title" (Not that I didn't think it was too generic but that's a first impression thing from a blind perspective before buying the game because, people like criticising alot and make a huge fuss these days and I see it way too much!)
Now back to what I was saying, I had a blast and heavily enjoyed this game despite the slow pacing and build up but what it did... it felt like something else. Something I hadn't witnessed. A new and fresh recipe. The execution was done so perfectly it WOW'ed me. I had to keep playing this game towards the ending of the first game and then jump onto the second game ASAP. (which I'm currently working my way through as I am writing this.) Oh and did I mention that Estelle is an well written character that has many dimensions within her? No I didn't! In fact, she's one of my favourite characters of all times in about anything. Whether it's games, movies or TV. Estelle is the perfect character personally.
Now let's talk about the pro's:
- Estelle and Joshua
- Well written and great main characters (Though Agate and Schezerad are somewhat lackluster but they make up for the second game from what I've played.)
- Story telling
- Story buildups
- Amazing ending that leaves you on the edge to the next game
- Well thought out, fun and good written dialogue
- Amazing and underrated soundtrack
- Great RPG mechanics and aspects
- Inspirational RPG items (Orbments) (For example: They're similar to Exspheres from Tales of Symphonia and Materia from Final Fantasy 7.) It makes it's own identity in a good way
- Nice artstyle
- Suprinsgly amazing world building (Whilst the game's graphics, power and budget look underwhelming I was impressed with the world building.)
- Awesome Lore and history of the Trails universe
- Turn based-Tactics gameplay is fun, thought provoking and great
- Good level designs
- Very enjoyable and light hearted
- No random encounters
- Very good replaybility factor
- Fun sidequests
- No grinding
- Time consuming amount of content
- Great PC port with great and very consistent optimization despite the one or two bug/crash issues
- The translations and localisation of the game.
Moving onto the indifferences:
- Graphics (This is understandable due to the budget that was put into this game and the PSP's power at the time wasn't so good)
- Slow pacing (Might put people off but my advice is to play the game from start to finish. It'll reward you in a great way)
- Date of the game (The game looks somewhat outdated but the gameplay isn't)
- Voice acting (Whilst I love the cast picks it can sound a bit cheesy but nothing major. Then again I think that's what it's trying to achieve. Not be realistic like what majority of games do these days
Moving onto the cons:
- May look or seem cliche, generic or bland in the first place
- Story builds up in a slow manner. (People who are into fast paced or action RPG's might not like the idea of that)
Overall Rating: 9.3/10
Worth the price? Most certainly! I feel bad for buying the game on sale and not buying it at full price and would've honestly paid more!
Conclusion: From my experince: Trails In The Sky was a new, fresh and breathtaking experince and set new standards and expectations for a JRPG. Sure there are JRPG games such as: Final Fantasy 6-10, Chrono Trigger or Mario RPG's that had the same or similar effect on the majority of people, but Trails In The Sky was the right game for me.  It took the 90's JRPG elements, aspects, troupes and the mechanics that everyone loved but did things differently to create it's own identity for a sole purpose. I must say that Trails In The Sky is an underrated JRPG and one of my favourite JRPG games. ALSO there's one other thing I might not have mentioned in this review. I HIGHLY SUGGEST you buy the first two Trails In The Sky games if you're willing to give this a shot.

While the graphics are extremely low-rent, once I turned off all the after effects (which is necassary to get the game running above 20FPS) I found myself liking them. The same way that pixel graphics are nostalgic for a slightly older audience, the MS Paint graphics reminiscent of games found on Newgrounds or Flash Player in the early 2000s really strike a chord with me. The story is fairly interesting, and I would even rank it above Hotline Miami 2 for having actual focus, rather than just portraying a series or vaguely related events. Gameplay is the obvious weak point, with a large amount of bugs and geometry problems. AI that starts shooting the second you get within 10ft. of enemies, regardless of where they are facing/if there is a wall, makes melee combat nigh-impossible. Even with this glaring flaw, I've had a lot of fun with this game, and am looking forward to the extra modes. If you like Hotline Miami and/or weird Russian stuff, wait for the price to drop a few bucks and give it a try.

Definition of a grind in videogaming:
When the player finds themself no longer enjoying the game after hitting a wall in difficulty, often unnatural feeling, and leaving the player to spend more time than they feel is necessary to "catch up". When content falls short and you end up repeating too familiar tasks over and over again.
Grind meet Punch Club.
In many respects this game is like a kairosoft game but somehow it just doesn't feel as satisfying or enjoyable. It's also less deep, if you could believe it, than most kairosoft games. Thus, feeling extremely grindy.
If they ever rebalance the game or add more content to justify grinding or at least make the grind feel more interesting, it may be worth it to everyone.
Until that doubtful day, only get this 75% off if you're a fan of kairosoft games and want an imperfect glimpse of that on PC.

I am so close to finishing this game, I'd say I'm about 5 hours away and so far its been a blast. The music is okay and the graphics are charming, though they may not appeal to everyone. The battles themselves can be a bit easy but there are some challenge monsters thrown in and optional side dungeons that you can tackle beforehand for more challenge, (including an 'optional' esqe boss). One of the problems though is that the game is on the easier side for most of the game and tends to have some diffuculty spikes "at random". Nothing too big I'd say but it can catch you off guard. Not only that but nearing the end game some of the optional enemy fights while not really difficult (as long as you plan a bit) they can drag on a bit. I will say this, no grinding needed. Though it might make those optional fights faster.
The combat system is nice as well. You collect currency from enemies which you then use to craft into crystals which will then, based upon the combination, allow you to access new moves. Each character you play as also have their own distinct personalities and fighting styles. That being said at any time you can only have up to 2 different members on your team due to Joshua and Estelle (main characters) being locked in.
Over all a fun game that really pulled me into the world. To fully enjoy it I would reccomend trying to do some of the side quests and collecting some "mundane things". Talk to the people as well. As events proceed in the game the characters will have new dialougue which makes the world feel more alive as well.

This game is the start to a series which has swiftly become my #1 favorite. None of the games in the Legend of Heroes series can beat Final Fantasy Tactics as my singular favorite video game but in my opinion, the series isn't meant to be viewed by it's individual parts but as the entire whole. The world of Zemuria feels ALIVE as plotlines connect between games in each sub-series and the sub-series between eachother. Plot points which you thought would never be touched after Trails in the Sky have impact even as recently as the climax of the most recent game (Trails of Cold Steel III / Sen no Kiseki III) which only just released in Japan.
All of this being said though, be forewarned, this series is a SLOW burn and won't be for everyone. However, If worldbuilding, expansive storylines and excellent character development is what you look for in video games, you will be hard-pressed to find a better series than the Legend of Heroes series. 5 of the 8 games have been localized in English and only 4 have been released to Steam (although the 5th, Trails of Cold Steel II, will be releasing on Steam in early 2018). Thankfully the Crossbell arc has fan translations available on youtube (although the quality of said translations are still being worked on) and Trails of Cold Steel III will most likely be receiving an offical translation.

This is a hard game to review. I wish there was a neutral option, but as there isn't, I'm going to lean in the direction of recommending it.
Pros:
-The gameplay is a lot of fun, especially missions with the quadcopter and the jumper. I feel like you have a lot more options for playing sneaky and stealthy than in the first game (and I'm one of those people who actually liked the first game, despite recognising it's flaws).
-The city is beautiful and alive. There have been countless occasions when I've been completely distracted by a mission, and ended up wandering down streets, taking in the sights.
Cons:
-The AI is a bit weak. One of the first things I saw in the game was a police car driving into a civilian's car as it turned at a junction. They sat and stared at each other for a few minutes, then the civilian got out of his car, walked ten feet away, and stood motionless, staring at his vehicle. After a few minutes, he got back in his car, where he immediately reacted to the collision again as if it had just happened, and got back out. This repeated over and over until a bus came along and just smashed through the whole mess, which brought ambulances to the scene which then crashed into the injured people. Good start, huh?
It's also a bit amusing how quickly enemies can go back to being calm after seeing a drone/jumper hovering around. I suppose it wouldn't be as fun if the were overly vigilant, but sometimes it feels a bit easy to get past guards with stealth. But, perhaps this will change as I get further towards the end of the game.
-The performance is not the best. It's nowhere near as bad as it was reported on launch, but I have a pretty decent set up that surpasses the recommended specs, and I just can't get this game to run as good as it should. I've probably spent more time tinkering with settings, and browsing forums on the matter, than I have actually playing, and that really breaks the immersion (and is probably why I haven't finished yet).
Driving, in particular, is the biggest issue for me. I've tried changing so many settings, but the only thing that has made driving bearable on my system is to completely turn off anti-aliasing. It doesn't look too bad in screenshots due to my resolution but the jagged edges are driving me nuts while playing, and everything is moving. It's a real shame to play such a pretty environment like this. I'm still tinkering with having anti-aliasing controlled by Nvidia control panel rather than the game itself, but so far I can't get it to look pretty without having driving feel like a laggy mess.
So yeah, it's not a bad game by any means, and I am enjoying playing it. I just think it has a few potential issues that people should take into account when buying. It you get it on sale, then it's a much better deal!

I just realized I haven't reviewed this for some reason.
I'd say it's easily one of the best games to come from the EA system and getting this is an easy no brainer if you like designing ships. If you are watching the videos and looking at it as someone who likes designing ships, but really would just like to play an RTS, it's something less of a no-brainer as designing is by far the more indepth part, but obviously something about the game is appealing to you, or you wouldn't be reading these reviews!
Basically, airships is a sort of super-lite 4x. You design and build ships using a plethora of different modules, and send them out to fight other fleets and conquer cities on a real time strategy map. This will earn you more funds for bigger, better ships, as well as various technologies that you can then incorporate into your ship. The combat itself is pretty much what it looks like in the videos, but can actually involve some fairly complex tactics.
Cons: Campaign isn't super fleshed out and is pretty simple in terms of what you can do. That said, it's evolved a TON since I bought this game a couple years ago, and is going in a good direction - it's gone from being basically just a map to look at in between fights to a fully moddable strategic game in and of itself, with a few different neat features. Still, this game is fundamentally a sandbox game, which depending on what you like may grow dull, and while a story may come some day, it's not a priority.
There's some limits placed on ship design, such as number of crew you can have, that might seem kind of arbitrary to someone with a decent PC, but are there to keep people with potatoes like mine from having performance issues.
From my understanding multiplayer only gets turned on at preset times unless you're playing a LAN game, mostly in an effort to have enough players online at the same time to make it fun.
Pros: Pretty much everything else, it really is a well-made, well-designed game.
It will run on crap computers.
Ship design is deep, and everything is easily moddable.
Actual combat can require a bit of skill.
You can't tell from the video, but the explosion effects, the smoke (it will build up and linger if there's no wind on a given map), the impact of cannon balls, it's just all very well done and the game itself is incredibly beautiful.
There's a replay feature that allows you to replay literally any fight you've had with the computer controlling both sides, so you can easily make .GIFs (using the built in button) or videos of cool stuff like you dumping 40 marines on to the top of an enemy blimp.
To restate it, the only reason I would not recommend this game to you is if you don't think you'll have fun designing airships and landships and forts and such, because it's a crucial, and often time consuming ('easy to learn, hard to master" type time consuming), part to the game.

FEZ is a joyous platforming experience that adds some unique usage of perspective and dimension. The overall story is definitely weird and something I cannot get into in-depth. But in any case, you wake up and find some powers that allow you to explore the 2D world by turning in into 2.5D/3D by rotating the areas around by 90 degrees at a time. From that point forward, the entire game is exploring areas, learning some insane puzzles, finding collectibles, and coming to a very confusing endpoint.
This game is very unique and one that I would tell anybody who hasn't played it to give it a try. I think it's one game that would fit many audience groups and isn't just stuck to a small group of people. Platformers are types of games for anybody, and you are adding in manipulation of the world while you move around!
The graphics style of FEZ is interesting, though some people complain of the pixelation. I understand that it definitely gets weird at places, but I think it allows for the stylistic changes it does in the world areas, such as the sewers. The audio of FEZ is simple and relaxing, though I can't say I remember anything standout despite just playing the game in the past couple of days.
Making your progress through the game requires immense exploration and puzzle solving. I would say about 75% of the puzzle solving does not require anything extensive, however - just some tricky platforming and logic. The other 25% requires a bit more work, such as understanding the alphabet of the game, or any puzzles that deal with symbols.
The only puzzle I have to say I simply hate is the QR code being in the game in a couple of places. It is definitely stupid for them to put that there, in my opinion, though some people seemed to like it. I just don't think bringing your phone in should be something necessary - it's not doing anything special by wanting you to download an app and scan something. It's not a puzzle. It's meaningless work.
FEZ is definitely relaxing to play. The areas are unique to explore. There's lot of questions that will come to your mind, and while not everything is answered, it's nice to think about this world and its strangeness. I felt great satisfaction when resolving many of the puzzles, and not much gave me frustration at all, which is very rare for a game. What I mean by that is usually a game is simply "too easy" or "too hard" - you'll usually feel anger or boredom, but not just accomplishment by itself. This game has that accomplishment.
I never thought I would feel so much happiness from running around rooms and solving puzzles for collectibles. But that happened.

Now I know what you're thinking:
is just a shameless ripoff of
.
Oh, if only.  No,
is a "hilarious" "parody" of
.  Or, put it another way, this is what
would look like if nobody involved with its development were over the age of fifteen, save for one unfortunate musician who was relentlessly badgered into providing the admittedly great soundtrack.
Naturally the game can't ape anything properly from its influence.  Whereas HM based its challenge around planning and tactics, BK instead opts for horrid controls and limited visibility.  Movement is incredibly awkward.  The player character lurches ahead too quickly for any kind of precision and often gets stuck on walls and furniture.  There's also no lock-on feature, so don't even bother fighting while moving.  Meanwhile, your visual range is very narrow, so most kills are made by firing blindly down the hall, and the eye-searing visual effects make it harder still to aim.
Fortunately, you do have two advantages: First, the AI is very dumb.  Once alerted, it will just bounce off the walls until it can line up a shot, which is highly exploitable if you're careful.  Second, it's very easy to glitch yourself in and out of the level, so if you don't have to kill anything in a stage you can just bypass the enemies and head straight to the goal.
Ultimately my breaking point was a vehicle section in which you must avoid two instant kills, one of which is positioned randomly.  Once I realized just how little control I had over the outcome, I gave it a few more hopeful tries and finally ragequit.
That's not even getting into the script, which is a cringeworthy mess of bad jokes, nonsensical profanity, and outdated internet memes.  It might amuse those who lied to get around this page's age gate, but adult players will most likely find it incredibly grating.  The only laughs I got out of it were when the abysmal English translation mangled a line beyond comprehension.

The Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky is the first serie of the Trails series, which tells about the journey of a young girl and boy who travel around the whole Liberl continent by foot. The story sets in a world with orbs, an item which basically can do anything - from lighting the lights to move an airship. With the orbs, comes a job called bracers - a mercenary like job which revolves in using orbs in battle. The young girl and boy, being newly appointed as a junior bracers, strives for reaching a senior bracers status.
The music in this game is awesome. All of them sounds relaxing and i don't really mind listening to them for a long time. There are some musics that's reused for different areas, but i don't really have a problem with it since the music is great. I especially like the music that's in the area before Jenis Royal Academy.
The world graphics look like old PS1 graphics, with a better UI and portrait images. I love how the character portraits are suited to the character's expression when they talk. The food looks a bit weird with the background though; it looks like a 2D image slapped between 3D objects. There are also some cutscenes in the game, although i have to say that it's blurry on some parts.
The game has a lot of characters. That being said, each characters have its own backgrounds and characteristics. I love seeing how they're talking with each other. Although the game doesn't focus much on the side characters, the game has a character development on its main characters. I also love the fact that the game has some backgrounds on its villains and their motives.
The story is mostly concentrated in each region, each -although a bit slowly- connects to a bigger part of the main story, which flows well together. However, the ending leaves a lot of questions, which i believe will be answered in the second serie.
Non story aside, the NPCs in the town always have their dialogue changed after main story progression.
Before you can start the game, you have to configure some options; mainly controls, input, and graphics. There are a lot of keyboard controls that you have to memorize and it might be quite hard to do at first. The mouse input really helps at first because i tend to forget the keyboard controls.
The configuration also offers turbo mode. If you're familiar with emulators, this is basically like the speed up button; you can speed up battles and/or fields up to 4x by simply clicking a button. The good thing is, music will still flow in normal speed. I don't think i can play any rpg game without turbo mode for a while after playing this game.
The game offers 3 difficulty: normal, hard, and nightmare. I choose to play in normal mode. The game itself is just like your usual rpg with a turn based battle where you can move your characters in a grid. The characters will have its set of equipments and orbs, which can be customized based on the available slot. Each orbs have their own types and effects, where the types can be comboed to learn a skill. However, some of the orb slot has a specific type requirements on it so it might be tricky to get the combination that you want. Type specific requirements aside, you can use the orbs freely to distinguish between an attacker or healer.. or a buffer, even.
Aside from the magic skill that you can learn with orbs, each characters also have their own specific skills that consumes CP to cast. The  CP gauge can be filled by taking and dealing damage (or by waiting in turns if you equip certain accessory). There is also a higher skill that requires a minimum of 100 CP, namely S-Craft, which is an ultimate skill that can be used in any turn.
The battle system also display the list of "turns", who will go next turn and such. There might be some special buffs listed in the list, such as recover HP, or even 100% critical hit on the said turn. Since the buffs are fixed on the turn slot, you can always change who'll get the buffs by using S-Craft or killing the enemies.
Setting the battles system aside, the game also offers cooking. You can mostly get the recipe by eating foods and while some foods can be stored in your inventory, there are some foods that can't be stored. These types of foods usually gives a better benefit than the "storeable foods".
The are also some books in the game that you can read. It's basically a story in a story since the book is talking about different fiction in the same (or different) world. It's quite interesting to read, especially if you're an avid reader.
The game usually follows a set of rules: you go to a place, do the task, and report it back on the guild. That's basically what you'll have to do, plus checking some sidequest on the bulletin board and notice some hidden quest in the game. Some quests will give better reward if you do specific tasks correctly.
Although you are travelling to a lot of regions in the game, you can't return to the previous region once you cross to other region. The game will notify you when this or something similar happens though. Plus, there will be a lot of situation where you have to save beforehand because you might not be able to return to the previous area for a while. Some events are also only available for a specific amount of time, so you might miss a lot if you only focus on the main story.
Pros:
- Turbo mode
- 3 difficulty settings
- 8 playable characters (changed in each chapter)
- Customizable character skills
- Cooking
Cons:
- A-lot-to-remember keyboard controls
- Unable to backtrack to previous area
- Missable items

The best worms game.
The Worms franchise is a very good idea executed very similarly over and over again. You have a bunch of cute little worms, with cute little physics-based weapons (well, sometimes they're not so little), trying to destroy each other. It's brilliant because it's ridiculously fun for both casual and hardcore gamers. The hardcore gamers get their kicks from practising their technique until they become unstoppably accurate with all their shots, whereas the causal gamers simply enjoy the trial-and-error fun of shooting bazookas at each other.
That's the entire Worms franchise. All the Worms games are more or less like this: quality games that are more or less interchangeable. That being said, I would have to say that Worms Armageddon is the best Worms game so far. It has a wide variety of weaponry, a huge capacity for customisation (although you need to beat the game to get the full options), very accessible level editor, interesting missions, training that is actually fun, as well as a "deathmatch" mode that is fun, intense, and has never since been replicated.
Although these are petty concerns, where WA falls short is in two respects: a slight lack of help in how to play the game, and in its online community. I found that, when I first played WA (when it came out), it was difficult to figure out all the little controls. There are two jump buttons, and pressing or double pressing produces different jumps, which was confusing at first. Also, customising grenades, such as changing the fuse time or making them bouncy, was never clearly explained. If you buy this game, consult the following page:
Most of the necessary controls you can pick up in the game, but the page is a useful reference when you really want to nail down your grenade shots or your ninja roping.
The other problem, as I mentioned, was the online community. When last I checked, WA had an entrenched and hostile online community, where the standard was absurdly high, and anyone not of this standard was abused and/or dropped from games. But, so long as you play with friends, this shouldn't be a problem.

I have played this game for 6 hours. 6 hours to beat and get all the achievements. I regret those 6 hours. The game is broken and a chore to play. EDIT: Apparently they added more achievements, but I am not wasting anymore time on this 'game'. This Hotline Miami knockoff is so bad that calling it a knockoff is actually a compliment.
-Gameplay
The gameplay is a 2D topdown similar to another game, but it is nothing like the game it takes "inspiration", as the game is so more gun focused that melee weapons are useless, as the player has the ablility to kick which can be used while having a gun. The kick makes melee weapons obselete as it gives the same amount of points. This is merely the tip of the unpolished gameplay, as playing the game feels floaty and weightless when you're moving the character, which leads for the character getting temporarily stuck on objects.  And the bugs, there was many times when the game barely chugged by and crashing. The whole gameplay consists of running and gunning which would be fine if the game was so broken and unpolished.
-Story
I don't know if I am too stupid to understand this "complex" story which was confusing and had horrible reasons for the whole story. The whole thing was vague and not in a good way. It was confusing as it had no basis for us to connect to. and was utterly bland from my vague understanding of it. The "dank maymays" and Russian "satire" fell flat for me and would probably fall flat for everyone else to.
-Graphics
Like the gameplay, it just looks so unpolished. The visuals area mess as all the screen effects do not mix well with the Microsoft Paint-like graphics. The whole style is hard to look at and feels generic.
-Soundtrack
The whole soundtrack is a mix, some are good but mostly are not a good unique music but rather generic sounding.
-Other
The game had originally advertised several features but now is proclaiming them as upcoming features. I doubt that they will actually be released, even if it was, it would be as unpolished and buggy as the rest of the game.
As the whole game is just one big, unpolished game. It was a waste of money and time. The one minute of whatever "fun" that might be squeezed out of this game is not worth it. 4/10.
Please do not buy this even ironically or as a joke gift.

I wish this game was better. I supported it, backed it on kickstarter, shared it with friends. The developers promised a Road Rash revival back in 2013 with a projected release date of aug 2014 for xbox 360, WiiU, and PC. What this game has become is a true disappointment. They developers have completely abandoned the xbox 360 and WiiU ports which they had specific backer tiers for on kickstarter with hundreds of backers. I have spoken to devs who have just let that fact stay quiet even while fully admitting privately that those ports are no longer possible.
However despite the questionable ethics involving the kickstarter the game is still in rough shape in its existing form. This is not the Road Rash revival that you were hoping for. The game feels off, bikes feel like they are floating around on the road, there is no sense of impact or weight. The game is played entirely with weapons, there isnt even an option to throw punches against other riders, and ever rider is equiped with weapons. The "races" are full of endless spawned bikers that have no effect on the standing of the race. The rooftop races are a total disaster with bugs that will have you endlessly falling with no way to stop but quiting the race entirely, losing your progress.
on top of the extremely mediocre execution of what should have been simple game mechanics the visuals do nothing to pick up the slack. I play the game on the highest possible settings and it is still pretty unimpressive, even for an early access game.
to summarize this game is mediocre at best, and doesnt look like at has much hope of leaving early access. Its been almost a year since the projected release date and they do not even have this game functioning in online multiplayer, or have a finished single player campaign.
I had originally written a less harsh review for this game, because I was still under the delusion that things would get better, but after closely looking over the timeline and having an extensive talk with one of the devs Ive decided to give up the ghost on this one. Maybe someday someone will fulfill on what this game promised... but I dont see that happening with Road Redemption. Buyer Beware.

Dang, this is hard.  So good, but seriously hard.
If you are into cryptography and love serious challenges, get this.  While I was able to figure out enough to "beat the game" i.e. get to the credit sequence, I know for a fact that never in my life will I be able to 100% this game.  I heard somewhere a great comparison: "The hard puzzles in Portal 2 are real thinkers.  You will sit back in your chair and think, 'how is this possible?', but 10 minutes later you will have solved the puzzle and be moving on.  The hard puzzles in Fez take 10 hours and a doctrate in mathematics."  That wasn't the exact quote, but it gives you the idea.  The hard puzzles are hard as hell.  Throughout the game there are two "languages" tha you will encounter that you have to break to continue.  The first is fairly simple (I got it after only about 4 hours of fiddling around) and the other is just insane.  Maybe I am missing somthing, but wow.
Gameplay itself is fantastic.  Super unique concept, being a 2D person in a 3D world, and it takes a bit to really wrap your mind aroud it.  The map you have is also quite challenging to understand at first, but trust me you can get the hang of it.
Tons of really intriguing puzzles all in one box.  Some easy, some borderline impossible.  Smooth gameplay, excellent concept.
Solid A+ game.  Took me about 7 hours to get to the credit sequence (but completing probably half the puzzles, total).

A pretty solid JRPG that succeeds in innovating and telling a decent story. Without going into too much detail, I really enjoyed Legend of Heroes since it definitely doesn't feel like any other RPG that I've played. The story doesn't feel too urgent until the latter half of the game, but I believe that keeps in pace of the story and rushing it would have felt unrealistic and forced.
One recommendation I would make is not to play it on Hard mode, it just made things annoyingly harder and I just had to grind to accomodate. Hard difficulty should have been smarter AI, not just buffed up stats on enemies (it only made 1 particular boss battle really fun, otherwise I regretted it).

If you want a story-rich game in a fully realized world, this is it. Every single detail of the world is explained and makes sense, all the NPCS have their own lives and react to the events of the story, and there is enough optional dialogue to fill a series of really thick books. Every detail of this game was lovingly crafted, and it shows. The characters are awesome too. This is definitely a game to try if you are into RPGs.

In some games, there is a right way and a wrong way to enjoy them. I approached Assassins' creed III in the wrong way, and in the end, I regretted it.
It is a game of contrasts - it is beautiful, but poorly optimized, failing to run maintain 1080p60fps on overpowered rigs, in certain areas. It has a huge open world, but the missions proper are heavily scripted and will frustrate anyone wanting to do them in their own way. It looks to be about being an assassin but it really is about being a runner and a brawler.
And yet... There is so much here. There is menu-driven resource management. Tons of weapons and armors to collect. A huge world to explore, full of secrets and challenges. Whole swats of gameplay that you can ignore, and likely will if you focus on the story like I did.
In the end, I felt regret for approaching the game in my own terms. Had I taken it easy, had I played it as a slow burn, exploring every nook and cranny of the marvelously realized world, I would have probably enjoyed it a lot more - and would likely have finished it around the time Assassins Creed 6 got here.

Pros:
-Great throwback to retro gaming and 80s-90s humor.
-Music, despite only consisting of a few tracks, is actually enjoyable to listen to even after hours on end.
-Feels extremely rewarding if you properly manage your character.
-Remains a challenge the whole way through.
Cons:
-Classes need rebalancing.  Strength builds get completely destroyed, Stamina builds take a while, and Agility builds own.
-No multiplayer feature, would be awesome to go against friends.
-Would have liked more opportunities to generate skill points.  Beaten the game a couple of times and never finished a tree despite doing as many fights as I could.
-Would be nice if you could pick a "sub stat" instead of just getting a secondary stat to boost your main stat.
-No way to customize character at all outside of name.
Summary:
This game is a "tycoon" game where you are given an initial set of resources to expand and grow an investment. In this game, you're given a quick backstory to the main character, a would-be boxer who has begun training to live up to and surpass his late father's legacy.  After a brief tutorial which shows you the mechanics of the game (Health, Hunger, Mood and Energy; Strength, Agility, Stamina; Time and Money), you are immediately left to your own devices and told only that you need to grow your stats and train hard to work your way through the ranks as a rookie boxer.  With each passing day, you will grow weaker if you don't train, but you must spend time in order to make money.  Without money, you cannot feed your boxer or get proper training.  The game entirely revolves around how well you can manage the resources at your disposal to efficiently train your boxer to become a champion.
I loved a lot of things about this game.  The art style was very well done, especially for a retro-themed game.  There's even a "retro effect" in the game that adds scanlines!  Despite only having one real song and a few other songs that pop in here and there, I actually didn't mind listening to that track for hours on end.  Various 80s and 90s references are littered throughout the game such as "Stoney" instead of "Rocky" and "Sport Sport" instead of "Blood Sport".  The various story arcs do a good job of leaving it up to you to determine how to go about making your boxer stronger.
The issue with this game is how one-sided the stat system can be for agility-based builds.  On top of dodging most attacks resulting in little-to-no damage being taken, agility-based fighters can learn a counter ability that inflicts half of the opponent's damage back to them when dodging.  Characters that would crush me in a few hits if their blows could land were killing themselves faster than I could as a result.  On top of that, my attacks cripple their agility, leaving them with no accuracy, further driving the gap.  At one point, my fighter was 2 Strength, 17 Agility, 9 Stamina and I managed to defeat a 20/13/16 fighter strictly because I had more agility than they did.  It's that overpowered. I feel like if you want a true challenge in this game, try a Strength or Stamina build.  Doing a Stamina build on my second playthrough proved to be much more challenging but I was still successful in beating the game.
I would have loved to see a multiplayer feature in this game, a lot of my friends have played this game and it would have been interesting to have my fighter go up against theirs.  I would also have enjoyed a better ending.  I could see it being a way to lead into Punch Club 2 but it's entirely obvious that there would be one.  It's possible the devs did this intentionally to see how successful this game was before promising a second game.
This game is definitely worth the $10.  You may find it on sale at some point as well, so that's a plus.  I managed to snag it for $5 from a TinyBuild sale.  Absolutely worth every penny even with the issues.

In short : Addictive and rewarding experience. It’s exactly what it looks like – a retro style from zero to hero story with grind based gameplay with a dose of management. Although monotonous at times, it’s tongue in cheek, stereotypical setting and gratifying level ups will keep you playing to the end which unfortunately is abrupt and disappointing.
In depth review :
Punch Club revolves around a young boxer wannabe who rises to the top in order to avenge his father, whatever sense it makes.
You start as lonely guy living in a small house with his cat and a fishtank. Oh, and you’re broke as hell. After series of mildly interesting events you’re given a chance as a boxer.
This introduces you to what is core element of Punch Club – training, stats and skills. If you’re familiar with Kairosoft’s mobile “Story” series you’ll probably get the picture.
There are three main branches of stats – strength, agility and stamina. The same goes for skills which are divided into a basic set of skills and three advanced, heavily stat-dependent styles.
In consequence you can choose to be a lightning fast fighter, sluggish but powerful heavy hitter or a damage soaking tank sponge. But hold on, it gets a little bit more complex.
One stat has an impact on another. Example – having high strength and punching hard depletes stamina drastically and low agility will make you more likely to miss. Character progression involves tactic, adequate stat training and carefully selected skills.
You’ll be spending lots of time on training which can raise your stats or give exp points for new abilities. But there is a twist. At the end of every day you lose portion of your stats so not only you have to improve them but also maintain them. This is tricky as you also have to find time to earn some money, rest and make stops at convenience store to refill your fridge. Punch Club will force you to manage your time, money and boxer’s path. It can be both frustrating and fun.
Let’s go to the meat of Punch Club, fighting that is. As I said before it relies heavily on stats and abilities. That’s because you have no influence on your bouts aside from setting up your skills and training. Fortunately, I must say that I enjoyed watching and cheering my boxer or moaning in disappointment as you normally would watching match on TV. Punch Club’s advantage is also a variety of fighting scenarios. You’ll be boxing in amateur leagues, professional championships but also in a street fights, illegal matches and special events.
It’s worth mentioning that Punch Club has a little more to it than a career – mostly special events. You may fall in love, chill with your new friend, do some dirty work for a mob boss or traditional fetch quests. Sadly, there’s not much to it. They’re trivial, rather short and in small amounts. There’s also a crossroad in the plot where you chose your path but still, final destination Is the same.
What seems obvious here is a huge, in-the-face influence of 80’s/90’s culture. It’s apparent in the plot, in side quests, in locations, in dialogue, basically everything has this cheesy, yet very likeable vibe to it. You’ll recognize a lot of references with a mild sense of humor – Rocky, Street Fighter, Mortal Kombat, TMNT (yup!) – you name it. With graphics resembling NES/SNES or even arcades it really adds to this feeling which is cozy and familiar.
That’s good and all but there are also some major flaws in Punch Club. It’s short soundtrack will get on your nerve pretty soon as it repeats over and over again. Though gameplay is addicting it’s also pretty repetitive and if you won’t believe the illusion of variety, you’ll get bored easily. What made me especially mad is weak story progression. Was it intended to emulate early action movies or not, it failed to be engaging or compelling. What’s worse, it ends abruptly and ridiculously making me not only disappointed but mad. It’s fun when the ride lasts but the destination makes you wish you never arrived.
Completion time : 13 hours
The good :
-	Addictive and fun gameplay
-	Good 80’s/90’s feeling
The bad :
-	Disasterous ending
-	Monotonous music
-	Rather short
Final score : 7/10

Ohhh Worms Armageddon, you NEED to play this game. Worms is a series that has been going on since the late 90's and this is actually just the third game in the series. Worms is a game where you control (duh) worms and they blow other worms up. The game is turn based and very strategic for how you want to use your turn. With Jet Packs, Ninja Ropes, and Parachutes for traversing terrain, You could go all the way out of your way to kill someone humiliatingly with the prod. Speaking of weapons, this game has a wide variety of weapons. Basic bazookas, grenades, air strikes, etc and then strange weapons like sheep, holy hand grenade, cows and other farm animals fill this game with very diverse weaponising.
One of the best parts of Worms Armageddon specifically is the jump from the original and Worms 2 in balance via weapons. My favorite part of Worms Armageddon is the maps, though. Isn't it fun to blow through rubble, detritus and other worms on your way to victory? I think it is. Worms Armageddon has a relative amount of player customization with being able to change custom things such as maps, fanfare, voices (australian, cad, english, Soul Man), gravestones, flags, and worm profile names.
Worms Armageddon has a feature of CPU opponents. The CPU's have a AI skill ranging from 1-5. On five, the AI will hit ridiculous wind-targeted rockets and grenades you couldn't have thought as possible. Level 1 CPU's tend to miss and blow themselves in to the water on occasion. If you use a fair weapon variety (my favorite is bazooka, air strike, grenade, shotgun) AI can be a formidable opponent. Oh yeah, SPEAKING of picking what weapons to use, that's another feature called game schemes. If you want to play with banana bombs, holy-hand grenades and armageddons only, then do it. Game schemes are very helpful.
This game also has a single player mode, which is training, playing deathmatch vs. computer (VERY HARD AFTER A WHILE) doing missions (Eliminating 18 level 5 CPU's with one worm) and quick, simple games vs cpu. The single player mode is for unlocking small things for the game, such as indestructible terrain, a cheat that makes worms bleed when attacked, and more!
For a game from 1999, it may be surprising to find out that it has an online multiplayer mode. If you jump into the land of WormNET, you will find different perspectives of worms armageddon such as Shopper, use ninja ropes and stuff to get crates with weapons, WxW, and Quickdraw. Worms Armageddon is vast worm world. Definitely one of my favorite games of all time.

The first 2 things I got to thinking about after beating this game:
1. This is one hell of a memorable game!  (I can't think of anything else like it)
2. Why is it so hard to
The best way I can describe this game as: is a hybrid point and click puzzler and platformer. There are parts that do require keyboard (which the game will let you know if it switches) and some areas that require some precision mouse only control.  Parts that are logic puzzles... and that's all i'm going to say about the gameplay.  I don't really want to divulge too much as the game has a great way of surprising the player and it's great just letting it unfold naturally. So my advice: (if you can resist or help it) avoid any gameplay videos or progress discussions until you've experienced it first.
My only warning to some is that the game transitions from puzzler to precision platformer often and could be jarring or frustrating if you can't be precise. Though with that being said, you're not punished by losing progress and making mistakes seems to add to some of the surreal charm the game has to offer.
The music is a phenominal mix of pleasant and up beat 16 bit style and nerve wracking ambient, mixes well with the gameplay and is quite good.
The graphics have a very charming old apple II or c64 look with various trippiness pepperred in.  There are parts where the art style changes drastically that is just surreal.
There is a story; You unravel the mystery of the character you play through main gameplay and by finding secrets that are peppered all over the place... I don't want to delve deeper beyond that as it's best for you to experience it.  If you're enjoying the game, there is incentive for multiple play throughs.
I'd estimate the game time to be about 2 to 6hrs, all depending whether you burn right through it or take your time, look for secrets and replay areas.

A clever play on The Oregon Trail that is much more deep and intelligent than it presents itself at first glance. Apart from an annoying tutorial section explaining the core mechanics, this game has a heart and wit that most zombie games don’t. It underwhelms you with it’s retro style graphics and convinces you that it’s going to be a simplistic parody, but subverts your expectations by growing more intense as you play. I’ve played quite a bit of the Oregon Trail and I still suck at it, so the same applies here. One thing you may notice is that it takes a lot longer to beat than Oregon, this one took me about two hours to beat whereas Oregon took me around half an hour (I also played this game on tablet).
Just like in X-COM, the best way to play in my opinion is to name your comrades after your friends or family. Overall this is a really unique take on the zombie theme and highly recommended.

Photography is one of my hobbies, and over the last year or so I've been diving into a bit of model photography, so when two games recently appeared on Steam covering this subject (Sonicomi being the other one) it perked my interest.
For this review I am only looking at this from from a photography point of view (read some other review if you want a different POV), and from that perspective I'm actually pleasantly surprised. Don't get me wrong - the game falls short of providing a real photography experience in a lot of ways and I could nit-pick it for hours (and I will in just a moment) - but, I went into this with low expectations and was surprised at how much control it did give me, and I largely enjoyed my time with it.
Firstly, the good - the game offers a number of photography scenarios, ranging from a studio, to a bedroom, dancing in a club, playing on the beach and several more. You can have the model wear a variety of outfits (which you must purchase using funds earned from any of several minigames), change her hair style, dye her hair different colours or wear contacts. There is only one model, but I found I was still able to achieve plenty of different looks with the available options.
Most of the scenarios have only one predefined pose or animation (there are several dance styles available for the club), but the studio offers far more flexibility as you are able to ask the model to pose in a large variety of ways (which cost money to unlock - seems a little odd as usually hiring a model costs money but then they would pose however you ask within reason - but I suppose this was done to have some progression in the game), and you have some control over the lighting.
The lighting options in the studio are of course significantly more limited than they would be in a real studio. You can choose to have the light come from a number of directions above the model, as well as directly in front, behind or below the model, and you can select a number of preset ambient lighting styles.  What is missing here is of course everything else - there are no soft boxes, no reflectors, no hair lights, no strobes, no umbrellas, no ring flashes, no way to create harsh or soft lighting, nothing you would expect to find in a real studio, and personally I've never really a fan of flat lighting - I would have liked to create a striking high contrast lighting effect with the light placed below the model to the side, but I could only achieve a low contrast effect with the light above the model to the side, and choose from a few preset ambient lighting styles that were kind of close to what I wanted.
I was disappointed that the studio did not offer any prop or background choices. Several of the available poses do include chairs or poles, and as mentioned above you can change the ambient lighting, but that is it - if you want a more interesting background you can't use the studio, but outside the studio you can't pose the model.
But, there's an elephant in the room: This is a VR game, but it is really aimed at one of the mobile phone VR devices and the PC port is essentially DK1 level tech - it only tracks head rotation, not position. This means whenever you move your head the entire world moves with you. I also found myself instinctively trying to move towards or away from the model when taking a photo if the focal length wasn't spot on (which cannot be adjusted - probably a 50mm prime), but because it doesn't have head tracking that didn't work, and the UI doesn't allow you to abort once you have selected the camera - you just have to take a photo (using up some rather expensive film - no digital here) before you can go back to adjust the position.
Which leads me to the second elephant in the room: The UI in this game is entirely driven by gaze - there is no support for the Vive's motion controllers (or as far as I could tell any other controller for that matter), which is just horrible. But the worst consequence of this is that it means adjusting the camera height, distance and rotation around the model is infuriatingly slow and difficult, and you cannot comfortably look at the model while doing so - my neck was getting quite craned by the end as I was constantly looking down to adjust the controls. And then the camera icon is in the middle of all the other adjustment icons, making it impossible to select without slightly altering the position first...
And this leads to another problem - since the game does not use a controller, you can't actually press the shutter. Instead it uses a three second timer to give you time to frame the shot, but this is of course problematic if the model is moving as it is not possible to time the shots perfectly (ok, since it's just a CG animation you could wait for it to loop and start gazing at the camera icon 5 seconds before you want to take the photo). In many ways it is better to just use Steam's built in screenshot feature, but the quality is lower (although at least it gives a stereo 3D screenshot, even if it does fail to understand the point of off-center rendering and places infinity at screen depth) and that somewhat defeats the point of the game.
For the uninitiated, the number one reason professional photographers (and most enthusiasts for that matter) use a DSLR above any other type of camera is because the controls are all right at your fingertips. Adjusting the shutter speed (which affects motion blur and exposure) is done by simply turning a wheel. The aperture (which affects depth of field / sharpness and exposure) is adjusted with another dial (or the same wheel while holding another button on the cheaper models). Adjusting the ISO gain (which can boost exposure at the cost of grainy photos) is one button followed by the wheel. The focal length (zoom) is simply adjusted by rotating a ring on the lens. The white balance is just a few button presses away (seriously, if you have never manually set the white balance on your camera you need to learn - your photos taken in the shade will instantly look a thousand times better with the white balance set to "shade" then they do on "auto"). The depth of field preview is one button.  Changing the shooting mode is another. There are of course many other advantages to a DSLR as well, but I've always felt that this is by far the most important, so having a photography simulator where most of these important controls don't even exist and the ones that do are operated by gazing at an icon for a few seconds...  sigh - it's worse than a phone camera.
It's also nice to see a game along these lines that is not from Japan (but still from Asia) - I hadn't really paid much attention to this and just assumed it would be from Japan until the model counted crabs in one of the minigames: "yī èr sān sì wǔ..." - that's Mandarin!
In summary: It is certainly a long way from hiring a real model and studio, and it definitely needs a lot more polish, but it is also considerably cheaper than hiring a real model and studio (not to mention the cost of the camera, lenses and all the other accessories you need before you can even think about trying
this for real) and it is still enjoyable ;-)

Disclaimer: beaten and completed the game outside Steam tracking. The review is light on spoilers.
Fez is an indie platformer revolving around introducing 3D comprehension into a (basically) 2D game, both plot-wise and gameplay-wise. It is also *the* indie platformer, as it was one of those gems, released in 2012, which helped indie game development gain popularity and wide-spread acclaim.
The game has the protagonist depart on a quest to save the world. Player uses the ability to jump between four different "faces" of an otherwise 2D landscape (akin to looking at a cube from sides) and tackle puzzles. Player is frequently expected to show a good grasp of timing, agility and management of different "faces" of the game world. Controls are both keyboard and joypad friendly. Fans of Metroidvania games will appreciate the open world design and the possibility to track progress using map.
Chiptune score suits the 16-bit graphics and follows the change in scenery. No matter the place, though, the game retains a positive and light tone; it has no age restrictions (rated E by PEGI).
Fez has no replayability value by design - it's a single-player game lacking any multiplayer capabilities. Length of time required to beat it falls anywhere in the range of 5-10 hours.
I can definitely recommend Fez for those who want a refresh of the "old" platforming experience. It's price nowadays is well below the point of having to consider its worth.

I wanted to play BattleBlock Theater for quite some time now but only recently picked it up when it was for sale for about 3€.
BB T is an INCREDIBLE platformer and i think the Hardcore Gamer review says it best:
"The amount of content, style and polish in BattleBlock Theater is incredible and puts the efforts of many AAA developers to shame. The story and writing alone could fill a comedy club, but the accessible, addictive gameplay demonstrates a mastery of platformer fundamentals."
I played BB T from start to finish (excluding 3 encore levels at the time of this review) in 46 hours and i got fun, quick and challenging gameplay enclosed in a fitting musical atmosphere, an insane + loveable narrator and perfectly polished mechanics.
I started the game on insane difficulty, and although i'd describe myself as a casual gamer, i finished all levels with an A++ (all gems + yarn looted, time bonus) after those 46 hours. I can't compare this to normal difficulty as i haven't tried it out, but i guess you get atleast 30 hours of gameplay out of a single player experience if you won't speedrun/rush the game.
I have to give this game a 10/10 as it is one of the best games i've played so far. If you don't like its humor, narrator or platformers in general i'd understand and i'd suggest a different genre of games, but even if you have different preferences it wouldn't distract from the fact that this is an absolutely polished game and a unique experience that i  hope gives everyone as much joy as it gave to me.
It's brilliant!
Side Notes:
- There are ~50 levels in story mode and to achieve A++ i grinded sometimes for an hour.
- The level design is incredible, every level is different.
- The game is totally worth its full price
- Works fluently on my crappy laptop
- I love the fact that every level can be mastered on A++ without the help of tools, but also that the tools (unlocked by gameplay) give you the ability to alter your playstyle a little and maybe even "cheat" on some levels. You are presented a challenge, and even if there is an intended way to solve them, you can try out different approaches.
- There are secret levels, and i probably missed some!
- I haven't even started multiplayer or custom created games (or anything other than the story mode).
I can fully recommend this game!
Thank you for reading, go ahead and start playing!

You won't find a better 80's boxing/kung fu fighting management tycoon game. That's not to say it's a perfect game but this game is undoubtedly one of the more management games I've ever played. Not to mention, this game has some of the best pop culture references I've seen in a while, so many familiar faces! However, before I give my opinion, allow me to explain how the game works.
In Punch Club, you take on the role of a fighter who's father was murdered by a mysterious red eyed, fedora toting ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who brings a gun to a fist fight. You will have to manage 3 main attributes which are STR (strength), AGI (Agility), and STA (Stamina). You increase these stats by training in the gym and use them to defeat opponents in fights. STR affects damage output but increases energy consumption. AGI increases your accuracy and your ability to dodge. STA affects how much energy you regenerate during the fight and at the end of each round. Each stat obviously has it's benefits but it's in your best interest to only focus on one or two, not all three. Having a well-balanced fighter is a bad thing when fighting specialized fighters.
You will also have to manage your health, hunger, sleep and mood. At first, it'll be tough to have enough money to eat yet still train so that you can compete against tougher fighters. My best advice to you is to work about 2 shifts, eat, sleep and train as much as you can before rinsing and repeating. Eventually, you'll get involved in ultimate fights which start to pay the bills and when you're finally able to beat the 'Rookie League,' you'll really start making money. Oh, you also go to Russia but that's all I'll say about that.
The largest focus of the game is the fights. Now this game is strange in the sense that it decided to take direct fighting control away from the player and instead base it on the aforementioned stats and seemingly unforgiving RNG mechanics. While this can be annoying, it's also led to some real nailbiters. It should also be noted that there are 3 fighting styles that can be unlocked as your character obtains Skill Points (SP). Along with these fighting styles, you'll unlock skills and perks that are used in combat. All of these skills are activated during combat automatically based on the amount of energy you have and perks are always active in a passive manner.
So what is my actual opinion of the game? Well, to be honest, I love it. It's a blast. It's annoying as hell but it's still a lot of fun and has a metric ton of charm. Sometimes the game is unbearably grindy like when I was trying to beat the Rookie League but then it suddenly gets super easy once get to Russia. Sometimes the fights feel like total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t when your character is significantly better than another fighter but he somehow gets lucky. Even with these issues, would I recommend it? For 10 bucks? Hell yeah, this is a game that everyone should experience. Especially fans of movies from the 80's and early 90's!
Definitely recommended.
