Watch Dogs 2 is a great game.
I was personally a huge fan of the original Watch Dogs, so of course I am slightly biased. Everyone seemed to think the original game's protagonist's personality was dull and unrelatable, which was mostly true. The storyline was pretty interesting, pretty unique. I really enjoyed the first game, having played it over six times.
I picked up Watch Dogs 2 several months before it was released with knowledge that it would be great.
I wasn't wrong! The game is fantastic. Here's some things the game does better that the original could have done better:
The characters that star in Watch Dogs 2 are surprisingly more unique, relatable, enjoyable but also slightly cringy. They're better than Aiden Pearce, and that's what matters.
The new hacking system is really unique and tremendously necessary. It makes the game more fun, honestly.
This includes the mobile RC car and the quadrocopter you can equip from the rather odd 3D printer. (I'll talk about that in one of the cons) These make the game far more strategic and less shooty.
Here are some things that the game could have done a bit better:
I'm still not a huge fan of the driving. It's acceptable, but they haven't done too much with it since they last promised.
The 3D Printer thing is really stupid honestly. I get the game was kind of trying to keep up with today's trends (specifically 3D printers) but the practically instantaneous fabrication time and outrageously expensive one-time prints are almost useless. You're better off just killing some initial enemies with your stun gun and steal their weapon, and work up from there.
The characters are extremely fun, but at the same time they are just too gangsterish. I don't know how to word it, but they are annoying at times with their verbal abuse of vulgar language that was completely unnecessary. I understand it's the area but I feel like Ubisoft was emphasizing this too much. Besides that, the characters are also very stereotypical. Don't get me wrong, I still love them! They're fun to play with and relatable.
Looking past these cons, the game is very well done and I recommend it to anyone who has $60 and is interested in this game.
TL;DR: Game is significantly better than original. Buy if have money!

Satazius is a fun little Shmup that closely pays homage to the Sega era of Shmups, it does a good job scratching that "itch" of wanting a good arcade Shmup to play. The level design plays more like a 90's Shmup with obstacles in the level design that mixs well with bullet hell mechanics. The game is not overly punishing, often starting you back at the last checkpoint upon "Game Over". Weapon powerups, while diverse in playstyle, are more traiditonal in how they're obtained. After each boss encounter and stage complete, you go back to the weapon select screen where you can try the new weapon powerup you just unlocked.
There were both good and bad things I found while playing Satazius that I feel you should take into consideration before purchasing this game:
+ New weapon powerups given after each level make your gameplay experience revitalizing and fresh for the next level.
+ Lots of powerups given throughout each level.
+ Well balanced stage difficulty, starting moderately hard at the beginning of the game which progressively gets harder.
+ Environmental obstacles mix well with a bullet hell environment.
+ Controls felt nice and tight; light taps feel accurate when trying to hug a wall for a powerup pickup.
+ Music has a catchy techno theme that goes well with the sci-fi theme of the game.
+ Sprite art are was a nice throwback to some of the older Sega Shmups, lots of great animations.
+ Every level was diverse in theming.
- Cannot "Pause" while in-game, must rely on a Windows 10 scheduled update popup instead. lol.
- After clicking “Start” on the main menu, you cannot go back to choose another option. You’re locked into starting the mission, or exiting the game entirely to go back to the main menu.
- In the weapon select screen before and after a stage, you have limited time to make a strategical decision of which weapons to choose for your upcoming level.
- No story, no cutscenes! I would have liked to see a "Starfox-esque" dialog system seen during the game, like an animated portrait that has textual dialog, or even voice acting.

I bought this while on sale not expecting much and I've enjoyed this game more than I thought I would. For an indie side-scrolling shmup, it's pretty well-done. It's not really innovative at all (it's essentially Gradius), but the levels are memorable, the weapons make sense and offer variety and strategy, and the game isn't a pure memorizer (where the only way to win is to memorize your ship movements down to the pixel, like R-Type and its ilk).
The difficulty isn't that bad either; a mid-level shmup player might be able to beat this in a weekend with a bit of work. It's neither too easy (like many games from people who haven't played arcade shmups and add things like health bars and leveling up) nor too punishing (like many games from people who have only played arcade shmups and expect you to spend hours to deduce The One True Path through the game to finish it). It's just a solid, old-school horizontal shooter.
Alright, now on to the complaints: the game has only one resolution and it'll resize all the windows on your desktop to that tiny size when you quit and the ESC key immediately bombs out to the desktop without any prompt (which is annoying if your muscle memory is to hit ESC to pause like most PC games).
This game needs a graphics and UI update badly, but it's worth picking up for the classic shmup player who has some time to kill.

Airships: Conquer the Skies is a highly enjoyable game that revolves around designing airships (also land vehicles and fortifications).  The setting is maybe a little bit "Steampunk" or maybe an alternate timeline set around the start of the industrial revolution.  I primarily play in "Conquest" mode, which is a very simple strategy game, but is still very enjoyable due to the primary strong point of the game, which is desigining and testing your creations.  The design interface is easy to use, and the individual components and necessary considerations have already created quite a lot of depth in a game that is not even released yet.  As a helpful hint for anyone that plays the game, try using the overlay tab in design mode.  You can build bombers, big ships with lots of cannons, ships with troops for boarding, tanks, and so on, and so forth.  I found combat in the game to be satisfying, and have already spent quite a bit of time testing the ships and learning the problems and strengths with each design, which has led to an awful lot of adjustments.  I think that gamers that enjoy building or designing in games and think that airships are cool should definitely check it out.

Legend.A computer worm is a standalone malware computer program that replicates itself in order to spread to other computers.[1] Often, it uses a computer network to spread itself, relying on security failures on the target computer to access it. Unlike a computer virus, it does not need to attach itself to an existing program.[2] Worms almost always cause at least some harm to the network, even if only by consuming bandwidth, whereas viruses almost always corrupt or modify files on a targeted computer.
Many worms that have been created are designed only to spread, and do not attempt to change the systems they pass through. However, as the Morris worm and Mydoom showed, even these "payload free" worms can cause major disruption by increasing network traffic and other unintended effects. A "payload" is code in the worm designed to do more than spread the worm—it might delete files on a host system (e.g., the ExploreZip worm), encrypt files in a ransomware attack, or send documents via e-mail. A very common payload for worms is to install a backdoor in the infected computer to allow the creation of a "zombie" computer under control of the worm author. Networks of such machines are often referred to as botnets and are very commonly used by spam senders for sending junk email or to cloak their website's address.[3] Spammers are therefore thought to be a source of funding for the creation of such worms,[4][5] and the worm writers have been caught selling lists of IP addresses of infected machines.[6] Others try to blackmail companies or schools with threatening DoS attacks.[7]
Users can minimize the threat posed by worms by keeping their computers' operating system and other software up to date, avoiding opening unrecognized or unexpected emails and running firewall and antivirus software.[8]

Can you play a game for over 50 hours where nothing really happens? You should ask yourself that before buying this game, because it has pretty much no plot until the end. EDIT: As of writing this review I have now finished the sequel, Trails in the Sky SC. While more stuff did happen in that game, expect a slow start, like for the first 5 chapters (it has 9 chapters). So it is not just this game that is slow paced, it's also the sequel. Haven't played the third game yet because I really need a break from this slow pace.

The gameplay is fairly linear, you journey throughout a country doing quests with the goal of becoming senior bracers. Bracers is kind of a guild that take on different jobs, but are independant from nations. The combat is turn-based, where different actions take different amount of turns so to speak. But they are dynamic, so the more speed your character have, the more turns he gets, the same is true for enemies. My only complaint is that there is a soft-cap on your level, so you can only grind levels up to a certain point. This is because for each level you gain, you lose half the xp value of monsters, even bosses, so eventually you will only gain 1 xp per monster until you continue with the story.
I should also mention that you will transfer your save to the next chapter and the level you start with depends on the level you got in this game. It ranges from 35-40, so if you became level 42 you will start as a level 40 in the next game. Same is true if you're under level 35 where you will start as a level 35. All the quests you've done are also saved and people will remember that you have helped them.
If you rather prefer a shorter game with better pacing, I would suggest you get Grandia 2. Because getting into this series is a major time investment.

As it is now, it's a pretty solid bike racing / fighting experience, in the spirit of the old Road Rash games, which is good because I loved that series and I've been waiting years for a game like this.
Anyway, keep in mind that this is an Early Access game, so it's safe to pick it up if you're a Road Rash fan like me, you'll most certainly love it, but it is
a finished product. It suffers from the poor performance issues of Unity 4, so until devs update it so it will run on Unity 5, the most crowded moments of the game will seriously drop your FPS, but overall it's playable, so it's not that big of a deal, considering that updates are released pretty regularly and I think that the transition to to Unity 5 will be only a matter of time.
Also, it currently lacks competitive multiplayer and online, so at the moment you'll be only able to play 2-4 players co-op. When competitive and online multiplayer comes out, it will be a great boost to the replayability factor of this game, which is already pretty high considering that the campaign is procedurally generated and the skill system along with the temporary upgrades that you can buy in the shop between races makes every campaign different from another.
Procedurally generated tracks are generally good, but are not so varied and tend to get a bit repetitive really fast (expecially rooftop ones, and it's a shame considering that at first it's a really fresh and fun concept). Also you can't save tracks in any way, so even if you loved a track and want to play it again sometimes, or with friends coming over at your house, you currently can't. I hope they'll add an editor of some sort or even a seeding option to play around with the track generator and why not, share tracks with the community.
Weapon variety and fighting are great, it's so funny to get rid of rivals by smacking them in the face with a spiked bat, grabbing them and ramming them into the upcoming traffic, or slicing them with a BATTLE AXE! Firearms are a bit OP obviously, this being a bike racing game, but they come with limited ammunition and if you like challenge, you can choose to not use them at all (but give the grenade launcher a try, it's funny as hell), since CPU rivals will not (save for a specific event in which there are some bikers with unlimited pipebombs). I hope they will be toned down a little when online and competitive MP will be added.
At the moment there's not a large choice of bikes and characters, and there are no upgrades that change bike stats (other than damage resistance) or its appearance.
So, to sum this review up, I give this game 7/10, only because it's clearly unfinished (after all, it
an Early Access game), and I recommend it to anyone who played any Road Rash and/or likes the concept of racing/brawling on motorbikes, and I recommend buying it in the meantime (consider buying it when it's on sale if you're not a diehard Road Rash fan or you're not sure you want to buy an Early Access game) to support developers, so updates will be released faster, and also because it's very likely that it will cost more when it will be finished. Also it's nice to see that devs take time to read our opinions and answer to them in the forums, so this is another good reason to buy it and play it so that your feedback will help making the game better and better. It really has potential, and with some tweaks here and there it could easily become the best game of its genre.

A great example of this is the skill tree, which should be scrapped entirely for a new unlock system that changes your starting weapons and unlocks new motorcycles. Increasing your health, xp gains, and cast earned isn't healthy game play fun - its grindy and does not feel rewarding to the player.
Instead, picture that you only start the game off with a single character and bike, no weapons, and have to earn your way up the ranks. As you spend your xp after each match you unlock new characters (that start with a single weapon) or bikes with real differences. You shouldnt start each game with 3 weapons immediately, already on stage 3, and nearly irrelevant bike choices just because you played through a few times. I know it's early access - but this is the kind of thing that is getting old quickly.
The game also completely lacks personality from the other racers, and to make it worse it is littered with a bunch of randomly spawned NPC's to up the action. Instead keep my 10 or so competitors and make them challenging, make them try to grab me and block my shots, or boost when I try to shoot at them. Give them names and pictures, dialouge, they need personality.
Lastly, since right now your current objectives are all random - it makes for some frustrating game play. I don't mind the tornado, explosions in the middle of the road constantly levels, or roof top timed challenge modes existing.... if there was a choice to it. If i could choose to want to play that or not it would really help. I want a core gameply driven experience when I hit campaign, and I want a challenge type scenario placed elsewhere. My campaign should be an experience of improvement and difficulty to be the best racer out there, not dodging randomly generated falling cars.
The game is still fun, but I am not recommending it until I see some real direction put into the game instead of a bunch of randomly placed together content and skill trees.

First off, I'm playing on Linux with an i7-4770k, GTX 770 4GB, 16 GB ram and a driving force GT (DFGT).
Feral Interactive did the port, and based on others reviews it seems they made it work better than Windows. Sure there's slightly worse performance and a few bugs here and there, but generally it's working great. Best of all, Feral responds to bug reports and actively tries to help!
Performance wise I get a steady 40-50 FPS with spikes up to 90-100. More consistent FPS would be nice, but it's an issue out of Ferals control. The game has never crashed for me either. Sound has wigged out once, but a simple restart of the game fixed it.
AI seems to be a popular complaint as well. I fully agree that they need improving, especially when they get blue flagged. It doesn't ruin the game for me though. I'd be happier seeing more AI difficulty options or at least less drastic skill differences between difficulties. The jump from hard to expert or legend is just a bit too big, especially when comparing qualifying performance to race performance (AI performs better in the race).
The final thing I'd like to see improved is Linux wheel support. If I wasn't as familiar with Linux, I'd have a hard to sorting out the wheel settings. For anyone running into problems my strategy has been to use ltwheelconf to set turn radius and such, then use jstest-gtk to calibrate the wheel and peddles. It has to be done once per time the wheels power is disconnected or your computer is restarted. I also set the steering saturation in game to around 40-60, otherwise the in game wheel isn't quite in sync.

Though there really isn't much dialogue or story to the game, the gist of SATAZIUS involves pirate-infested planet Satazius, and assault ship Tralfagar's crew taking immeasurable odds on to wade through fleet after fleet of enemies, and destroy the pirates' base situated there.
The customization of the game is quite interesting. You're granted a Main weapon, which will always fire when the button is held down, and two Sub weapons, which you can switch between, and will fire alongside your main weapon. (The homing orbs in particular are my favorite, possibly because I'm no crack shot when it comes to these sort of games.) In addition, you're given a more powerful Charge weapon, which you can fire off once you've fired with your Main/Sub weapons long enough.
Now, to actual gameplay. On the field, you'll find powerups that augment your currently equipped weapons (however, the Sub weapon powerup will only affect the currently active Sub weapon, so be careful!), speed, score, and a powerup that will generate a shield around you, effectively making you invincible for one shot.  Oh, and like most traditional shooters, one shot will mean the end for you. (Alternatively, you can crash into a wall, like me.) However, you're given three more retries, until it's the end. Make those count.
... Or don't, and finish the game without dying, like the professional shooter veteran that you are.
Alternatively, don't do that either, because even if you're skilled at the genre, it's a pretty brutal game.

Early Access reviews can be pretty rough because the game is not finished.  It can be tough on the reviewer too because after playing the game, one can see the vision of the developer, but the unsanded edges of their work also stick out like a sore thumb.
Train Station Simulator falls into a category that I would describe as "good for early access".  With the market currently flooded with cookie cutter management sims that are never updated and use borrowed art it's nice to see that Appliks Apps Studios have gone with a more original style of artwork and design.
The game itself is a bit rudimentary right now and suffers mostly because it stands unfinished.  As of this writing there is no in game guide or manual which leaves the player to suss out exactly what they need to do in order to be successful.  It took me about 2 or 3 hours to figure out the basic game mechanics and start to get a grip on the overall mechanics
From a gameplay point of view there are at least three issues holding the game back:
1) The building tools for walls/doors etc is a bit clunky and should be reworked.  It is unclear to a new user where they are and are not allowed to build.  It's not a major issue but could use some tweaking.
2) Scheduling of trains and buses.  At this time, it's seems scheduling is rather random.  In my most recent playthrough I did not even bother to do more than set all the buses and trams to deliver at random throughout the day and it seemed to have no impact at all on the success of the station.  Train scheduling is important in that you need trains in your station to get passengers out, however I stumbled upon and issue with scheduling that is related to the third issue...
3) The most major issue lies in passenger AI.  As of this writing each day passengers enter your train station and appear to move and act in completely random and arbitrary ways.  This makes it quite difficult to manage the station efficiently.  The game provides an ability to watch and follow a single passenger in your station.  So for example I have witnessed a passenger enter the station, walk to a random corner of the station, leave the station, come back in and then use the bathroom, then buy a train ticket.  I am sure in the history of the real world someone in real life has done this for some unexplained reason.  But I think it would be exceedingly rare to see.  In game at this time such activity is quite the regular sight.  And this now ties back to scheduling trains.
Unlike most normal thinking creatures the passengers in this game do not buy a ticket and then go to the platform their train is scheduled to arrive at.  Instead almost all passengers buy a ticket (there are several classes of ticket) and then wander around the station doing various activities.  When a train arrives all the passengers in the station that have a ticket then start to attempt to get on that train, even if their ticket is not for that train.  So only the passengers with the correct ticket get on (and most of them miss the train because they were doing something else across the station when the train arrived) and the rest of the passengers are left standing on the platform or go back to wandering the station.
This becomes quite the issue when you start to have multiple platforms.  For example if you have 4 platforms and a local train and a commuter train come in on track 1 and 4 respectively, then you are almost guaranteed to have half of each type of passenger to miss their train.  Some random selection will go to track 1, and the others will go to track 4.  If they have the right ticket then they board, if not they stay in the station.  Add in a third train or a train that comes in an hour later and you have this mass herd moving around the station trying to see if they can get on a train.  In short the passengers treat their tickets like a lottery instead of a train ticket.  Because of this limitation I was left with scheduling trains on 2 adjacent tracks almost the entire day (despite having 5 platforms) in order to bounce the passengers back and forth and get the most on the trains each day.  This is a major flaw at this time in my opinion and limits what the player can accomplish
The AI needs to be tweaked so that the passengers at least appear to have an idea that they have a train to catch and what train it is and where it is going to arrive.  IRL a passenger buys a ticket, knows where and when the train is arriving, does the business it needs to conduct and then goes to that location to meet the train.  In this game the passenger buys a ticket and then acts as if they have no idea what train, what time or what platform they will be leaving from and so instead run around randomly hoping that they guess the correct train.
Overall the game is definitely playable and enjoyable once you start to bend the AI to your will, but in order to really become simulation level it needs to work on the AI and flesh out some of the in game options.
As far as an early acess title I would rate this game a 6 out of 10.  With continued development the game should improve and become more enjoyable.  If you are looking to purchase the game just beware of it's current limitations.

There are dozens of railway management simulations on Steam. You might have already played some and you think that you know the basics and seen it all. Today I’m reviewing a game that wishes to focus even more on the management side and logistics of railway travel rather than setting up tracks between points  A to B while constantly improving the means of transportation. No, Train Station Simulator just as its name suggests shall offer you a perspective into the intricacies of the gateway itself, so to speak. An ambitious Steam debut by Appliks Apps Studios with relatively few flaws and a lot of potential even in its current Early Access stage.
While campaign missions are certainly present in Train Station Simulator, an actual storyline is not. For now you’ll have to contend with the open-ended structure of the assignments given during each mission you tackle from the game’s Main Menu. They range in both complexity and duration. Some operations focus on restoring prebuilt train stations back to their former glory, yet the most challenging missions are still the ones related to full creative freedom while on a tight in-game budget. Even without a story, the title performs its tasks as expected and the only visible flaw I could notice in regards to its narrative structure, is the absence of a tutorial.
“Pop-up” tips & tricks are hardly a substitute for a comprehensive explanation of the game’s features or even basic economy. It is perfectly fine for new players to try out economic simulations even without previous experience for this particular genre. We all started out from pretty much the same point before accumulating the needed know-how. Tutorials smoothed the transition from simple to complex gameplay mechanics, for a genre that’s more about creating virtual jobs and making an equally virtual profit instead of shooting people in the face. So Appliks Apps, please make your project accessible to all gamers on Steam and offer them a tutorial that might take them step by step towards their first successfully ran train station. The trial & error method is a viabile alternative, but it won’t endear you to economic sim novices.
The graphics engine powering Train Station Simulator is custom-made and not even Modb could pin it down to a certain asset manufacturer. It did remind me of my Roller Coaster Tycoon exploits from “back in the day”. If you’re going to say that the looks are not on par with the gameplay, know that true simulations never need eye candy in order to convey their intended vision for a focused job description. I’m not going to be hypocritical either and deny the many benefits of a full 3D environment, but my point refers to the efficiency of the game itself which given the genre we’re discussing now, the 2D assets are more than able to satisfy an established fan base. Never judge a book by its cover.
Most sound assets are simplistic yet within acceptable parameters. Voice acting or not, there’s still a station announcer notifying passagers of incoming or outgoing trains. That was expected as were the various sound effects for the traffic outside the station or the restless crowd which doubles as your potential customers.
Which brings us to the really strong points of this title. Commuters or simply occasional tourists represent your main source of income. In order to manage a successful train station you’ll need to cater to the many needs of any who enter the premises. Customers on one hand and the station employees on the other. I’m pleased  by the attention to detail which went into the simulation of the human resources department. Any manager worth his salt knows that hiring staff is more than just the simple and more often than not, cold procedure of examining a dossier while seeking the best qualified person willing to work for the smallest paycheck. Low wages are obviously going to reflect into the same manner of services and level of motivation.
The first lesson you’ll learn when starting a new mission in this game, is that respect is earned, not instantly won or enforced in any manner. You will have to hire individuals from several categories of the workforce, ranging from hygiene technicians, security personnel, engineers and last but not least, medical staff for any potential emergencies. By letting the players choose both the wage and the work hours, the dev team have included the options for working in multiple shifts while being able to set custom salaries. Maximizing profits may be the end goal of far too many greedy companies in our real life, but there’s no reason not to properly motivate your virtual employees and also keep the customer satisfaction on a similar level. Mutual respect is the key to long term profits.
By focusing on the train station and its secondary amenities, you won’t be able to draft or influence routes but you can enhance the local infrastructure up until the point at which bullet trains will replace any other form of railway transportation.  A hefty number of customers will overflow your station after you’ve built advanced bus stations or limousine parking lots. It may seem a bit strange that someone which can afford a limo service may travel by train instead of plane, but perhaps they might be afraid of the commercial aviation. Players shall keep a close eye on the needs and expectations of all who work inside the station or use it for traveling purposes. It goes without saying that maintaining the place properly cleaned, in working order  and well decorated, shall draw in numerous customers and eventually extend your profit margin.
Since there’s no pause button yet, players have to shift their focus between human and immaterial assets in real time. Pausing in strategy titles (economic sims are a form of strategy, of course) is vital. It should be an option as ubiquitous as saving the game state. I’ve learned through the initial slow development and even financial failures that you should only work on expanding and redecorating the train station outside of the working hours. You need as many customers as you can get during daytime and while you may conceive your next building projects whenever you wish, set those plans into motion at night. The old adage for “working smarter, not harder” is fitting like a glove in these continuous scenarios that can only be sped up and never paused.
More diversity for the visual and sounds assets or a simulated weather system would be welcome, but the crucial issues that require immediate attention stem from the lack of a pause option and a proper tutorial. There’s a decent amount of Achievements to stimulate players and one can only hope that Trading Cards could be introduced eventually. What’s certain however is that you won’t get bored even in the title’s Early Access. Do try out the sandbox mode with nearly unlimited funds, until you learn the ropes and feel confident enough for the challenging missions.
+ Replay value.
+ Steam Achievements.
+ A simulation of decent complexity.
- No option to pause the game.
- Complete lack of a tutorial.
- No Steam Trading Cards.

If you like to tinker and experiment around in games, if you have a knack for city builders and like to construct an efficient system, then observe it for a while and modify again to optimize, get this game.
If you like utter chaos and screenshakey explosions, pirates, mech spiders and house-sized buzzsaw weaponry, get this game.
There's many ways to play this, and it really is one of those games where losing is fun, not only because it's a learning experience, but it also manages to drive home the atmosphere with the sound and effects. And yes, I'm aware that many people criticize the screenshots, but just wait and see until you've finished your first conquest. The outside view of the vessels isn't as important as what goes on inside, anyway.
See through the torn-open walls of a burning, battered bunker, corpses littering all the hallways, and just one guy still alive, trying to fight the flames until he runs out of water. Then he accepts his fate and stands there, trapped by the fire until the entire structure explodes in a mushroom cloud of awesomeness.
Force your crew to focus on firing the cannons while the rest of the ship behind them is already breaking apart and falling from the sky, so at least they can take some of the enemy down with them.
Or laugh at your own stupidity when you forget to add enough coal storehouses and your entire armada just drops like a brick in the middle of the fight, crushing the hostile landship underneath them in a huge, suicidal fireball.
Also, no bugs on my end, so far!

How can I explain how much I enjoy this game? I know! I bought it twice. Yes, bought twice. First time on iOS when it first came out, then again on Steam about a week after I joined. And I was glad to do it.
Organ Trail isn't original; it's an homage. It's a bizarre, hilarious, utterly enjoyable take on the classic Apple IIe Oregon Trail. You remember: the one where everyone died of dysentery and you were left wondering just what the heck a "wagon tongue" was. Well, you trade in the Conestoga wagon for a station wagon (which bears a strong resemblance to Clark Griswold's Family Truckster, or possibly a Plymouth Reliant K) and instead of hunting buffalo, you're shooting zombies. The sound, graphics, and gameplay are all so close to the original Oregon trail that you're going to have elementary school flashbacks. (Since they have such a sense of humor, clicking in-game buttons has a sound effect: the distinctive CLUNK of a IIe keyboard.)
The one and ONLY one slight ding against it is the repair minigame, but you know, that's totally forgiveable. Just because it's not my cup of tea doesn't mean it was a bad design choice or really a problem with the game. Every game has a feature or two you're not particularly fond of.
Tremendous replay value, practically guaranteed hilarity, and outstanding minigames. And, of course, dysentery.

Alright, iv been playing this game on and off for years now. No matter what mmo or other game i try our i always end up back at tera. The amount of hours on steam are nothing, i used to play before it was on steam.
THIS IS NOT P2W AT ALL - everything can be earnt in game or bought with in game gold on the brokerage except server transfers should you ever wish you change to a different server.
Levelling - follow the red quests and make sure you are queued up for dungeons at all times as they give insane xp, around 2-4 levels per dungeon at lower levels, then at higher levels you get 2 - 3 times more xp from a dunegon than you will from finishing a quest.
Gearing at max level - at lvl 65 you get given idoneal armour which is basic max level armour that doesnt require enchanting. Its good enough to run the first few dungeons which get you your next set of gear or alternatively there is a quest on the island of dawn that rewards you with gear and some items to help you enchant it if you kill so many bams (big♥♥♥♥♥monsters). Dunegons drop all the gear you will ever need. Top gear can only be made by crafting it and the materials for crafting it are dropped in dungeons however it is RNG with whoever rolls the highest number getting the item. I personally will NEVER buy or make top teir gear as they release new gear so often. The next teir down, once enchanted to +12 is usually good enough to do every dungeon in the game anyway. To me top tier gear is normally just for bragging rights or elitest idiots.
PVP - Im on mount tyrannis server and open world pvp is very active but only in certain areas. levelling up you encounter people quite often who are the same level as you and will try and kill you over a few mobs, which can be fun, especially if you end up winning. However on channels other than channel 1 pvp does not really occur. Battlegrounds.. What can i say, i LOVE corsairs stronghold. Every match you play is different from the previous one. You can win and lose in the same way over and over again but your team and the enemy team are always different. It takes a while for the other battlegrounds to pop (10-20 min queues even as heal/tank) so i dont often play those. Gridiron and fraywind canyon are almost straight up pvp deathmatches which can be fun as hell but often you'll get one team way better than the other so that can take the fun away from it and cause frustration.
PVE - Dungeons are fun, i have high ping (250ms avg) so i cant run some of the high level dungeons at all because im dying to things that arent even on my screen yet. A lot of them have mechanics where you have to respond within a certain time frame or else you are one hit and with high ping that makes it very difficult for me. Timescape is one of my all time favourite and most repeatable dunegons of all time. The mechanics are fun, the bosses are fun and it can be an awesome time with a group of friends. Pugging (random) dungeon matching can be annoying if no one in your party knows what to do but sometimes that makes it even better as they arent going to rush through and do things without you and you all get to learn together. However, when you have multiple characters, running the same 4 or 5 dungeons every day does get boring pretty fast.
Cons - Finding a good guild is hard. Finding a guild who isnt elistest, doesnt want you to have the top gear before even applying, doesnt expect you to be on teamspeak or some voice chat app the WHOLE time you are logged in is hard. I have been kicked from a guild because I wouldnt use teamspeak, even when i was just farming credit points and not even doing dungeons. Even when I knew the dungeon inside and out, could run it without dying, they still expected you to be on teamspeak. Finding a guild that is relaxed, just about having fun and running pvp/pve content together is pretty hard and I havent managed to find one yet so im often doing things solo or having to use dungeon matching to find a group which can suck as id love a group of core friends to hang out and do things with.
Other than that this is a great game who are constantly updating and releasing new content whether its dungeons, costumes, random mini events, new gear, new classes and so on. Plus the combat, its amazeballs!

While it says I've only played for 8.7 hours this week, I've actually played this game for years before it came to Steam. This is a decent F2P MMORPG but I've come to the realization that it's not as good as I thought it was when I first started playing.
PROS
- Good graphics
- Big numbers for DPS
- Good character animations
- Good music
- Fast gameplay
- Many cosmetic options for those who like that stuff
- Wide variety of items from the Cash Shop
CONS
- By and large, the community is horrible. Many of the players are disrespectful to newcomers or even veterans who make a silly mistake. It is even worse in PvP where people will kill you, then trash you for no reason.
- There is no end game aside from grinding dungeons, farming materials to sell on the market board, buying costumes and mounts, and then AFKing in a highly populated area for attention on you new attire.
- There are people who P2W and you will know who they are. You may not be able to buy gear with real money, but you can buy items and sell them on the market board or just sell your EMP for gold. It becomes even more apparent in unequalized PVP where people already have maxed PvP gear within about 2 weeks of the new gear coming out.
- You are severely restricted on the number of dungeon runs you can do while unsubcribed, giving you a disadvantage to Elite players
- There are ALWAYS people who spam in chat. While you can simply turn those chats off, the priniciple of the matter is that those people exist within the game, plus having to disable those chats removes the boon having said chats provide.
- It is highly unlikely that you will get well geared at end game unless you're in a static. So, for those of you that don't play with friends, good luck. Even within a guild, people like to do their own thing and aren't always avilable to help you grind materials for gear.
- Monsters are regurgitated over and over but with different skins come new updates
- The game is HORRIBLY, I mean,
unoptimized. It doesn't matter how good your PC is, the game is not optimized to take advantage of your PC specs. You will have constant FPS drops, lag, rubberbanding, and stuttering. These issues make PvP even harder and more aggravating.
- There will be trolls. More trolls than any MMO I've played. They will make it difficult, if not, impossible, to complete a battleground or dungeon. Trolls are even more worrisome when you're playing Corsair's Stronghold, a large scale battleground, in which peopl need to work as a team. The language barriers, the lack of communication, and the fact people simply don't care enough to help others makes the team based PvP in this game absolutely atrocious. The leader will issue a strategy and instead of everyone following it, they will go off and PvP random people. People just don't care.
Try the game. You may like it as I did. You may also get to the end game, see all it's flaws, then stop playing, as I did. The game is decent but you will end up more frustrated than not.

Aside from that, there is also a separate meter for craft skills. These are used for character specific attacks and abilities and all characters have them. As characters take their active turns in combat, icons to the right of the turn order window will show up and they can get bonuses like a minor hp heal or a free critical when its their active turn. Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky...First of all, it's extremely heavy on dialogue and the pacing is a bit slow so I hope you're patient going into it.
This game does everything a solid JRPG should have right: engaging combat, solid story, entertaining characters, side-quests, airships and a plot twist at the end that might as well been pulled from M. Night Shamallamadingdong's desk drawer.
A general overview of the story: two adopted siblings travel the continent to prosper as junior "bracers", which are the goody-two-shoes guild that help the citizens with tasks while also looking for their father. As it goes on, some spooky corrupt spookyness happens and♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan. Want the details? Play the game, you goof.
Characters are a bit stereotypical yet not entirely one-dimensional which somehow makes them all so loveable; the polar opposite personalities between Estelle and Joshua playing into conversation and decision making works perfectly; emotion vs. reason. Normally hyper, overly-emotional characters like Estelle annoy the hell out of me, yet somehow she was my favorite, not just to see how she would overreact in a situation
but also how well defined and developed her character actually was. I wish there was more drunk Schera though. There wasn't enough of that.
Combat is turn-based on a small grid-layout battle scene. You move around and select your attacks and such, standard fare. Think Tactics Ogre but on a much smaller scale.
The music overall was pretty good but I generally had my own tunes playing instead out of preference.
Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky is easily one of the best games I've played in the last couple years, and by FAR one of the best JRPGs I've played in the last couple years. If you finish it, and havent had your fill...there's two direct sequels, and supposedly, they're even longer.

Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Once upon a time in the nineties, relaxation after a hard day at school was emitting a sigh of relief, booting the PlayStation to hear the dulcet tones of Road Rash 3D (and by dulcet tones, I mean real metal songs like 'Rusty Cage'. That might not seem much now, but before the GTA series this was something of a rariety in a game).
Apparently, according to wikipedia Road Rash 3D wasn't well received at the time. Well it was by me having by that point probably wasted months in the Road Rash games on the megadrive. As such, this modern day
homage has an awful lot to live up to.
Things are still rough and ready, but the core of the game is there.
On the bad hand; the split screen multiplayer is workable but has bugs, the network play is still completely missing and the bikes feel like they are cruising far too smoothly and quickly over the road surface - it's not just the final "rainbow road" style track that makes you think you could be playing a karting game.
This should be unforgiveable, but...it's somehow not.
It's a testament to the Road Rash legacy for those who grew up with it that Road Redemption still makes me grin every time I fire it up after an update, whether it's surviving a pile up, loosing a lorry load of logs off a passing trailer on a trecherous bend with a well placed sword swipe or kicking an opposing rider off a bridge.
It also has something I don't remember in Road Rash, guns!
Simply put, this game has massive potential. In my mind's eye I imagine netplay with clans of bikers riding a race or grudge match against one another. I can almost hear the grenade launcher calling out for it. I can hear the swearing and the laughter over the voice comm.
For now, Road Redempton is worth supporting as no one else is doing a similar game. Buy it (or con someone else into doing so :D) give it a play through, then get a few ciders in and try the split screen with some buddies, preferably on the hallucinogenic chemical zone level, where cars fall from the sky. There are far worse ways to waste your day.

It's a well-made  traditional STG (as in a non bullet hell) unlike Astro Port's other STG Super Robot Vulkaiser (which is bullet hell).
It's enough like Gradius that I would certainly recommend it if you are a fan of that series. It features  a very simalar aesthetic and shares some of the retro design philosophies (I.E being in the right place at the right time) that made the earlier games irritating, but it's nowhere near as unforgiving. You choose your weapons as you would in Gradius, a primary, two switchable sub-weapons and powerful charge weapon.
Your weapons are pretty much ripped straight from other STGs. Gradius, mainly, but you even have the Hunter from Thunder Force.
The powerups work differently. Intead of collecting cores from enemies to highlight a bar you collect them from stationary boxes and each core has a letter on it. S for sheild, and a P for power which powers up either you main, your equipped Sub, or your charge.
Bosses are also exteremely easy. You won't need to aim for the core and a few of them will even go down with a single hit from your charge weapon.

When people said this was similar to Gradius they weren't kidding. There are numerous instances of deja vu for fans of shooters such as Gradius, Darius, R-Type, and Axelay. That's not a bad thing and it still manages to be a great shooter on its own. There are better shooters out there, but considering the scarcity of shooters in this vein nowadays, it's still a worthwhile expierience.

If you want a new shoot 'em up specifically in the vein of Gradius, you'll find it here. While the graphics and music might be a little cheesy or off-putting, the weapons, stages, and bosses will literally blow you away, and you'll love every second of it. I've started a new run maybe thirty times and only recently beat it, so expect plenty of deaths and game overs, but pushing yourself a little harder to reach the next insane boss or stage is totally worth it.
The weapons are pretty standard, but the power-up system is just different enough to catch you off guard when you finally bite it and lose a few points and your weapons power down. Thankfully, while the game is pretty hardcore and the bosses are totally nuts, there are several checkpoints and mid-points during stages and boss fights that give you a few upgrades so you're not totally ruined when you twitched into a ceiling or missile just seconds from a victory.

Graphics are good. Music is decent. Good level design. Lots of different weapons, most of which are pretty cool and effective. Big boss battles. All in all, very reminiscent of Gradius games.
So why do I not recommend it?
Because if you can't play it properly, then the rest means nothing.
This game forces you to use the analog stick with no option of using the Dpad. I've been a huge fan of shoot 'em ups since the NES days, and while I'm no expert, I am pretty darn good at them. In this game, however, I was dying from the simplest of things (things that the developers probably hadn't even intended to be a threat) merely because the analog stick makes it too difficult to maneuver your ship with precision. I see no reason to limit the directional controls in a 2D game to the analog stick.
If a patch comes out that allows the directional controls to be changed to the Dpad, I will instantly change my rating to a thumbs up.

Side-scrolling shooter in the vein of Gradius and R-Type. May be a decent shooter, but I wouldn't know because I'm sick and ♥♥♥♥ing tired of games that force analog control instead of allowing the use of the d-pad.

An honest review from a long-time Codies and F1 fan:
Let me start by saying I don't play multiplayer often so this review has nothing to do with that section of the game.
Having until now held back from purchasing this game due to the lack of career mode and the discussions of game-breaking bugs and crap AI, I can honestly say I was surprised at how not-broken this game really is.
- Is it clearly a rushed job in terms of menus and extra content (i.e. challenge modes) from previous titles? Yes.
- Is it a shame that there's only a 'championship season' mode rather than career? Yes, hugely!
However, this game is NOT broken. Sure, there are some optimisation issues that mean that I can't run it on ultra, whereas my machine specs might otherwise have allowed it. But it looks very pretty on 'high' settings--far better than any F1 game has looked by far. Furthermore, since the modes are kind of bare-bones, the most important aspect of the entire game has to be the car mechanics and the racing. The mechanics themselves, while not perfect, feel really nice. This is NOT an arcade F1 game: with assists off you're fighting your back end out of the corners and trying to manage fuel/tyres in a way never before achieved in an F1 game. There's improvement to be made, but it's heading in a really great direction for F1 2016. For those really into the technical stuff, adjusting brake-bias and other settings are far more important now when it comes to preventing tyre lock-ups that now actually will destroy individual tyres. The AI is pretty dumb at times, admittedly. But it isn't game breaking (perhaps it was fixed over time).
But if you're like me and you were an F1 fan itching for F1 2016, hesitating to buy this one or having completely written it off, with the discount it's a really good buy. It is no longer a broken game as many reviews will tell you and it's actually a lot of fun. It's not the F1 2015 we were all hoping for, without career mode. But they focused on the racing, the feel of the cars, and they've done that really well. To tide you over until 2016 is released in August, I would definitely recommend this. More casual racing fans ought to stay away and wait until 2016 which will undoubtedly be better and more polished.
Overall: 7/10

Punch Club is a very unique blend of fighter and RPG.  I cannot off the top of my head recollect another title I would count as its peer.  That said, it would be important to evaluate it purely on its own merits and not attempt to compare it to any previous offering.  That too is a unique opportunity.
What is Punch Club then?  Well it's more of a management sim than anything else.  The RPG elements are strong but the majority of your input in this game is balancing your fighter's activities to build up for the fights.  The skill trees are interesting and present some real head-scratching moments where you'll be making some very defining choices for your fighter.
I beat this game in about 9 hours.  For a $10 game, that's not outside of what I would have expected.  The grindy nature of the game became VERY apparent in the final two to three hours of gameplay.  The novelty of the training and balancing your other activities will be gone by them time you're building up to your final ten fights.  There are some missed chances for some more cinematic presentations for those final fights too.  The opponents are less generic and it would have been an excellent opportunity to have special entrances, custom music, or maybe even mid-fight events.  Instead they become just another stepping stone to concluding the story.  At that point in the game, you've likely locked down your fight strategy so the probability that you're actually making meaningful adjustments is low.   Essentially you'll just be trying to maintain your stats between fights, and twiddling your fingers until the next match.
The exploration and story elements in the first half of the game are extremely solid.  You are introduced to a number of characters and branching story lines that allow you to spend some time outside of the organized fights.  Unfortunately that pace falls off about 60% through the game and it finished on a wimper rather than a bang.
For $10 I would recommend the game for those looking for something a bit different.  Don't expect a long and immersive experience, but a fun and interesting short one.

Yes, the new Worms games are fun. Yes, even the 3D ones that some people hate for one reason or another, but Worms Armageddon is (and will probably always be) my favourite Worms game of all time. And this is coming from someone who's been with the series since the very beginning.
All of the "beta" updates that the game has received since its initial release (1999!) keeps the game optimized and up-to-date with current technology, and the removal of the former multi-team worm cap (allowing the maximum of 48 worms in a 6-player game) and the unlocked map boundaries makes an already great game even better.
And it still has online servers to play on! (Take THAT, *insert game that recently had its servers taken down*!)

(Hours logged in-game only apply to the Steam version of W:A I purchased. The actual amount of time I've spent playing this game is incalculable.)
Best game ever made, hands down.
Better than all of the newer Worms titles. (Although we shall see if W.M.D. ends up being any good.) Unbeatable replay value and deeply strategic gaming. This game literally never gets old.
I've been playing it online since 1999 and I'll be playing it until I die, probably.
Looks are deceiving - what appears to be a simplistic, cartoony game for kids is actually the best online multi-player turn-based strategy game there is. The learning curve is practically endless. No matter how much you've played, you can always improve.
This is also a fantastic choice for less hardcore Worms players if you merely want to have some 6-player action with your friends and laugh your heads off.
I really don't understand why this game isn't more popular. To this day I have yet to find any game with as much replay value due to how customizable it is, and community-created schemes and maps are abundant.
One word of warning to newbies: People have been playing this game for a LONG time. If you find yourself losing (and you will), don't be put off by it. Every match is a learning experience and this game takes time to master. Nobody becomes good at this overnight. The community in general is friendly and willing to answer questions.
This game is digital crack cocaine. Yes, the graphics are dated, but the gameplay is outstanding.
If you have even the slightest interest in the Worms series, this is the game you want. Best balanced, largest community and most actively patched of the series. Can not recommend highly enough.
Just buy it!

By far the best Worms game in the series as far as the sheer amount of multiplayer options available to you.  Not to mention the game has been receiving updates for years and there is still an active community.  Skip the newer Worms games and get this instead, even if you have to wait for a sale.

You may think you don't need to buy this Worms game because you already own another one. If you buy Worms Armageddon, you won't need any other Worms games. WA has stood the test of time much better than many of the recent games.
The price tag may seem a bit steep for a game that is, at this point, over 14 years old, but the game continues to get software updates to this day. It's compatible all the way up to Windows 8, and it even plays nicely with Wine if you're the sort of sadist who thinks playing games on Linux is a sensible way to pass your time.

"What's the best Worms game" is surely a matter of intense debate over a very long series of installments. And sure, some of the most recent titles have been pretty solid. But I dunno. Maybe I'm biased when I say there's just something about Worms Armageddon, but I think you could make a pretty solid case that this one was just the best. I'm sure someone would agree. And hey, pretty much the entire map will now fit on your super futuristic enormous desktop resolution. Ha!

I can't even begin to estimate how much time in middle school I spent with this one.  I remember taking the CD of this game over to friends' houses, where we'd team up against the computer in the most outlandish scenarios we could think of.  Yes, we'd sometimes kill half our own team with an extremely poorly-planned super banana bomb, but we didn't care.  In this game, the hilarity of mistakes outclassed even the feeling of finally throwing that perfect grenade. It was stupid, perfect fun no matter what happened.
Don't just get Armageddon for the nostalgia value, though.  Get it because it's still as great as it was in 1999.  Get because it's still being patched and has a big community behind it even today. Get it because there hasn't been a greater Worms game since.

I’m the type of guy that to this day still has my Sega Genesis with Road Rash hooked up to my Television, so when I learned about Road Redemption it was an instant buy for me. When I first started playing, I was a little leery, as it is so clearly early access. The models aren’t the best (especially the collision models); it’s poorly optimized, there are no key re-bindings… but above all, it’s still a blast to play. The level design is great, the combat system is like Road Rash on steroids, the weapon selection is massive ( who doesn’t love taking someone out with a claymore, mace, or harpoon gun?), and the developers actually care about feedback. The game still has a long way to go before it’s finished, but the concept is solid and the team is obviously dedicated to making a great game. I highly recommend it, even in its current state.

- Early Access Review -
This game is a love-letter to the Road Rash series. Even in its current state, if you have any fond nostalgia for those games, you owe it to your inner-child to pick this title up.
Currently, the game is limited to a campaign mode of progressive areas and difficulty. There is racing against the timer, racing against a specific rival gang, night driving, icy tracks, cars raining down from the sky, police chases, exploding vehicles, rooftop racing... and I enjoyed every satisfying slash and crash that forcibly de-seated my fellow racers as I burned past them. Every time you die, all of your XP earned through that play-through can be spent on permanent player upgrades, adding to your health, damage, weapon durability, ammuntion, etc... so on each successive run, you'll have even more of an edge on your side.
The game plays fast and feels fast with little stuttering (running on an i3 processor with a GTX 640 Nvidia card), though there are instances of SUDDENLY-CARS, because the draw distance seems a little close to your bike. The way the bikes handle feels instinctive (using an x360 controller), and the button layout is workable... though not perfect. The ability to remap the keys isn't currently implemented, but it is one of the features on the list to be added. Based on the level of polish the game already has, this is definitely not a project with sloppy devs... I would highly believe that patches, new game modes, and features are en route.
For downsides, though... with only one current play-mode, the game will grow repetitive after a while. The AI routines of the opponent riders is somewhat predictable, and once you learn the timing of the weapon swings, they frequently fall for a basic swerve-n-strike pattern. There are plenty of weapons to experiment with, including the grappling hook which is a blast to use, but its still an issue of slowly becoming familiar and then boring. There is no automatic lock-on for any firing weapon... that takes a while to get used to, as your ability to aim is also your camera control... perfect for the shotgun, but very tricky for the uzi. The roads themselves are far more lethal than the other riders, and while this is an excellent thing, currently specific conditions like the raining cars can make those races VERY difficult, and can completely shut down a run.
Its an awesome thing to see, mind you... driving through a downpour of debris, but that feature needs to be scaled back enough to be able to actually navigate through the falling wrecks.
Multiplayer is a listed feature of the game. That would seriously increase this game's replayability factor, and it would be AWESOME to be able to race against other players with this engine, but currently that feature isn't available.
All that said, I still HIGHLY recommend this game in its current state. Its very playable, low on the glitches, a TON of fun, and I have full confidence that upcoming features and fixes will just make this even more enjoyable of an experience.

Satazius is a horizontal shoot em up in which the environments are far more dangerous than the enemies you will be fighting. You have multiple weapons to choose from and unlock more the further you progress. It is not a bullet hell as enemies fire reasonable amounts of projectiles, at least in the first two unlocked difficulties. You have a basic fire and two alt fires which you can switch between, all which can be switched for different unique weapons to make your ship like one of a kind. One shot will kill you if you don't pick up a shield power up but scraping into the environment will kill you regardless. One thing to be noted is that the game worked perfectly fine from the get go with my 360 pad even though it doesn't say that it has controller compatibility on the Steam page
The one thing that was weird with the controller was that you can not bind the pause button to it which  can be problematic. No dpad support either which is not too great considering the environments require pixel perfect navigation. On top of your already massive fire power you have a special rechargeable move which is really helpful against bosses. There is also powerups scattered around the level to further increase your damage and speed. All this makes you sound overpowered as heck, and you are actually pretty overpowered and the devs know it.  They will constantly sucker punch you with things you had no way to see coming instead of offering a fair challenge.
You are offered 9 continues each which grants you three lives a pop. Most of my deaths felt pretty cheap and made it into a trail and error type of game until you memorize the level. If you don't enjoy flying through very narrow insta-kill environments with little time to react this is not the game for you. Being only 7 levels long means having a high difficulty is kind of necessary but knowing that doesn't make it any less annoying when you have to traverse a ton of hazards, get sucker punched and have to repeat that section again. Each time you die you are thrown back into a previous checkpoint instead of simply respawning. It does lengthen the game and it does feel like an arcade game for better or worse.
Graphics are nice and have a decent amount of detail to them. The explosions and debris flying around after you shoot down enemies look great as well.  It runs at 60fps which is another point in it's favor. Even the music is pretty catchy. Outside of the main mode you have a “practice” mode where you can choose any level to play but you don't have any continues which makes it harder than playing through the actual game. Do not press the escape key or you will shut down the game. The key to pause the game is “Q” for some reason. This game does feature cool looking giant bosses but most get absolutely devastated when you use your special move making them kind of a pushover.
Satazius is by no means a bad game. It's just that if you are expecting some fun shooting there is very little of that here. You will just be holding down the fire button and trying to navigate the environments which pose a far greater threat to you. And having to control your ship with the analog stick or keyboard makes it far more difficult than it should be. It is difficult and unfair but it is still fun to mix and match your weapons to blast through levels. Overall this is a solid title if you are in to arcade like shoot em ups and is recommended to those that can deal without a dpad.

So going into this game I was worried.
They slapped a five dollar price tag on their sequal, to a game that I like. But looking at the original, I though to myself I would not have bought it, even as much as I enjoyed it. So if they expect me to buy their sequal, it oughta be damn good!
And... it's not.
The "choices" you make in this game aren't even choices really. They're more you just answering questions the girls ask you. These questions include asking if you're a virgin, if you drink and if you'd ever want to settle down and make a family. The only real "choice" in the game is to answer the same to both girls, as in do you give the same answers to both of them? If so, great! You get the good ending. If not, boo-hoo. You get the bad ending where they call you out and it's sad.
And that's about the whole game. I got the bad ending my first run because I told the girl I didn't like as much (Evelyn) that I was a virgin, but told the girl I liked more (Emily) I wasn't. I did this because I was not comfortable telling Evelyn that I had banged before. So at the end of the game when Emily is willing to stop talking to me because of that, I didn't feel sad or like crying, I felt like I'd just gone through some bs. What makes the game worse is that after Chapter 3 it doesn't really matter which girl you chose because they both behave and talk the same.
To be clear, even looking past the lack of choices, the game's story sucks. Girls ask you questions, you can lie to one of them and they'll find out, then they'll break up with you. That's it. The original had a much more interesting story and did not try to disguises itself as some 'choose your own adventure game', it was linear and it had a good, sad story.
Tl;dr, the game is very linear, you don't really have any choices to make at all and even beyond that the story isn't very good. Lie to girl, girl get mad, the end.
Some pros would be the immersion is really good, you really do feel like you're in 2006 chattin' up some babes. The addition of 'YouToob' and 'Facenook' were neat.

JRPGs that have a focus on story tend to be less open ended and more linear. While Trails in the Sky is one such JRPG, the story is incredibly interesting and well written. It's not your typical 'you must collect X amount of special orbs or whatever to save the world' plot, in fact, it's not really even a ' you must save the world' plot. The story follows two siblings, Estelle and Joshua, who are travelling around the country of Liberl as part of their training to become Bracers (basically this worlds' version of police). Things start off fairly slow, but start to get really interesting as more characters appear and they start to get involved in solving mysteries involving things like terrorism and government corruption, while also focusing in-depth on character development and relations.
Gameplay is, for the most part, fairly standard for a JRPG. While it tries to establish it's own mechanics, it ends up seeming more like a rehash of mechanics used in other games. It's not like it isn't fun, but it's not anything groundbreaking. I imagine there are many JRPGs that have this problem, so that shouldn't be a dealbreaker.
It's also worth noting that this game has an amazing soundtrack.

The Legend of Heroes (LoH) is
turn-based JRPG that can appeal to any RPG fans out there.  LoH is one of the most acclaimed RPG's on PC, and it rightfully earns all the praise that it gets; the game's story is interesting and intricate, the characters have depth and meaningful progression, the turn-based combat system is bar-none the most mechanically sound out there, and the game's simple but pretty visuals are a pleasure to enjoy.
Note: My playtime hours are low because I originally owned this game on GOG, where I played a significant portion of the title.
I'm a long-time player of turn-based RPG's, from Pokemon Red on launch day, through nearly every Final Fantasy game that's been released - if it's a popular title I've probably played it. LoH does it better than any other game out there.
First, initiating the system makes sense.  Enemies are invisible in the world until you come within a certain proximity of them, upon which time you can clearly see the enemies (no random splash screens into battles here).  This allows the player to both have to be cautious of where enemies could turn up, and decide whether or not they want to engage enemies when they appear.  There is plenty of time to avoid fights shoudl you choose to.
Second, the actual combat system is engaging and efficient.  Combat is quick, intuitive, and allows for taking a variety of different angles to combat; whether you'll be using full-attack strats, defensive buffs and heals, ranged magic or AoE attacks, or single physical abilities.  You can clearly see when your turn to attack is, what and when enemies will have the opportunity to attack, and adjust your characters appropriately using the movement system.  Them movement system is a grid-pattern that allows you to move a certain number of "blocks" each turn; this adds a dimension of strategy to fights (rather than just mashing attack patterns) and allows you to use positioning to your advantage.
LoH has about as perfect a balance between complexity and simplicity of RPG elements as you're going to find in a game.
Each character has their own items that can be equipped and changed, but since item drops are relatively rare you won't be adjusting equipment constantly.
Characters also have their own stats which can be upgraded to unlock various abilities; in essence, there are different stats that allow for relatively similar types of magic abilities such as healing (blue/water), pure damage (red/fire), debuffs (black/dark), and so on. Other than which TYPE of stats you want to allocate to your characters, there is no further micromanaging required; simply choose what kind of stats you want to allocate based on a desired character role (healer/dps/buffs), abilities will unlock for those particular stats, and choose what abilities to use in battle.
Unlike many turn-based RPG's you do not have to manage many different characters, and which ones you will bring into battle. For the most part, you will always have the same 2 characters at your disposal that you can focus your efforts on, and any additional characters that are added to your party are temporary and require little-to-no skill management.  I prefer this system and think it works well.
LoH does a great job at creating an intricate story that the player can appreciate, while also not having that story unnecessarily intrude on the gameplay experience.  There are no cutscenes to disjoint your playtime, and instead the story is conveyed through read dialogue between characters that allows you to always go through story elements at your own pace.  Even more important than the story are the characters in LoH - they are absolutely fantastic.  Characters all have their own depth, progression, and quirks that make them likeable, unique, and of actual interest to the player.  The characters also do a great job of playing off of one another to highlight their strengths, faults, and how they connect to one another.  In short, the characters of LoH are what make the story absolutely shine.
The art and soundtrack in LoH are pretty standout as well.  Because the game is a JRPG, it's definitely got a Japanese/Anime look to it when it comes to the character sprites in dialogue, however it's not so overt to turn any players off of the game.  During gameplay, the graphics/visuals are reminescient of Super Nintendo-Era pseudo-3D sprites within a colorful 3D world.  It's clean, simple, and works well.
Though I'd rate LoH as a solid 9/10, it's one flaw is pacing.  At times, particularly in the beginning of the game, the story can become drawn out and a bit tiring due to exposition related to certain characters, plot points, or the like.  While it can be a bit tiring at times, it's made up for by the fact that any of the content of these slower portions of the game is (generally) quite relevant to later major parts of the game/story.

Boy, was I excited when the latest Worms installment "Worms Revolution" had been announced. 2010's "Worms Reloaded" – while not terrible by any means – didn't manage to meet the high standards of the classic titles like "Armageddon" or "World Party". It was obvious that it had been designed with the arcade or mobile audience in mind, who don't desire a lot of customization. It was basically a PSP port ("Open Warfare 2" from 2007) with just a few tweaks, and it did show!
Cutting to the chase, "Worms Revolution" turned out to be a disappointment on almost all levels, BUT the best thing about pre-ordering it was the free copy of 1999 classic "Worms Armageddon"! In contrast to the watered-down "Revolution" "Armageddon" lets you customize almost every single aspect of the game – From weapon power, crate contents and choosing random or timed mines to the number of landscape objects or the probability level of first aid kit drops: Every player was able to tailor his very own game modes and this led to a huge variety of amusing play styles, which could also be experienced in the game's online multiplayer mode.
Speaking of online, Armageddon's online community is still very strong after all these years. I've been playing this game 200+ (!) hours within the last few months and there was never any shortage of online opponents.
I can understand Team17 were trying a reboot with "Revolution", attempting to appeal to younger players. It's not a bad game on its own merits. But if you do know "Armageddon" or "World Party" it's just inevitable to scratch your head over some of the design choices they've made on "Revolution". It's just incomprehensible that "Armageddon", a game from 14 years ago, feels superior and is in fact more feature-packed than the latest offering.
So, if you want a classic and complete Worms experience, I suggest skipping every franchise title made past 2001 altogether and get "Worms Armageddon" or "Worms World Party". Both are equally good, but to my knowledge "Armageddon" has the stronger online community.
"Armageddon" is currently not available to purchase via Steam. I hope this will change in the near future. It really deserves to expand its audience.

I entered into this game not really knowing what to expect and was confronted with a puzzle before I could even start the game, though I guess this means I already had? It is difficult to describe Pony Island; it has elements from a number of genres but I guess could be loosely defined as a puzzle game/mind f**k.
The game has a glitchy 90’s feel and for the most part uses a black and white, pixelated art style; there are some more colourful sections but these are not any less dark. The music keeps to the same retro style and does match the game but I did start to find it repetitive after a while in some parts. I sometimes wondered if the controls were a bit unresponsive and clunky, however the game is so bizarre this could be intentional!
The game involves navigating your way around a computer, hacking away and deleting core files. I can’t explain why without giving too much away, it is an interesting concept though. I enjoyed the puzzles for the most part but the randomness of the pony sections made them frustrating at times. There are games within the games and games within those; a bit like a freaky game of Inception, just with more ponies.
I completed the game in just over 6 hours, with 12/20 achievements. It confused me in so many different ways, some more agreeable than others, but good fun overall. I bought this in the Humble microBundle and paid less than the quite reasonable full price of £3.99. I did get asked repeatedly to insert my soul; I’m not sure if this is a kind of paid DLC but the price seems very steep and there wasn’t much info so I gave it a miss!
Now to ponder the moral dilemma of whether or not to uninstall the game.

Another issue is that sometimes the character does not go where you want to, causing miss-jumps especially when you're chasing down the almanacs.  However, I believe this is a problem in almost all AC games, and I've also encountered this same issue in the new AC Black Flag.  Probably just the way the engine deals with pathing, or maybe my fingers are not doing as what my brain tells them to.
Technical issues aside, I quite enjoyed the story and was interested to continue on and see how a part of American History is perceived in an alternative manner.
The Washington DLC is also quite decent, especially with the powers that comes with Ep1 and Ep2.  I was wishing such powers would be available at the end of the main story, or unlocked in the main story once this DLC is completed.
