Assassin's Creed III is another solid entry to the series. While it has some negatives overall it is a strong entry and definitely feels like a numerical entry to the series after the Ezio trilogy.
The game play does a great job of stream lining many of the elements introduced since AC2. No longer having to constantly hold one of the triggers helps make combat more smooth and brings it closer to the combat you experience in the Batman series by Rock Steady. Running through the forest adds a new element to the series and helped with immersion and felt fluid. It was the highlight of the game and makes you feel like a true assassin tracking prey through the tree tops and pouncing on them from above.
The story does a nice job of moving things along and telling a coherent tale from both Desmond and Connors perspective. While you start as a different character for the rather long tutorial (took me around 5 hours because I had to reach all the eagle views in Boston) it does a fantastic job of setting up the game world and introducing you to characters you meet down the road. It also has an interesting twist that I did not see coming.
The weakest part of the story I found was the main character Connor. The voice acting was flat and monotone. He seemed to grab on to the stoic Native stereotype and never let go of it.  Most of the other characters gave at least passible emotional range but Connor seemed to have a cloud of ennuyeux about him.
Other than Connor I really enjoyed the Desmond story line because it finally started to make some sense instead of being tremendously vague about what was going on and the Connor line had a number of twists and turns I truly did not see coming.
If you are an Assassin’s Creed fan or just looking to jump into the series this is a great point to start. The game play is modern and the story is something to not miss. If you can stand having to listen to Connors inability to change the pitch of his voice no matter the circumstances you will enjoy the ride.

Hm, what's to say? Well... it's okay at best. I got this on sale for $2 and I can't say it's worth more than that. The game is all of 30 minutes long maybe, assuming you play the zombie mini-game. Basically, Gynophobia is about a young male of indeterminate age with a paralyzing phobia of spiders and females. His mother slips him some strange potion and he goes on a mental bender within a dream, fighting his fears to overcome them. That's basically Gynophobia in a nutshell. While I feel like there is an idea of a better story to be had here, the work simply hasn't been put into it.
To start, Gynophobia has some buggy walking detection. The difference between a street and a curb can cause your character to bounce up and down while sometimes loading in from a continue screen leaves your movement (and controls frozen). Additionally, you can surf atop of enemies! Land squarely on an enemy's head and you'll be taken for a ride wherever they go. Dead foes also present walking obstacles until they fade into the ground.
Concerning the art, outside of the last boss, it's generally very low. The female zombie-like enemies resemble something from a cruder version of the first Timesplitters with poorly stretched out textures and barely recognizable humanoid shapes. The spiders are somewhat better off, but I'm not certain as to why. According to the developer, these are stock assets. Understood, but they really don't make things look all that great.
This is the kind of title that's bad enough to be amusing and I suspect it capitalizes on that concept so people like Jim Quisition (who gets referenced in this game) will give it free advertising and cash in value. Gynophobia DOES have the potential to be an interesting game, but it's so short and cheaply done that all the tongue in cheek references can't make it genuinely good. I honestly wish someone more competent could have helmed this titled because the concept is there, but the execution is barely worth the penny. The game is so-so at best.

Gynophobia has a unique concept and its quirkiness is something that can only be appreciated by fans of Eastern European game developers. If you enjoy games like Painkiller, You Are Empty, and Serious Sam, or if you're a fan of games that aren't afraid to do something 'niche', then you might enjoy this game.

First off, these games run on a toaster and can be played entirely with mouse alone.
The Trails in the Sky series is known for its
- amazing worldbuilding
- great characters (even the random town NPCs!) and story
- Estelle Bright, one of the all-time best female JRPG protagonists
- Olivier
- Falcom soundtrack goodness
- lots of text
- length (we're talking 40-60 hours for the first game and 1.5 - 2 times that for the second game).
- NPC dialog that changes after every little main story progress, telling you about their lives, problems, relations and the world itself. Their little sidestories can even span multiple games!
- and Olivier
While these games don't throw you into an epic adventure right off the bat, their slow build- and set-up deliver huge pay-offs if you're willing to stick with it. Basically, treat it like a good book and immerse yourself in its world.
Combat is turn-based with slight positional elements and an intricate 'magic' system (Orbments and Quartz) that allow you to greatly customise the abilities of your party.
And did I mention Olivier already?
If there's one thing I would consider a clear negative, then it's the battle speed. They feel just a little too slow, and since those games are long and you're going to be fighting a lot, that certainly adds up and can get very tiring.
Fortunately, there's a solution for that! Use CheatEngine's speedhack functionality, which works right out of the box with the Trails games. 1.5x is a nice modifier that makes combat snappy while not being ridiculous. I'd even say this should have been the default speed.

In the past, I watched Markiplier play all the entirety of the first "Emily is Away" game.  I thought it was quite amazing and very good—especially for a free game—even if it was fairly short.  When I saw the first episode of Jacksepticeye's playthrough of "Emily is Away Too", I was completely surprised on how much more immersive and detailed this one seemed to be.  This game clearly was going for immersion and emulating the feeling of living in the era where the internet was about to hit its growth spurt.  This game had so much going for it.
One of the things that I noticed right away from it was the nice multiple person talking mechanic.  In the first "Emily is Away", it was always just you and Emily—nothing more, nothing less.  In this game, however, it was more than just you and Emily speaking.  It made it feel more dynamic and more immersive as it approaches to hit the classic AIM feel.  The conversations within the AIM parody also felt fairly geniune and realistic; to a fair degree that is considered.  The biggest part that moved me was the realization that I cannot make everyone truly happy.  Conflictions can and will occur—just like in real life.  Upon realizing that, it really warped my playthrough for the better as I was struggling with all my might trying to make everyone as happy as can be to me focusing on a select person(s).
Overall, if you are one to enjoy stories told through only the characters as well as stories that focus primarily on development of the characters, then this will be one great emotional ride for you.  Otherwise, I recommend checking out "Emily is Away" first and then decide whether "Emily is Away Too" is worth the purchase.

I'm a writer by trade, so in a sense playing AdvertCity was treading familiar ground. Self-promotion and advertisements are an essential part of getting eyes on your work, after all. Those eyes on your work are ultimately what puts food on your table.
Out there, floating through my procedurally-generated city, I had a real sense of sudden connectivity with what I do in the real world. Picking my targets and watching, in real-time, how the campaign unfolded gave me a quiet thrill. If anything, I wanted more information on the outcome of each campaign: not just the amount of views, but the reaction of the viewers, their demographics... information I could use to more carefully craft future advertising programs.
It was then that I realised that AdvertCity had me. For all its flaws, I was revelling in it, pursuing more information, seeking approval, weighing up my finances -- more, more, more!
AdvertCity is a tycoon game with a cyberpunk flavour. As the owner of AdSplay -- a futuristic analogue of Google Adsense -- your goal is to advance the reach and sales of a suite of Megacorps through your advertising. Back them, gain their trust, and then buy them: the ultimate objective is a complete city takeover. Advertising is done both in meatspace and cyberspace by navigating to buildings or websites and selecting your method and company. As your funds and influence build, you'll unlock new methods and technologies to keep pace with your crushing loan with the Happy Banking Corp -- who, incidentally, are ripe for a little hostile takeover.
Unfortunately, AdvertCity is held back by its relentless conformity to an older style of game. Much in the same vein as Dwarf Fortress, the UI is a mess -- opacity between text windows means that it can be difficult to pick out pieces of information.
The uniform grey, slab-like cyberpunk city is thematically appropriate but it makes locating individual or specific buildings next to impossible. Constantly scaling debt and a lack of a method to pause the game means that, at least initially, spraying and praying becomes your best advertising policy.
Controls are another beast. Keyboard navigation is aptly floaty, which can take a little getting used to. The problematic part is mouse control. With no way to adjust sensitivity in-game, I found myself spinning wildly through meatspace and cyberspace alike. The game promises partial controller support, but it isn't clear what or how this is achieved.
Feedback on your actions is minimal. A lack of sound cues does not help. In a sense, though, that's an understandable decision: AdvertCity's soundtrack is absolutely fantastic. The bleak, acidic jazz perfectly matches the tone of the game. The hour-long soundtrack is sold separately and is well worth considering.
Overall, subtle touches combined and a strongly principled approach from its developers left me with a positive impression of AdvertCity. If Steam used a star rating system, I'd go with 3/5 stars. The game's flaws aren't always easy to overlook, but the immersive atmosphere, fantastic soundtrack, and engaging gameplay are worth the struggle.

Probably the only review I am ever going to write, but after trying to get into this game for a longer than I'd like I just want this perspective out there. I was not nearly as big of a critic of the first Watch Dogs game as most seemed to be. I thought the city was beautiful to walk around in ("BUT THE GRAPHICS WEREN'T AS GOOD AS THEY PROMISE" shut up, they were fine.) and I enjoyed the story. Now I know that's where a lot of people took issue with the original Watch Dogs. They think that Aiden talked too much about getting revenge for his niece, that he wouldn't lighten up. I mean, I think it's reasonable to be a bit vindictive after someone kills your young niece, but whatever.
Although apparently the directors for Watch Dogs 2 took that message to heart. Seeing as how in Watch Dogs 2 you play as this nerdy but supposedly funny SJW that, inbetween getting wasted on the beach, going to burning man to cheer up, and nerding out over a new cheesy movie with his friends, likes to solve the social problems of our world by playing "sick pranks" on the evil corporate masterminds. That includes tricking a Pharma CEO into spending a million dollars on a new rap album that doesn't exist, or stealing the prop car for a new movie that is making fun of hackers and taking it on a joy ride around San Fransisco. And the most bewildering part of these pranks is that you are murdering between 1-10 security guards and cops just so you can pull off your dope pranks. It makes no sense! They aren't some gang bangers who are selling crack to the youth of SF, they're just some blue color employee who get gunned down by a meme slinging hacker who is just looking to have fun. Hit the 50+ hrs on record played mark, so I figured to write a review on the game. And what a game this is!
The Developer, David Stark, pushes out updates singlehandedly, every once a while. Although it's still in Early Access Mode, it already has the markings of a fully enjoyable game. The community's input, regarding Workshop content, is two-fold: players can upload their creations while Modders can upload alterations & other content.
Firstmost, it is steampunk with its own distinct lore. Second, a world designed with Leonardo da Vinci and Niccolò Machiavelli seemingly at the helm of conquest matters. Third, marvel in the creation of "ant colonies" and the ensuing conflicts that come to play.
One will be designing airships, landships and buildings in order to find what works. Some of the technologies required are obtained through annexation of foreign regions. One will face additional difficulty through financial management, varied weather, spy operations and the occasional wildlife incursion.
It starts with the emblem, which is personalized through style, symbols (with optional bonus) and colors. Then there's the created designs that involve construction, armor, paint, decoration and naming. Creations can be up- and downloaded from Steam Workshop, while Mods can enrich the design space with various assets.
And on that bombshell, I will conclude this review. Do I recommend it? I do, the game grows the longer one plays, as if one is listening to an opera of creation.

Punch Club is a special game. While the strategy games have been done before, this one makes me feel a little like Mr. Balboa. The gameplay is simple enough, click items on the screen to interact with them, click on a location on the map to whisk away to that location. But the meat of the game takes one deeper and deeper into the world of punches and kicks. There are skill trees that will help you build a fighter that will suit your style (Hit 'em hard and heavy, dodge everything and pummel to victory, and have a ton of stamina). The actual fighting is passive, you choose a number of moves to pull off and the computer does the rest, choosing moves to use based on your stamina. At the end of every round you can make adjustments to your moveset or just get back in the ring. Simple yet with a voluminous skill tree there certainly is a high potential for strategy.
While you're not fighting you can be doing other things, like exercising, hanging out with pals, working to make ends meet, buying groceries, and getting into street fights. The strategy here comes from balancing your schedules around your current stats (Mood, Energy, Hunger, etc....) and events that are coming up in-game. A fight usually happens every three days and you must use your knowledge of the opponent you are up against to better prepare. Within the core of the fighting there are three fighting stats that you can raise, Strength, Stamina, and Agility. Higher strength hits harder, higher stamina hits more, higher agility dodges switftly. By working out at the gym you can raise those stats to better prepare you for the fight ahead. Here's the kicker though, your fighting stats will deplenish a little bit at the end of every day. Now, there are skills you can unlock to prevent total depletion from lack of focus in one stat but that's not the whole picture. Once you get further into the game the opponents obviously get harder so you will have to be more cognizant of your training day by day. And on top of that you must keep an eye on your hunger, energy, mood, and everything else; so, no, you can't just train all day. Also, exercising on one machine for too long will wear you out so you must use a different machine for a little while.
Of course, in that world as well as this, money talks and keeps the world spinning. There is a cost to just about everything and the only way you can make money (at least initially) is by taking on side jobs. These jobs also take away your energy and make you hungry and all that so there is that extra wrinkle to the strategy you must employ. All of this to further the story.
Yes there is a story to this game and the way you progress it is by completing objects found in a story tree. It's really a rather clever way of conveying progression to the player. While not every objective is made known right off the back, you can get a good idea of how every objective ties into the narrative. You simply are a man whose father was killed a long time ago and he now is trying to get ahead doing what he loves, fighting. It all starts off innocently enough but suddenly you can take performance enhancing drugs and take part in illegal street league fighting (which could seriously injure you so be wary of that). I admit I haven't had the time to progress too far in the story but what I have seen is interesting and leads me to want to see more.
I need to discuss the art style. It's great. The pixel SNES era graphical style is pleasing to the eyes and looks like they gave a damn in building the world of Punch Club. Being a huge fan of that graphical style I can't praise it enough. Really, that's about it. It's great. There's a retro look option that makes the game look even more pixely. But enough of that.
How about the sound? The 8bit style sounds complement the game nicely and the chiptune style soundtrack keeps me pumped and thinking my initials are R.B.
Finally, worth noting, while the game has a more serious tone, there are little bits of humor that interject their way to the player. There's some clever humor here and the understated style of delivery makes it that much better.
So what, you still need more convincing? If you like strategy heavy games and schedule balancing time management playstyles (is that a thing? Maybe......) then by all means give it a play. You won't be disappointed.

I would recommend Satazius to both fans of the genre and curious newcomers.
Satazius borrows some of the best elements of older games like Gradius and other horizontal shoot-em-ups, and is more forgiving than the arcade of games of yore.
Let's take the weapon system. In Gradius the player could choose their ship build at the start of a credit, while in Satazius the player also gets that opportunity at the start of each level, allowing them to select the best tool for the job at the right moment. Weapons are powered up in a similar way to Gradius, though here each weapon remains powered up as you switch between them. This gives the player the option of focusing on just a select few favourites, or else improving a wider range of weapons at a slower rate. Spreading the love, as it were. Upon death, the player is not stripped of all power; instead their weapons are just downgraded a few notches. This means death is not a double punishment, and failing once does not mean you're twice as likely to fail on the next try.
The levels are full of exciting set pieces, high speed chases and environmental hazards. Indeed, the environment is as much your enemy here as the enemies themselves, reminding me fondly of another classic horizontal shmup, Thunderforce III.
Which is a good point to turn to Satazius' few bad points. In those high speed sections the player simply cannot survive if their ship is not a fast one, whereas in tight quarters a nimble ship is easy to crash. The player should be able to switch at will, a la Thunderforce III, rather than having indirect control through power-ups.
And secondly, the music doesn't match the catchy melodies of the above mentioned games, or so many other old-school shmups. That would have just been the cherry on top of the cake.

In the past, I watched Markiplier play all the entirety of the first "Emily is Away" game.  I thought it was quite amazing and very good—especially for a free game—even if it was fairly short.  When I saw the first episode of Jacksepticeye's playthrough of "Emily is Away Too", I was completely surprised on how much more immersive and detailed this one seemed to be.  This game clearly was going for immersion and emulating the feeling of living in the era where the internet was about to hit its growth spurt.  This game had so much going for it.
One of the things that I noticed right away from it was the nice multiple person talking mechanic.  In the first "Emily is Away", it was always just you and Emily—nothing more, nothing less.  In this game, however, it was more than just you and Emily speaking.  It made it feel more dynamic and more immersive as it approaches to hit the classic AIM feel.  The conversations within the AIM parody also felt fairly geniune and realistic; to a fair degree that is considered.  The biggest part that moved me was the realization that I cannot make everyone truly happy.  Conflictions can and will occur—just like in real life.  Upon realizing that, it really warped my playthrough for the better as I was struggling with all my might trying to make everyone as happy as can be to me focusing on a select person(s).
Overall, if you are one to enjoy stories told through only the characters as well as stories that focus primarily on development of the characters, then this will be one great emotional ride for you.  Otherwise, I recommend checking out "Emily is Away" first and then decide whether "Emily is Away Too" is worth the purchase.

First things first: don't ever use the internet for looking up puzzle solutions - you will regret it and the fun of the game will be gone (forever!). Resist the urge to search for a solution as long as possible and you will be rewarded with much satisfaction upon cracking a conundrum!
Fez is a simple puzzle game. Join Gomez on an epic quest to save the very fabric of reality! Employ your spacial imagination to traverse the world of almost 3D! All you will be needing is: a few keyboard buttons; lots of logical thinking; even more intuition; a high-level of perception, decent observation skills and the resolve to not give up.
In less poetic terms, you traverse a 2D world collecting cubes. There is one catch to the 2D world tho - it's actually 3D, only the perception of beings living in it is 2D - you however are bestowed with a fez by an alien lifeform, which allows you to see another dimension. Thus you can turn your perspective around by 90 degrees and see the world from another angle! More to explore, woot!
Finding cubes is usually connected to solving puzzles and that is its main aim - as such it is fairly challenging. It doesn't lead you by the hand and you pretty much have to surmise/guess/reason your way out of each situation.
I would recommend this game to people who would like something more challenging in the brain department - except for common-sense instructions on how to move etc. you have to find your way around completely on your own. There's even a completely different sign alphabet which it'd be advisable to try deciphering at some point in-game - just imagine how frustrating it is when you don't understand what people are telling you!

One caveat before I start.  This game is still unfinished.  There are really only three tracks, and half of a campaign to play through as of my last playthrough.
With that out of the way, this is pretty much the absolutely insane Road Rash successor that I didn't know I wanted.
The main campaign mode (the only thing implmented in the version I've played) is semi randomly generated (meaning that you'll get random victory conditions on the tracks), and has rogue like elements like permadeath and an ability to buy stats with the money you collected during a run.  The campaign, so far as I can tell, still follows a basic track structure.  It goes desert tracks for a few races, rooftop tracks (which is where most of the glitches seem to currently reside), winter track (which is basically a greyier version of the desert track), and quite literally Rainbow Road from Mario Kart.  What really makes these tracks dynamic is the random effects you can get.  Like all oncoming traffic, weather effects, or even raining and explosive cars.  Some of these effects are amazing, and really push the races from fun but basic to absolutely crazy.
The actual bike handling is pretty forgiving, if a little stiff.  It's pretty easy to stay on the track, barring some occasional blind turns.  I do kinda wish there was more tactile feel to the handling, since it really doesn't feel like you are even on a bike.  But in the context of the game it isn't so bad.  Because it works well with the game's combat system.
Which is the meat and potatoes of this game.  It is amazingly satisfying to club someone over the head with a pipe.  Most of my time in the campaign mode was chasing down and braining rival racers.  The more racers you take out, the more money and better weapons you are granted, thus continuing the cycle of violence.  The gun play seemed okay, but I honestly didnt try it much, since I really just wanted to beat more racers (and police, and random traffic) with melee objects.
Of the games three basic tracks, the desert/winter ones are the best realized.  The rooftop tracks I had issues falling out of the level geometry and getting stuck.  And the Rainbow Road alike track makes for an interesting easter egg, but wasn't much fun to race on, with constant tight turns and narrow track width, and no traffic to interact with.  But these are things I'd assume would be smoothed out over time.
Overall, thus far there's not a wealth of features in the game, but what is there is quite fun.  The combat is fun enough that I found myself slowing down just to hit more racers with blunt objects.  And doing so while cars are dropping from the sky and exploding is quite amazing.  I'd recommend it once it becomes a more complete product.  Even now it's pretty fun, but the glitches and lack of content mar it currently.  If a totally crazy and still very playable bike combat game sounds up your alley though, I'd go ahead and recommend it now.

Tycoon games always have a special place in my heart. Nothing like running a business, growing big, and smashing all the other competitors, and AdvertCity doesn't disappoint. Playing as an ad agency in a cyberpunk world, you must plaster name brands on every surface possible.
First, I want to point out what the game does really well. You can create a new city through the random number seed, and you basically have a completely different city every time, which is nice. The business aspect of the whole game is mixed with meatspace and netspace, which you must control both to get the best out of your advertising. Meatspace entails sending out fliers to setting up billboards while netspace deals with text ads and such. There's always the goal of expanding and stretching out your ad agency's empire, and it's a great feeling when you plaster the whole city with your own ads and rolling in the credits.
The atmosphere is great, and it's coupled with a fantastic soundtrack that makes you feel like you really are in a cyberpunk world. Even the little things like switching between real world and the internet also tweaks the music a bit to grant more immersion.
The game runs great with no hiccups whatsoever, and I hear it's optimized for multiple operating systems (I only have windows, so I don't know how it runs on other OSes). The graphics work well for the game, and does a good job of creating a cyberpunk atmosphere.
Unfortunately, the game does come with its share of problems. First of all, the GUI in the game could definitely use some work. It's hard to tell what buildings are and how many people are in them until you click them, so you'll be clicking through A LOT of buildings to better target ads, which is time consuming. It would be nice to know what building is the HQ of a corp, especially when you're looking for the bank to get a loan. The visuals definitely give a great cyberpunk feel, but at certain angles, it's hard to see some buildings that blend into the background.
The game also seems to like hiding some of its features. It's hard to tell what effect your ads are having on people, how it affects other corporations or even how it affects the building you're targeting since each building is owned by a different corporation. More management screens or something that's telling what's happening could definitely improve the game.
On a personal note, I would also love to see more corporate warfare. Maybe hire hackers or thugs to sabotage other corporations or something like that, but that's the cyberpunk fan in me wanting a little more.
Overall, the game is definitely worth checking out especially if you like the cyberpunk theme. At it's current price point of $20, it's a hard investment to put into a game. Maybe catch it on sale or wait until the price goes down.

TL;DR: It's not bad but... Definitely not worth 20€.
In fact, I feel a bit disappointed because when I spotted this game on Steam's Upcoming Releases, i was excited about the concept and bought it just as it released. Sadly, in my opinion, it fails to deliver the depth one might expect at that price.
What feels pretty good about the game :
- A brand new take on the Tycoon games concept
- Atmosphere and Music is pretty great
- Interaction between CyberSpace and MeatSpace
- Everything is dynamic, cashflow is realtime, city is affected by adverts... or supposed to be (see below)
- Multiple OS support (thanks!)
- In-game display of the ads
- Runs rather smooth
- Apparently has Trading Cards support despite not being on store page
- Occulus Rift Support (couldn't try it myself)
Sadly it has a number of problems:
- Basically no kind of game setup settings or anything. City size, difficulty, number of companies.. Nope.
- No options beyond video. I couldn't even find where to change keyboard layout (WASD on AZERTY ? what a pain)
- Game runs fast, and apparently without timing controls. All i could find was pause. When you begin the game and are advised to take a loan, you're going to owe twice the loan in a matter of minutes while you're figuring controls out.
- Most of the dynamism is completely hidden, it's hard to tell what you do has any actual effect
- It's a tycoon & management game. You would expect a few fancy visualisation screens and stats to guide your choices. There's pretty much none beyond a rough cash/debt graph and corp value.
- I couldn't find anything like a tutorial, so game start is pretty much planting ads left and right and hoping to make a profit. I have to mention you don't even start in the 'right place', and i had to click around to find out i had an HQ with an actual influence area.
- Because of the lack of feedback about what's actually happening, all you can do is spray'n'pray and watch your cashflow. What's going on behind the scenes ? No clue.
All in all, it's not really a bad concept... But for 20€, it's definitely not polished and deep enough. Don't buy it at this price, or you're definitely going to be disappointed.

Pros:
- Incredible attention to detail. All NPC dialogue adapts to the current state of the in-game world, all important NPCs have relevant tidbits to say regarding your achievements and your relationships with them. Villages and cities are beautifully realized.
- Charming characters that remind me of classic SNES JRPGs rather than the angsty and one-dimensional teenagers of other modern series I won't name.
- Good mouse/keyboard/gamepad support with rebindable buttons
- Slow pacing that lets you appreciate the buildup and aftermath of each chapter, and see the characters evolve few shortcuts or "fade to black" tricks. The daily life of the main characters is way more believable than in most RPGs (though that comes with the "slow" downside below).
- Turn-based combat, that is as fluid as traditional JRPG combat while having some real positional and tactical elements built-in
- Nice music, the track variety is a bit lacking but some of them set the tone of a place perfectly.
- Automatic difficulty reduction for fights that you retry over and over. As someone who has no time for this anymore, I think it's a better alternative to banging your head against the wall or grinding two hours to be able to beat a boss like we did in games of old. You can turn off this feature though, it might be off by default if you play above normal.
- Captivating story that really gripped me
- Somewhat linear progression. You move from hub area to hub area with room for sidequests and completely optional areas to explore. I still prefer JRPGs which let you loose in the world in search of the next plot hook, but this is a bit more relaxing and I'm enjoying it in that sense.
Cons:
- Veeeeerrrryyyyy Sloooowoowww tooooo geeeeetttt gooooiiiinnnnggggggg - 8 hours in, I hadn't even finished the prologue and they had only started to hint at some elements of the intrigue.
- Combat gets repetitive fast and I didn't find any way to speed up the animations (EDIT: I now use CheatEngine's speedhack bound to left trigger on gamepad. Heaven! All hail PC gaming!). You're also encouraged to grind early for gems to unlock ability slots.
- Enemies are damage sponges - I've outleveled and out-geared some of them which deal 0-5 damage to me when they attack, and they still take more than one regular attack to kill! You can't possibly lose, but you still have to go through the motions (or flee, but that feels lame), very boring.
- Huge difficulty spikes between regular wandering monsters, and the chest guardians or story fights. This is in part because usually you'll be able to attack wandering monsters from behind and have an extra turn to beat them up, killing most of them before they even get to move. The pacing feels all wrong because of this, at least compared to SNES Final Fantasies where I was fighting for dear life when entering a new area, which means I really had mastered the tactics when I finally got to a boss. Here you're basically running through and then getting a door slammed in your face.
- Leveling up feels anticlimactic, it acts as instaheal and (probably) increases your stats but it doesn't even tell you which ones it did increase. You get rare ability/"crafts" unlocks but not often enough to redeem the whole thing.
- While the houses' interiors are very detailed, there's little to no incentive to explore them because unlike other JRPGs, there's no hidden treasure, no objects to examine, no weird books in bookcases and no out-of-the way quest-givers. I guess they did it to cut the compulsion of checking out every single crate, but they went too far in their streamlining.
- Camera is annoying to manage when navigating towns and dungeons.
- Obtuse magic system with bonus-carrying crystals that you must slot correctly to sum up various elemental values and unlock spells. I found that it took way too much fiddling to distribute those optimally across your four characters, especially as the story keeps adding and removing those from your party.
On normal difficulty it seems that you can get by with only doing the story quests and the forced fights, the game will be much shorter this way but you'll miss on some cute areas and dialogue. If you are the completionist type who does all quests, finds all chests and grinds even a tiny bit to upgrade your characters, I can guarantee that playing on normal will be too easy.
In conclusion I'm recommending the game because I liked the world, the level design, the characters and tremendously enjoyed the story and it's conclusion. The combat was also mostly fun despite the pacing issues. Just don't let the Very Positive review score make you think that this is a flawless game... without a speedhack I think I wouldn't have finished it and would've watched the story bits on Youtube.

You are introduced to a big cast over the course of the game, wich is nice, so there should be a character you can like somewhere, although most characters are quite steriotypical.
Now for the bad. Yeah i know, it's not much good...
This game starts out instantly showing of what the rest of the game will be like, so if you like the first houer, you might like the rest of the game. It is extremly slow, there are tons of unneccisary dialouge that are supposed to emerse you into the world, but it missfires by a mile, only becoming tedious.
Maybe it would be better if we could get some early intresting story that would drive us forward, but no, there is nothing for HOURS. You don't get a taste of the main plot until the end of chapter 2, wich for me was like 20h in, and then its just a tiny small bit of relevent story.
If you like a LONG game, then this looks to be amazing, but it is long for all the wrong reasons.
Speaking of slow. The battle animations are soooo slow. It's not a problem at the start of the game, but later on you will be forced to cast spells that have 20 second animations repeatedly on ridicolously tought bosses, becuase as i mentioned, quicker physical attacks have no effect on them.
The mains story is very unintresting, with a villain that are supposed to be extremly cool and overly powerful, so the only reason in the end that you succed in doing anytihng is that you were manipulated all along. The game lays up big reveals wich are extremly obvious.
The female main character is so stupid and naive it's sad. During the entire game people tell her that her father is a big warhero, she even get to see him preform amazing combat feats at one point. So in the last chapter, after we've heard over and over again how utterly amazing her father is, she is still totally surprised when someone mentions it. Maybe she suffers from memory loss.
The developers are really proud over the character development, and how amazing personalities the charactes have. So proud in fact that they have to point it out several times, so that we know there have been character development.
(As for any character development, the main character matures a tiny bit during the game, wich is not saying much since she is ridiculously clueless at the start and mid part of the game.)
As for the quests, there are some that are ridiculously annoying, like you have to chase a cat pretty early on. You see the cat run into an alley, so you follow it and nothing happens. Run around the place and look everywhere, nothing happens. You have to enter the same street, but from a different direction for the cutscen to trigger..... But it gets worse.
In chapter 3 the there is the worst quest in gaming history. You have to search the city for different things, based on clues, like you need to find a 3-eyed giant or something. What might that be? Well you dont know, because it is impossible to see what the game refers to as the "3 eyes" if you are scouting the city. When you press a really small lighthouse, the camera pans upwards, showing the lamp of the lighthouse, wich happen to have 3 sockets......... and then there are like 3 more clues to do, wich are almost as bad.
There are tons of sidequest, and they are all quite generic. There are a few wich are okay.
Overall, the game gets a 3/10.

I'm honestly not sure why this is a Watch_Dogs game considering how rarely hacking is necessary, beyond simply calling a guard's cellphone to distract them before hitting them with the stun gun. The game offers you skills like Mass Vehicle Hack and Blackouts and whatnot, but I never faced a single scenario that came close to needing them. I'm not saying I was expecting a realistic hacking simulator, but if you're basing your game around the conceit that the player's cellphone can manipulate an entire city's infrastructure and the populace, you really should be able to come up with better scenarios than "Go to office building, hack computer" over and over and over and over again. What good are God-like powers if there's never any need to use them, and no creative ways to use them? This is basically an average, middle of the road open-world game with a "Press LB to do mildly useful thing" mechanic. Not exactly riveting stuff.
Story's hit-and-miss, leaning heavily towards miss. There are a few genuinely cool parts - Marcus and Wrench's friendship, the occasional bit of meta (Marcus fanboying over Aidan Pearce), some of the obvious digs at real world events. The core Deadsec group is a likeable enough bunch, well written and well acted. But the game has no narrative momentum at all - it's pretty much established at the start that Blume and ctOS are evil, and 20 hours later... yep, they're still evil alright. The game never builds up to a big reveal, or a "We have to stop them before they X," or any kind of narrative payoff. You kinda just♥♥♥♥♥♥around and mess with the bad guy until he arbitrarily decides he's had enough, at which point you get the "This is the Final Mission" prompt.
There's lots of small narrative threads that never really get explained, and many writing snafus (Sitara teases one mission with "You'd better bring explosives," yet when you arrive for the mission briefing, she says "Blowing up voting machines? Doesn't that seem a little extreme?"). You and your comrades also have a total lack of self-awareness, but I guess playing as people who realize what massive hypocrites they are doesn't test well. And there's gangs for some reason, but they are completely irrelevant until the game wants to make a really haphazard attempt at yanking your heartstrings near the end. They become relevant for two missions, then go right back to not mattering. All in all, this is not the game for you if you want a compelling or coherent story.
(Also, was the public really crying out for the return of Raymond Kenney? He's bland-on-a-stick. There's nothing even remotely interesting about him, but apparently he needs to show up to provide TENSION~ that never really goes anywhere.)
There's nothing about WD2 that's really awful. It's functional. The gameplay works (though it's easily exploited: if ever your RC car is spotted, just use Phone Distract on whoever spotted it - instant amnesia!). But much like it's hacking systems, the game is just completely inessential. It's unnecessary. It provides little to nothing of value. There's nothing this game does that hasn't been done better a dozen times over. If you want an interesting city to explore, get GTA5. If you want an open world game with a good story, get Sleeping Dogs. If you want a fun sandbox to play in, get Saints Row.

Once upon a time Rocky said to me: No pain!

Few millenials, reluctantly or not, will fail to remember Rocky's metaphorical ascension in the famed "steps" scene, catapulting viewers into Avildsen's diegetic spatio-temporal struggles. A seemingly simple character study, a
which was to resonate throughout subsequent decades and rarely grow
. Yet, gentle readers may be wondering what my exposition has to do with this rather more purposeful Tycoon, and caustic "2.0 children" may be neurotically snapping into a "Ur an idiot, lol *spout 21st century expletives and bile*."
Punch club provides a glimpse into those very struggles, and it makes sure you feel the pain too. Though at heart belonging more to the Tycoon-management genre, it blends elements of a character-driven romp and point-and-click adventure into a delightful miniature, one worth picking up despite the evident frustrating elements. A frustration by design, one that is intended; no success story is that simple, and rewards are sweeter if obstructed by seemingly unsurmountable obstacles.
The game's 80s cultural references do not stop here though, as it brings up a melange of tropes from a variety of mediums, including quoting video games in truly post-modern fashion, and it melds everything into a savoury broth spiced up by an appropriate measure of comedy. To TL;DR you; it's got Rocky, Big Trouble in little China, Sub-Zero and will make you laugh.
"How does it play?" You may ask. "As frustratingly as reading this adjective-peppered review" I may answer. In fact, I just did. The formula is "work-train-eat-sleep" and looking at bars filling up while you gain stats isn't fun, but once your character starts growing the sense of accomplishment is strong. The choice of skills and skill trees makes for enough variety in builds, despite some players indicating broken mechanics, and replayability is strong. Not to mention that watching your "end-product" knock everyone out in trainwreck fashion gives an evident sense of pride, like your grand-oeuvre is complete.
There is little pretense in "Punch Out" and it is evident that a lot of care and work has gone into the core mechanics, and the story is not half bad despite being slightly confusing. To a superficial and dismissive observer it may look like it underlies clandestine micro-transaction mechanics, perhaps initially conceived to quench the thirst of mobile-platform whales; but it is not aspiring to be Zynga on PC, serving a dish that is much more deep and complex.
Highly recommended, but not for the faint-hearted.

A great game with a lot of freedom in creating your steampunk machines - air, land and buildings. Play sandbox mode with everything available and the option to pit your creations against others in custom combat, or play randomly generated campaigns where you have to earn money through cities to construct your vessels, which you then use to capture new or defend the cities you own.
Currently, all it probably lacks is more depth, and maybe some tweaks. The campaign, for example, offers no diplomacy, no "empire building" except forces and conquest (so, no research, no upgrading of cities or sectors except through defensive buildings). And while they are a good amount of different parts, it still feels like the game could need a good batch more - to also offer more alternatives in what to build. Some items you'd expect to be a staple of an airship, like balloons to generate lift, feel useless, as they are easily destroyed and there is no real disadvantage to use a more advanced technology for lift - as even the price difference in campaign mode is almost negible. But these are all things that could be improved on, over time, as the base game is fun and stable.
Make sure you opt into the beta branch after buying the game.

This game feels like a hidden gem, which in itself feels incredibly rare these days now that the internet and youtube blow games like this up all the time. Something this good shouldnt be this obscure.
Yet it is.
Airships is a steampunk (Less brass and unnecessary pipes, and more just old timey tech on spider walkers and flying airships with zero aerodynamic properties) themed sandbox game where you design and battle airships, landships, and buildings. Its has 2D pixelated graphics, and construction is achieved via placing modular parts together on a grid.
The games balance is achieved via budget, typically you set a money limit to a match, and thats what your ships must meet, whether you use many small cheap ships, or one big expensive ship.
Its downright fun and easy to get into designing your ships, I often find myself getting into cold war arms races with myself, designing a ship and then designing another ship to counter it, and find its weaknesses, pitting my own designs against each other.
The game is in early access, but at its current asking price of 10$ it definately has 10$ worth of content, much like how Kerbal Space Program felt like a complete experience early on, the early access is less of a "I wonder if the devs will ever finish this and make it worthwhile" and more a promise of more content to come. The modding community appears to be if nothing else very dedicated, so if you find yourself yearning for more, you can always pop down to the steam workshop and grab a few new mods.
I highly recomend this game, it deserves more attention.

Aight, so here's some basic pros and cons
Pros:

In comparison, EA is filled with tones of shallow or short game for twice the price of this.
-Smart AI. Instead of just sending their ship straight at your guns, the AI will continue to manuever it's ships all the time to get in your ship's blind spots and vulnerable areas.
-Good pixel graphics, also makes it easier to design complex ships and for the community to make mods.
Cons:

-It's Early Access. So it's incomplete and might hits unexpected problems if the suddenly something happen with the devs.

As someone who doesn't normally enjoy horror games, this one surprised me.
Pony Island is a story-driven experience that starts off as a simple platformer and unfolds into a puzzle game that tries to outsmart you at every turn. It sells its atmosphere very well, and despite not having any jump scares or cheap gimmicks, it's chilling and captivating at the same time. The creepiest parts of this game are the places where it's completely unscary - where the game returns to 'normal' and you're just waiting in suspence for the chaos to return.
The game makes use its framing device (an old PC game on an old desktop) in many creative ways, and on several occasions it uses your actual computer's environment as a tool. The puzzle segments revolve around manipulating code blocks (using GOTOs and such) to change the game and would actually make for a really interesting game on their own. Overall, the gameplay in Pony Island meshes very well to its story and are challenging without becoming punishing.
The story itself is also very well done, and it's communicated through just about everything in the game. While I'm not going to reveal any details, I will say this: If you liked Undertale's story, you'll like this one. This game uses similar tools to propel its narrative and there are some common themes. Again, it's very good. There's not much more to say without delving into it.

Gynophobia tries really hard to symbolize a deep, dark meaning, but unfortunately does a very poor job at explaining or hinting to it. There's little to no continuity in the little bit of story that peeks through, levels don't match and feel stitched together, and the game ends as abruptly as it starts. The time I have logged in is almost enough to beat the game twice (it crashed towards the end my first time).
Spoilers Inbound:
Without extrapolating more information than I need to, you play as a young man with an acute fear of spiders and women, living with his mother in a rather small apartment. The game starts with you staring out the window in your mother's room. Quickly growing tired of this, you decide to go play PC games, but on the way there you are "ambushed" by a tarantula-sized spider walking across your hallway. After it passes, you are free to enter your room where you begin the first portion of the game, a crappy Left 4 Dead knock-off consisting of two short zombie-shootin' levels. After this is complete (no more than 10 minutes later), the doorbell rings and you are terrified to learn that it is a young woman with a very low-cut top. Spooky! You make a dash to the kitchen to drink your stress medicine out of a very ornate silver bottle. This makes you tired, so you need to return to the bedroom and rest, starting the second (and final) portion of the game: a dungeon-crawling shooter that plays exactly like the first portion, except now you have spiders to worry about in addition to the all-female zombie horde. Oh, and weird floaty head things. After a quick jog through two generic dungeon/cave levels and a simple boss battle, you awaken to find your courage restored. You charge out of the room, squish that pesky spider, and throw open the door to greet the young woman who had apparently been standing outside during your entire nap, and the game ends.
In Short:
Gynophobia lacks so much that I'm not sure I could even qualify it as a game. There's no variety, no continuity, no explanations, and not much of a game to play. As I mentioned above, I'm sure the developer had every intention to make this game as symbolic and deep as he could, but failed to realize what his game was short on: everything.

This game sucks, so lets start with it's redeeming qualities.
The combat is kinda fine. I played on hard, and the areas you visist basicly level caps you, wich i like, becasue the game gets more challenging. However, on hard at least, almoste all major fight comes down to you spamming magic on the boss, becuase they have insanely high defence, so physical deal little to no damage on them. I even had the best equipment possible for every single region, but still wasen't able to deal much physical damage, wich maxed damage from orbments (this games "materia system"). Apart from that, the battle is fine, even fun at times.
The Orbments or "materia (ff7)" is sort of intresting, but the menuing makes it tedious trying to figure out what combos you need to get in order to get the magic you want. When you are in the Orbment menu, you have to press the exit button up to 3 times, then go to items, find the bracer guide book, enter it, search it's pages for the one that explains what combos you need to make to get what magic, then memorise it and go all the way back to the Orbment menu. The menu in general is pretty bad.
After each battle you gain diffrently colored crystals wich you use to buy orbments to power up later. That system was fun, made each fight feel rewarding, more so then gaining som money and a random (often useless) item like most jrpg's do.
The art and facial expressions then characters talk are pretty standard, so it gets a pass. The into and ending animations are well done.
You are introduced to a big cast over the course of the game, wich is nice, so there should be a character you can like somewhere, although most characters are quite steriotypical.
Now for the bad. Yeah i know, it's not much good...
This game starts out instantly showing of what the rest of the game will be like, so if you like the first houer, you might like the rest of the game. It is extremly slow, there are tons of unneccisary dialouge that are supposed to emerse you into the world, but it missfires by a mile, only becoming tedious.
Maybe it would be better if we could get some early intresting story that would drive us forward, but no, there is nothing for HOURS. You don't get a taste of the main plot until the end of chapter 2, wich for me was like 20h in, and then its just a tiny small bit of relevent story.
If you like a LONG game, then this looks to be amazing, but it is long for all the wrong reasons.
Speaking of slow. The battle animations are soooo slow. It's not a problem at the start of the game, but later on you will be forced to cast spells that have 20 second animations repeatedly on ridicolously tought bosses, becuase as i mentioned, quicker physical attacks have no effect on them.
The mains story is very unintresting, with a villain that are supposed to be extremly cool and overly powerful, so the only reason in the end that you succed in doing anytihng is that you were manipulated all along. The game lays up big reveals wich are extremly obvious.
The female main character is so stupid and naive it's sad. During the entire game people tell her that her father is a big warhero, she even get to see him preform amazing combat feats at one point. So in the last chapter, after we've heard over and over again how utterly amazing her father is, she is still totally surprised when someone mentions it. Maybe she suffers from memory loss.
The developers are really proud over the character development, and how amazing personalities the charactes have. So proud in fact that they have to point it out several times, so that we know there have been character development.
(As for any character development, the main character matures a tiny bit during the game, wich is not saying much since she is ridiculously clueless at the start and mid part of the game.)
As for the quests, there are some that are ridiculously annoying, like you have to chase a cat pretty early on. You see the cat run into an alley, so you follow it and nothing happens. Run around the place and look everywhere, nothing happens. You have to enter the same street, but from a different direction for the cutscen to trigger..... But it gets worse.
In chapter 3 the there is the worst quest in gaming history. You have to search the city for different things, based on clues, like you need to find a 3-eyed giant or something. What might that be? Well you dont know, because it is impossible to see what the game refers to as the "3 eyes" if you are scouting the city. When you press a really small lighthouse, the camera pans upwards, showing the lamp of the lighthouse, wich happen to have 3 sockets......... and then there are like 3 more clues to do, wich are almost as bad.
There are tons of sidequest, and they are all quite generic. There are a few wich are okay.
Overall, the game gets a 3/10.

TLDR: Although it's not without its interesting features, I can't reccomend this game because its combat is boring, unrewarding, and at times, unfair. The story is also fairly generic and has too much needless dialogue.
I'm playing it on hard. I'm an experienced RPG player, and I don't mind dying in a game when it's fair. In hard, there are fights that are plain unfair. The games combat turns works in a similar style to FF10, the turn order is displayed down the side of the screen, and if one character is fast enough, they can get two actions in the time someone else gets one. Using magic takes up two turns, but the time between those two turns is reduced.
This is a small problem. You never know the turn order reliably, nor do you know more than one or two turns in advance.
By far the most frustrating thing about this game is the levelling system. You start the game at level 3. Each enemy you kill gives you maybe 10 exp. By level 5, these enemies give you 1 exp. There is no reward for battling, and even though you are two levels higher than the enemy, they aren't THAT much easier to kill. You lose virtually all reward, but you may get hurt badly enough that you need to use some of your mana to heal, mana being a very limited and important resource. I understand why the game wants to limit the amount of experience you can get, but it ends up just making battles feel like a waste of time. I fought a boss in which my main character was 2-hit, obviously I tried desperately to revive her. I ran out of revives, so she ended the battle dead, meaning she would not get battle experience. The other party members got 7 exp each. 7 exp for a boss that could 2 hit me.
Magic takes two turns, and your mana at the beginning is understandably limited. Unless an enemy is very weak to a specific type of magic, spells only do slightly less than double damage compared to basic attacks. Theorhetically, this would mean that there is no use for magic that isnt super effective against an enemy. The game devs must have thought of this, because they made basic attacks miss insultingly often, and made a few early enemies basically imune to physical damage. If you come against these kinds of enemies low on mana, you can't really do anything except run away.
These are just two small issues. I would also like to highlight some cool aspects of the combat. After each fight, you get elemental gemstones. The element of the gemstones is determined by the enemy you fight, For example, a plant enemy may drop 2 water gems and two air gems. These gems can be either sold, collected into groups of 30, 50, etc to open new spell slots, or used to make new spells.
This is fun and cool, but you are repeatedly fighting the same enemies, so I had about 240 earth gems, but only 7 fire gems. To open a new spell slot, you need 30, then 50, then 80 (continuously increasing amounts) of EACH KIND of gem. So to open the 3rd spell slot, I needed 50 earth and water and fire etc. It is exceedingly frustrating to have so many of one kind of gem, and so little of another, because it means you need to farm the first enemy you see over and over to get the fire gems.
As for the story, many of the positive reviews state that the game has a great story and stuff like that. In the first 7-8 hours, the story is fairly generic, and I agree with one of the other negative reviews that say it isnt so much story heavy as it is dialogue heavy. You spend the first hour reading, but you learn very little from all of that time. There are also some very odd sequences of dialogue. For example, when a passed out kid is brought into your home, your father starts randomly talking about how "auburn" the passed out kids eyes are. Why do we need to know? We don't, and that sums up a fair bit of the early dialogue.
This isn't an awful game, I've focused a lot on the negatives here, but those are the only things that really stand out. It's pretty generic, which is fine, but it isn't as good as it could be.

-The overarching plot is predictable.
-There is a lot of cheesy dialogue, especially in the early part of the game.
Pros:
-Grinding is quick and rewarding, but not necessary at any point.
-Combat is well-balanced and difficulty progresses at the perfect pace.
-Almost every NPC has a name and a narrative that continues to develop as the story progresses.
-Lots to collect and complete (Bracer Points, Recipe Book, Monster Guide, quartz, equipment, books, newspapers, etc.)
-Excellent soundtrack
There are also some recipes (most notably Apple Ice Cream) whose ingredients are sold in shops. The cost of the ingredients is less than price the cooked version sells for. This means that you can buy the ingredients, cook up to 99, then sell the finished product for a profit. Depending on the type of player you are, this could be a pro or a con.

I could not believe the disappointment I have felt when playing this game. So allow me to express my negative opinion of this game for you.
First off, I will be the first to admit that my Laptop ain't too great in the graphics, sound and processing department and is not the most up to date, so I would expect the game to be rather unplayable by mid-high graphics and sound settings wise; I have no problem admitting that playing a high quality graphics based MMORPG like Tera right here, so I set the graphics and sound quality to their lowest possible to make the gameplay experience rather justified. But not even that could save me from the dread of lag. I am typically an MMO Player, I play quite a few of them actually and I can run them really fine actually with my not so great laptop with very minimal lag, but I swear that simply pressing just any key seemed to cause a slight issue with my processor!
When I finally went through the loading times and started creating a character, I had felt rather disappointed by the lack of choices and options for making the character, even the clothing styles were limited but I was fond of one of the designs so I picked it. When I finally loaded my character onto the server. NONE and I mean NONE of my choices for the characters in designs apparently loaded in. My Armor/Clothing Choice, Hair, Eyebrows, Race, even the class of my character was not what I picked. I don't know why this happened, I assumed it was a glitch or that maybe I had to earn my look and design, but so far from playing, I did not see anything that implied that idea, even then I would prefer some context as to why this happened.
I am also not fond of the gameplay style where the game adopted two of the most famous MMORPG gameplay styles but melds them together in my opinion the not so greatest way. The control layout is not reccommended for people who enjoy using keyboards, it is better for if you have a game controller of sorts; but the layout is not very good and the problem is, figuring out how to change the layout was a pain to discover, I found out how to do it by doing some internet research which I found redundant because of the fact that it should be within the Options Interface. Overall the gameplay was the best thing about the game to be completely honest but even that I think is given a little too much creedence in it's regard because of it's derivative nature.
The story was not that great, mostly because of what I had played of the game told me very little; I honestly have no clue or idea what it is that I am doing or protecting or why protecting this tree is important or the signifigance of the land I was in. The story has potential but it falls flat because of what is not revealed. I at least expect to know who or what it is that I am supposed to be defending the land against personally.
I am sorry but I cannot reccommend this game to be honest. It just has a little too much problems that I think hold it back.

I'm honestly not sure why this is a Watch_Dogs game considering how rarely hacking is necessary, beyond simply calling a guard's cellphone to distract them before hitting them with the stun gun. The game offers you skills like Mass Vehicle Hack and Blackouts and whatnot, but I never faced a single scenario that came close to needing them. I'm not saying I was expecting a realistic hacking simulator, but if you're basing your game around the conceit that the player's cellphone can manipulate an entire city's infrastructure and the populace, you really should be able to come up with better scenarios than "Go to office building, hack computer" over and over and over and over again. What good are God-like powers if there's never any need to use them, and no creative ways to use them? This is basically an average, middle of the road open-world game with a "Press LB to do mildly useful thing" mechanic. Not exactly riveting stuff.
Story's hit-and-miss, leaning heavily towards miss. There are a few genuinely cool parts - Marcus and Wrench's friendship, the occasional bit of meta (Marcus fanboying over Aidan Pearce), some of the obvious digs at real world events. The core Deadsec group is a likeable enough bunch, well written and well acted. But the game has no narrative momentum at all - it's pretty much established at the start that Blume and ctOS are evil, and 20 hours later... yep, they're still evil alright. The game never builds up to a big reveal, or a "We have to stop them before they X," or any kind of narrative payoff. You kinda just♥♥♥♥♥♥around and mess with the bad guy until he arbitrarily decides he's had enough, at which point you get the "This is the Final Mission" prompt.
There's lots of small narrative threads that never really get explained, and many writing snafus (Sitara teases one mission with "You'd better bring explosives," yet when you arrive for the mission briefing, she says "Blowing up voting machines? Doesn't that seem a little extreme?"). You and your comrades also have a total lack of self-awareness, but I guess playing as people who realize what massive hypocrites they are doesn't test well. And there's gangs for some reason, but they are completely irrelevant until the game wants to make a really haphazard attempt at yanking your heartstrings near the end. They become relevant for two missions, then go right back to not mattering. All in all, this is not the game for you if you want a compelling or coherent story.
(Also, was the public really crying out for the return of Raymond Kenney? He's bland-on-a-stick. There's nothing even remotely interesting about him, but apparently he needs to show up to provide TENSION~ that never really goes anywhere.)
There's nothing about WD2 that's really awful. It's functional. The gameplay works (though it's easily exploited: if ever your RC car is spotted, just use Phone Distract on whoever spotted it - instant amnesia!). But much like it's hacking systems, the game is just completely inessential. It's unnecessary. It provides little to nothing of value. There's nothing this game does that hasn't been done better a dozen times over. If you want an interesting city to explore, get GTA5. If you want an open world game with a good story, get Sleeping Dogs. If you want a fun sandbox to play in, get Saints Row.

Organ Trail is a very fun game. And it's very comfy. But honestly, you're better off not buying this. The full game is riddled with bugs that'll make it freeze. I have never had that problem in the the flash game version. If you are seriously considering getting this, play the flash game first. If you still like that, consider if you're willing to wade through a heap of bull in the (pretty high) chance it locks up when you beat the game. This isn't even a rare occurence, this is a well known, reported, practically game breaking bug that has not been fixed in apparently months of it being known. And what does this version add over the flash game? Harder difficulties, but they're still pretty easy; Scavenging is absolutely overpowered even with the more difficult shooting controls. Extra content as far as picking what sprite your character uses, special buyable power ups, and unlockable starting vehicles. Plus, there's a minigame that's very similar to Spongebob's Boat-O-Cross. Not really a huge step up; the only major points are the new job system and being able to pick alternate routes at certain spots on the map. All in all, if you want to play, you should really just stick with the flash game unles you get this version cheap. Even so, be prepared to deal with lock ups.

As someone who doesn't normally enjoy horror games, this one surprised me.
Pony Island is a story-driven experience that starts off as a simple platformer and unfolds into a puzzle game that tries to outsmart you at every turn. It sells its atmosphere very well, and despite not having any jump scares or cheap gimmicks, it's chilling and captivating at the same time. The creepiest parts of this game are the places where it's completely unscary - where the game returns to 'normal' and you're just waiting in suspence for the chaos to return.
The game makes use its framing device (an old PC game on an old desktop) in many creative ways, and on several occasions it uses your actual computer's environment as a tool. The puzzle segments revolve around manipulating code blocks (using GOTOs and such) to change the game and would actually make for a really interesting game on their own. Overall, the gameplay in Pony Island meshes very well to its story and are challenging without becoming punishing.
The story itself is also very well done, and it's communicated through just about everything in the game. While I'm not going to reveal any details, I will say this: If you liked Undertale's story, you'll like this one. This game uses similar tools to propel its narrative and there are some common themes. Again, it's very good. There's not much more to say without delving into it.
While I have uninstalled this game (as it instructed me to), Pony Island is a fantastic game that takes a couple hours or so to complete and is well worth your time. For its price especially, this game is a must-play if you're looking for something unique and memorable.
It's a delightful meta adventure. Telling much more is a spoiler. Has 1 or 2 frustrating bits though.
The fact that this game is compared to Undertale and Frog Fractions is an insult to those two brilliant games.
Love it. Don't read anymore reviews, just play the game before it gets spoiled for you.

Picked this one up over the Steam Sale since the reviews were good and the price was low. For a dollar and some cents, it was definitely worth the price of admission. However, I can't recommend the game overall.
It has a humorous, well-written storyline and an interesting subversion of gameplay that allows and forces you to solve "coding" puzzles in order to progress. The puzzles are a superb highlight, and some of the storyline twists that alter them are brilliant and satisfying to solve. And it's also fun to click around and explore some of the more quirky aspects of the operating system for secrets and easter eggs. I especailly liked gaining an achievement for playing a certain infamous/famous hobby board game. That's MY type of humor.
But, then there's this other half of the game where you're wonkily controling a pony through faux-atari levels. It starts off relatively innocuous and boring, then progressively becomes more difficult as different weapons, enemies and challenges are unlocked. The control scheme never feels comfortable as it's a mixture of mouse movement and keyboard button presses, and the slightest mistake sends you back to the start of a stage. I was able to defeat the first two major sections of the game (complete with interesting bosses), but I stopped soon after and have never returned.
I enjoy difficult games, but they have to be fun. Every death felt less like a challenge and more like another wasted minute of time. I didn't rage-quit; I quit out of tedium. It felt like work to proceed to the next fun puzzle and I was no longer enjoying the quirky meta-videogaming veneer. I loved half of the game and dreaded the other half for all the wrong reasons.

On first look, I found the first game interesting, I didn't originally play it myself because learned it all ends the same, but watching I felt the pain the game was suppose to give you. It was an interesting experience that taught you a lot of things, like don't wait for someone and be daring. (even though neither of those options mattered to the game, but its the illusion on the first play that it made you think it did)
Come back to the next game, and for the first two chapters especially, it felt awesome, you actually get real choice in game, so I decided in my first play to see what happens, be honest and play it where it falls. Play myself pretty much. Doing this I had no problems,
So I continued the game, only thinking that was weird but that it had no hold on me.

That really ruined the game for me. On one side, it made me think even harder on my choices, but I became obsessive and paranoid about every choice I made that I was unable to play anymore games with the intention of playing me or a character, I ended up designing a strategy to best the game, (as I oddly seem to do when I start to notice breaks in the illusion, I did the same thing with the Mass Effect series, call me crazy) which I really didn't want to do when I first got it. I went from trying to play the game the "right" way to gaming it, and that is something you shouldn't need to want to do with this game. Aside from that, this game honestly has very little replayability. I mean better than the first one, and while better than like Mass Effect 3 in sense of ending choices, the game is not as clever with hiding its trick on the second playthrough, (which it clearly expects given all the secrets that require replays, granted you could look them up, but it seems that was at best an afterthought) I mean the choices you made being reiterated perfectly verbatim feel kinda flat for both characters, Evelyn and Emily can end up saying almost the exact same things with some simple choice flips, and your player choice changes due to the character are no longer hidden in any way from the player, I don't recall any real changes from chapter to chapter on the second playthrough that don't involve the little extras you unlock, and I've yet to see if they affect the "plot." (but I doubt it) All that given, there isn't really anything new to playthrough a second time at all, except the endings, which are probably more effort than they're worth to get, given how the conversations stay pretty much the same all the way to the fifth chapter.
One thing I think about this game is the dev was thinking that instead of reiterating an emily is away sequel where it does the same thing, he was trying to do something new. Doing so, he pulled probably one of the most popular ideas of "the happy ending" people and "give me real choice" people. And while it did make it interesting, what he wrote up and designed out didn't line up with those "features," (or objectives if you'd like) and it seems more like a lot of the attempt was too heavily mixed with trying to implement more design of the original game back. As a result, while in select moments Evelyn and Emily both seem unique, especially in dialogue, there are way too many times they are functionally equal, and it if not for the writing, they may have been easy to confuse. I think if Kyle wanted to push this idea, his design needed to be much more devoted to creating an experience that made the characters feel different, and not by just stating it, but by acting it out, cause as of now, the ingame actions of both characters are basically the same and the only difference between any particular action is who you choose. (or none in that case too, which I haven't seen or tried yet)
Given all this, I do recommend it, I'm a little sketchy on five dollars for it, while fun and interesting first time through, (
) unless the content gets changed, updated, or we get workshop content, it'll probably be a waste for most, as the current core game offers very little actual payback after the first playthrough. I'm hoping Kyle sees this type of critque (and I'm hoping I'm not alone in it) and is willing to do one of those things, (I'd really like him to do all three, but even just a longer and more planned out experience would put this game far enough to ignore the price tag) but as of yet, great game, sketchy ending (
) with only one really interesting unique design choice, but it has potential to be improved upon, as long as the dev continues to improve its design. (and maybe some more content, and/or add player made content)
So yeah, I recommend it, but I also recommend you wait and see if Kyle plans to do more with it first before buying.
