Even looking on the release horizon Im not sure we will get another game like tera any time soon.
Its probably still worth checking out if you are a new player, although I guess this review really just turned into me waxing nostalgic and isnt much use to new people looking to try. I say go for it, just...dont expect to stay long.  I wish I could give this a sideways thumb for the current game.

Section 8: Prejudice is a Sci-fi First-person shooter developed by TimeGate Studios and released in 2011. Section 8: Prejudice implements different characteristics to break up the monotony of standard First-person shooter competitive multiplayer gameplay.
Section 8: Prejudice takes place after it's predecessor “Section 8”
. Alex Corde,
is reviewing basic training and learning how to use the various weapons and tools with the 8th Armored Infantry.
Suddenly the 8th Armored Infantry is threatened and the United States Empire
goes to war again with a group known as the “Arm of Orion”. The basic gist of the rest of the game is: completing various objectives on different planets and trying to track down the leader of the Arm of Orion.
Section 8: Prejudice had many unique qualities making it a great game competitive multiplayer First-person shooter, unfortunately there aren't very many people playing it anymore, so multiplier has mostly dried up.
Rather then focus on the qualities that Section 8: Prejudice shares with mostly all First-person shooters (usual classes, usual weapons, usual game modes), some different qualities are:
When you spawn, you drop through the atmosphere from drop ships above the map, you can select where to spawn, unless someone has placed an Anti-Air Turret …then you'll probably die from Anti-Air Fire unless you're extremely well armored.
The classes are completely customization, with different armor skins, various weapons, stats, and armor boosts.
You can purchase vehicles, turrets, sensors and supply depots by using “Requisition points” that you earn from accomplishing various tasks, challenges, and kills.
One final tool to mention, and also my personal favorite the “repair tool”, you can use this tool to repair your armor, your vehicles, your turrets, just about anything with a health bar. You can also set it up so that you siphon health from enemies.
There are no
achievements for Section 8: Prejudice, however you do unlock Xbox achievements.
There are 59 achievements with a total of 1250 points, the DLC: Overdrive Map Pack also has 9 achievements.
These achievements require a pretty good team of people to accomplish “Win a game on each map in swarm on Hard or Insane difficulty”. About half of these achievements are easily obtainable, a fourth are hard earned, and the last fourth require intense grinding and team work.
Section 8: Prejudice is priced at $9.99 on it's own, it's a pretty solid title and you can easily spend 10 hours in the game working on the campaign and offline achievements.
I do not own any of the DLC, but just to warn people ahead of time, the DLC does not work for this game, so don't purchase any DLC.
References:
Story: worthy of at least one play through. Gameplay: A nice change of pace from your standard First-person shooter styles. Customization, different game modes, classes, weapons, and repair tool all make Section 8: Prejudice enjoyable. Achievements: none on steam, but you can scratch that itch via Xbox achievements. Price: perfect for the game, however it doesn't hurt to wait for a sale.
I recommend Section 8: Prejudice to people who enjoy First-person shooters, and Sci-fi themes. Brace yourself for very little multiplayer activity, there are still people who love this game, and you might be able to start or join a group to schedule game days, but all in all you'll probably be playing mostly by yourself.

Originally I left a negative review for FEZ because I didn't enjoy playing it. I've come back to leave a positive review after putting more work into experiencing it.
I think that I finally realized why I don't necessarily enjoy playing FEZ. It makes me feel lost and confused as I wander through an abstract maze in order to gather tiny blocks in order to save a universe that I know very little about and don't care about much at all. Whenever I can't seem to reach a block it doesn't seem far out of reach if I just keep tapping the trigger buttons and rotating the world. When I can't get to a block or I'm forced to take one path instead of another, it's painful knowing that I will need to backtrack through the annoying maze of a world once again later on down the line.
However, the game is awesome in it's own strange, painful, and beautiful way. The graphics and the level of detail and the level of care that is put into the design of each area is amazing. You can really feel the work that was put into this game, but it is almost painful when you imagine that it was the work of one man. I can imagine what a confusing nightmare that the design must have been like, and it makes me appreciate the game more. I think that I can enjoy FEZ in small doess, so I intend to keep coming back to it. I'm sure that the payoff will be remarkable if ever force myself to finish the game.

Stephen's Sausage Roll is a hard sell in many ways. The graphics are extremely blocky and simplistic, the music is mostly procedurally generated and kept in the background, and there's initially very little in terms of story or any sort of context. There's no tutorial to ease new players into the fiendishly difficult puzzles - many people with only a passing interest in the genre will likely quit after seeing just the first few levels. The vague trailer, description and hefty price tag probably don't help either.
Still, once you strip all of that away you're left with one of the best puzzle game experiences available on Steam.
The basic premise for each level is that there are some sausages, some grills, and armed with your fork you must cook every sausage and return to the start to complete the level. The levels are made of tiles, and sausages are two tiles long, have two sides that require to be cooked, and cannot be overcooked or dropped into the ocean. Every level plays around with this simple premise, and almost all of them manage to introduce a new twist or encourage a different method of thinking - the game has almost no filler or tedium. This applies to the levels themselves: each level is tightly designed such that almost every traversable tile or obstacle carries some significance to the puzzle, and the later puzzles introduce a surprising amount of verticality (the '3D puzzle game' description really doesn't lie). The puzzles start off difficult and only get harder from there - you can expect to spend upwards of an hour trying to solve a single puzzle. In fact, one potential negative may be that some puzzles do appear too early relative to the player's familiarity with the game (
) and may prove extremely intimidating. However, the payoff of figuring out the trick to each puzzle and solving it feels incredibly rewarding, and it does convey a real sense of progression in terms of mastering the mechanics of the game.
An obvious game to compare this to is The Witness. Past the graphics and exploration aspects (for which The Witness certainly wins), the underlying idea is much the same. Both games don't explicitly reveal anything about their mechanics, instead leaving it to the player to figure the rules out. This concept is as essential to the game as the puzzles themselves, but Stephen's Sausage Roll does this more subtly, only allowing the player to experiment as much as the levels accommodate for it. Unlike The Witness, which have distinct types of line puzzles, it doesn't feel like new mechanics or abilities are outright introduced to the player; rather these abilities are discovered through normal play; sometimes even on accident. It's these discoveries that lead to the most mindblowing moments of the game; it's as though an entirely new layer of the game opens up, presenting multiple avenues for more complexity and teasing many potential applications of these mechanics. There's also the story element that The Witness has taken some flak for - here the story is simpler and told far more directly, but it still manages to be surprisingly endearing
.
So all in all, would I universally recommend this game to everyone? Absolutely not - this is a puzzle game at its purest that would appeal to a very specific niche of players, and you'll need a lot of patience and perseverance to overcome each of its challenges. If you're willing to make that commitment, then Stephen's Sausage Roll is well worth the asking price, and it may well be one of the most rewarding experiences you'll have in a puzzle game.

Emily is Away was honestly one of my favorite games of all time, just for the sake of it being so true to the ways I felt in those periods of my life and how I handled my relationships, and this game has built upon that and improved.
I honestly lived a very similar situaiton to the person you play in this game. I dated someone just like Emily just before I ended up dating a person just like Evelyn a week later in 2013, and it was one of the most heart wrenching things I ever went through. In my first playthrough, I chose to puruse Evelyn (who liked the same music and acted the same way as my first serious girlfriend), and everything she said brought back so many memories that literally brought tears to my eyes. When she sent me a link for Your Guardian Angel by The Red Jumpsuit Aparatus, I was immediately sent back to that night that the first girl I ever loved unconditionally sent me the same song and told me that she loved me for the first time. This game will pull at your heartstrings, even more so if you've lived these kinds of situations.
The dialogue felt very realistic to how I and others I knew around senior year of high school talked, and the timed answers mechanic worked well for how the story plays out. I felt like utter♥♥♥♥♥♥for not getting to an answer quick enough for Emily and watching her log out because of me hit me just like the first game, and my heart pounded in my chest when Evelyn said she thought she loved me, just like the first time I heard it from my ex. This game made me smile genuinely and feel terrible all in 2 hours, which I love so much. If you're on the fence about it, save 5 bucks and please get it. This game is expanding my perspective on what makes a game good and how much influence it can have on how we think and feel.

What if the devil programmed an arcade game with cutesey graphics to trap people's souls? That's the premise here, and it could've just been a simple, stupid 10-minute Flash game. Instead, Pony Island is a fleshed-out experience that moves along at a brisk pace, but really puts thought and attention to detail into every aspect. Expect metahumor and clever twists, somewhat like the Stanley Parable. However, while The Stanley Parable was a very literate deconstruction of narrative in games, Pony Island doesn't really care about depth. So this is early access and in alpha.
It's pretty much Road Rash taken to 11.  You get guns, a samurai sword, c4, all kinds of weapons, a nitro boost, a jetpack maneuver, a really responsive drift, oceans of traffic, and various objectives.
It is also very much like a rogue-like.  You earn experience and cash by beating up other racers and completing objectives.  You start with one life and you buy yourself upgrades and/or lives with cash to continue beating random, escalating scenarios. You spend experience on permanent upgrades after you run out of lives and those upgrades will carry over to a fresh cycle (pun not intended).
Graphics are very good, but lacking an artistic direction to really set it over the top to make it something unique and special.  The music covers many different genres, and it is basically all very good and upbeat.
Also, there is ragdoll.
I don't recommend buying at the price they're offering.  I would recommend it at five bucks.  It's one of the better arcade experiences I've played and it's only in alpha.

In it's current state, v0.813, the game is already an incredible amount of fun.

Weapons ranging from sledgehammers to battle axes to C4 give enough variation to wanna try them all.
The campaign mode currently exists out a number of missions to complete like a normal race, attract police, kill a number of enemies (sometimes without using weapons). These modes are mixed up with some crazy stuff like cars dropping from the sky, driving on rooftops or even using jumpjets. Gotta say the first time those cars came down I was like 'What up with that? AWESOME!!!' On the other hand it can also be slightly frustrating in the later levels, cause if you die you start from scratch. The game uses two types of 'powerups' one persisted and bought by XP the other only counting a lifetime and are bought with money earned for taking down enemies and winning races. These 'powerups' are mainly about, get more life, get stronger, get more ammo for weapons etc.
The races itself are extremly frantic and fast paced, this will cause you to crash from your bike every now and then showing a ragdoll effects which reminds me much of fallout 2. And with all the sillyness in the game already who knows it might get a stunt mode as well? :D
This version does not have the competitive mode yet so i'm really looking forward to that, cause that could make or break a game like this.
Now to sum up what I really like about the game
- Awesome fast paced racing and combat
- Funny diversions like raining cars and jumpjets.
- A good set of weapons.
- The temporary skills (don't like the permanent ones so much, it makes the game a lot easier).
- It's easy to drop in for just a few races.
So far i've run into a few issues:
- Inifite loading bug, usually occurs around mission 11 for me, havent been able to play that mission yet.
- Framerate can be a bit low in certain places (however i don't doubt this will be fixed).
- Firing weapons with a gamepad can be a bit tricky, the default rb key to shoot doesn't feel right for me. I also kinda doubt that using a gamepad for competitive mode later on will be a real option since shooting with the mouse is way to accurate to be fair.
All in all I can only say I think this game is on it's way to being awesome.
For an early access title it's already very playable aside from the loading bug and the framerate issues.
Considering it's an early access title I would rate this 8/10.

Tons of funny references, a catchy soundtrack that's bound to get stuck in your brain, and a variety of ways to build up your fighter. You start out trying to avenge your father's death by recovering the Medallion he gave to you and your brother. Along the way you gain allies and rivals as you build yourself up to being a true Contender.
Pros: Great 16-bit looking graphics and music. The music was catchy and the fights remind me of an elaborate game of rock-paper-scissors. Managing all the aspects of your career (money, health, stamina, hunger, strength, agility, and stamina) is challenging and you really need to think about what you are going to prioritize. The game has some replay value as you'll probably find your second run through MUCH easier than the first. The game also takes place over several locations, allowing a change of scenery. Looking back after my initial start there are several 'mercy' options available if you get 'stuck'.
Cons: The game can be extremely grindy. Each day your stats automatically go down, so you're constantly having to train to keep them up. The only thing that really 'stays' are your skills/perks. Losing fights can be a major setback, requiring long periods of re-training and recovery. Running out of money and being too hungry/tired to work can be a pitfall for some players. These can be circumvented, but it tends to nudge the player toward min-maxing in order to ensure a smooth progression.
Overall it is a really fun game, and definitely worth $9.99 . I'm really looking forward to future balancing by the devs, to make a great game fantastic.

Punch Club! is a throwback to everything 80s. You're a punk out to avenge your father's death through YOUR GODDAMN FISTS. Life's hard and you have to work hard and train hard. Think it's okay to spend a day chilling with your bro,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥the day away? World champs don't have time for that.
Punch club shows the difficulty of trying to maintain a life balance whilst trying to hone your body. Yes that day at the gym will be wasted if you spend a whole week delivrring pizzas. But a man has got to eat and how else will you put something on the dinner table whilst a scrapping the barrel of the rookie league boards?
Punch club gives you the choice of trying to find the killer by being a legit world class struggling to make ends meet or go through the underworld where you may face other challenges with a branching storyline.
As for the gameplay, punch club forces you to balance your time and money. Your stats: Strength, Agility and Stamina are increased by using gym equipment ( one kind of training has a fatigue meter forcing you to use less efficient ones if you wish to train one stat more in a time frame) and stats degrade daily. Eventually to surpass certain limits you will need to make training a full time duty.  There are also Skills which are unlocked from skill points earnt from fights. Therefore combat experience will allow the benefits of training to come to fruition. The skill tree branches according to which stat you wish to focus on.
Fights are mostly automatic where you choose the skills you want for the round and then watch. Rounds last 30s and vary in number depending on 'tournament' rules. Will you focus on high accuracy moves to catch the pesky dodgers, attempt to exhaust them with blocks and hard throws or become whirlwind counter attacker? You can see your upcoming opponent usually and spend the days of training crafting your strategy to beat them - this can be quite important! You don't want try to tire out a boundless ball of energy or focus on hard hitting but inaccurate slugs against a nimble foe.
However don't expect to learn more than 1 or 2 moves before your next fight. One snag of strategy is the imbalance between builds. As of now, agility based builds are generally considered superior. What good is your strength if not only to your exhausting yet killer punches not only fail to connect at all but also injure yourself for a proportional amount? My high level strength character had to rely on basic boxing punches to catch moderate agility foes without raising agility equal to theirs and a repeated misses would devastate myself; meanwhile their weakness is just a lower Hp pool with their damage based on doing my damage back to me albeit more reliably!. Hopefully the developers will even the routes out and even days after release have been working tirelessly to address our criticisms. Agility currently is an absolute must to maintain a bare minimum of near parity with your opponent whilst the other two are optional. This may be as simple to fix as just lowering the dodge chances however so expect this game to be in a better state soon.
Is it worth it now? Mostly depends on how much much you like grinding. Those liking jrpgs shouldn't have much issue but if you want something suited for quick blasts, no. Right now the game can be a bit frustating at times before you've developed your style and hav eexperimented around. At the same time part of the charm is the difficulty; I do not think there is any sort of gameover mechanic i.e. death, running out of time etc., stat degradation can mean you may find yourself in a slump where progression feels challenging. If you're having a hard time maybe someone might just offer you a 'magic potion'. Either way any fan of 80s TV and old fighting games will be sure to love all the cheeky nods.

The emPHAsis is on the wrong SylLABle.

This game would do better with more emphasis on the fights, and less time spent managing an eat/sleep/work/training schedule, or at least a way to scheudle and automate it. RPG Goodness
Very enjoyable RPG from the Trese Brothers.  Similar to Baldur's Gate, etc... Build and lead your team of 4 through a story-driven tale, with combat, big dungeons, towns, side missions, character development.  Upgrade various facets of each team member over time, improve their armor, skills and weapons. Variety of maps, enemies, bosses.  Recent performance and UI improvements, further strengthening of the story and storyline interactions are simply delicious icing on this game.  Every release gets better and better.
Value
After 80 hours of gameplay, I finished Episode 1 of the game, and there are 4 total so far.  All without DLC.  Gameplay is deeper the longer you play, and there are 4 difficulty levels, and an optional upgrade for 4 additional characters is available.  Replay value is high due to ability to mix and match characters.  Note: I am primarily playing my current game on iPad, so have well over 150 hours total, and I'm nearing completion of episode 3.  The devs are working on expanding episode 4, so there is incredible value in this game.
Accessible Developers and Community
The developers are very active with this game (all of their games actually), and continually upgrade, improve gameplay, squash bugs based on user feedback and advice.  They have a forum for their games, and the community is mature, helpful.  Questions about strategies? Stuck on a map? Want ideas on team builds/upgrades? Replies from uber-players and the developers come within hours, if not minutes.

For an I-phone port to steam this title plays beautifully and has a unexpected level of tactical depth and over all appeal.

Of special note is the outstanding customer service of the Trese Brothers, I got a dev response on their forums within 20 minutes of reporting a bug, and that same bug was patched less than 72 hours later.
For turn based tactic veterans the game has a nice pick up and play feel, and provides an enjoyable challenge at higher difficulties, and even beginners will find the game easy to learn thanks to the introduction that covers all the important game play elements without being overwhelming.
For a light weight turn based dungeon crawler the fun factor is consistent, and it's easy to spend an afternoon exploring the various locations and finding some of the hidden treasures of the underground. (From magic rings to armor sets)
Granted the game might not be on the complexity level of Final Fantasy Tactics for depth, but it delivers a solid turn based tactical dungeon crawl that's well worth the price; and is a surprisingly long game for its size. (10+ hours in and I'm still on the first chapter.)
Give it a try, you won't be disappointed.

This is one of the best games, if not the best game, that I've ever played. The story is the main focus of the game, and it'll introduce to you an exciting, yet meaningful world. You'll meet and fall in love with many characters; you'll get hyped as every dialogue or action gains meaning over time. The story never falls short, and at every moment I was thrilled to learn more about it.
The music is also superb. With 57 tracks, there is an adequate one for every situation. Even after finishing the game, I keep listening to its soundtrack, reliving every moment of its grandeur. From remembering the casual setting of Rolent, when my adventure had just begun, to being impressed by the final zone, with all of its glory and mystery, the music is always there to make me feel the game again.
Last, but far from least, is the gameplay. While this game doesn't have the features of tactical RPGs, the combat is streamlined and entertaining. You'll meet a large diversity of enemies, each one with its own particularities, and those enemies are what will make one battle different from another.
This game marked me forever. Interestingly, I've purchased this game by chance, on a Steam Sale. Don't let you chance pass. Buy this game, and enjoy this masterpiece.

Although this game was originally released more than 10 years ago, the graphics still hold up well today and the high resolution textures are nothing to scoff at. Menus and characters are still very sharp. The background textures are beginning to show its age, but the diverse locales definitely make up for it. The game also employs a chibi art style which is timeless and will definitely endear you to the characters.
What really sets this apart from other JRPGs is its great world building. Throughout the story, you will visit all the different locales and witness many events. The game frequently references other countries in the Trails in the Sky world and even gives some history of the world. NPCs also have their own little stories and whenever you complete a sequences in the story, the NPCs change their dialogue. This was a nifty addition to the game as you can follow the NPCs in their daily struggles and even laugh at some of their misfortunes. The locales, events, history and NPC sub-stories, truly make you part of the story instead of being a simple observer.
The main story is at times very intriguing also worthy of following. If you like stories where the main plot is slowly revealed to you then you will definitely like this. Dialogue for the game is also excellent with the main characters being able to make you laugh and cry and even inspired to do the world some good. Props to the excellent localization of the game as the sheer amount of dialogue this game contains was translated well to English and the emotions of the characters and gist of the jokes are not lost.
The only downside I can see in the game is that combat gets tedious after a while. I wish that there was some sort of auto-combat support as you can play most of the non-boss encounters by simply auto attacking. However, the customization of this game via “orbments” is rich and will provide you good entertainment if you enjoy min-maxing.

Do you recommend this game?
Not at full price and even then, not unless you really care about the story.
I played this game over the past week and I am honestly surprised as to what really justifies a rating of 8.
This game is nothing more than an interactive story with very little to offer in terms of gameplay.
Before you wonder "How could you have played this game for a week if you don't like it?"
I always finish the games that I start, no matter how bad they are.
Here's a quick breakdown on what's about to follow:
Artwork, Story, Combat, Puzzles, Multiplayer
Artwork:
The artwork does a good job giving the player an impression of the time-period of the action and allows proper immersion into the story. Going from zone design to housing to outfits. The Design for Connor (one of the protagonists) sadly is not very impressive, compared not only to other games released in the same year, but also compared to other games in the AC series. I am being more harsh on this subject, considering that this game is AAA rated and has a dedicated design team.
Story:
I know others consider the story of this game to be cliche, but I personally like the story. To fully enjoy the story you really need to explore everything starting with AC and all the way to Black Flag. Like a lot of other AAA games the stories really shine. This being said, the game is sadly nothing more to me than an interactive story.
Combat:
While the combat looks impressive, as do the assassinations. There is no real combat in this game the entire combat revolves around countering and attacking. You can't counter the same way on all opponents to make it slightly more difficult, but the difficulty scale is still laughable. In other terms... wait for slow motion, press counter, wait for slow motion disarm/throw/kill.
The combat is not satisfying at all, no matter how impressive the attacks look. Perhaps the combat designers should check out some real action games and come back after they learned a thing or two.
Puzzles:
The few puzzles I encountered revolved around Quick Time Events, reading BOLDED TEXT WITH GREATER FONT in "hidden" texts marked by a magnifying glass with riddles so difficult you feel you're being asked to untie the gordian knot.
Here's a dumbed down example: "Grand Lodge Above All (up), men and women in balance" Grand Lodge Icon (top, men left, women right, scales bottom)... I feel as if somebody asked me to tie their shoes. Such an impossible task can't be performed by a mere mortal as myself. These puzzles have obviously been designed for the sake of having puzzles in the game.
Multiplayer:
I must say the multiplayer experience I had was quite fun, even though I got my♥♥♥♥♥kicked a lot by more experienced players. In multiplayer you have to complete missions to buy upgrades, however you are confronted with higher level opponents right from the start, creating a rather ridiculous matchmaking. This is however not as punishing as it may sound, since leveling up is not very difficult. You have different types of missions: Identify & Assassinate a specific player while being chased by another player yourself. This sounds simpler than it seems at first sight, but I can see this becoming either very dull or very addictive very quick.
What did you like overall?
I enjoyed the story and the multiplayer experience, although imbalanced
What did you dislike most?
Combat and puzzles. The simplicity of both was quite insulting. Label the game for 3 year olds, why don't you.
Conclusions:
Beats me why AC2, AC:B, AC:R, AC3 and AC4 aren't all expansions of AC1. The engine is the same. Could easily have been a content patch and would have allowed for owners of the previous games to join together in a multiplayer experience, allowing for a larger player-base. But I suppose this would have made it more difficult to milk the cash-cow, similar to sports games.
Inbetween the story bits and pieces, the singleplayer experience was EXTREMELY boring. Sure roaming is fun for the first 2-3hrs but afterwards it becomes dull. I'd rather take a stroll in the park if I want to see nature (it's higher resolution too).
I play games for the gameplay, and this game had almost none. Shame on you Ubisoft, running from A->B for 15min does not count as 15min of playtime, I don't care what your statistics say.
At full price this game is overpriced, grab it for the story if you like, but don't expect anything else, since multiplayer will likely move on to Black Flag, leaving this game deserted and those with a competitive desire rather unsatisfied.
Awesome game. Lot things to do with intresting storyline. I Highly recommend this to anyone familiar with the series. PS. Axes in combat <3

This game is a shambolic mess of poor controls, oversimplified gameplay and failed stealth.  Whereas previous games in the series featured extensive roof networks (AC) and towering monuments (ACII), Ubisoft had decided that engaging cities were not, in the grand scheme of things, all that important, and ditched the huge, colourful Renaissance hubs for the mud and thatch American Revolution era villages.  Gone are the paved streets, replaced by mud ruts, gone are the beautiful ivy-covered courtyards.  It's a wholly uninviting and squat place to explore.
The crowds of ACIII are hardly convincing.  The children seem only to have one recorded sound, consisting of a laugh track which they will repeat in broken-record style until you run away.  Civilians can no longer be killed for an easy diversion.  Glitches abound, both in animation and in AI stealthing detection.
Character development is also inadequate.  Conor is by far the least significant, least fleshed-out character of the series.  He moves with the grace of an elephant, talks as if he has had no education whatsoever (to be fair, he probably hadn't) and seems to have no real motivation for being an assassin.  Whereas Altair of AC was a ruthless, faceless angel of death whose questioning of his cult led to his humbling, and Ezio was a brash and reckless young man whose family death caused him great anguish, Conor is an unwanted child who one day returned to find his home on fire and who promptly did absolutely NOTHING of consequence.  We don't care about Conor because he seems to be the sole contributor to Desmond's personality.  There is nothing in Conor that we would ever wish to be, and no amount of shoddy combat can ever fix such failure in story.
AC's combat was a bit rough around the edges, but it involved a fair amount of timing which could be passed off as "skill" in the sense that if one won entire wars with single button presses, then becoming expeditious at pressing that one button might be something to be proud of.  Nevertheless, there was a certain satisfaction in killing the final templar with a single strike; in that one perfect moment, facing his (then) greatest enemy, Altair truly seemed to be a weapon without equal in his effortless dispatch of anyone in his way.  Ezio wasn't quite as good as this, but at least he had nifty climbing abilities and additional fighting moves, and was still able to fight in a flowing manner more reminiscent of a dancer than a thug.  Conor unfortunately is just a thug.  He moves like a clown (vaulting over walls with more effort than Mr. Bean) and his attacks are purely brute force, which would suit Hitman's Agent 47 more than a supposed Assassin.  His attacks are also purely contextual animations; if no one is in range when an attack is initiated, he flails his arms around in a poor flourish rather than actually swinging his weapon, and it looks ridiculous.
The controls are the final nail in the coffin.  The mouse control should remain the same in menu and game; it doesn't.  AC I required two buttons to be held to run, one separating "high profile" actions from "low," and it worked reasonably well.  ACII upped this with the sprint, which was a welcome change.  In both games the Spacebar, E key and Shift performed actions that required little directional input (except for grab, but that was a small thing), which was crucial because the left hand on PC spends most of its time covering the WSAD keys.  ACIII decided that it was preferable to suddenly change the Counter command from Right Mouse Button + Left Mouse Button to an E key binding, and dispose of the "High profile" in favour of making Right Mouse Button "Sprint."  Surely if one button is to be made Sprint it should be Shift, given its close proximity to the WSAD and the fact that the left hand controls character movement.  Common sense would surely dictate that the second most important controlling button, RMB, should not be stripped of its previous functions and relegated to a purely ancillary role.  All these things come second nature with any measure of good judgement.
Ultimately, common sense and good judgement are exactly what this game lacks.
*Edited time for accuracy.

This is, at the time of this review, an Early Access title with some definite rough edges.  However, it is already a very playable game that, although somewhat Spartan (See: Starkly functional, not kicking people into pits) in it's presentation don't let that fool you.  There is quite a bit going on under the hood.
The theme reminds me of World War I scaling combined with H.G. Wells-like steampunk and fanciful technology with just a little sprinkling of fantasy in there.  The world is locked in bleak war with giant airships and landships at the front of the battle.  Rather than helium, your airships are held aloft with "suspendium", either as a dust in balloons or as a sort of engine housed in the ship's interior.
Ship design is an interesting balance between weight, lift, propulsion, durability, crew requirements, and cost.  Sure, you could sacrifice some armor to drop some weight and add an extra weapon, but you risk going up like a matchstick if you do.  Or perhaps you want to build a secondary suspendium chamber for extra lift and redundancy in case the other one is taken out?  Good idea, but remember that you need coal to power the various functions of your ship, which means more modules, more weight, more cost.
You also can design "land ships" which is pretty much the same as designing an airship sans lift components.  Instead you have a selection of mech-like legs and tank-like tracks to choose from.  They don't have the advantage of flight, but this also means weight isn't quite as much of a concern and they can make great, heavily-armored, mobile anti-air platforms as a result.
Lastly, you can also design non-mobile buildings as the centerpieces of defense in your territories.  You can really stack on the armor and weaponry there.  Just be sure you design the building to be resistant against fire, invasion, and attacks from multiple angles! Careful though, every module in this game has weight and physics and it's a huge disaster if parts of your structures begin to collapse on themselves!
There is a campaign to be played which is at the moment extremely simplistic but fun.  You send spies to neighboring states so that you can see their defenses.  Then you pay to sabotage them or build up your forces enough to overcome theirs and then invade.  As you control more territitories you gain more income, technology, and ship building ports.  Ships have upkeep costs to consider, and you need to budget your secret police (to prevent enemies from sabotaging you).  There isn't much to it other than that.
The game really expressly shines in the design and combat aspects.  The interface for design is a little bit cumbersome, but doesn't detract from the fun of snapping together modules on a grid.  There is also a bit of a personal touch there as you create unique shapes and decorate the ships with paint, banners, and decals.  You can then test your designs against the AI (or pit AI against AI) in the sandbox combat arena.
The combat itself can be pretty exciting despite how simple the game looks.  The way your crew operates reminds me a lot of FTL without the micromanagement.  That is to say that your little air sailors really do move around the ship and man the various stations, but you don't control them directly.  When you give the order to move, the crew runs to take coal from your coal stores and shovel them into the engine.  When you fire on a target, some sailors man the weapons while others haul up ammo.  Fires break out and sailors scramble to put them out with water, etc.  As you lose sailors in battle this diminishes your capabilty to run your ship efficiently, or can often leave you dead in the skies.
Combat is impactful, with holes being punched through armor, and entire sections of your ships being blasted apart.  Fires break out and burn out of control.  Boarders scramble in through your windows using their tiny little grappling hooks.  Battering rams smash you to pieces.  It's all pretty intense and battles rarely play out the exact same way twice.  Sometimes a very lucky shot is all it takes to entirely turn the tide.  Other times what seems like a bad thing - like your ship falling out of the sky - might end up a good thing, like that falling ship absolutely squashing an enemy ship that was unlucky enough to be underneath it.
There is multiplayer here but in an extremely limited fashion (EG - no multiplayer campaigns), but that could possibly change down the road as this game is still under development.
This game was a delightful surprise for an Early Access title.  It offers quite a bit of meat at the current stage of things, and is what I would call "fully playable".  I've already sunk many hours mostly just designing ships and combat scenarios alone.
With that said, there are some definite improvements that I'd love to see.  First in my mind are the landships.  Unless they are absurdly large, they are sort of ironically terrible at traveling on land.  This makes them far less generally useful than airships.
Also some aspects of design likewise seem entirely more useful than others.  Other than in cheap, small, suicide attacker airships, I found that using suspendium dust balloons is of pretty dubious use other than as a supplemental means of lift to suspendium chambers.  They are always targeted first by AI and are destroyed very easily.  So creating a giant Zeppelin-like craft or a Final Fantasy style airship isn't terribly feasible.
It'd be great to see traditional matchmaking for multiplayer as well as multiplayer campaigns someday as well.
All in all, though, it's all very solid and very fun.  If the screenshots/videos of the ship building appeal to you at all, then this is already a must for you.  Like mercilessly blasting apart your enemy with a 12 heavy cannon behemoth, you won't regret it.

Punch club is a fighting sim/rpg/tycoon style game.  It's very passive in play style, much like some anime style time-management games where you schedule your characters actions per day and try to have the skills and stats unlocked to accomplish goals.  There's content enough for at least two plays through the game depending on the choices you make.  There are some balance issues that still need to be addressed and the daily stat drain is brutal, but, that's mostly because they want you to play the game a specific way and the specific way is through unlocking and choosing the correct skills versus simply getting high stats.  This forcing of a specific play style is further evidenced by how overpowered some particular choices are versus the other obvious avenues.  Agility is way stronger and easier to play compared to Stamina or Strength.
It's a fun game worth checking out.  It's chock full of 80's references and jokes.  It's amusing enough to have kept me interested for 8+ hours which is decent value for the cost, assuming I'm not going to finish it in the next 15 minutes.

If you go into this game expecting an RPG or Punchout you will be disappointed. This is an retro style manager sim that requires a lot of planning and thought into each action you take and when you take it. If you want a sports manager with a differnt take, a  story and some awesome pixel art, or you grew up loving games like Monster Rancher, then this is for you. If you want an RPG where you just pump points into things. move along. This is not a game about instant gratification.
Those saying the fights are predetermined by stats have not really figured out how the game works. Which is fair as it does leave a lot to the player to learn on their own, much like with real kick boxing. The fights won't make much sense until you get the scout perk, which lets you see the stats for each move and how your stats impact them.
Early in my playtime I had to focus on stanima attacks as my opponents were stronger, absorbed most of the damage, had high health and could block pretty much everything. I was out stated across the board. But, they were using high energy cost attacks. By attacking their stanima with the snap kick I was quickly able to wear them down in the first round.  This meant in round 2 they couldn't use high stanima attacks frequently and would just run out of energy, leaving them open to being hit for high damage knock downs and unable to block my low damage attacks. You can easily underdog a fight if you plan several rounds ahead, you can also get destroyed if you don't (using dodge when you should use block can change a whole fight.)
Eventually you can start planing 4 days a head by focusing on certain stats, visiting the gf for stats boosts, and planning rest and work days. You will get to a point where you can keep the fridge fully stocked and rarely need to work (fights start paying cash rewards for wins.) You need to build a routine for your fighter that works and use perks to fortify that routine/fight style. For example once I got the perk that keeps my agility at no lower then 8, I then started focusing on strength as it was only at 2. If I get it to 4 I can lock it in with a perk and ensure my hits deal some decent damage, but without losing the agility I need for dodging and landing hits. I use the agility tech tree, so this is a perfect balance for how I play and plan my fights.
It's about building your fighter up slowly, over time learning from each success and failure. Not just training one stat and being awesome.

How do you review a game that doesn't have to be good? Road Redemption needs just a few things to succeed, and being good isn't one of them:
1. Motorcycles
2. High speeds
3. Hitting the riders of other motorcyle with things.
Everything else is gravy, and Road Redemption NAILS that. You have all sorts of really satisfying things to hit, shoot, or blow up other bikers with, and the entire game is a corny excuse to make you do that a lot. You can ignore the wonky physics, the incredibly unbalanced level system, the unlockable riders full of lame gimped abilities, the corny "roguelike" nature of the campaign that's about five levels too long, the terrible rooftop levels that show off the game's horrible uncontrollable physics, the sheer amount of random cars that leap out of nowhere to dismount you, the obscene late game damage scaling that limits your options down to the cheesiest, most spammy play...
None of that matters because RR does not need any of that. As an excuse to do some really, really fun hitting dudes on bikes, RR delivers. That's all it needs to do, that's all you're here for, and you're gonna have a blast doing it.

As you may have already gotten from the Steam Videos, this game involves you riding around on a motorcycle in an infinitely generating world, where the track can take you anywhere from rooftops to the dusty deserts. Map generation is absolutely gorgeous as twisty hills and traps are generated all over the place, including hazardous traffic. Immidiately i was having flashbacks to an awesome game back on the Amiga and other consoles of my childhood, because as you, on your bike meet up with opponent racers with a 'Catch-Up' speed system, and knock them off their bikes with swinging a lead pipe to their faces...my childhood heart started pumping again as it felt like Road Rash was finally coming back to me, the game i had always wanted to be re-made.
The game is VERY familiar to Road Rash players, but it goes so much further than that, with the ability to ride an upgraded bike that can jump into the air with booster jets, and swing from helicopters with a hookshot. Even the Cars can sometimes be your greatest opponents in this game as they too, compete against you in many campaign missions.
Weaponry involves many melee weapons of different ranges and different strengths all the way to UZi submachine guns and grenade launchers, but here-in comes one of the greatest issues of the game at least as a PC user, KeyBoard and Mouse controls are VERY difficult to master as they become extremely twisty and you havent enough ability to drive, aim, attack, handbrake and all the rest at the same time. It is hard to play (but manageable) with a keyboard and mouse, but ultimately this is a game for a Controller. I Highly advise you grab a dual-analog controller and plug it in to maximize your control here. WASD is not very good at how sensitive you should steer your bike and you are going to need to drive with all of your skills here as the difficulty is quite high.
You will certainly get a blast out of this game, especially when the multiplayer module comes out, as PvP in this game is set to be one of the most fun things you have done in many years, all about the skill and not about the diceroll. The game is definitely worth your cash, but also a little patience as it is early access and of course, there are bugs and several things needed to be worked out.
--In Depth Review--
Graphics: 7/10
As you can imagine, worlds which are generated tend to look like they have been generated, rather than natural looking, but that's what makes the race tracks all the more fun than realistic, but the graphics in general are great with lovely lighting and shadows, incredible carcrash physics, lots of particles and bits of things flying everywhere, its great. There are however some major issues which lose the game some points here. There is always this kind of Dust Particle which approaches your screen at almost all times, which actually heats up the computer and in some cases, kills framerate even on powerful rigs like the one im running. Another issue is that large car crashes or great moments of vehicle damage causes the game's framerate to take a divebomb down to like 2 frames per second, which often forces you to kill the game and lose your progress. It's still early access so it's very easy to understand that this sorta thing will happen :)
Sound: 10/10
Countless games fall victim to a lack of sountrack, a lack of variation, and a lack of adrenaline and emotion to boot, but this game features a large playlist of music, each which will pump up your heart rate and convince you to keep driving and keep smacking people off their bike, the wonderful track lineup really keeps you playing the game so you can listen to them all. I hope in the future, like all games that have featured a kickass playlist (MAX Power Racing, Wipeout 2097 etc etc), will allow you to change track in the Pause menu, because i want to play my favorites over and over again! Maybe they could add buttons to utilize 'Next Track' and 'Previous Track' compatability. Weapons feel so realistic whenever you're in combat, from the sound of slapping meat to teeth-grinding chings of an iron weapon meeting someones skull, it sounds terrifyingly good. I have absolutely nothing to suggest when it comes to their sound lineup.
Gameplay: 6/10
It feels immidiately familiar to Road Rash players and brings back some well needed nostalgia, adding to what is an adrenaline filled game where every gut wrenching moment you fear for traffic over a hill knocking you off your bike, to battling a horde of cop cars and bikes, to avoiding the bullets and melee tools of an opponent biker and for the love of god keep your eyes on the road else you wont last long :D even the race track is twisty, bendy, requires sharp turns, and wants to kill you. It's very difficult doing all of this at once, but that's the beauty of this game and ones like it in the past, it NEEDS to be difficult and challenging...well it certainly is, sometimes feeling even unfair andd cruelly hard when actually sometimes there is nothing to do when you have been overwhelmed but try to stay alive. My only issue is that Police Cars are far too aggressive, where if a single police car hassles you from the beginning of a race, it is too easy and fast for that car to absolutely obliterate you and you dont always have a gun or powerful weapon to deal with it, making your entire race like trying to push or outrun Superman. As i have already mentioned, this game is hard, VERY hard, which is where i would like to suggest a Difficulty option, so that not-so-skilled players, or casuals can drive on easier tracks, with less aggressive AI and perhaps play a more casual and fun game.
There is a lack of Online multiplayer and game-modes right now, but give it some time as there already are plans to include them. It is very likely in the future, the 6 rating i have given, will turn into an 8 or 9 after it has been more developed on :)
(after development you could even see up to 9/10)
You can tell the game is still early access with several bugs, cars suddenly driving on the incorrect lanes, particle and physical framerate slowdowns and ruthless Car AI, but after these are fixed and more game-modes are included, i would hope with a difficulty slider so people can play at their own pace and level, this game is definitely on it's way to being an instant classic, relivving old memories of games long forgotten but better. The development team are very generous, are listening to community feedback, and are hopefully working hard on this title, because Road Redemption if it continues on this path, is going to be a rolling success. It's just missing one thing, YOU.

Previously I gave this game a 'no' review. There have been some changes that have made the game playable and even enjoyable. The physics of the bike in the air is ridiculous... but then again so is the whole idea of the game. There is some satisfaction to be had in planting a bomb on a rival gang member's bike or grappling them until they are hit by an on-coming car. Then there's the 'cars raining from the sky' which isn't a bug but an actual developers' choice for a thing to be happening while you are trying to dodge cars and bikers.
The biggest issue at the moment on my system is that the game crashes out when trying to load levels. This appears to be due to the game using up all available memory and can be delayed by setting it at the the graphics to 'fastest'. The developers are aware of this and are trying to sort it out.
As this game has no plot it can be very satisfying to just jump in a race, smash of few bikers down and then walk away. The weapons have different characteristics and learning to time the strikes is interesting.
I wouldn't say the game is worth $20 in its current state but, with the effort being put in to fix the errors, I would say that it will be.

Allow me to start this off with my ratings before I go into the actual review. Surely this will help those who are in a hurry.
So, on with the review.
Your first question might be, what exactly is Trails in the Sky? Trails in the Sky is a JRPG, and if you don't know what that is, then just look up Final Fantasy. However, although it is a JRPG, it has many things that define it and set it apart from its competition. Such as its battle system and the design of its NPCs, but I'll get into both of these things later. Trails in the Sky is a challenging game with a very long story, the 50 hour playtime mentioned on the store page is an understatement, not an exaggeration, and you're looking at 100 for the sequel, and roughly 70 or so for the 3rd. If any of this has caused you to lose interest, I suggest you stop reading now. But if you're interested, here's the details:
The story of Trails in the Sky is quite long as I've said. However, to be fair, it won't be 50 hours if you don't do
(or all) of the sidequests, which I highly recommend you do, as some of them can be quite fun. However, the story is heavily focused on the characters and the world they live in, so if you don't like stories that start off a tad slow and don't like waiting for the big climatic event, you might not like this. I myself found it enjoyable.
What makes the story so great is how there's so much more to it than what it presents you with in a basic playthrough. This is because every NPC in Trails in the Sky has a name of their own, and almost all of them have a story to tell that evolves as the game progresses. Every time something happens, every time there's something new going on, you can talk to almost any of the NPCs and you're likely to find the next part of their little inner stories you can keep up with. This makes the world very hard to not be interested in, and definitely helps with the story itself.
The most important part of any story that closely follows the characters is to have the characters be well-written, and that's certainly the case in this game. All of the characters are interesting or likeable in their own ways, with well-defined personalities and good character development, especially in SC.
The only downside, however, is that you will not get the full story with this game alone. Without spoiling anything, the game ends on a cliffhanger with a lot of questions left unanswered and the plot without a conclusion, meaning you will
to buy SC to see the rest, as SC continues off right from where FC leaves us at. However, both games are worth it, so just buy them both during a sale if you're short on cash, or support the devs who most certainly deserve it and buy them both at full price. If what I've said thus far sounds good to you, you won't regret it.
The gameplay in Trails in the Sky is something that I enjoyed, but some did not. Trails in the Sky is a
text-heavy game. It is not a visual novel by any means, but you will be reading almost as much as you would if it were, and you have to, because not reading means not understanding what is happening. This means that if you want to buy Trails in the Sky, you have to be coming for the story just as much as you are the gameplay itself.
Then there's the exploration. This game has quite the large world for you to explore, and you will be doing a lot of walking through it. By a lot, I mean
. This is even more noticed if you aim to complete every side-quest. Fortunately, the game's world is very artistically designed, and if you enjoy exploring and traveling manually rather than using the fast-travels and warps we've come accustomed to from other games, then you will find yourself at home.
The other mixed aspect of the game is its combat. Unlike most JRPGs which would have you hitting random commands left and right to make things happen, Trails in the Sky offers a more strategic battle system involving a grid and the ability to move your characters about it. If you've ever played XCOM or any game like it, this can be related to that in a way. It's a bit more complicated than most RPG battle systems, and it definitely isn't perfect, but it offers a good challenge, and in my experience, was very entertaining, especially during certain boss battles that made great use of the system.
The magic system in this JRPG, however, is honestly one of the most in-depth ones I have ever seen. Fun, too! Rather than just hand you powers for levelling up as though your character visited the charity of magical-thingstuff along the way and got best grabs, this game gives you orbments. The game explains it in more depth, but the short explanation is you get to shove colored spheres into slots and based on what spheres they are, what their element values are, and how they're arranged, you will get different kinds of powers. It starts out simple, but toward endgame, you will have quite the variety to choose from.
The most noteworthy thing about the gameplay, however, is its challenge. This is a game developed by Falcom, and it definitely lives up to their reputation. But don't let that discourage you! The game can certainly be beaten by a newcomer on Normal difficulty, but if you're looking for a more hardcore experience, the higher difficulties can do the job. You'll have to play very smart, be very strategic with your use of items and powers, and have a bit of luck on your side if you want to beat this game on the highest difficulty.
Trails in the Sky is a wonderful JRPG that we are lucky to have on Steam where anyone can buy and experience it. Though its graphics may be old, they maintain a charm that is still appealing today, and the game itself has aged quite well. Though you may have to walk around a lot and the combat system could be a bit better than it is, neither one is necessarily bad, and though you may have to buy SC to get the full experience, the story, characters, world, and especially the music more than makes up for any short-comings. A definite recommendation from me.

I'll start off by saying that FEZ is sort of a love/hate game.  It's definitely not for everyone, but I still think it's worth trying out.
To get the bad out of the way, there are quite a few extremely, EXTREMELY cryptic puzzles in the game.  I won't lie, I resorted to using guides for most of them, as I lack the patience for this kind of stuff, but if you're someone who refuses to use guides, prepare to get a pen and paper, and put on your thinking cap.  Some of the puzzles just feel overly cryptic, and you have to do a lot of brainstorming, experimenting, and trial and error to solve them.
That's honestly my only real complaint with the game.  The world and art style of the game are very charming and nostalgic in a way, and the soundtrack is amazing.  The 3D world rotation mechanic that the game is built around works well, and is very fun to play around with.
If you're a fan of puzzle platformers, I'd highly recommend the game.

This is a pretty fun games as it currently stands (as of version Alpha 8.14).
The game is as it says on the tin, design air (or land) ships in a steam punk environment, and send them against your enemies.
The design of these ships is also quite sensible, since there are lose conditions that may hit you at any point during battle for each one of your ships, which you can mitigate based on how you assembled your vehicle.
Build your ship poorly, with only one access corridor to the water supply, and you're going to have a bad time. Especially once the coal store ignites.
Run out of coal for your "suspendium" engine that keeps your airship afloat, and you will fall out of the sky.
Run out of ammo, and, welp, all those giant cannons you have there might work as a battering ram if you're lucky.
Don't have any water on board? Have fun watching the ammo store turn into a fireworks show when it inevitably catches fire!
Don't have any guards on board? Have fun letting your enemies capture the ship and turn it against you.
There are very many pieces of a ship you can use to assemble essentially whatever you can think of, provided you stay within a few specified constraints, which you can change, depending on what you can afford. Most of these restraints from what I've dealt with had to do with overloading my vessels by adding too much gun, or by trying to armor my entire tank with bricks (harder to break completely compared to metal which doesn't like to explode).
At the moment there are 2 gamemodes.
1. Combat mode, which is as you would guess. Throws you onto a blank map, where you deploy your own, and you enemies ships, duke it out and see what happens. This mode is essentially the sandbox mode of the game, as there are no financial restrictions. This is also the only mode that is currently available in multiplayer.
2. Campaign mode is a mode where the game generates a map for you and up to 12 other AI empires to face each other with reasonably good tactical battles and planning.
At the moment the campaign is a bit thread bare as the only language any empire speaks seems to be "shoot them in the face". This isn't exactly a bad thing, as the mode is quite entertaining, especially since the AI does seem to be quite competent with how it handles it's forces and resources.
Each city captured will have different resources or tech you can exploit, like cheaper wood for example, reducing the cost of wood armored ships, and maybe a different city will have the technology of flamethrowers.
Unfortunately at the moment there is no way to steal, research, or reverse engineer tech without taking the city which contains it, but this is a flaw which I can see being fixed reasonably soon probably, considering we are still in early(ish) alpha. I've completed my first victorious large campaign in just under an hour, granted most of that time was spent designing ships to counter my enemies.
The game itself is actually very pretty considering the pixel art graphics, and can run on essentially a toaster oven.
I feel the current price of 9.99 is actually quite a reasonable price for the game with the current ammount of features present in the game, as this game is quite the time sink if you want it to be (I've probably got about 6 or more hours in offline mode that steam doesn't track). I would happily reccomend this game to anyone that asks about it.

Imagine a puzzle game where, rather than waste time on fancy graphics and characterisation, a developer channeled all of their time and energy into completely mind-opening level design. That is, at its core, what Stephen's Sausage Roll is. It starts off simple enough, almost like some mobile game, however even at that early stage many of the puzzles appear to have obvious solutions that just don't
work. The second area is where things start to really pick up, and for the first 5 areas, each area introduces another technique for puzzle solving. The neat thing is how these techniques come into play; the second area, for instance, introduces a trick involving an interaction between sausages and walls (I won't go into more detail because it'll spoil the surprise). However, in the first area you would never come upon this trick, as the first area has no walls. Areas 3, 4, and 5 introduce similarly game-changing techniques, giving the player more tools to attack the often fiendish problems the game poses. However, these 5 areas (comprising roughly 2/3 of the game in terms of sausages grilled) serve mainly as a tutorial for the final section of the game, which is filled with puzzles so original they could almost be new games by themselves. This section is reminiscent of the second half of Portal, in that the lines between individual puzzles become more and more blurred.
There is a narrative of sorts, although much like Portal this only really picks up during the final section, and it never interferes with gameplay in any way. I decided to wait until I finished the game before writing this review, and I'm pleased I did because the ending is both satisfying and conclusive (there are
sausages in the game). In terms of difficulty i would say it is somewhere around the level of a Zachtronics game, however there's a big difference in style, as the puzzles in those games don't tend to have one intended solution and revolve around system design.
If you're still wondering about the price, I have two suggestions for you:
In my opinion, despite its initial appearance, this is pretty much the best puzzle game there is at the moment, and i would recommend it to anyone and everyone. Worth every single penny.

Easily my least favorite title in the series.  It is very pretty and they did a fairly good job with the boating mechanic, I'll grant it that, but that's really about all I can say that's good about it.  The story is God Awful, if you're looking for a good story, steer clear.
Connor is a horribly dull character, his motives constantly conflict, he never matures, and he is quite possibly the least dimensional character since Desmond Miles.
The freerunning is massivly toned down, as the buildings are all reletivly small and they have a guard on every single roof, you'll never want to run atop the towns, but rather just stick to the roads.  There is the notable exception of the tree freerunning, which was nicely done, but unfortunatly it's not really utilized outside of a desolate forest that gives you no real reason to explore, save for finding a few collectibles.
If you're looking for assassinations or stealth you won't find them in this game.  Connor will randomly enter combat within cities for absolutly no reason, and there is only 1 actual assassination in the game.  While you do kill people, they are almost always part of some scripted event.  so rather than climbing atop buildings and trees to get that perfect arial strike, you get a cutscene to a small fight scene to another cutscene.
Connor's Arsenal has also been altered, now allowing him to carry more weapons he will never need to use.  The combat is what you'd exepct from an Assassin's Creed title, way too easy.  All the extra weapons are only for show as every bit of combat can be done with just your hidden blades.  Excluding ranged attacks though.  For whatever reason they've decided to replace Ezio's amazing hidden gun, which combined both stealth and power, with the worst sets of pistols and rifles in any video games ever.  Each one get's one shot before needing a 10 second reload, meaning in the heat of combat you only get to fire one shot.  The shots are also pathetically weak and will rarely, if ever, kill anyone.
I can safely say give this one a pass.  Go get Brotherhood or Black Flag instead.

This game has a lot of potential, but is bogged down by excessive amounts of grinding and little actual content. The story totally could've been interesting, but it's lacking a lot of events in between, not to mention that you're so busy trying to survive the stat reduction you might not even have time to do them. There's just SO. MUCH. GRIND. Everything in the world is against you; the random robbers event, the daily stat reduction, the ridiculous cost (probably dumped tens of thousand dollars into that god forsaken gym just to train and spar; how the hell is Silver not a billionaire already?), consumption rate, travelling time (somehow, the protagonist takes a full hour to walk ONE KILOMETER ONLY) and so on and so on.
In fact, I just don't see the point of playing through the game again with a different skillset - or as bad guy, which offers slightly different storyline and unlockable locations - because it took me 9 hours of crazy grinding - the end game actually features even WORSE, INSANELY REPETITIVE grinding, if you can actually believe it - to finally beat the game. The ending isn't even satisfactory; it leaves you with a cliffhanger and a storyline that confuse the hell out of people, and naturally there's no option to replay that particular cutscene because this is a 'retro' game. Uuuuuugh.
Also, someone mentioned in the discussions that this game is built around the concept of mobile F2P. I can see it, except that if it actually was F2P I would toss it out of the window in a milisecond. Even ZENONIA isn't as boringly grindy as this game, and that one's a KRPG.
As of now, I seriously cannot recommend this game to anyone. Yes, it can be fun. Yes, a core part of such sim games is to grind. But jesus, at least Sunrider Academy has boobs to look at (although that game's grind is even more pointless, at least it doesn't PHYSICALLY DISGUST ME WITH ITS MECHANICS). Heck even Love Dating Sim, a game since the 2000s EASILY trumps this game in terms of replayability and sheer fun. This one's just TEDIOUS, UNPRODUCTIVE WORK. I would play Pro Gamer Manager, an early access game with no end game over this. At least that one's relaxing.

I was born in 1985 so this game totally brought me back to my childood on so many levels. and the attention to detail in both the graphics, music, and references just have me feeling like a kid again.  I also got so emotional when i turned on the retro mode as my TV once again had the type of screen that it did when i was 10 that i actually just listened to the opening music and stared nostalgically at the main menu screen in the main theme for about ten minutes simply taking in and flashing back.  I miss those days...
The game isn't easy, because they never used to be.  Games never held your hand, they were not your sparring partner, they were your enemy.  Games used to kick the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me and laugh, and I kept coming back for more.  Why?  BECAUSE THATS HOW I GOT BETTER.  Not by having constant respawns and automatic save points, but by dying three times and having to start all the way back at the beginning.  On that note I found myself attempting to exploit a potential weakness that had the potential to break a core mechanic of the game.  I soon realized realize that the devs had accounted for it.  They knew I had grown soft in todays gaming market, and they were here to make me pay.
....In the beginning of the game, Mick (yes THAT mick) says that if you need a hot meal to come and see him.  Thinking that this was a no questions asked kind of deal, i tried to take full advantage of this foolish old mans hospitality.  The first time my character, who I named Billy (If you don't get this reference then LEAVE), got really hungry, I went at ate at Micks.  Then I tried going over for a mid day snack.  Thats when I realized Mick would only feed my character if he was super hungry.  So as I was saving up for home workout equipment (using the gym is expensive)  I figured I'd save money by starving myself, then going to Micks for a free meal... Mick knew my scheme, he knew I had cash and basically told me to go to hell.  So then I decided to live the life of a poor but determined fighter, spend all of my time training, earning no money, and just treat micks like a "god damn soup kitchen" (go watch "ROCKY").  The old man had finally had enough.  After a warning about this being my last meal there, he never fed me again.  Having not learned my lesson, I wound up being too hungry to work,, broke my arm in an underground fight, and had to restart my game due to starvation.... for half a second I tried to reach for a reset button.  Gonna say it once more, I love this game.
Devs, I have a couple reccommendations (Wishes?) regarding the actual fights, ones which I don't believe would screw up any sort of coding if implement.  During fights, i found myself looking for a couple animations which i assumed would be there given the 16 bit retro nature of the game.
1.  An "exhaustion stance" when a stamina bar or Energy bar (or both?) is low.  Just a slighjtly different animation than the usual fighting stance.  Saturday Night Slam Masters implemented this back in the day on the SNES and it really added an extra level of emersion.
2.  It would be cool to see the winner of a fighter preen for a second like all retro fighting game characters did.
3.  Just an extra frame or two of animation as a character rises from the mat in the vein of  Mike Tyson's Punch-Out and Double Dragon 2
4.  A couple sprays of blood (Obviously being able to be turned off for the squeamish) every couple of punches wouldnt hurt from a 90's stand point.  No need to go TIME KILLERS with it, but you get the idea :)
again, not a coder, don't know how easy or hard it is to implement these things, but would it add a layer of immersion which I feel is missing from the game.
Thank you Devs.
I'm happy to say that you've nailed what a retro game is both asthetically as well as  is at its heart and soul better than any game out there on the market.  Hope to play more games of yours in the future...

This game's "Story Rich" tag is an understatement. This is not an Action RPG. There is a lot of reading involved. The gameplay and pacing are a slow burn, but the payoff is immense. The level of detail in this game is beyond words. If you're a completionist who explores every nook and cranny, and talks to every NPC no matter how mundane or unimportant they may seem, then you will strike gold with this game. Every line of dialogue in this game contributes to a level of world-building that is so awesome, it makes other JRPGs pale in comparison.
As an added benefit, this game is the 1st in a trilogy, and that trilogy is also part of a larger saga. I never heard of the Legend of Heroes series before this game, but after playing this game, I now check Steam frequently for more ports and localizations of other games in this series.
- Phenomenal plot; last two scenes really make you crave the second chapter in this trilogy
- Highly-developed playable characters and NPCs
- Extensive natural-sounding dialogue, including a multitude of humorous moments (I took dozens of Steam screenshots just to immortalize many of these scenes)
- Hybrid turn-based, grid-based combat system that brings a level of freshness and strategy not found in many JRPGs
- Customizable character builds ("Quartz" system is similar to the Materia system from Final Fantasy 7)
- Challenging boss encounters
- Almost 90 "side" quests (in fact, side-questing is a core concept of the game)
- Great graphics
- Engaging music that adds excitement to many scenes due to reoccuring themes
- Truly challenging Steam achievements (such as finding every treasure chest in the game)
- Difficulty scaling is somewhat off; monsters are often too easy or too hard
- Some content is easily missable; you may not realize this until you complete the game and realize you are missing some Steam Achievements
Final rating: 9.5/10

I played this game during a period when I didn't have much free time, so it took me 6 months to finish. I played it in sessions of 1-3 hours at a time and that worked very well for me. The game doesn't force you into sequences where you feel like you can't stop now.
Also, the game has a calm, relaxing feeling to it. Most of the locations feel serene and immersive. For example, this game makes excellent use of it's in-town NPCs. They go about their daily lives with their own relationships, troubles and dreams. If you speak with them regularly as you are playing the game, you will find how their own stories evolve alongside yours and they often end in hilarity.
Another good point about the world building is the game's sense of adventure. During the majority of the game there is no imminent evil that has to be defeated. The main characters just travel between different locations without having to chase a bad guy. This gives the feeling of a relaxing journey taken at a steady pace. This doesn't mean that there is no meaning to the characters actions and their travels. Over the course of the journey different events happen that foreshadow the main conflict and everything culminates satisfyingly at the end.
However, there are no user choices that affect the main storyline. This game simply lets you follow the journey of the main characters. Thus, this game might not be for people that enjoy forging their own adventure.
I'm not going to go into game mechanincs or other such specifics. This game has a very typical JRPG gameplay and is a well-crafted example of the genre. Unlike you might expect from a JRPG, there is not need for grinding sessions and I never felt the need for those.
Overall, this game was a very pleasant experience for me. If you are looking for a relaxing game with a slower pace that you can pick and drop at any point, this is probably a good choice for you.
