A great game, though not without its faults of course. Specifics as follows:
PROS:
- Fascinating and engaging storyline with very little in the way of plot holes and the like.
- Some of the best dialogue I've ever seen in a JRPG - period. I don't joke when I say the writing puts most of Square Enix's work to shame.
- Outstanding characterization. This game has some of the best developed characters I've seen in an RPG. After about 15 hours of gameplay, you start to feel very close to the characters and you'll smile or feel saddened when they succeed or fail. And it's not just the main protoganists either, but also the supporting cast.
- Gameplay is easy to get into and is fun to play around with.
- Charming art style
CONS:
- Though the dialogue is well written, sometimes conversations can go on a bit TOO long and wind up coming off as padding for the game's running time.
- Occasionally buggy user interface. IE: Sometimes an item's description won't show up in the text box so you wind up wondering what the hell that item does.
- Map design is a bit linear.
- Not a whole lot in terms of extra things to do like mini games or what not. A small gripe.
- The music (most of the time) is mediocre at best and flat out teeth grinding at worst. The tracks play on a very short loop and do not age well after the 20th time you've heard them. The game does have a FEW good tracks though.

Gomez wakes up on a sunny day and leaves the house to receive an important letter that’s about to change his life. Who is Gomez? He’s a weird-looking blob of white pixels living in a colorful flat world of neon green platforms hanging across the cyan sky. The message in the mailbox asks you to meet one-eyed Geezer at the top of the village. That meeting is going to change the life of the protagonist in a most peculiar way. Gomez will receive a fez. The red hat isn’t just an exotic accessory. It allows you to manipulate the world by rotating it sideways. And of course you don’t just receive it: getting ahold of such a powerful artifact is accompanied by the appearance of a giant golden hexahedron spewing cyphered messages at you, tearing the space-time continuum and “resetting” the game.
You wake up once again and go out of the familiar house. At first glance — nearly nothing’s changed. Villagers still wander around minding their own 2D business, but you know you can see more, can reach places you couldn’t reach before. And that will help you on your quest that your newest Zelda-referencing flying companion, four-dimensional hypercube named Dot tells you about. Collect the cubes. Open the doors. Save the world… perhaps?
Fez rightfully assumes that for now all you need is more of that gorgeous scenery. It was enough for the game to receive two IGF awards despite being still in development both times. And it is in its right being so confident about its looks. Visual styles so distinctive and appealing don’t appear every day. It’s retro and modern at the same time, a lovechild of technological experimentation multiplied by childhood nostalgia. It took its creator Phil Fish more than five years to build a game around the initial trixel idea, which makes you wonder just how much of that time has been spent scraping the work results and redoing stuff all over again. That doesn’t save you from having game-breaking bugs in the final product, but it nearly guarantees having a puzzle so difficult, that it took the community a whole year to crack it “properly”.
The mystery of the black monolith was initially brute-forced by collective online effort. But of course that solution was far from satisfying to say the least. Uncovering the logic behind the artifact that was not so easy to discover in the first place would be a proper way. There was no shortage of fourth-wall breaking hints before with QR codes, pop-culture references and messages encoded in binary with the star patterns of first “regular” ending. Fez teases you, challenges you to solve it; the game gives you the deciphering key to its baffling coded messages with a visual representation of a famous pangram.
There was no shortage of theories surrounding an obvious 2001: A Space Odyssey reference, but the reasoning behind it was elusive. Much like the original Clarke's black monolith its counterpart from the game’s gotten its share of explanations, but still stayed unfathomable. Maybe it was its meaning — that we can’t have all the answers. Or maybe it was the ultimate prank of Phil Fish, who managed to keep a three-dimensional nature of the game a secret when it was unveiled in 2007 at TIGSource. In 2008 when the rotating mechanic became known the second cryptic part of the game remained undisclosed. One can only imagine what it takes to keep your mouth shut for so long and not hint it even once.
Your perception of Fez shifts and rotates much like you do within the game world. A slow relaxation of a starting zone gives way to some underlying mystery; then you’re distracted from that with some really smart puzzles that don’t even seem like puzzles at first glance. Finally, when (if) you get through all of this, you get to see the fourth side of the cube. And it blows your mind. These transitions are subtle. You can’t really put your finger on what’s changed at first (except for the big final development). And is that really a change? Maybe it’s just a look from a different angle, a perspective alteration revealing content that was always there, but you were too distracted to notice it. Just to prove this point Fez doesn’t really reward you with anything. It just starts anew leaving you with nothing more than a buzz in your head from all those riddles and suspicious hints to a bigger story.
Supposedly some of them were meant to be picked up in a sequel, but we aren’t getting it anytime soon. Well, time to rotate that cube again then. Maybe there’s something on the side that you’ve missed?

So the time has come. After extensive gameplay, I can finally get my conclusions on this game. Yep, it's a thumbs up review against 60% negative reviews... ouch.
Okay, let's go. The first point of disappointment around the community is the lack of content that Codemasters had been announcing since October last year. They basically said that physics and handling were taken to a new level of realism, graphics were made realistic and detailed thanks to an all new engine, the player would be more involved in the action thanks the larger variety of cutscenes, a new team radio system with which you can actually interact with the engineer, 2014 season for free, more online modes, two brand new full championship modes, car technical updates as they come in real life... Promising, isn't it? If we look into the game and play it, the guys at Codemasters haven't said a lie. Well, just one: They haven't laid any car update since the day-1 patch, which included team Manor and McLaren's new livery  (what about the new Mercedes rear wing, Force India nosecone, McLaren new short nosecone, Ferrari new sidepods...?). With that exception, everything they said is in the actual game.
- Handling, physics and tyre model is just amazing. Seriously, it really is. F1 games are no longer a lazily built arcade with random curb spin and nonexistent grip feel on turns and braking points, but and incredibly detailed simulator-like which transmits the power of the cars in all its glory. Now you have torque wheelspin which you can correct with quick steering movements to put the car straight and make it find grip, which makes the car nervous as in real life.
- Some people moan about the inability to change dead zone and saturation setups on wheels and pads. I have mixed opinions about that: For compatible devices like the Xbox 360/One pad or the main wheels on the market like Logiteg G27/29 or certain Thrustmaster devices the developer has brought a preset setup which adapts to what they want the game to handle like. Change the settings and you completely ruined the car behaviour. On the other hand, this has a drawback. If you have a wheel which hasn't got a preset, forget about ever trying to use it with this game. It would be nice to set up a comfortable setting for it because Force Feedback will mess around and steering will be completely unrealistic and close to impossible.
- Most PC users report constant bugs. I haven't found any type of glitch during my gameplay, of any kind. Try checking out your GPU drivers before directly blaming the game. Some Youtubers and users make "bug compilation" videos and screenshots of gross bugs with the initial version of the game, without the Day-1 patch. That's not fair, and don't take them into account. If you really want to get feedback about glitches, ask people, document yourself with patch fixes and the PC those users have and their drivers version. Again, I haven't found any bug in like 40 hours of gameplay.
- Setups are much deeper and they change realistically the behaviour of the car, mostly because the physics take into account many more real-time factors like, say, a fully working weight balance system. Now it comes with five setup presets which you can choose to adapt the car to the circuit you are at plus you can save your own. Tyre model is now enhanced and integrates a much more complex tyre wear system, so choosing the right setup makes a huge difference in tyre management.
- As to graphics, what they made was basically go back to the F1 2010 model which consisted in using light effects to make beautiful and realistic scenes, but of course they've enhanced textures, added some nice motion blur, a long awaited ambient occlusion and refined colours. Rain effects are also enhanced and rather impressive, and night circuits have a much more accurate reflections and lighting effect.
- Sounds make a big difference and are probably one of the fields that have been worked out the most. The engine has an impressive range of sounds, from the dynamic roar of the V6 along the revs panorama to the subtle whistle of the turbo, including the electric engines' distinctive sound. Aero sounds are more detailed and go further from the strange noise that sometimes appeared on the previous games when attempting to make it. There's the reverb of the sound when getting close to walls and barriers and more detailed tyre squeak, among other cool effects. Team radio is at its best, providing useful information and with a larger variety of sentences.
Now let's move to the drawbacks, because it doesn't matter how much you're enjoying this game, they're there as a wound. Where to begin... Oh, yeah. The optimization.
Unlike the rest of the games by Codemasters, F1 2015 is really, really, really badly optimised (I mean, really). Seriously, I don't know what they did there. Frame rate will be the same on the lowest settings as on the Highest, and some tracks have some nasty drops at some points. Pit Stops are somehow capped to some ridiculous 15 FPS and after leaving the pit lane you're back at the normal frame rate. Thank God you haven't got to do anything during pit stops, because otherwise it would have been impossible. Some patches have improved performance and frame rate is more stable now. Game is fully playable though, so no need to panic. I'd take the excuse that this is their first title under the all-new-bright-and-shiny graphics engine so they haven't had enough time to make it as perfect as the previous EGO engine was by the last games it powered...
- Online. Man, this is by far the worst part of the game. Well, you can't even say it is a part of the game, because it's just broken. As if it wasn't there. No online. One of the additions to this game is, as said before, a new bunch of online game modes, "hoppers" as they call them. These are simply preset lobbies, so you can enter any type of race you want. Looks good, huh? Nope. It doesn't make it easier to find the exact race setting you want, although not because of the game, but the very few people that switches to online. Enter a hopper: No lobbies. Different hopper: No lobbies. Another hopper: Enter a lobby. Lobby already racing ( -.- ).There's also the custom match lobby, of course, but for some reason it cannot be public (only friend invite). Don't want to lose time searching open lobbies and you just want to go online? NOPE! For some reason, they removed the "Joker" of Quick Matchmaking. Manage to enter a lobby and start racing? NOPE! Bound to be kicked from session. To be fair, Codemasters has never had proper servers. 70% of the times in F1 2012 you or anyone else in the lobby would get Disconnected. DiRT 3 was glitchy at some points. But these issues in F1 2015 aren't even normal.
- The lack of Safety Car, to be honest, doesn't make any difference at all. I have around 200 hours of playtime in F1 2012 and most of the time I play 25%-50% races. Haven't seen a single Safety Car. If so, some red flags. If from 2012 to 2014 the Safety Car was as common as seeing a four-leaved shamrock, why not having it in 2015 is a big deal? My point of view is that the damage system is so bad that there's no reason to lay the Safety Car on track. Massive incident, front wing and wheels off, car and parts disappear, resume racing. With the new graphics engine they could have enhanced the damage system to add debris on track that could cause punctures, gravel spread on the tarmac, marshals picking up pieces... In those occasions it would be easier and reasonable to deploy the Safety Car, but as the damage system only added more realism on flatting tyres against walls and more parts of the front wing that you can lose, there's no reason to do. That's a disappointing drawback, the damage system.

If there’s one thing to say about Behemoth is that they always want to try new things. First they made a 2D shooter called Alien Hominid. The it was the Beat-em Up Castle Crashers. The have a tactical RPG in the works called Pit People which has a glorious tutorial. And the subject of this review, the platformer Battleblock Theatre.
Story
Usual I give a brief summary of the premise but I really can’t do it justice. Just go watch the Intro and opening level and come back. I’ll wait....
You finished. Now, you may be finding either your ribs are aching or you struggling to breath from all the laughter that's happening and the whole story is like that. I could go over characters or themes but there isn’t anything like that. Just silliness and nonsense as things are getting worse for everyone.
Gameplay
Remember that mini game in Alien Hominid about the stick man going through little platform levels to get to the exit. Well, here’s that idea fully realised. All the blocks from that mini return like the water, the boat, the spikes and the rocks. Maybe a few other I might’ve forgotten.  And for new blocks, we got fire blocks that bounce you around, fans that push you away and blocks that harmlessly explode as soon as you touch them to name a few.
In each level you must collect at least three gems out of a maximum of seven in most levels to open the exit. These gems are mainly use to buy new heads for customising, trading or just to get an achievement. There is also a ball of yarn hidden in each level and these can be trade in for weapons against the cats including grenades, boomerangs, a dart gun and exotics animal that explode. I haven’t seen much use for the yarn after you bought all the weapons so that could be a flaw.
At first I was disappointed when I found out the bosses would be time trials but damn are these levels hard. These are basically wake-up calls as you have to do two levels in a row in a short amount of time and dying only makes the level take longer so screwing up isn’t and taking your time isn’t an option.
There’s also level editor but I haven’t really look into it but I have dabbled into the user made levels and the few I played were pretty good. There was a Pokemon theme one were each level was based on a Pokemon type and it was pretty good.
Presentation
Lets get this out of the way, the narrator is brilliant.  Every line that pours from his mouth is just golden, which is good for a game that doesn’t have much characterisation for its cast. I’m also a fan of the art work here. All the Behemoth games have this style of cuteness no matter weird it is odd shape heads and beady eyes.
And the cutscenes really capture the puppet show look they were going and although they are clearly animated, they almost look real at first. And for the music, it’s pretty good and some are bond to be favourites. I like the menu theme, the final boss song, and one of the level track but lets not forget the secret song.
Verdict
I’ve played three of the Behemoth games and all of them are hits. This is definitely a developer to keep an eye out if you haven’t already.

Hahaha, get it? It's like Oregon Trail, but...
No, it really is Oregon Trail with zombies. But instead of being a one-note joke, Organ Trail actually improves on the original formula in significant ways. If you somehow never encountered an Apple IIe in school, the basic idea of ______ Trail games is that you have a party of 4 or so travelers on their way to a distant destination. Random things happen on the way, sometimes you get a choice to make, other times not. Settlements give you the chance to shop, barter, or scavenge for supplies. Organ Trail sets this up as you and your 4 pals escaping D.C. in a beat-up station wagon, carrying as much food, ammo, car parts, and fuel as you can. In addition to the random horrible things that happen, you'll also encounter minigames like dodging zombie deer and motorcycle gangs on the highway, or making a clutch shot to save a friend from a kidnapper. These interactive events really help break up the monotony of watching your beater roll down the highway while bad things happen to you all.
Settlements are where the game really shines, because there are a wealth of options for managing your journey. In terms of supplies alone, you can buy and sell for cash, wait for trade offers on your goods, scavenge by playing a little top-down action minigame, and do side missions (also minigames) to get paid in goods. There are additional options for managing the health of your team, for maintaining and upgrading your ride, and even learning new special skills for your player character that help in minigames. Learning how much you need of what resources and what upgrades you should spring for can take time, so be prepared to either lose a few times or start on Easy. The first time I picked this game up I got rather frustrated because my car broke down and I got trapped in a settlement with no way to repair it. But after a few more rounds I learned the power of scavenging and practiced my minigaming and now everything runs smooth... on Normal, anyway.
It's a pretty deep game for a literal Oregon Trail clone, and the zombie aspect fits the style well without being tired. There are some cute pop culture references that are clever enough not to annoy, and plenty of replay value. As long as the ultra low-res graphics and learning curve don't put you off, this is a grand little coffee break game.

Great game, all around!
Airships is mostly a real time strategy game, with resource managing elements. I have not played the multiplayer very much, but the single player is some of the most fun to be had with 10$ that you'll ever find!
The graphics are neat pixel art, and available in a wide range of resolutions. Very crisp, though sometimes the colors can be a little bland (menus and such tend to be all brown or black, which is to be expected of the genre yes, but perhaps a little higher contrast would make things easier to see).
Gameplay is extremely solid. I've only encountered extremely mild bugs (a certain airship design never replaced the cannon when repaired, I had to refit it with one every time). You use the mouse to select commands for the airships (usually just movement) and this can seem simplistic at first, but quickly gets hectic once you start having more than 6 ships in a battle at the same time, which is by no means a bad thing! (protip: try to manuever your ships so that when one goes down, it doesnt take 3 others directly below with it, causing a massive fiery explosion destroying half your fleet).
sound deisign is spot on, weapons have varying sound effects that allow you to tell what is being fired by listening alone, music is good, though there's only like 3 different songs in the whole game. You don't really notice this though, as i'd liken it to the hangar building music in Kerbal Space Program; just sort of there, not really in the forground.
Some changes i'd love to see would be a custom sizing option for the menus, with the building menu sometimes it's difficult to select which module you want (at least on my 1080p screen, not sure about smaller resolutions). It would also be wonderful to see some more offline modes, perhaps having only a single airship and upgrading in order to complete tasks or something.
And finally, I would love to be able to personally change which workers do what, or at least assign them myself. for example, if I have 6 airshipmen, an ammo depot (4 workers max), two cannons (1 worker each) and a water tank (2 workers max), the game will automatically decide where the workers go. so i might have 2 workers on the water tank, two for the cannons, and two for the ammo depot. But sometimes i'd rather have 3 on the depot, and only 1 on the water tank. nitpicky perhaps, but it would help a little.

Section 8: Prejudice is a surprisingly decent, if not painfully short, FPS. The main campaign will probably only run you about 3-4 hours or so, with a decent amount of that time stuck in loading screens.
It feels like an attempt to replicate the feel of the Halo franchise in a way, by making your characters kind of "floaty", as well as everything having a general "Halo"-like feel to it, from the character design to the weapons.
The story, however, is rather lackluster, and doesn't really have any memorable moments to it at all. Something about aliens, or a rebel task force... or... Something. Nothing really sticks with you. The cut scenes really don't add any substance to the game at all.
Graphically, the game actually looks really nice. Nothing amazing, but definitely on par with what I would expect from something that's trying very hard to replicate the look and feel of Halo. The environments are polished all the characters look really amazing.
I'd have to say that one of the biggest flaws this game suffers from is that it's using Games for Windows Live, which poses a huge detriment to actually enjoying the game. I made the mistake of forgetting what account I used to register the game with initially, and now I can never fully enjoy the game again, as GFWL does not let you access many features of the game without being logged in, nor does it let you save your Campaign Mode progress. So if you ever forget your GFWL password, you'll never be able to just jump back into the game; you'll have to play it from start to finish in one run.
The multiplayer is decent, for what it's worth, though I had difficulty finding anybody to actually play with. The actual gameplay in the multiplayer mode was okay. Nothing I'd ever look back on and say "Boy, I want to do that again!", but it wasn't bad, either. Just like the rest of the game, it was just "okay".
I'd say if you want to play a decent sci-fi FPS, it wouldn't hurt to pick up this game. Just don't expect this to be game-changing or anything.

This game took me by surprise, and then kept me occupied for — according to Steam — over 90 hours of playtime. Geez.
It is very, very heavy on dialogue and story in general. I used to think Suikoden V had a slow start, where it took maybe 6 hours for the story to really get going; Trails in the Sky FC easily doubled that time (for me, anyway). But oh man, was it worth it. Character customization for combat is fairly satisfying and gets more interesting as the game progresses, but the actual combat is somewhat slow-paced. This goes from being hard to get used to in the beginning (and adding to the slowness of the intro...), to feeling just right towards the middle and end — where playing strategically and planning your moves really starts to matter.
Ultimately though, where this game shines the brightest is in its likable cast of characters and its world building and overall story-telling. If you're the sort that loves seeing literally every single NPC in the whole chapter update their dialogue after every. single. change in the story... this game is for you! If you enjoy delving into the social interactions of the townspeople and watching them progress as your main story does, you'll likely love this. The only downside to this is, of course, that you'll probably end up doing a LOT of running around and talking to people every time something significant happens. But technically this isn't at all necessary to actually progress the main story.
If you're a completionist, you'll absolutely WANT to do the extra running around and exploring, though: the game is extremely sneaky about hiding items, dialogue and entire side quest chains. On the one hand this could be seen as annoying or frustrating; I certainly did miss a few quests and was bummed about that. But on the other hand, it is immensely rewarding to just accidentally stumble onto an interesting side story or mystery or monster extermination quest when you aren't expecting to.
The game does an amazing job of familiarizing you with its setting — be it its lore and ancient history, or the current political, social and militaristic state of your country (Liberl) and its surrounding nations. The only thing that I've played that comes close to doing this as well as Trails in the Sky is, well, the Suikoden series.
...Speaking of which, a lot of the music in this game reminds me of Suikoden. And aside from maybe a couple somewhat repetitive town tracks, the soundtrack is really, really good. I just wish it was purchaseable DLC on Steam.
TL;DR: Very, very long game. Lots of dialogue. Story is the focus, combat is secondary. Many hidden things. Great music. Very likable characters. Super duper highly recommend! ...Oh and it ends in such a way that you're going to really, badly want more of it. Thankfully the second chapter is on Steam already. :)

Alright, here goes. After two and a half hours, I really enjoy this game. It looks great, the combat is fun, the story is decent (if not exactly original), and i really love the characters. In many ways, it should be easy to recommend to everyone. In a perfect world, this would be a well-known classic.
However... as I said, I'm two and a half hours in. About twenty minutes of this has been actual gameplay, and that includes walking around in a town and learning about the skill system. That's really not a whole lot of "gameplay". I have heard a lot of people defend it by saying the story matters and so on, but I don't really agree. Final Fantasy XIII got a lot of hate for being a corridor the first 30+ hours, yet the same people like Trails in the Sky even if it's yet another corridor? That doesn't make sense to me. Why hate one game and praise another for the exact same reason? And yes, I did enjoy FFXIII a lot. But I think it had a nice ratio of cutscenes vs gameplay. Some cutscenes, some gameplay, some cutscenes, some gameplay etc. Trails in the Sky has very long cutscenes, then some brief, extremely linear gameplay, then yet another looooong cutscene. Again, two and a half hours in, and have played around 20 minutes. If that.
Also, I love games like "999: 9 Hours, 9 Persons, 9 Doors" (though I always get the door, person, hour order wrong), and those games are 90% cutscenes. But they are *intended* to be cutscenes. I knew what I was getting myself into right away. Trails in the Sky is intended to be a JRPG with strategy-RPG elements (move around the battlefield etc), and the story isn't really anything new. So why this endless focus on cutscenes?
But if you can get past that, I recommend this game. It looks great, the characters are awesome and the combat fun. And who knows? Maybe it opens up later. Fingers crossed. :)

Firstly, I love this game because you can drive all over Europe. You have to manage your money, and make sure that, when you get out a loan from the bank, you have enough money to pay it back, or are at least making enough daily profit to pay it back.
You also manage a business. You can hire drivers to work for you, and they will complete jobs for you, but you have to pay them a wage, plus some for every journey they complete. You can always do 'Quick Jobs', and these are when the employer provides the truck, and you just go where they tell you. This is fun, but it starts to get boring, only doing short deliverys, so you can buy a truck, so that you can go further distances, and get more money.

Fez is clearly a love letter to old-school side-scrolling platformers like Super Mario and Metroid. It's 8-bit aesthetics and sound are distinctive and charming, and the gameplay is incredibly therapeutic. Playing Fez isn't stressful at all, which is in line with creator Phil Fish's vision for a game that harkens back to children just playing and exploring without any clear objective. The rotation mechanic is a very creative addition to spice up the gameplay of traditional platformers. The ending is pretty remarkable in that it makes references to string theory and physics. Awesome game!

The game demands more skill in puzzle-solving than in platforming. It's not meant to be 100% completed in one playthrough; in New Game+, the player gets an ability to find more clues to solving the puzzles.
The puzzles constitute most of the game, and although it's possible to get lucky in solving them, the solutions definitely have strong reasoning behind them. The mechanics and clues behind the puzzles are among the most creative that I have seen.

I quit playing the game after not too long, since, though I like simulator games, this game was just way too simplistic, and way too unrealistic... But after playing it some more, the game really started to grow on me. As I played, I found that it's wildly addicting. I've always been able to appreciate sim games, the kind where you just click on buttons and check stats, but this was something more. I never have liked simple things, but I found that the simplicity has a sort of charm to it. It seemed like such a boring game at first, but as I built up my supplies, I started to become quite attached to my characters. Though the game doesn't allow for much good storytelling, it just leaves it more up to the imagination. It seemed just lazy, but I eventually started to like the little things like, how you don't have an inventory, but rather a set of a few random variables, and how, when in a fight, the game accounts for no background aside from you and the zombies, just leaving a black backdrop. It really is a great game, just takes some getting used to.

This is a really fun little game. Section 8: Prejudice is basically a low budget, science fiction Battlefield, with a few neat touches of its own to boot. An important part of the game, it that trully makes you feel you are a futuristic super-soldier, with the ability to sprint blindingly fast, jetpack into the air, and use a limited lock-on ability with your weapons, all right from the get go.
The primary goal of each map is to capture points around the map, much like Battlefield, but interestingly, small side-missions pop up while the larger battle is going on, which can net your team additional points. This keeps the battle dynamic and a little unpredictable, keeping a handful of capture points from being the sole focus of all combatants.
I also really enjoyed that vehicles and other supplies need to purchased and dropped in from space, rather than just respawning after a period of time. The same is true when you die; you are given the option of being dropped from orbit, allowing you to land behind enemy lines, provided they haven't set up anti-air auto-cannons to destroy you in mid-air.
S8 also includes a fun four-player co-op mode, similiar to a horde defense mode from other shooters. While the single player is pretty boring and repetitive, and not worth the time, the different multiplayer modes are all great. It's unfortunate this game didn't do very well, despite its bargain bin price. It's unlikely there's much of an active community left, as it was on the smaller side even on release in 2011, but if you have three friends, I recommend picking up the four-pack for the co-op at the very least. It's one of the best budget shooters out there, and some of its innovations outdo the bells and whistles of the FPS heavy hitters out there.

The way I see it. The point of Road Redemption is to depict the most critical moments of every bike event (be it a "race", take out bikers, attract the police, etc), where tension and danger have build up to their highest.
If you consider that and keep that in mind, than this game delivers it very well. Its very action packed and keeps you at the edge of your seat 99% of the time (even that not being the ideal for me, personally, but that is a matter of taste).
I think its fair to see people disapointed with this game because they expected a Road Rash remake, and you can't acctually blame them because the developers used the Road Rash hype to get attention directed to them. But you can't also blame the developers for wanting to make their product to stand out on their own and bring their own ideias to light.
--x--

is a 3D fantasy themed massively multiplayer online role-playing game (MMORPG) developed by Bluehole Studio. The game was released in South Korea on January 25, 2011, in Japan on August 18, 2011, in North America on May 1, 2012, and in Europe on May 3, 2012, with closed and open beta testings taking place before the launch dates. NHN Corporation, NHN Japan Corporation, En Masse Entertainment and Frogster Interactive Pictures publishes the game in these regions, respectively. In February 2013 the game was renamed to TERA: Rising concurrently with the game's launch to the free-to-play model.
TERA has typical MMORPG features such as questing, crafting, and player versus player action. The game's combat uses a real-time battle system that incorporates third-person camera view. The player targets an enemy with a cross-hair cursor rather than clicking or tabbing an individual opponent (which is called the "Non-Target battle system" by the developer). The Players need to actively dodge enemy attacks. A keyboard and mouse or a control pad can be used to control the character.
The developers collaborated with CCP Games and their successful use of "PLEX" for Eve Online as a way of deterring gold farmers. As a result, TERA released a currency called "Chronoscrolls" that works similarly, as it allows game time to be purchased with real money and sold for in-game gold. The use of Chronoscrolls is only available to users who have purchased the game either digitally or physically. Those with the "Discovery Edition" cannot use Chronoscrolls.
In February 2013, Tera in North America and Europe transitioned to "Tera Rising", which changed the subscription model to a "freemium" design (free play plus buyable premium status and customization options). The developer has promised no time, level, or content restrictions for free players after this update. Players who purchase a 30-day "Elite" status will receive increased dungeon rewards, in-game discounts and other metagame advantages. Due to the new model, the "Chronoscrolls" mentioned above are being phased out, and are no longer sold by the developer, nor usable to extend game time. Existing chronoscrolls can be sold to merchants for 2,000 gold.
The Japanese and Korean versions of Tera also became free to play in December 2012 and January 2013, respectively.
Characters may be one of seven races:
-  The Aman, a race of draconian humanoids
-  The Baraka, a giant, intelligent race
-  The Castanics, a demon-like race
-  The Elins, an innocent nature loving race
-  The High Elves, a race of traditional and elegant humanoids
-  The Humans
-  The Popori, an animal-like race.
The Baraka, Elin, and Popori are gender locked (only male Baraka and Popori, and female Elin exist). Both males and females are playable for the rest of the races. The Elin were originally projected as Female Popori in the early stages of the game creation.
Each race has a set of unique "racial skills" that gives them minor advantages. For instance, Elins and Popori have skills that increase out-of-combat movement speed, while High Elves can restore all of their MP on a long (2 hour) cooldown. Races also have their own unique animations for many class-specific skills, leading to small advantages and disadvantages in framerate, animation speed, movement distance, attack distance, or other attributes for each individual skill depending on which race the player has chosen.

Depending on your class, you typically can wait anywhere from an instant to 15min of matching time. If you're a DPS class, I would expect something of at least 5min and upward. If you're a tank, (Lancer specifically,) I would expect a very short matching, (approx. immediately to 2min,) and if you're a healer, (Priest or Mystic,) around 2min and upwards. Nobody likes an uncooked, soggy sausage.
Took me 42 minutes to beat the 'easiest' puzzle in the game. No doubt it will get easier as I go along so I look forward to breezing through this in a few hours tops.

+ Decepively simple. You might look at the trailer or start a level and think "This game looks easy, I got this no sweat!" ...but the game will taunt you as you get stumped on each and every level.
+ The gameplay is pretty simple and easy to learn. The goal is to cook sausages on the burner. You must cook the sausage once on both sides to complete the level. If you cook them twice or knock the sausage into the water you lose.
+ "Undo button" which allows you to easily traceback your steps without having to restart the level from the beginning.
+ Very challenging, great for veteran puzzle solvers. One thing that makes the game so hard is that each level is on a very small grid which limits your available moves severely. One wrong move and you will be in deadlock, so you have to carefully plan out each move.
+ relaxing soundtrack
+ Just a personal note, but this is one of those game that you have a friend or family member play and laugh at them while they sturggle to get past the first few levels.
- The game is incredibly difficult from start to finish. This may throw off casual players who will likely not finish 5 levels before giving up.
- I feel like the movement controls could be improved a bit. Sometimes you want to turn around, but your characters will turn in the oppisite direction causing you to accidentally hit a sausage, which can be a bit annoying.
[Side Note: I seldem mention price points in my reviews, but this game is currently priced at $30!... that's a bit steep and may impact how much you enjoy the game]

If you want to cut your teeth on the Final Boss of box-pushing puzzle games, then have I got the game for you.
Right out of the gate SSR offers a somewhat uneven mix of real head-scratchers and what I can only describe as pity puzzles, but quickly reveals itself to be the sort of puzzler that mandates particularly extensive sessions of staring at the seemingly inconsequential number of tiles onscreen and poking experimentally at them until something starts to click. This demands a little more patience than I ordinarily have, but I was starting to appreciate the design as I acclimatized to it.
Then I arrived at The Great Tower level (in only the second subsection of the overworld), which all at once foists about 4 times more pieces on you than you've dealt with previously, while simultaneously introducing a Z-axis and the concept of using pieces as platforms mid-puzzle.
SSR does have a well-executed and forgiving Undo function with basically unlimited storage which is a great thing to have up until the time spent rewinding would outweigh the time spent to simply restart the puzzle and do over; the only way it could be made practical on a level that large would be if you had a full-on timeline scrubber like in the rerelease of Duke Nukem 3D.
There's patience, there's logic, and then there's
I play puzzle games to try and
stress, not the other way round. It's a solid design, and I'd probably recommend it to the REALLY die-hard logicians and puzzle fanatics. To the sort like me who enjoy puzzles but prefer there to be some sort of ceiling to their complexity, Gaben help you if you're going to try and soldier through this thing. I would even call Infinifactory a lot more accessible than this is.

Super hard, no handholding, but there's a steady progression and figuring out the solution always feels SO good! Every single level has a new idea to it to solve it. Every part of a level is carefully placed. For example, if there's a 5 tiles high tower with a ladder on it, you'll need to use it. This way, there's the almost non-verbal "language" that you'll start to understand. "Oh, there's only one tile grill here, I probably have to push the sausage over it, vertically", etc, etc. Around world 4 or 5 things start getting crazy and there's new mechanics you'd have never guessed possible in the starting areas, all built around the very simple base idea of pushing sausages around.
A bizzarre game that needs hardcore dedication but if you're into it for the gameplay rather than cut scenes and spectacle, this is one of the most rewarding games out there. Know what you're getting yourself into, though!

So, the game has improved a lot. You find my original review down there.
But let me say, that the game in it's current form is a good game. Most of the bugs were fixed and multiplayer actually works, if you find people to play.
So If you do not need to have the new licences and just want a fun racing game to play now and then, you should get this one, because it's surely going to be cheaper than the new F1 2016.
Original Review:
The game is really not that bad as it sounds, and it would definitely deserve a good rating, once the bugs are fixed.
The game does some thing right of course and it's not all bad. You do have the new engine which is pretty great graphically, the new physics are really good and it's really fun to play. The AI is also better then the years before. They drive more agressively (i.e. attack you on the outside of a corner etc.) and make less misstakes just by themselves, but of course also try to overtake you with smokeing tyres sometimes. Good job there. But then you run into a bug...
And that's the problem, there are many bugs, which sometimes prevent you from even finishing a race (getting stuck in the pits or something like that). There are some other glitches which are pretty annoying. Some people even say, that the game crashes from time to time, which, I must say, has never happened to me so far. But there is one dealbreaker which makes game game bad right now...
Multiplayer on PC simply is not playable. 90% of the time, you don't even find a lobby and when you do, most of the times the game gives you a disconnect just short before the start of the race.
So is the game bad? No it's not, it's just not out of beta test as of now. There is a really strong foundation here, and it would really be a good game, once all the bugs are fixed. So my verdict is:
If you just want to play single player and enjoy good racing against AI, you could get the game if you don't mind a bug here or there... You could of course also wait till the bugs are fixed.
If, however, you want to play multiplayer, don't get it! Wait till the bugs are confirmed to be fixed, and then you have yourself a good game to play.

Secondly, there are lots of bugs, yes but the majority of the game-breaking ones are fixed and the game is actually a pleasure to play. I do however hope to see the ones that are in the game still ironed out and I do NOT forgive Codemasters for releasing a broken game.

Overall, yes I recommend this game, however make sure that you have a compatable controller or wheel prior to buying it, I use a wireless Xbox 360 controller and some cheap reciever and they're okay. It's fun and if you don't mind waiting for some features or for bugs to be fixed then definitely pick this game up.

I played the original Emily Is Away when that came out and I was very excited when I heard there was a second game coming out. While I admit I was a bit skeptical at first when I saw it was going to cost money, unlike the original, I bought the game and played it all in one sitting. It was in my opinion the best game of 2017 so far. The fact that there's so many more things in it now besides just messaging Emily is really helping with the feeling of realism in the game. There's of course a lot of replay value as can be expected from a game that's all about choices. I love the way it really tries to make you feel like you're back in the mid-2000s, something it is very succesful at. Overall I am very impressed by this game and I can't wait to see what else the developer has in store for us!

What I like:
- This is a great piece of mid 00s notalgia.
- The conversations feel incredibly real. If you grew up chatting online at this time it feels like a real conversation you would have.
- The story rides a good line between corny and real, patronizing and independant. The characters all seemed pretty cool.
- The other content that is brought into this game through Youtube and "Facenbook" is great, a genius way to add to this game.
What I don't like:
- Minor: I couldn't access the "desktop" portion and it wasn't clear how to do that. Luckily it didn't affect the game play.
- Minor: There were a few times where the text that was input didn't match what I selected and that was annoying.
- Minor: In 2006 this would be Gmail, not AOL. lol
- Major: It seems like the central mechanic of the game is a time based answer mechanic where it has a lot more to do with the time the computer takes to type the words then it does for you to write your response and is annoying.
All told this is a great game, and if you have $5 you should get it, but it's probably worth closer to $2.50. I will check out the prequel/sequel.

I can't truly put to words how much I hate this game. Connor is unlikeable and plastic, and I never really bonded with him in the same way I bonded with Ezio and Altair. The setting is also very plastic, almost like walking through a miniature model of Boston as a tiny toy soldier. Graphics are watery and low-resolution at best, and Connors base-set of Assassin's Garb is so uninspired it hurts. Glitches are everywhere, from flying horse carriages, to dead bodies stretching out across the entire eastern seaboard, it is nigh impossible to get immersed. The control set also changed from 2-Brotherhood-Revelations, and if you played all of those games you'll more likely than not spend half the game trying to use the old controls you got used to and failing and fumbling about. Honestly, the biggest drawback is that it's set in Colonial America; there's nothing new or exciting to be had in Colonial America, it's all 'been there, seen that' (At least from the standpoint of being born and raised in America.), with the feeling that they took a crash elementary-level US History course before writing the plot. The only thing it has going for it is the crafting and caravan management, which even that is riddled with horrid bugs and hidden behind a god-awful UI that makes doing anything a chore. Overall, I give this game a 3/10. Spend your money elsewhere.

SPIDERBIKE! SPIDERBIKE!
More like SPIDER RASH... I backed this thing up because I'm hopelessly addicted to the 1995 Roadrash for PC (remember the friggin awesome Soundtracks on that one?) the rail rider mechanic (having the screen pull your bike around wherever the road bends and you got to pull in that direction to keep in lane or avoid collisions). Expect me to endlessly compare this UNITY engine stinker to the good ol' boy classic. My name is Milwaukee Jon !
Now I know this is Early Access and I am writing TWO notes here to edit this review whenever I see significant changes.
First off: Unity? FFFFFUUUUUUUUU...
Runs like @$$. I'm serious. I have seen better Tetris 3D clones with more destruction and particle effects that run like a waterfall (constant). I have just recently grabbed Receiver (thx Bundle store) for free and I am willing to accept its low poly plastic look that runs as $H!T as anything else with the touch of the Unitron.
I guess the engine was picked for a reason (looking at you Linux and MacOS) but ffs is it underperforming.
Could be because I do not own a 1337 PC GAMING MASTER RACE accredited machine. I don't give two about that becaue I played games in the past decade that a) run like hell and b) look like paradise at the same time while you get your lil avatar♥♥♥♥♥raped by the superb AI that handles most of your surroundings. All the while my machine was switched to energy saving settings.
Anyway:
Soundtrack is a bit here and there. I really like some of those electro tunes (shiz beatz and all the shebang) but on the other side the metal tunes cannot possibly compare to the grunge awesome that was included in the classic. However if you compare the stage themes (there were 5 in the classic) and this one that puts random themes everytime you reload a stage I guess it is somewhat better because you know it is an actual track and not a MIDI tune with fake instruments from the system repository.
Controls: As I expected it is an upgrade in dimensions. You have thrusters to do quick jumps and doubletap to activate a constant booster instead of boost capsules that needed to be timed well in the classic to have an effect. You can turn around, drive here and there, only limited by the camera pitch towards the center but OH WAIT, mouse now controls the camera and the combat. The one hit takedowns work nicely and blocking seems to be OK. There is even a hook gun that when mastered can become your best tool while chasing rivals or evading obstacles. Spiderman approved!
Video and Settings: Change resolution, windowed or FS, AA, VS. all that $H!T takes a nose dive because on weak rigs you can pretty much forget about it. Doesn't matter what you pick. Fastest is still beyond min. playability. The more is happening on screen the worse stuttering gets. I usually just skipped the city rooftop stages whenever I lost too much HP cause they are pointless when the best I get are 12 FPS...
Gameplay:
One hit takedowns (crticals) are often, booster gets me up to max speed when I need it but doesn't help chasing well placed opponents although the game cuts you some slack like the classic did. The opponents are often gathered near frontrunner so if you manage to drive fast and not fly off your bike or get
SUPER GLUED  to the rear of a car (wtf man?) then you have a good chance to overtake all them suckas at once (thx to the popo beating up everyone and occasional car storms (yes you heard right, CARS dropping out of the sky onto the track like ultra heavy rain drops of the apocalypse!!!). I felt like a D@m/\/ wizard while a few hundred meters in front of me cars spawned out of nowhere and crushed the opposition and pesky pigs.
As mentioned in the beginning. Hook gun comes complete with bungee rope and all that gud stuff. While midair you can turn directions like Mario and not give a flying pair of ducks about inertia or silly physics. YOU ARE THE PHYSICS! Oh what is that, a huge boulder? NOPE! it's a perfectly fine ramp. Just dash into it and get catapulted back on track while blasting fools from above with your hitscan AK, UMP, Shotie and grenade launcher. Hell yeah.
I guess at this point I gotta pull the emergency brakes: See, the classic was inspired by the console versions. The combat felt up close and personal because you AND your rivals had a health bar that regenerated once downed. It was fists vs. fists, chains, bats. The opponents had names displayed in the corner. They even had UNIQUE outfits and bike colors ffs (d@mn boy (speaking of Early Road Redemption), you gettin yo 4$$ handed to ya by a 20 year old game you tried to surpass). That's right, rival gangs, popo and all that SHARE most of the looks. One surprise I found was that some random racers drove CARS! Wohoo, I can't bash your teeth in but I sure can blow you up with sticky TNT or that nice 40mm launcher.
Then again, the basic get up in the classic was a helmet, a two colored bodysuit, and the color of your bike. The popo had fat bikes and leather with an open helmet so you could see their faces when punching them off their bikes. This one surprises me.
Nobody wears helmets (only random ♥♥♥♥♥ drivers wear those), everyone is beating everyone of different color, the cars just run into you when you try to slow down, Coppers don't play it save, the cars do incredible amounts of colateral damage, the police is more interested in murdering than in real life minus the use of guns (would be too OP I guess).
What I am trying to say here is that basically I like some of the new stuff but laugh at the lack of detail that's been put in the visuals and the behaviour. Everyone is bat$H!T insane and the truck drivers are dropping deadly logs on purpose causing endless waves of crashing cars and taking you off your bike (I guess those things get nerfed sooner or later). It makes the feels go away and make way to a different kind of frustrating. Needs way more polish guys.
One example in combat dynamics:
Here only the toughest makes it out alive (most of the time it is you because everybody else gets knocked the EFF out from one hit criticals or quick 2 hit combos or simply mowed down by gunfire thank god it isn't autoaiming like in some other bike racing games *cough* Jacked *cough*). Once you manage to crash enough times (mostly thrice) then it is bye bye and you gotta restart your career in a parallel universe as the Game Over screen keeps tellin yo stOopid @$$ (or spend EXP on a "NEW" concept of advancing the plot. Yes, a PERK let's you skip the beginning stages).
The perk system is very funny at that it COMPLETELY bypasses SHOP, CLUB HOUSE, SAVE TOILET. Yep.
Want a better bike? only 100XP for starters, want higher character stats? moar EXP please. Want to gain more for less? EXP is currency, money is for the YOLO campaign items. The concept of YOLO is exactly that. Where the save feature made devastating bike damage pointless in Rash: oh you failed, bike is gone, money is gone, go back to square one and ... oh wait just load your last save. Redemption goes: PFFUUU...CK saving, better transcend space and time and possess another racer that looks exactly like you and condemn him to the same if not worse bone shattering death! Oh and go back to the beginning lowie.
Character traits are gone completely. You are the same a-hole all the time occasionaly your dummy driver comes with a helmet. Watch out we got a badass over here. You can steal weapons from everybody else but why would you when the missions are short and your own stash of multiple murdering tools is more than enough. Oh right. Weapon degradation. No ammo refills, no slice and dice. Every hit takes a chunk out of weapon condition. No more endlessly swinging your bat in the face of oncoming rivals.
What I expect in the future:
Biker Names - at least the Opposition
Moar creativity with the bikes - customization
MUCH longer stages. MUCH LONGER.
5/10

Sixteen hours.
That is how much time I have devoted to sitting down in this game, and giving it an honest look-at. It sat for sixteen hours not mindlessly playing, but paying attention to lore and gameplay mechanics. I observed what makes this game, and what breaks it. There are many things that I can solidly say I love about this game, but I want to also list my reasons why I'm not playing another minutes.
This game for starters is breathtaking. I normally am not one for the light fantasy settings, meaning the rainbows and the overall happy tone to it, but I found this game amazingly detailed and beautiful. I loved the lands you could roam, I loved the views that were offered, and I took the paths given as well as some places where not many go. If there is one thing this game is, it's beautiful. Not heavenly, but it's good enough for me to call art.
Secondly, the combat is delightful. I love the choices that allow me to be completely overpowered so I can finally solo, not liking to play with groups all that much. I found myself having a blast with larger semi-boss mobs, the lengthened fights and the heavy hits if I did not avoid them. The fluidity of the combat is also wonderful, being a cannon wielder, I found it hard to compare any other class I have played in previous games that has fluid movement and versatility like that.
Lastly, I'm somewhat happy with the world being at peace with eachother (somewhat), the major races anyway. I understand needing division within the game, like in WoW with the two major choices being presented. But I like the idea of being able to be the unthinkable ally (in most fantasy games) of a high-elf like being with a dark-elf like being (gah, can't remember their names.) The division in this game will come from players themselves and their guilds, mostly tests of mocho to see who is better. Look to the skys and see who is dominating!
But with every good, there is a bad.
Firstly, I want to state that I'm not happy with the armor that is given to female characters. Being a gunner, I had to play as two of the most attriactive females. I don't think there is anything wrong with giving your character something sexy to wear, but having nothing but skimpy clothing up until ~20 isn't right, moreso if I can't have something I can't play with a open door in my room.
Secondly, there is nothing outstanding about the story. A world in peace---> 'Darkness' ----> ??? ---> Game
This is the basic format that I have gathered. While I understand that they are trying to make a game, something with more detail to why it is happening instead of "random island!" is kinda... Silly. I mean, there might be more explained in later levels, but I would rather know my lore right off the bat and learn non-essential lore later on, instead of the reverse.
I said my fair share, and provided something major changes for something different in the game, I won't be revisiting this game. From my own play, I don't like it, and i don't recommend it.
But, this might be someone's thing, who knows, different pallets for each person.
So, play at your own risk.

This game alternately makes me feel smart and dumb as hell. I haven't gotten too far into it yet, but I see myself developing a Stockholm Syndrome love-hate relationship with the fiendishness of the puzzles. It's like Dark Souls for your spatial reasoning instead of your reflexes.

"A simple 3D puzzle game" is an apt description - simplicity is where its greatness lies. It is notorious for being difficult, but while it can take a bit of time to figure out the rules that govern the movement of your character and the sausages (some of these rules feel a bit arbitrary), after you do the difficulty gradient is negative. It felt like the middle of the game was where it peaked in difficulty.
The game allows you an infinite stack of undos, since it's easy to make a puzzle unsolvable. The best puzzles are those where you really have to use constructive reasoning to rule out sets of possible moves, and there are lots of puzzles like that. For some others the trick is relatively simple and it feels more like trial and error as you try to avoid moving sausages to inaccessible positions, particularly towards the end of the game.
The level design is consistently creative. Each level feels genuinely different from the last; the game only repeats tricks to introduce new ones. To top it off, each level is integrated into a huge overworld; on activating a puzzle, the unnecessary land drops away and you are left with some sausages to roll and a grill. The overworld is fun to explore, and the freedom to tackle puzzles - within an area - in the order you choose means you can postpone difficult puzzles for later. Without the overworld the game simply wouldn't be as interesting, or as user-friendly.
The graphics are as you see. Crude, but for a game like this, the most important thing is that it's easy on the eyes. The music is subdued and soothing. The game is relaxing to play and doesn't try to assault your senses.
Is £20 a misguided price for this game? Yes. Do you get your money's worth of utility from it? Absolutely. It's quite a long game, and you get to solve puzzles which genuinely require thought.
I played the DRM-free version and I think I spent about 20 hours finishing it, give or take 5. You can get both the DRM-free version and a Steam key for the same price, and they share the same directory for save data.

Stephen's Sausage Roll must be one of the purest puzzle games to come around in years. It is 100% created for its mechanics and the way they are incorporated into the staggering amount of puzzles is sheerly baffling.
Somehow each level showcases a new concept. This is an incredbile feat as there are no "powerups",
special keyboard prompts or any other standard gaming conventions to promote variety: the sausages, fork and Stephen are all that are needed.
This game is not for the feint of heart. The begining levels are likely to take upwards of 5 to 10 minutes each to figure out how to properly navigate a perfectly cooked sausage and it is very likely some puzzles will take hours to solve. There is not an unfair puzzle, no red herrings or cheap tricks, just pure rational problem solving.
The puzzles in this game have two general ways of being solved. The first is organically as you move around the level. Slowly you'll see movements that will get you closer and closer to your goal, its then just up to putting those movements in the correct order. Its a very satisfying feeling slowly building up your understanding of the puzzle until you can see the whole picture and have those tasty sausages pop away.
The second way problems get solved is by uncovering the underlying mechanics of the game and this is where it truely shines. There are no tutorials to teach you any mechanic other then moving and rewinding mistakes, a flawless mercy that lets you undo any action step by step for as long as the current play session (or if there is another limitation I've never expeienced it after rewinding dozens of minutes away just by holding down a single button). Its so well implimented that you can even undo exiting a level, making sure all those minutes of sausage rolling will never be in vein. Every time you discover a "new" mechanic is a moment of awe as your brain tries to process how many new possibilites this new option will provide. Do yourself a favour and never, NEVER, look any puzzle up. There are logical solutions to all of them and you will eventually be able to create it; a moment that will give you pure bliss until the next puzzle.
The art style at first feels very basic but the more time you spend with this game the more you understand the benefits of its simplicity. Everything has been created to make the best possible puzzle expeience and this art style allows for a clear sense of spacing for all aspects of the level as well as being able to frame most levels so that they fit in one screen. The little details like particle effects on flowers, the day-night cycle, the different sound effects for everything and even the music all show the attention to detail that this game went through.
All in all this is one of the greatest examples of not only the puzzle genre but of games in general. If more games could treat their mechanics with such care and expand them as far as Stephen's Sausage Roll the industry could only benefit.

I just finished the main storyline and I have to say, I don't feel like I'm done with the game. It very much feels like GTAV in that way.
So, what did I like?
The actual game world.
The game is visually gorgeous. The city is pretty damned accurate, and everything looks different depending on the weather and time of day, right down to shadows going in the right angles and water filling up low spots in the ground.
The sound is damned good overall, and the conversations between NPCs as you pass help make the game feel alive. The music is also really good, and one of my favorite parts was a "boss battle" with a song by The Prodigy going in the background.
The characters in the game are the best part, I think. Every one of the main characters in the story feels believable. I like most of them, and the tension between some of them is very genuine, be it friendship, mistrust, or even attraction. A lot of care and effort was put in to how these people react to each other.
The story was pretty good, and I liked how it all came together.
The hacking puzzles were mostly fun, and I really liked the side-quests and collectables scattered around the map.
So what didn't I like?
Mechanical stuff.
Cover based mechanics weren't perfect (too innacurate or too unresponsive. Or both).
Enemy NPC aggro and accuracy was a huge pain considering how tough most of them are.
Driving can be a chore (unless you are on a sweet bike and it's a relatively straight road).
Weapons were mostly a liablity, except for the upgraded stun gun.
Grenades were far too hard to throw accurately, and blowing them up wasn't always possible considering how inaccurate hacking on the fly tends to be in a gunfight.
A lack of jump made a lot of puzzles harder than they had to be, and jumping across gaps in buildings mostly impossible.
Micro-transactions for clothes and paint jobs (neither of which there are enough of in the game, IMO).
Overall, I loved this game. I still feel like playing it, despite the fact that I'm done with the main story. The negatives DID frustrate me from time to time to point of real anger, but they bothered me pretty infrequently if at all. The game is addictive, and it's (and I want to stress how frickin' weird this is)....
A GOOD Ubisoft game. No joke. Micro-transactions aside, the game is worth spending money on. Especially if it goes on sale. $60 might be a bit steep for many, but if it hits that sweet spot of $40 or below, it is well worth it.

When the first Watch Dogs was announced at E3 2012, I was one of the few that wasn't entirely engrossed by it. It came out and was met with a positive yet still underwhelming reception after the two-year build-up of hype. In E3 2016, Ubisoft, in a similar fashion to Bethesda's release of Fallout 4, debuted the first trailers and gameplay videos of Watch Dogs 2 and released it later in the year. Again, I wasn't really interested and like many people, thought it was going to be super cringey and edgy, especially seeing the masked emoji character. I was wrong (even about the masked fella).
Positives:
- San Francisco and the Bay Area are recreated beautifully, with many familiar landmarks and sites
- Graphics and PC port look nice and run fairly well
- Art and environments are well-detailed and alluring
- Being able to approach most missions and side content by only using hacking skills and your two drones, a lot of times without even having Marcus enter the objective's restricted area
- Likable and well-developed characters that emanate a greatly amicable sense of camaraderie as the story progresses
- Decent story diving deep into Silicon Valley involving several electronics and software companies making a contemporary cyberpunk-lite atmosphere
- Respectable and intelligible antagonist
- Many of the tracks in the original score are very well-done, some of my favorites being around the end of the game, though some can be a little off or mediocre
- Decent list of assorted songs in the radio/music playlists
- Majority of side content is decently produced and enjoyable, or serve a direct benefit to the player in terms of gameplay unlocks or vehicle/drone paintjobs, rather than being meaningless collectibles
- All NPCs are able to be hacked and manipulated
- Random occurences on the streets can be growingly amusing with the several many different NPC interactions and conversations there are in the game world, and even being able to call the cops or a gang attack on any random person
- Clever incorporations of familiar IRL phone apps
- Has a generally light-hearted and humorous tone, though shifts to serious affairs frequently all-throughout yet deftly
Negatives:
- Should be a lesser presence of lethal weapons and approaches to missions in accordance with how the hacker group 'DedSec' (you're a part of) isn't perceived to be necessarily violent in the narrative
- No real incentive of taking out people non-lethally
- Driving vehicles and handling could be a little better (though from what it sounds like, it's an improvement over the first)
- Hacking puzzles are mostly fine and fairly challenging but I really would've liked even more complex and intricate puzzles
- It might be too much to ask for, but there are many repeated character models that fill the game world, and very few different face designs, with different assortments of hair and head accessories
- As some people mentioned, with SuperBunnyHop on YouTube being a prominent voice, an even bigger emphasis on stealth might've favored the design of the game.
After 2016's long year of shooters (albeit of high quality), Watch Dogs 2 was a stand-out open-world game that was done right. Ubisoft seemed to take many criticisms of Watch Dogs 1 to heart and built a sequel that reigns superior, not unlike the transition from Assassin's Creed 1 to Assassin's Creed 2. Unfortunately it seemed that Watch Dogs 2 wasn't very successful in terms of sales, or at least not real close to the financial success of the first game. Here's to hoping it was good enough to warrant a Watch Dogs 3 that improves even more of the downsides of this game.

Okay, I don't usualy write reviews, but I chose to (this time).
I love this game.  It's one of the best city builders I have played within the past decade.  The other one is Cities XL, which I played heavily before Cities Skylies came out (unfortunately that game, Cities XL, is outdated and just wearing; not good for long play).
This game, however, if lively, bright, inviting, smooth, and fun.
I know a lot of people have an issue with Paradox's "DLC policy" but you're not required to buy DLC to enjoy this game.  The game itself is fun and has updates on its own.  Also, the game is open to mods, which means you can add assets and other things created by other fans of the game from the workshop without having to worry about the DLC.
...and I wonder jsut how many people may argue about the DLC may have bought an expansion pack for an online game (WoW or any other,... Final Fantasy 14 in my case).  I can't knock these worked on mini-expansions small prices when I spend $50 on an expansion for an online game that allows me to use 3 new jobs and travel to a new area...even thought I will be right next to people who can access these things without me having them (meaning the $50 was just a glorified unlock code, essentially)
I mean they could wait and make a massive expansion and release a fullsized expansion but I don't see the issue with sevelal small "expansions" called DLC.  DLC that one could wait until it goes on sale and buy them a bit along.
And that is why I recommend this game.  A company that continually wants to expand on their property to keep it alive.  If you see it as them just being greedy, you're not oblidged to buy it, but it's clear that people are still buying them.  Why?  because they enjoy the game.
That's the point of games.  To enjoy them.  Why not have more things added to further that enjoyment.  Much less have stuff added that is official, stable, and compatable.
Or, if you're not happy with it, you're free to go buy the old and outdated city builders that avaiable on Steam here.  SimCity4 is available...but you'll never get to see any new content or enjoy any mods with that game.

[POST-REVIEW EDIT:] Well, after some careful consideration, and a few additional playthroughs, i'm rendering a final, FINAL decision for this damn masterpiece of a game. It truly has been one of my Top 10's for best of 2017 thus far. It's simple, sure. But the pure emotion and thought-provoking story make up for the simplicity more than ten-fold. If you've ever had any doubts about playing Emily is Away Too, I can tell you it's worth it. For five USD, you're getting a ticket for one hell of a ride. I'm also raising my final rating to the highest 10/10 I can possibly give it. That makes it the first of the year. I don't know what it is about this game, but it really struck a chord with me. And I can tell that it's going to hold a very special place in my heart for some time to come. "If I could see all my friends tonight..."
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Before I begin, I will preface with saying that as a "Choose-Your-Own-Adventure" style game, Emily is Away Too excels. It's a cut above your average hour-long romp of trial-and error storytelling that you see from most games of this calibre nowadays. It deals with some actual real-life situations and handles them very well. In a fashion that makes sense...for the most part. But we'll get into that later. Seeing as how this isn't an entirely "complex" game, i'm not going to go about using my normal review style. Instead, i'm just going to give you a short list of pro's, con's, and my in-depth thoughts on specific listed aspects in either catagory. Let's begin.
-A pleasant and visually pleasing art-style remeniscant of the era being portrayed, and all the nostalgia that goes along with it.
-Generally great pacing.
-Two interesting, and in-depth main characters, although there's this one little instance...Well, we'll talk about that later.
-A helluva nostalgia trip due to the setting. But, may I take a moment to say:
Really though, the setting is engaging, and it sets the stage for the story very well.
-Actually reduces the window you play the game in down in size quite considerably, which isn't necessarily a bad thing. It is very remeniscant of the old-school instant messaging programs you'd see back in the day. That's the point, after all.
-An marvelous misadventure of a mini-game with knock-off Rick & Morty.
-An exaggeration of an entire Internet inside the game, which is suprisingly interactable.
-It gave me a cool wallpaper.
-Lots of little secret icons to unlock.
-Multiple endings.
-The introduction and mentioning of multiple side-characters, but no real way to interact with them. Some of these people sound like pretty interesting characters! Let me talk to them, god-dammit!
-The limitation to only a few dialouge options at a time. And most of the time, they're really generic and corny responses.  And sometimes, you'll find yourself with a bar full of options that ultimately mean the same thing, or the option you select will be changed by your character when he's typing it out! (That's how I got ♥♥♥♥ed over in the end.)
-The lack of an option to punch Evelyn in the god-damn throat.
SO, now that we've got that out of the way, let's pull a few things from the list, and talk in-depth about them. First-off:
WARNING: SPOILERS AHEAD!
This instance is a slap across the face of the player, and I sincerely hope that it gets patched soon to avoid frustration. Now, If you're just reading this portion to avoid spoilers, and you're going to be set on hooking up with Emily, I would advise you
to select "No, not really." when presented with a question about your virginity from Evelyn. Now...let's talk about something positive. The overall premise of the game is great for the league it's in. You'd be pressed to find some of the better CYOA games out there of this formula. The art-style is great, the developer's got some great taste in music, I find the pseudo-Internet thing really charming, and the real-life-esque scenarios you're presented with are believable and engaging. I also find all the old, nostalgic sounds of the old OS's, and hard-drives oddly theraputic.
*sigh* As you can probably tell if you read through my little rant given above, i'm kind of salty over a single fault in the game's design. But in all seriousness, it's a great CYOA game, and a great story in-and-of itself. You'll be getting around two hours of well-written dialouge, and interactive story, possibly three if you take the time to really dig deep into the psuedo-Internet in the game. And I say it's well-worth the price of admission.
TL;DR: Great CYOA game. Check it out. It's five bucks.
Final Rating: 10/10

I have to say Punch Club is surprisingly addictive.
After participating in Twitch Plays Punch Club and struggling to copy paste the steam codes from the Twitch chat (which is very difficult if the code refuses to stand still and someone already beats you to it).
Pretty much what the game is about is managing your boxer's day, having him train, work, sleep, eat.
If you don't train enough his strength, agility, stamina will deteriorate.
If you don't work, he wont' have money to buy food.
If you don't have food, he can't train.
If you work too much he will be unhappy which will make him train slower.
It's all about trying to find the perfect balance throughout your workers day.
It may sound tedious at first, but soon enough you get into it and find a ideal routine to make your boxer the best there is. Throughout the game you meet various people, gain new equipment, fight a Teenage Mutant Ninja
Crocodile, get a girlfriend, make difficult decisions, and maybe learn about your father's killer. You can train your guy to be like Mike Tyson and knockout your opponents in just a few hits, or make him like Bruce Lee and do some amazing kicks, or become a boxer that can't be easily knocked down.
Overall this is actually a very entertaining management game that I can just waste hours on. With various ways to build your character, discovering multiple routes throughout the story, and some very nice pixel art (and there is also a option for a retro mode), I can guarantee that you can also get as addicted as I did.
Final Rating:
