Stephen's Sausage Roll is a game that the developer doesn't want normal people to buy, it seems. The description is literally, "A simple 3d puzzle game.", there is one video that shows you nothing about the game, and it's priced at $32 CND.
Fortunately, I'm here to tell you to get off your♥♥♥♥♥and to buy this wonderful game. The graphics are alright, the music is OK, but the puzzles are sublime.
In each level, the goal is the same: cook all the sausages and exit the level by standing on the exit level sign in the right orientation. You cook sausages by pushing them over a grill. Like in sokoban games, you can't pull the sausage (yet...), only push it. Another huge wrinkle is that sides of the sausage can only touch the grill once. If you touch a cooked side of a sausage to the grill, it will be burned and you fail the level. This little wrinkle will make you pull your hair out in some levels as you try and figure out how the hell you are going to maneuver the sausages around so they get cooked properly. A neat thing about the game is that if you fail, you can still continue playing the level, which might help you figure out how to play it.
You'll have a section (part of an island) that has a number of puzzles for you to solve in any order, so if you get stuck, you can try another one (until you get to the last puzzle of the section). Once you complete a section, a new section will open up with more puzzles.
Your little guy has tank controls, which you will find extremely useful, as turning to the left or right near a sausage will push it in different directions. A nice detail is that the all of the puzzles make up the island section. When you activate a puzzle, the rest of the island drops away into the sea, leaving you on a tiny puzzle island.
Each section introduces new mechanics into the game. First you'll just be pushing the sausages, but then you'll be stacking them, skewering them (you would think this would make things easier, but no! You can't turn when you have a skewered sausage!), walking on them...
I would say that these levels are on the level of Snakebird, though I found many of them easier than Snakebird's puzzles (maybe I'm better at sokoban games than I know?). These are the kind of puzzles that you walk away from frustrated, but come back to a few hours later with the solution. This is the game where there are so many ah-ha! moments that make you feel smart. You have no idea what to do at first, but eventually you get better and better. You might not see solutions at first, but you begin to see where you need to go to solve the puzzle, and then work backwards from there. It's wonderful!
If you're having trouble, there's a community guide that has all the solutions, which is super helpful (though not as much when I was playing because it wasn't complete!).
It might be expensive, but I took 36 hours to solve all the puzzles and it was worth every penny.

Overall, an excellent JRPG. Great story, great characters, and good mechanics. This is certainly a game to get into if people want a good story to follow. While slow pace, the story is never boring and this is one of the few games I've had a connection with the characters and story. You will need the second chapter (SC) if you want to get into this.
The cons of this game are two-fold:
The PC port is shotty. I've played this on the PSP before and had no problems, but on PC (with an overkill PC and SSD) there's certain maps and areas that studder and gitter within 50-125fps that feels like it's running at 4fps. The menu sometimes doesn't want to show labels on items. Sometimes you won't be able to load up the saved games are at start-up. I've had more crashes than with a Bethesda game. Luckily the autosave is good. None of this is game-breaking, but rather dissapointing. Although I'm unsure if this is somehow only a problem on my system.
The gameplay is rather bleh~. Battle system is standard. There's not a whole lot of customizability with equipment and upgrade (you get better stuff progressively). Difficulties are whacked. Normal is rather challenging without grinding (I only grind before the final battle so I would have less headaches). Hard is a nightmare, and beyond... you've got to be a masochist because it's health/attack based difficutly. There's only a few good fights where the opponents try to fight smart, otherwise they become bullet sponges. If you play on normal, nothing will be teeth-grindingly bad, just not very challenging without. Once you turn it up to hard, you get kicked in the balls. Oh, and you can't change difficulties later on so choose wisely.
Side problem: The graphics are decent for the most part other than the sprites. They scream 2004! If that was changed, people would probably think this was a recent lower(ish)-budget title.
If you play on normal and suffer through the small port/localization problems, it's a really enjoyable game. Nice to sit back and play to enjoy the story with some small battle challenges here and there.

There's a good game under here somewhere. Unfortunately, there's just too much wrong with it for me to be able to recommend it, at any price.
I had this game on my wishlist for some time, as the premise sounds interesting, and I ended up picking it up in a bundle.
Even at bundle prices, though, I'm having a hard time feeling that this game is worth my time.
5 hours in at the time of writing this, I'm forcing myself to play to see if things get better. The game just crashed for the Xth number of time, so I'm taking a break to write this.
Crashes are an issue. Looking at the forum, it seems it's not overly uncommon, though it's not something that everybody has issues with; your mileage may vary.
My biggest issue is probably the UI, which is atrocious. Given Stardock's experience with 4x games (Galactic Civilization series, Sins of a Solar Empire series and the Elemental/Fallen Enchantress/Sorcerer King series), you'd think they'd know better, but... no. This is honestly the worst UI I've seen in a long time, clunky and unpleasant to navigate.
There seems to be pathing issues as well: it's happened a few times where mousing over a location on the map would say that my units could get there in one turn, but when I actually gave them the order to move, they didn't make it all the way.
I've also had idle units not be recognized as being idles, with the "end turn" prompt appearing when a unit still had moves left. If I hadn't remembered about the unit, I'm not sure what would have happened. Would the turn have ended, skipping the unit's turn, or would it have selected the idle unit at the last second? Either way, it's bad.
This really feels like an Early Access game, despite being a year-old stand-alone expansion to a game that came out in 2015 (stand-alone "expansions"; another one of Stardock's bad habits, on par with the AAA industry's filthy love of "Super Extra Collector's Edition Director's Cut" re-releases).
Again, though... there really seems to be a good game hiding under here somewhere...
I like that there's a wide unit variety, lots of craftable equipment (not just for your heroes, but for your regular units as well), lots of spells to learn and cast, lots of "races/leaders" to choose from (which you can customize).
The empire-building/4X aspect is a bit odd, being very limited in where you can build cities at first (only on specifically-designated "fertile" tiles), but as the game progresses, you learn spells which allow you to turn regular tiles into fertile ones, thus expanding your empire. I'm not at that point in the game yet, so I'm not sure how that exactly plays out, but it's something different and interesting to look forward to.
Can't say I'm a fan of the pace: I'm playing on easy difficulty, figuring that would let me not worry too much about sucking and advance at a decent pace while learning the game, but... no. There's a lot of waiting around, and you're quite limited in what you can do in the early game. Enemies are impressively tough, even on easy, which really limits what you can do early on.
No doubt part of that is because I don't exactly know what I'm doing and I'm still learning the game, but I've played enough 4X in general and a bit of Fallen Enchantress in particular (which is very similar to this title) to feel that it's not just my lack of skill that's holding me back.
I'll keep playing this a bit more, but I'm thinking I should just go back to Fallen Enchantress and play that, which I haven't done in a long time. Too long to really compare the two games, but my foggy memory seems to indicate that this is simply a worse version of that.
So... don't waste your time with this title, and maybe check out Fallen Enchantress instead. Not a perfect game in its own right, but a better version of this, at least.

Radium is a game based on your skill to navigate a ball through hazardous environments, by controlling the ball with two control points that exert force on the ball. Some levels include collecting tokens to open the exit. You should watch that short video on the store page, screenshots can't depict how the interaction with the ball works.
It's very simple, and I found it challenging in exactly the right way. Difficult, but not frustrating. Getting a feel for the physics, retrying and learning the levels is a big element, and you will make progress and it feels very rewarding. There are no random elements in this game, when you fail it will be your fault and you will happily try again. The experience is very smooth, with a very short 2 seconds countdown before the timer starts, and a key that instantly restarts the level if you're about to fail. The levels are quite short, rarely more than a minute long, most of them around 30 seconds I guess.
Then there are time limits to beat to collect stars, and this game becomes essentially a racing game where you have to take corners with the right amount of speed, you will steer and drift and use walls or try other approaches through parts of a level, to try and optimize your time.
There are several gameplay mechanics that the game employs to change things up and keep you entertained (very successfully so, I might add):
- collecting tokens: in some levels, they are distributed around a maze or nonlinear network of tunnels that you have to learn or to optimize your path through them. In other levels they just are scattered in an open area with some hazards, and you have to see how to collect them quickly by just steering the ball as precise as possible around the hazards. You'll often have to weigh risk of collisions against speed.
- special tokens that reverse the ball control, from pulling towards the control points to pushing away from the control points. Often they cannot be bypassed and you have to be ready to adapt to that other "mode", which is always a chance for disaster :)
- limited visibility in some levels: sometimes there's darkness and only your ball's surroundings are illuminated to some extent, which emphasizes your learning the level, with each retry getting better and anticipating the point where to break or where to initiate a curve or something. Like car racing in fog, on a track you are familiarizing yourself with. Some maze levels employ this limited visibility to make you try out branches of paths, and to beat a certain time limit you'll have to remember and take the direct path to the exit.
- many of the later levels have moving hazards (for example sawblades) that follow a path, and timing your movements and controlling the speed of the ball becomes even more important. Things can get tight and you have to be quite precise in controlling the ball. The movements of those hazards are predetermined and never random, so retrying a level will eventually help you master it.
Most of the levels have a very nice difficulty, I rarely spent more than 20 minutes on single level until I was able to beat the hardest time limit to earn 3 stars. Often it was more like 3 minutes. But it's not easy either, it's very normal to initially fail a level a couple of times by colliding with a hazard, or to make it through but not beating any time limit and thus earning only 1 star.
I noticed that within most levels the most challenging/risky parts of that level come up near the level beginning, which is a player-friendly way of designing things because this way you're not wasting time on any part that leads to the risky part where failure is probable. I've seen other games make that mistake but Radium keeps you motivated to retry, and keeps boredom low. There are some exceptions in the last levels though.
For people who care about achievements and 100%ing their games: this game is absolutely friendly in this regard, the later levels pose a challenge but it's not a matter of luck but a matter of skill, there are no broken achievements and the achievements are not grindy.

I've played several other MMOs before this; Ragnarok Online, Maple Story & Phantasy Star Online 2.
TERA is one of the better MMORPGs around as its action oriented and skill based rather than the usual stat based 'press a button' type of MMO. This alllows you to take on mobs several levels higher than you as you can dodge or block based on you own reflexes and reading of the enemy's "body language" instead of your PC's stats. The mini-field boss class monsters are good fun to fight.
Also the PC customisation during creation is quite detailed with the option to fine tune several aspects of the PC's face or you could simply choose a preset and change the hair style, color,  skin tone & make up to make that character truly yours. My only gripe is that they didn't give the option to select body build type, height, the fact that they tied eye color with make up and that the 'horns' for the Castanic race is tied to hair style (so no pick and mix in those areas).
The classes are many and varied with you being able to play any race/gender with any class with the exception of two classes (Gunner & Reaper).
The armor and weapon sets (lol skimpy armour for female PCs FTW) look really well detailed and are beautifully designed though there isn't alot of variation appearance-wise with many of them being merely different colored versions of each other, but its no big deal.
The quest log system is well organized and easy to use though like every other MMO the quests are fairly generic in nature, dungeons are individually instanced so there's no need to wait for a previous group to exit before you or your party can go in (yes you can solo a dungeon).
Also this game seems to have to have no restrictions on the sale of its paid content in the normal marketplace as some of those premium items can be found in the player to player marketplace, so you won't have to spend any real $$ as you can buy those items with IG currency.
That's all I can say about the game for now; as I haven't been playing long enough to utilize some of the more advanced meta-games within TERA.

One of the best games I've played in a while, and easily one of my favorite RPGs...and thats after one playthrough, 50 hours long.  Definitely getting the next chapter of this series.
The only caveat I would give anybody is that you need to put in the time to get the full effect from this game.  Because the game delivers a long story with some extremely detailed characters, you have to immerse yourself into the game to enjoy it thoroughly.  Once you do though, it is so rewarding.  I could go on and on about the characters especially, but to save space I'll just say they feel like actual humans with complex stories and feelings, making them very easy to relate to.  Of course, the interactions and comic relief are abundant too, and quite effective (I lost it ater "Princess Joshua").
The gameplay elements also deliver, as there are some really interesting features including basically shaping your characters' abilities through sepith, quartz, and Arts (magic, if you will).  Between that and the turn order and battle grid, there is quite a bit of strategy and preparation involved, so while the game isnt overly difficult, you can put yourself in a pretty big hole if you give the game the chance, or give yourself an advantage.  You also can craft healing items, but I think I only ever used 3-4 of the couple dozen items available, so its more filler than anything.  If you're a completionist like me, you won't need to do much grinding since you'll be fighting a lot of monsters on these quests, but it can get tedious to fight off so many of the same monsters in the same place again and again, but the ability to "bump" into enemies you want to fight and the 100% escape rate make it manageable.
Without question, this game is absolutely worth the price tag.  If you enjoy RPGs and storytelling, this game is perfect for you.

The battle system is satisfying. Fighting takes place on a big grid (so positioning actually matters) using "Arts & Crafts". The Orbment system is a little abstract at first but eventually you get used to it. Quartz are basically like FFVII Materia except nothing like Materia. Look at the in-game journal to find out which Quartz gives you the Arts (magic) you want. Even though the game can occasionally feel like a real slog in some of the larger late-game encounters, it never becomes too much of a problem and the majority of battles are pretty well balanced. Even as I'm writing this up I'm getting the urge to start up the game again - I just really enjoyed the battles that much.
The writing is pretty good. The characters are well realized. Sometimes characters can be grating but its okay because they are teenagers and that fits. Even so the dialogue works well enough to keep character interaction entertaining and interesting. The humor is hit and miss for me. Some of the gags and jokes are just too corny and/or sweet. However the empty chest messages are fun - so much so I felt compelled to find every chest I could just to see the messages. At times the game can feel like words words words but not so much to make me drop it.
The story doesn't do anything groundbreaking but serves its purpose well enough. Its an adventure that actually feels like an adventure. The game follows two teenage step-siblings Esteban and Joe of the small town Rolento in the Kingdom of Liberal after fate sends them on an adventure across the land searching for their missing father and sleuthing for the privately owned, government contracted police force. They travel the Kingdom visiting wonderfully detailed city-hubs: Bose™, Juan, Zoo, and finally ending up at the capitol of Granpa. Along the way Esteban and Joe team up with all sorts of fun characters such as Charizard, A gate, Tifa, Chloe, Zane, Oliver and many many more.
The soundtrack is alright. A lot of the tracks are super catchy. One song in particular is still stuck in my head.
The game is a time vampire. Honestly if you are on this page and considering purchasing a jrpg, you already knew this. It isn't even that long reletave to other games in the genre. Still though ~50 hours is a good chunk of time. Fair warning.

This is one of those games I wish Steam alowed a middle ground.  While I will say that there is a lot of enjoyable gameplay offered up here, but there's an equal amount of pure frustration.  Even on easy difficulty it takes a long time to upgrade your army, and yet they can get killed off really easily.  At which point you're so late in the game you're screwed.  I end up saving a lot and reloading a lot to get by this.  Of course you can only reload a few times before the game crashes.
As far as I'm concerned the biggest problem is the amount that random elements can have such a huge impact on any one game.  If you don't get metal next to your first base, don't bother continuing just restart.  I've had games where It took me dozens of turns to find any metal and then it turns out that you can't place either an outpost or a settlement near it because of the terrain.  There is a global spell to fix this, but you have to research the spell and what spells you have available to research is pure chance.  So yeah the chance factor of the game utterly destroys the tactical elements.
So over all I can't recommend this game unless you are willing to restart the game a lot.  When things line up this can be quite a fun game, but that is actually kind of rare.

Most people didn't like this game for the following reasons : a) It's very buggy and b) Is shallow compared to our predecessor.
While all the above are true to a certain extent, Sorcerer King rivals is a fun and fresh approach to the world of elemental.
I'm from the guys who really enjoyed FE:LH despite its bugs and latest updates that kinda messed the thing up. Sorcerer King rivals isn't your ultimate civ alternative to civilization with a heavy fantasy twist like FE:LH was (or at least tried to).
SK:R is different. While some design features like empire management and army customization were stripped out, other features like crafting and army/creatures equipment were added in order to offer a fresh approach to the series at the cost of certain depth and customization scope. It generaly feels a lot more like Heroes of Might and Magic or King's bounty rather than Fallen Enchantress. It's merrier, it's funnier and generaly a joy to play if you're into that sort of thing.
Marketing a game as the next chapter in a saga where you decide to reshuffle the deck and add/remove things, is generaly a bold move and it didn't pay well in this case. If it was marketed differnt, e.g as a pararell story or a brand new franchise it might have worked better because despite its bugs and different approach to FA:LH, it's an wonderful adventure with a vivid twist in the series.
Be aware though that the game is buggy. Save often and have multiple saves, cause save files tend to get corrupted and freeze while loading or crash to desktop.

I try to review games based on what it seems the game was trying to accomplish and how well it did so. Ultimately, I feel like this game did an excellent job bringing me back to the days when I was in high school and silly conversations over AIM managed to feel like some of the most intense♥♥♥♥♥♥ever. It was easily worth the modest asking price of 5$ and I beat it in roughly 2-3 hours while playing at a very leisurely pace and pausing to converse with friends occasionally. More enjoyment derived here than 5$ at a fast food restaurant, for sure.
Gameplay is simple. The game thankfully subverts some of the more trite aspects of interpersonal simulations in other games, in that you can still form meaningful bonds with the main characters even if your character doesn't necessarily like all the same music and/or movie genres they like. Characters notice more than traits in common and will also pay attention to how consistent, genuine, and honest you are. The only thing I didn't care for was the timed responses sequences. The game is fair about how they're introduced - before timed interactions play any sort of meaningful part in the story it tests you with a timed sequence just to introduce the concept to you. That aside, ten seconds to type a reply isn't a lot of time even if you ARE paying attention. It's a bit jarring how suddenly this results in blowback in the story, but ultimately, it didn't hamper my enjoyment entirely.
Messing around with the online components of Emily Is Away Too was enjoyable and neat, and I was able to get pretty immersed. With my first playthrough, I'm tempted to call this game 'best friend simulator'.
I have yet to take on another playthrough and honestly, I'm not sure I want to. I enjoyed my first experience through it guide-free without worrying about achievements and seeing every possible outcome. I'm sure eventually I'll go through the rest, but for now, I encourage you to try this game and just sit back and get as into it as you can. Be you, and be the best friend you can be. Maybe you'll find love. Maybe you'll make a friendship or two that will last a lifetime. Or maybe you'll screw it up!

If you think Sorcerer King: Rivals (SKR) is Fallen Enchantess (FE), you are half right.  The premise of the game is you were one of the losing factions in that game and are racing against time and the environment to stop the Sorcerer King.  After one play through at normal difficulty I never really felt the time crunch and was basically in control by the half way mark.  I pretty much knew I was going to win.
Part of the problem is the AI is not strong.  At the strategic level it builds lots of little armies and a few big ones.  So you whittle down the easier armies then build up experience.  At a tactical level SKR is equally weak, even when moderately outmatched you’ll have good odds at winning easily as the player uses its tactical options better.  Wonky AI has always been Stardock’s biggest problem, no changes here.
Remember that half right part of SKR being FE, you are also half wrong.  The Level of detail, management and content in SKR is a boiled down version of that game.  It is vastly more simplistic from cities to units to quests.  Gone are customized units you build, buildings determine what you can build.  Gone are tech trees, rather you research spells.  Gone are deep skill trees, but heroes are also now more focused so that is somewhat of a wash.  Your mage has its own skill tree and does not develop like a hero.  On negative about heroes is you will not have many and the last couple will be so late in the game they will be unusable for front line armies.
One huge plus in SKR is crafting.  You get stuff from resource tiles, encounters, combat, spells or dungeons.  The amount of stuff you can build is akin to what you could buy from the stores in FE, but this has a more organic feel.  Piling onto this crafting system is enchanting, which uses the same resources to provide statistical perks, spells or effects.  Every magic item has one slot and later you get two.  There is quite a bit less loot doled out, but once in a blue moon something really good crops up.
Graphically SKR is lush, though a bit cartoony for a game that feels more post apocalyptic.  Many of the same graphics assets are in this game, but there are some new ones that FE could have used.  For example dwarves.  The lack of fantasy race diversity in FE was palatable, something SKR better handled.
Ultimately though Sorcerer King: Rivals is a step back in Stardock’s fantasy series which is a shame as it did have some really nice elements.  If this game came out and its good parts went into Fallen Enchantress you would have a brilliant game.  My recommendation is to, sadly, skip SKR and pick up FE with the DLC, it is a better game.  It is not a bad game, it is a game that doesn’t really need to be played.

As narrow as a fork, as deep as a sausage.  This is the best puzzle game out there.
The minimalist advertising is done for a reason.  This is a game about being dropped into a world with no idea how to play or what to do, just so you can figure it all out.  This is an idea that progresses throughout the full game.  It starts as a series of puzzles where you are just trying to figure out how to move sausages onto grill spots to perfectly cook them without burning them or plunging them into water.  This concept quickly and elegantly ramps up in complexity.  Where world 1 could likely work just as well in a 2D space, you will find this changes afterwards, and continues to ramp up new natural rules and ideas until the end of the game.
Each world has a variety of levels to select from in an open ended fashion that explore different consequences of the game design.  There are no tutorial puzzles, there are no easy puzzles, all the fat has been trimmed into a neat package that still stretches into a ridiculous number of levels.  This adventure will take most people well over 30 hours, which if you were worried about the price point, you will get your money's worth.  My only complaint is once you get down to the last one or two puzzles of a world, you are stuck needing to solve them before you can move on.  Unfortunate, but I can't think of a better solution for this problem either.
As you play, you will find puzzles will start to demand more forethought.  Many of the stages have what looks like an easy solution, until it doesn't.  You might try to brute force your way through them, you won't succeed.  This is a key difference from a game like The Witness, which, considering the sometimes small possibility space offered by that game's panels, could be brute forced with no understanding of the solution.  That does not happen in Stephen's Sausage Roll.  This game is raw problem solving and extrapolation.  If this does not intimidate you, good.
Rather mercifully, the game has unlimited undo's and a level reset button which can also be undone.  These are not only lifesavers, but keep the game from ever getting frustrating.  With the later longer puzzles, especially ones you could have partially solved, it is a god send to be able to undo as many moves as you need without an outright reset.
Speaking of The Witness, if you were disappointed by the lack of narrative, you'll be pleased to find out that this game actually offers one.  What starts off as a seemingly throw away plot starts to develop a lot as you progress and is surprisingly dark.
The visuals look exactly like they do in the trailer.  They aren't amazing, but they get the job done.  It is simple and clean, which is nice for a puzzle game.  It has an ambient soundtrack that plays throughout, and works well for the pace and tone of the game.  Considering the time and mental energy this game will require compared to other games, the minimalist soundtrack is probably a good thing.
I imagine that because of the difficulty, many will not be able to beat this game without a guide.  If you are not up for a challenging puzzle game, this will not be for you.  For everyone else, this game is challenging, and for all the right reasons.  Every puzzle will give you a strong ‘aha!’ moment.  The mechanics end up having significant depth, and the level design is masterful from start to finish.  If you are looking for the next game to truly challenge you, you found it.
Just be aware that you will start dreaming about sausages.

Radium is a puzzle game where you have to go through obstacles to reach the end of the level. If you complete a level in a certain time period, you will receive three "stars". As you progress through the game, the levels gradually become more and more difficult, so difficult you would either smash your keyboard or throw your mouse at the wall. If you like a challenging mind game or any kind of puzzle game, Radium is the perfect game for you. If you are more into FPS games you probably would find it quite uninteresting and would not enjoy Radium as much as others. Nevertheless, this is a great game where you can spend hours trying to complete a level with three stars.

Pony Island is a game that has to be played to understand what it's all about.
The game is difficult to describe.  You'll spend a decent portion of it playing a bare bones moving platformer and the other part of it hacking the game via puzzles.  There's a fair amount of dialogue as well since you'll often have people talking to you.  There are collectible tickets which unlock a hidden ending if you collect them all.
It's hard to talk much about the game without spoiling anything.  It's interesting, I beat it in one sitting because I wanted to know what was going to happen next.  It's also very clever.  You'll likely find yourself laughing at some of the dialogue or things that happen.  The game is also very unique.  I would have a hard time thinking of another game like it that I've played.
Only a couple gripes about the game.  1.  It's short.  Expect anywhere from 2-3 hours unless you're really looking around hard for those tickets or other secrets.  2.  I didn't mind playing the platformer mini-game most of the time, but there are 1-2 areas where it goes on a little overly long and it can be a tad tedious during those segments.  3.  While most of the puzzles are fun, they are also often pretty simple.  You'll usually blow through them pretty quickly.  There are 1-2 late game puzzles that are somewhat obtuse in their solutions which could take a couple minutes of thinking or just random guessing to get through.
Pony Island is a game that provides a fun, interesting, and unique experience. The strengths of the game allow it to overcome the few shortcomings that it has.  Certainly a game that I'm happy I played.

I can't stand MMORPGs. Pretty much despise them. 99% of that dislike is the combat mechanic. Click the bad guy, sit back and watch until one of you dies. Click the next bad guy, hit 1, 2, 3, and watch your guy pull off combo attacks. If I wanted a game where I clicked a button then sat back  and watched things happen, I would hit a button on the remote and watch a movie. Because of my dislike of that combat, I haven't played many MMORPGs. I tried Elder Scrolls Online based on a youtube vid saying the combat was very NOT MMORPG. It wasn't bad, but when a guy starts swinging a sword at me and I run 30 feet awat, his sword should NOT still hit me! If I start swinging a sword at a guy and he runs behind me, my sword should not still hit him!
TERA. The combat still isn't perfect. Still isn't on par with an offline Elder Scrolls or Witcher, BUT you can avoid attacks, you can run away, you can MISS with a melee or ranged attack. You can fight one or two enemies, or get them aggressive towards you, run past them, and 'activate' a couple more to fight a bunch at once. As far as MMORPG combat goes, this is fluid and extremely fun!
Also, I'm not a very social person, and I've found myself having decent chats with complete strangers. The community I've experienced so far is quite friendly. It's free, you have nothing to lose by trying it, and if you've avoided MMORPGs for the same combat reasons I have, this game should leave you with a warm fuzzy feeling.

Goblin Defenders: Steel 'n' Wood, is a tower defense strategy game, developed and published by Alawar Entertainment.
First glance it looked like it was developed for mobile devices. My guess it was originally made for mobile devices before it was ported.
There's a second game for this series but unfortunately it's for mobile devices only.
I want to mentioned that the visuals for this game is well done even it's simplistic.
There a couple of complaints about the user interface takes up plenty of space at the lower portion of the screen. The user interface vanishes when a defense tower is dragged onto the field. It reappears when the defense tower has been place.
There's a option available, dragging and zooming, to view the entire field. This feature is very handy and makes planning a bit easier.
I want to mentioned that the audio for this game is well done even if it's simplistic and somewhat repetitive. The audio can be adjusted in the option menu as well.
There are only two game difficulty modes to choose from which is Normal and Hard.
There are two game modes to choose from and they're Campaign and Survival. The campagin game mode features five different areas with two levels each. The survival game mode is where the player is being bombarded with waves after waves of enemies.
The defense towers can be upgraded to its' highest level but it does requires a bit of coins. The highest upgrade level must be purchased from the shop using gems. These upgrades doesn't come cheap after all.
There are various game achievements but they're only in game. Each of these  achievements has certain requirements before they can be unlocked.
There are total of six different trading cards. You only get the three of those cards from the game. There are several ways to get the rest of the trading card: Purchased from Steam's Market; Trade with friends; Booster Packs and it's Booster Pack Creator.
My final thoughts, this tower defense game, fairly easy for those who haven't played these types of game before. But for those who had played tower defense games before won't find it challenging enough. I would recommend this game but not at the full price value.

This game is fantastic so far, definitely a huge improvement over the first Watch_Dogs. The world actually feels alive and populated, helped by the ability to listen in to people's conversations of their phones and interact with the world in other ways. The characters (while they look like♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ are actually likeable, funny, and pretty damn believable. They come across as millenials in a near future without feeling too forced and cringeworthy.
The gameplay is fun and tight, with the stealth executed well if not pretty generically. Interweaving camera systems let you stake out certain areas, or you can try and drive you RC Car or fly the Quadcopter through the building to do your research. The hacking doesn't feel restrictive or gimmicky and actually lends itself to the stealthing really well. I had multiple moments where I tried something simple out of desperation, like opening a door, only for it to work and leave me going "That never works in games normally!" The gunplay is simple as it should be and the parkour elements work well to make the game more manuverable. This is one of the few games where I really feel that there are everchanging ways to approach missions.
Finally, the online. I've only experienced small bits of it but I like what I've done so far. As well as being able to join friends for co-op and free roam, the game with randomly connect you to other players' session when an available PvP mission is nearby. It works in a system much like Dark Souls, where the goal is to hack the other player without being detected using whatever's around you or to eliminate them. I can't give much input on this yet but I really do enjoy how it is executed.
Watch_Dogs 2 was a pretty nice surprise. I thought it looked better than the first one but it exceeded expectations. It doesn't take itself so seriously like W_D1 did, which is a much better design choice. It feels like it let the devs kick their feet up and make the game a charasmatic, fun, and very different title than from what came out previously. Even in the face of performance issues (in the city I was 99% of the time stuck at 30-40, my rig isn't great), I have never not have fun in this game, even if I'm just walking down the street.

This review is based on playing with a Ferrari F1 Wheel Integral T500

- it just feels a lot more fluent and fun to drive
- rain races are a lot better now compared to 2014
- Tire management really is a thing now, you'll get rewarded for looking after your tires (harder for controller users, benefiting wheel users)
- Leaderboads now offer you to copy someones setup, so you can really see who's better
- Might not seem like a big deal, but you got 2015 and 2014 seasons available
- AI is more aggressive, they don't back out like in the old games and can actually overtake you now
- No big deal for me, but a huge letdown for some people
- Kinda sucks, but better for multiplayer actually, since people liked to abuse it
- Public lobbies with lots of issues, private lobbies via invites mostly working fine
- No forecast for the whole weekend, only the present day
- Though the engine was improved, the damage model is more or less the same as before, which is disappointing
- A bit too low for me, balance between cars isn't good (Mercedes AI extremely overpowered, rest is really slow)
The game surely isn't perfect and needs quite some work, but aside from the bugs, which can be really annoying sometimes, this is definitely the best codemasters game yet. Make sure to pick it up on a sale though.
Overall, I've had more fun than frustration playing this game so far, so I'm gonna recommend it!
If you aren't sure, I suggest waiting some more time before buying it.

No matter how much I would like to leave a positive review, I just can't bring myself to do it. This game is just a mess.
1)Balance:
Just in like in Heroes 6, Magic oriented heroes are a lot stronger than might oriented heroes. This is especially notable in some campaigns. My example is in the Sylvan campaign, second mission. When I reached an island with a city an enemy magic hero appeared from the fog of war. Decided to engage him since his army was weaker and he was the same level as me I thought I would have minimal losses. Was I wrong. At the first turn of combat he cast one spell and left me with 3 units from my originally 30+ stack of archers. I know they're not supposed to be tanks, but all of them dying just like that was stupid.
Can't say much about balance between the different races and match ups. Haven't played enough. I just remember that I had an easier time with the Haven campaign compared to the Stronghold one.
2)Voice acting: Sub par. It mostly made me cringe, especially when I listened to the orcs talking.
3)Graphics: Nothing really amazing. Take a long time to load as well and I'm not playing on a toaster, either.
4)Music: It was ok, though not very memorable.
5)Gameplay:
- one good thing I can say is that they added a flanking feature. This makes you more careful about your unit's positioning  on the battlefield and lets you exploits the opponents mistakes. Combat is otherwise the same as in 6, but more buggy. Would get prompts to use my hero, despite me already having used it.
- leveling system is a mix of Heroes 5 and 6. It takes the different skills which you could learn and abilities that come with said skill from Heroes 5 and it takes the liberty of you choosing what to upgrade from 6. Can't say I have any complaints regarding this mechanic.
- spells are learned through mage's guilds which can specialize in one school of magic. That means that you will get one spell from the school of magic in which you specialized your mage's guild for every circle of magic. Every race has different options for this specialization.
- resources are now 7 again. Would have prefered to keep the old crystal, gem, mercury, sulfur, wood, ore and gold, but that's not a game changer. You can also raid enemy mines to take several days worth of production and prevent it from producing for more. To take control of mines you need to control the fort or town which holds it in it's area of control just like in Heroes 6.
- a nice touch is that they added 2 champion creatures for each race. It's nice in the sense that it allows you to switch it up a bit when you get bored, but I don't think it matters much in most cases.
- they removed the racial abilities during combat such as divine shield, raise dead, gate and such which were introduced in HoMM 6.
- one thing which really bothered me since Heroes 6 is the duration of combat animations. They take too long. Entering combat as well. Increasing the speed of units is also irritating when they move like rats on crack. Hated that part of 6, too. Combat animations also feel desynced.
Overall, I'd say steer clear of this game and just get the superior Heroes 3 Complete on GoG or Heroes 5 Tribes of the East.

Same as with many people here, I'd initially heard about this game from Jonathan Blow. He'd been touting it as incredible for a while, but in a way that you couldn't quite tell if he was being serious or not. Add to that the fact that all the promotional material out there also makes you question if this is even a real game or not, and it being relatively expensive among its puzzle game peers, I was a bit weary.
Well, I've just finished playing through the whole thing, and I can tell you it's not a joke at all. In fact,
I clocked in just slightly over 40 hours, which should give you an idea of how meaty this game is. The mechanics have so much complexity to them, and the game goes sooo deep in exploring every single little intricacy of them, it's ridiculous. And it does so with the utmost elegance. The amount of times I went to bed in awe of a puzzle I'd solved earlier is so large that I lost count.
One big thing that is so remarkable about this game is how contextual its mechanics are. In the majority of puzzle games out there you have common game interfaces used as a vehicles to explore unrelated abstract concepts. For example, in Braid you use basic Mario 2D platforming as a vehicle to explore time mechanics. But the time mechanics have no intrinsic logical connection to your little guy jumping around or picking up keys and whatnot. Which is fine, but it's so much more impressive when there is a logical connection.
In Stephen's Sausage Roll, just about everything you do makes sense with common real world physics. The way you interact with the sausages and the environment all looks like it should logically work, with few exceptions.
If you're a puzzle game lover then this is a dream game.
If you're still unsold, check out the Giant Bomb quick look. It's pretty okay in giving you an idea what it is, and in not giving away spoilers. But know that that's just the tip of the iceberg, and there's so much stuff beyond that.
Cooking sausages is pretty fun I guess.

Before I start this review, let me make something very clear: this is a puzzle game lover's puzzle game. 99% of the enjoyment that this game has to offer is simply the excitement that comes when you finally figure out how to solve a difficult puzzle. There is no form of progression in the game other than moving from one puzzle to the next, and the graphics, music, and story, while fitting for the purpose, are minimal. So, if you require some form of external motivation to stay interested in a puzzle game, I can safely say this game is not for you.
Got that? Good. Now I can talk about why Stephen's Sausage Roll is the greatest puzzle game I've ever played, and what exactly it does that makes it so great.
The creator of the game, Stephen Lavelle, is no stranger to puzzle games. He has released hundreds of short, experimental games, including many puzzle games, on
for free. He also released a previous commercial puzzle game, English Country Tune, which is available on Steam. He even created an open-source puzzle game engine called PuzzleScript, which many other game developers have used to create simple web-based puzzle games. But it's clear that Stephen's Sausage Roll is his most ambitious project to date.
At first, it seems ridiculous that this game could have possibly been four years in the making. When you first boot up the game, you are greeted by a silly menu theme and a title screen that looks like it was made in 15 minutes in Photoshop, complete with stock fonts. Combined with the absurd topic of the game (who in their right mind would make a game about
?), you might begin to suspect that the entire game and its surrounding praise is just an elaborate inside joke if you didn't know better. But as soon as you create your save file and enter the overworld map, you begin to realize what makes this game special.
The first aspect of the game that immediately strikes you is the player character's movement. The only keys used for movement are the arrow keys, but it as not as simple as a press on one of those keys creating a movement in that direction. Your character wields a giant fork as big as the character itself, and while it is invaluable in helping push sausages around, it also restricts the ways that you can move. If you want to move in a direction that is perpendicular to the direction that your fork is pointing towards, you first have to rotate your fork so that the fork is now parallel to the direction you want to move in. At first, this system can feel clunky and frustrating, and simply entering the puzzles on the map may prove to be a challenge, as you have to align yourself and your fork with the ghosts on the map in order to enter the corresponding puzzle. After a while, though, the movement system begins to feel natural, and you get to appreciate the depth that this system allows for.
When you do manage to enter a puzzle and the surrounding terrain falls away to leave room for the level, you realize the second aspect of the game that stands out: that it's really, really, hard. The goal of each puzzle is simply to grill each sausage on the level to perfection, with no square inch of the sausage raw or burnt. A sausage takes up an area of 2 by 1 tiles, with each tile of the sausage having a top and bottom that can be grilled separately for a total of 4 cookable segments. The sausages can be grilled on the various grill tiles in the level, and each segment must touch the grill tile only once in order for it to be perfectly cooked. Despite the simplicity of these rules (which are actually not even stated in the game, you would normally have to figure them out through trial and error), the puzzles that are created with them are fiendishly difficult. It is all too easy to accidentally push a sausage into the surrounding water when trying to move, burn a sausage by moving it in a direction you shouldn't have, or get yourself in a situation where it is impossible to progress because you placed a sausage in a location where you can't retrieve it. You mercifully get unlimited undos to reverse any mistakes you made, but oftentimes the biggest challenge is figuring out how to get the sausages to the grills in the first place, and that is where the game's design comes into its own.
Stephen's Sausage Roll descends from an old Japanese computer game called Sokoban, which literally means "warehouse keeper". In Sokoban, you have to push crates onto their required target locations to complete each level, similarly to how you push sausages onto grills in Stephen's Sausage Roll. Despite this heritage, Stephen's Sausage Roll plays very differently from Sokoban. Sokoban's levels are highly claustrophobic due to their narrow corridors and the inability to push more than one crate at once. By contrast, Stephen's Sausage Roll's levels tend to have few walls, and you are able to push more than one sausage at once. More importantly, though, while Sokoban's challenge tends to come from figuring out the exact sequence of pushes required to complete the level, Stephen's Sausage Roll's challenge comes from figuring out a broader concept that arises from the game's mechanics.
Stephen's Sausage Roll only introduces new gameplay elements once per world, and the new gameplay elements feel like a natural consequence of the existing ruleset rather than something that was added because the existing puzzles were getting boring. For example, the second world introduces walls that you can stab sausages against, allowing for a new method of transporting them that helps get them out of sticky situations, but also prevents you from rotating your fork. The third world explores the consequences of adding a third dimension to the game, letting you roll on sausages by getting on top of them and letting you stack sausages on top of each other, but also introducing three-dimensional obstacles that are even more fiendish than the ones before. Despite the simplicity of these additions, the different challenges and strategies that they allow for are vast, and the possibilities are always fully explored before adding another mechanic to the game.
As of this writing, the game costs a full thirty US dollars, so some might be worried about the amount of content that you get for the price. Fortunately, there are many hours of enjoyment you can get out of the game. I like to think that I'm pretty good at puzzle games, and it took me 32 hours to finish every puzzle in the game. That's less than a dollar per hour, which is a very good value proposition for anybody who enjoys their time with puzzle games. There are actually only 86 puzzles in the game, which doesn't seem like a lot, but that only speaks to how well-crafted the puzzles in the game are. There are no 'filler' puzzles that are just basic applications of principles that you already knew, and puzzles aren't wasted to teach you those principles without providing a significant challenge, either. Every single puzzle will give you that 'aha!' moment that is the joy of all puzzle game fans.
In conclusion: if you enjoy puzzle games, then Stephen's Sausage Roll is a must-play. The puzzles may be very difficult, but if you persist long enough to solve them on your own, the feeling of satisfaction you'll get from them is unrivaled. And for those who think games today are too dumbed down: this is probably the least dumb game you'll ever play. Be ready to think
when you play this game!

Short Version: Having completed the game, I can say without qualification that this is one of the best puzzle games I have ever played. To anyone who likes this genre, buy it now.
Long Version: This game was great. More than great really. It is one of the most finely crafted puzzle games I have ever played. To say it is a pure puzzle game would be wrong because it obvious that a lot of care and heart went into it. However, those who go in expecting something like Portal will be disappointed. It is much harder for starters and has a minimalistic story. Some might say it has no story at all. I would disagree, but go into it knowing that you might find nothing more than hours worth of difficult brain teasers.
If you don't like puzzle games, don't buy it. If you don't have money, wait until it is on sale. However, I will say that personally, this was completely worth the price.

This game is fantastic so far, definitely a huge improvement over the first Watch_Dogs. The world actually feels alive and populated, helped by the ability to listen in to people's conversations of their phones and interact with the world in other ways. The characters (while they look like♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ are actually likeable, funny, and pretty damn believable. They come across as millenials in a near future without feeling too forced and cringeworthy.
The gameplay is fun and tight, with the stealth executed well if not pretty generically. Interweaving camera systems let you stake out certain areas, or you can try and drive you RC Car or fly the Quadcopter through the building to do your research. The hacking doesn't feel restrictive or gimmicky and actually lends itself to the stealthing really well. I had multiple moments where I tried something simple out of desperation, like opening a door, only for it to work and leave me going "That never works in games normally!" The gunplay is simple as it should be and the parkour elements work well to make the game more manuverable. This is one of the few games where I really feel that there are everchanging ways to approach missions.
Finally, the online. I've only experienced small bits of it but I like what I've done so far. As well as being able to join friends for co-op and free roam, the game with randomly connect you to other players' session when an available PvP mission is nearby. It works in a system much like Dark Souls, where the goal is to hack the other player without being detected using whatever's around you or to eliminate them. I can't give much input on this yet but I really do enjoy how it is executed.
Watch_Dogs 2 was a pretty nice surprise. I thought it looked better than the first one but it exceeded expectations. It doesn't take itself so seriously like W_D1 did, which is a much better design choice. It feels like it let the devs kick their feet up and make the game a charasmatic, fun, and very different title than from what came out previously. Even in the face of performance issues (in the city I was 99% of the time stuck at 30-40, my rig isn't great), I have never not have fun in this game, even if I'm just walking down the street.

Assassin's Creed III is a 2012 action-adventure video game developed by Ubisoft Montreal and published by Ubisoft for playstation 3, Xbox 360, Wii U, and Microsoft Windows. It is the fifth major installment in the Assassin's Creed series, and a direct sequel to 2011's Assassin's Creed: Revelations. The game was released worldwide for PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360, beginning in North America on October 30, 2012, with a Wii U and Microsoft Windows release following in November 2012.
The plot is set in a fictional history of real world events and follows the centuries old struggle between the Assassins, who fight for peace with free will, and the Templars, who desire peace through control. The framing story is set in the 21st century and features series protagonist Desmond Miles who, with the aid of a machine known as the Animus, relives the memories of his ancestors to find a way to avert the 2012 apocalypse. The story proper is set in the 18th century, before, during and after the American Revolution from 1753 to 1783, and follows Desmond's half-English, half-Mohawk ancestor, Ratonhnhaké:ton, also known as Connor, as he fights the Templars' attempts to gain control of the newly forming nation.
Assassin's Creed III is set in an open world and presented from the third-person perspective with a primary focus on using Desmond and Connor's combat and stealth abilities to eliminate targets and explore the environment. Connor is able to freely explore 18th-century Boston, New York and the American frontier to complete side missions away from the primary storyline. The game also features a multiplayer component, allowing players to compete online to complete solo and team based objectives including assassinations and evading pursuers. Ubisoft developed a new game engine, Anvil Next, for the game. The game was met with positive reviews and has sold 12 million copies worldwide.
A continuation of the series, entitled Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag, was announced in early 2013, and is set to follow Ratonhnhaké:ton's grandfather - Edward Kenway - a pirate and Assassin operating in the Caribbean.

While it has its flaws and the Assassin's Creed grind, I enjoyed the game the first time through, enough so that I'm playing it a second time.
The default control scheme is awkward (as far as I can tell, this is a concensus), but a few things make it less so.  Note that I might be using some of them as default, but I'm unable to tell at this time.  Under Options -> Customize Controls, try the following:
Jump - Space
Interact - Left Shift
Attack - Mouse Left
Tools* - E
Precision Mode - F
Recruit Menu - T
High Profile - Mouse Right
Weapon Selector - Q
Eagle Vision - V
*Tools are all manner of items including traps, horse whistle, and the like.  However, they also include most of Connor's ranged weapons such as the Rope Dart, Poison Dart, Pistol, Bow and Arrow, and Musket.  Having the activation key on E made it more comfortable in combat.  Also functions as reload when appropriate.
-Interact on Shift means you'll start missions with Shift, but it also delegates a number of other actions that previously would've been done with shift in past AC titles.
-Q as Weapon Selector is to keep it close at hand, which you'll want since you only have four quick selects while keeping as many as four main weapons (I think) and at least half a dozen frequently used tools (Bow for Stealth, Pistol for combat, Rope Dart for combat, Horse Whistle, Snares, and Bait just to name a few).  Personally, I use Quick Selects for combat options.  1 Hidden Blade 2 Primary Weapon 3 Rope Dart 4 Pistol.  Everything else will be less frequently used inside of conflict, meaning more immersion.

An excellent game limited by it's lack of variation and choices.
Replayability is very large but long-play-at-once is harmed by lack of variation and repetitiveness. Very fun to try another game at harder difficulties, but if it drags on for too long you eventually become exhausted of the lack of surprises and it's very hard to keep interest. This happened in my first run. Scavenging consists of picking randomly appearing items on a limited map as zombies randomly spawn and get close to you, for 40 seconds. Sometimes you'll need to scavenge many times in a row. Yeah.
Music is one of the best i've seen around, a frankenstein composed of chiptune music mixed with real instruments, super capable of conveying the emotions of having to put down your now-8-bit best friend after realizing you weren't going to have enough food to make it to safe haven at this pace.
Could have had a lot of variation item wise, and would have been nice to have more things to look at, talking to strangers just consists of a text screen, and you can do it anywhere, even when not in towns. It made you question the solidity of the plot; just how many people are going on the roads at once if you can talk to anybody at anytime? Why is it dangerous then?
Once you learn the mechanics it's very, very hard to die. Resting can get over any disease, broken leg, or bullet wound. There's no apparent benefit from keeping your friends  alive other than having extra support at finales and the score multiplier. They won't complain about your choices, you'll never be kicked off being a leader or care too much if someone gets bitten, after all, they won't die if they get bitten unless their health goes really low. Which is prevented with resting a few hours per town. Yeah.
Otherwise, the game is really great and the first run you'll be covering your face hoping the scrap you managed to collect before you starved is able to fix your car so you can get to the next town and hopefully buy food. Real tense moments where your hands are tied and you must project into the future to know what to do, maybe Bobby doesn't deserve coming with you guys if he ruined food by sitting on it or throwing your only muffler at a zombie. Or maybe you could sell Karen to cannibals for 250 dollars. Hm. Or you are very wounded but Joe needs the medkit because he's suffering from radiation poisoning and his skin is ♥♥♥♥ing falling off.

As a gamepad user, this has the best controls on a Codies F1 game yet - FAR ahead of both 2013 and 2014
Outside of the controls, the AI is better (it doesn't give-up places even on lower difficulties) and the track bounds are tougher on corner-cutters which is long overdue.

Trail braking (braking into a corner) is punished more now - you need to be tidier, you can't save your mistakes so easily!!
Graphics are certainly more detailed but they're also pretty demanding - i5 4440/650 Ti Boost sees 45-60fps on med/high settings which isn't brilliant but isn't as bad as it sounds/is perfectly playable (and lowering settings doesn't really improve fps numbers anyway)
An outstanding bug seems to be your own engine being too quiet (other cars actually drown it out in all but cockpit view) but that's teaching me to look at the revcounter instead of trusting my ears (these hybrids aren't really designed to be revved-out to the limiter anyway)
I did have a couple of crashes (to desktop that is!!) but a "Verify Game Files" sorted those out.
I don't really play online so I can't comment on that
I'm happy tho - as a pad player, it's the best F1 'drive' yet.

Ingenious skill game in arcade style. You must drag a ball with 2 tractorbeams through a maze of spikes and other traps. The Interface looks pretty much like an Etch-a-Sketch from the 90ies. If the tractor beam turns yellow (after a swirl) it goes into repulse mode. Be aware to link that into your brain. All 130 levels are quite challenging. You can earn 3 stars on a certain time limit and on each 8th level there's an achievement. Unfortunately the game concept contains a levelcap. Which means you must play some other levels to proceed to the next levelset. But altogether a very nice challenging fun.
This is a physics based game! You have to use lasers to guide the ball to the target. In order to move to the next set of levels you must have a certain amount of points! This game is so addicting!

It should be noted:  Everything is against the clock.  If you don't complete all the puzzles on a level in at least the "par" time, you cannot advance to the next level.   Obviously, this gets harder and harder as the game progresses.  Not what I would call casual or relaxing.  If you can live with it on those terms, I guess it is fun.  I don't like competing with clocks.

What's so interesting about this game is how deceivingly simple it looks (like how The Witness for example looks like it would be simple from the outside, but is actually a very complex and varied game).
Under all of SSR's funny packaging and simple art is an amazingly designed and fun game. The way SSR hides new "mechanics" and has you figure them out will have you jumping out of your seat. Not only that, but each puzzle is there to teach you something new, so nothing gets repetitive. The game is also very very difficult. And it doesn't care to slowly baby you to the hard ones, your first puzzle will probably take you a while.
I know people may see this game and be questionable about it, but if you like puzzle games, you need to play this.

Stephen's Sausage Roll takes Sokoban and adds a hefty dose of mechanical complexity to pretty much every part of the formula. The changes both extend and limit the player's abilities in ways that are extensively -- but not exaustively -- explored by the game.
Like many good puzzle games, this one is best played until frustrated, then left alone for a while, and returned to. I did make it through without hints or walkthroughs, though after getting stuck on a relatively early level I considered writing a planner. In the end, setting the game down and picking it up again over the course of a week got me moving again.
Generally, the levels that I found most troublesome were ones where a new mechanic was possible to use but not required to finish the level; I'd find myself focusing on using the newly available mechanic rather than solving without it.
As in "English Country Tune" there are a few somewhat exhausting levels (that is, levels where the solution is clear but the execution takes a fair bit of time). But, in "Stephen's Sausage Roll" I found that generally the execution was less daunting than I feared.

There are many small things I would improve about this game if I could have my wish, but most of them simply boil down to wanting more of it. More modules, bigger battles, longer campaigns, more detailed tech tree, etc.
At the end of the day, it's a early access indie title that only costs $10 USD, so you have to be a bit realistic about what is possible. In that mindset it has a lot going for it:
1. I've not encountered any noticeable bugs
2. It runs fine on a laptop not built for gaming
3. Gameplay is fairly straightforward to learn and amenable to both casual and intense playstyles
4. Game balance is reasonable with multiple viable strategies
5. The developer is
with plenty of interesting and attainable ideas for the future
Content-wise (as of v7.4), you're looking at about 15 to 20 hours worth of gameplay value for a singleplayer-only experience if you have only a modest interest in ship design. If you happen to have a friend or two for regular multiplayer sessions or happen to really love designing things just to watch them explode, I can easily see that going upwards of 40 hours.
------
Even if you're not convinced this is for you, it is worth watching for future updates. The game seems to only get better with age.
